name: Alaska Beacon
title: Incumbent congressional candidates skip Alaska Native convention’s forum
text:
An audience member records the U.S. Senate candidate forum held on Friday at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention in Anchorage. On the left, former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat challening U.S. Senator Dan Sullivan, is the only candidate on the stage. Sullivan did not attend. Seated next to Peltola is journalist Antonia Gonzalez, who served as the moderator. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Mary Peltola, a Democrat in a tight race that might determine control of the U.S. Senate, stood on stage at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention in Anchorage and threw some barbs at the candidate who was not there: incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Peltola, in a late-afternoon candidate forum on Friday, addressed the news shock of the day: a lawsuit filed by the Trump administration that aims to “not acknowledge a win if the incumbent does not win.”
“This is just flagrant, flagrant corruption, in my opinion,” Peltola said.
Earlier in the day, Peltola criticized the lawsuit, which President Donald Trump confirmed had been filed on his orders. Sullivan is “using his D.C. allies to try to keep himself in power and put his own interests ahead of Alaskans,” the Democratic candidate said in a Facebook message. She discussed the lawsuit in an interview on MSNBC as well. The Sullivan campaign has said it was surprised by the lawsuit.
In a break with past tradition, the incumbent senator declined to attend the AFN candidate forum, which in past campaign years has been one of the most high-profile candidate events. Also breaking with tradition was U.S. Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, who declined to attend the House candidate forum also held by AFN on Friday.[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Exactly why Sullivan was not present at the Friday afternoon AFN forum was unclear. AFN leaders said his campaign had cited “security” issues and protests. However, campaign spokesman Nate Adams said that was not correct, but did not specify the reason for Sullivan skipping the Friday forum.
Sullivan did speak at the AFN convention the day before, delivering a wide-ranging speech lasting for over 40 minutes that touted his work in the Senate. It was one of the speeches delivered by the three sitting members of Alaska’s congressional delegation; such speeches are routine during the annual AFN conventions.
 

U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks on Oct. 22, 2026, at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention in Anchorage. Held from Oct. 22 to 24, it was the 60th annual AFN convention. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Peltola, too, has skipped campaign forums, most recently a scheduled debate hosted earlier in the week by the Greater Fairbanks Chamber of Commerce. The Sullivan campaign on Monday issued a statement criticizing her for missing that and other events in Girdwood, Anchorage and the Kenai-Soldotna area. The statement called her “No Show Peltola.”
However, the AFN candidate events are usually highly anticipated. The federation is the largest organization representing Alaska’s Indigenous people, and its convention is the nation’s largest representative gathering of Native peoples, according to AFN. This year’s event was a milestone for the organization, its 60th convention.
Without Sullivan, Friday’s forum with Peltola was not really a debate but a friendly discussion. Peltola is Yup’ik and from Western Alaska, and she was an active participant in AFN conventions and other events well before she was elected to her single term in the U.S. House in 2022.
The discussion covered a variety of issues important to Indigenous Alaskans, fishers and the public in general.
Much of her time was devoted to the importance of subsistence food-gathering. The word “subsistence,” she said, “is a very inadequate term because ‘subsistence’ implies bare minimum, in my opinion. And being able to hunt off the land and live off the land and teach our children our values through hunting and fishing, that to me is the maximum quality of life.”
Key laws of importance to Alaska Natives and to fishers, such as the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, are overdue for updates, she said. Those laws “have got to be reauthorized to acknowledge the changes that we’re seeing in the demographics of our communities, in the different threats and challenges to the issues of abundance,” she said.
 

A plastic statue representing U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, labeled “Yes Man Dan,” stands on Oct. 23, 2026, at a booth manned by the liberal-leaning 907 Initiative at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention arts fair. The “Yes Man Dan” slogan is part of the group’s criticism of Sullivan for his allegiance to President Donald Trump. The booth also features banners criticizing Sullivan on fishery management issues. Nearby is a booth promoting Sullivan’s reelection and manned by the senator’s wife, Julie Fate Sullivan. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	She addressed the increased cost of living, especially in rural Alaska, where energy prices have soared. “No Alaskan should ever have to choose between heating their home and feeding their family, and that is exactly the predicament we’re in,” she said, repeating a line she has used frequently on the campaign trail.
On energy, she said she favors an “all-of-the-above approach.” Petroleum will continue to be important for the foreseeable future, she said, “But that doesn’t mean that we stop working on renewables.” She fought back tears when she was asked about violence against women and the crisis of missing and murdered Indigenous people. “These aren’t just statistics. These are real people,” she said.
She followed comments about Alaska’s role in the Arctic with a criticism of the Iran War, which she said “is leaving us exposed,” and is “unnecessary” and expensive.
“We need to stop fighting ‘forever wars.’ And that was one of the promises that we heard in the last cycle: ‘No more forever wars.’ And here we are in the most damaging war that I can remember,” she said.
Peltola has repeatedly criticized Sullivan for supporting President Donald Trump’s Iran War efforts. He has voted against War Powers Resolutions that would limit or end the conflict 14 times.
A question about climate change drew more criticism of Sullivan. Climate change is seen in the storm damages affecting coastal Alaska communities, she said. Yet Sullivan has backed Trump administration policies that canceled projects aimed at mitigating climate change, she said.
 

Attendees from the Bering Straits region listen to a speech by U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan on Oct. 22, 2026, at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“One of the issues that I have with Dan Sullivan is that he takes credit for disaster relief and investments in the Railbelt, but he clawed back investments in renewable energy,” she said.
Sullivan, in his Thursday speech to the convention, touted his record over 12 years in the Senate and celebrated federal investments that he said he helped secure. He touched on a broad range of subjects such as energy, federal relations with for-profit Native corporations and public safety.
He took credit in the speech for billions of dollars of military spending in Alaska. “We are undertaking in Alaska the largest buildup of our military since World War II, maybe ever,” he said. The biggest increases have been in the U.S. Coast Guard, which cost $25 billion in the last budget. The Coast Guard is planning to homeport four new icebreakers in Alaska, he said. “Think about that: It took our country 250 years to figure out that you should put the icebreakers in the state with the ice,” he said on Thursday.
He spoke about the Bycatch Reduction Act he introduced this year, which he said is “the most comprehensive bycatch legislation ever to reduce bycatch, protect seafloor habitat, strengthen transparency and accountability in federal fisheries management.”
And he spoke confidently about the massive pipeline project that has been proposed for half a century to transport stranded North Slope natural gas to markets.
 “First of all, don’t listen to the naysayers. They’ve never built a thing,” he said. “We’re never been further along in this project. The federal government is now in the lead. We’re going to get it done.”
 

Julie Fate Sullivan, the wife of U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks to a supporter on Oct. 24. 2026, at the art fair set up at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention in Anchorage. The fair, which includes information booths as well as artists’ work, is a regular feature of the annual convention. Sullivan is running for re-election, and his wife manned a campaign booth during the convention. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	As he does frequently, he criticized Sen. Chuck Schumer, the New York Democrat who is the Senate minority leader, and the Biden administration.
While Sullivan did not appear at the candidate forum on Friday, his campaign released a statement that day promoting endorsements from the Safari Club International political action committee, as well as the Safari Club Alaska and two regional chapters of the pro-sport-hunting organization.
The Safari Club and its affiliates have been at odds at times with the Alaska Federation of Natives and other Native organizations over tribal rights. The Safari Club has advocated for the removal of tribal representation from the Federal Subsistence Board, over the objections of AFN, for example.
Before Peltola took the stage, Bill Hill was the only candidate participating in a U.S. House candidate forum.
Hill, an independent, is challenging U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III, a Republican completing his first term. 
Like Sullivan, Begich did not attend the forum, but he did deliver a speech at the convention on Thursday, as did U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, who is not up for reelection.
 

Independent candidate Bill Hill, who is challenging U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III, speaks at a campaign event held Oct. 22, 2026, at Fire Island Bakery in downtown Anchorage, a few blocks from the Dena’ina Civic and Convention Center, site of the Alaska Federation of Natives annual convention. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	The Begich campaign did not respond to an email query about the failure to participate in the forum.
Like Peltola, Hill is Alaska Native. He is Dena’ina Athabascan from the Bristol Bay region.
And like Peltola, he was asked at the forum to describe subsistence.
He spoke about growing up in the village of Kokhanok on Iliamna Lake.
“Every spring we’d see the whole community pack up and move down to fish camp. And they spend the summer down there, and they put up fish for the winter. And they enjoyed their culture. They enjoyed their connection to the land and the water. They taught their children and their grandchildren what their culture was about and how they connected them to not just only who they were but who they were from and where they were from,” he said.
“How can you define that with a single word?”
A young supporter of Mary Peltola holds up a paddle bearing the Democratic candidate’s image as she walks on Oct. 24. 2026, through the arts fair that is part of the Alaska Federation of Natives annual convention. Peltola, who is Yup’ik, is challenging incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

name: Delaware
title: FBI examining New Castle County job offer made before recorder of deeds primary according to WHYY
text:
The FBI is examining a controversial job offer made by longtime New Castle County Recorder of Deeds Michael Kozikowski to County Councilman David Tackett shortly before Tackett entered the Democratic primary against him, according to a report Friday by WHYY News. image created on 10/24 using AI.
Karen Hartley-Nagle’s earlier investigation raised questions about whether the $76,295 position offered to David Tackett existed in county budgets, pay plans or legislation.
WILMINGTON — The FBI is examining a controversial job offer made by longtime New Castle County Recorder of Deeds Michael Kozikowski to County Councilman David Tackett shortly before Tackett entered the Democratic primary against him, according to a report Friday by WHYY News.
The federal inquiry brings renewed attention to a June 24 meeting between the two men and to questions previously raised by former New Castle County Council President Karen Hartley-Nagle about the county position Kozikowski offered Tackett.
WHYY reported that an FBI special agent in the bureau’s Wilmington office requested and received an audio recording Tackett made of the approximately 90-minute meeting. Emails reviewed by WHYY show the agent requested the recording Oct. 1 and that it was provided Oct. 8.
Federal authorities have not publicly described the scope of their review, and no criminal charges have been filed.
U.S. Attorney for Delaware Benjamin Wallace told WHYY that Justice Department policy prevented him from confirming the existence of an investigation. The Delaware Attorney General’s Office also declined to comment. Kozikowski did not respond to WHYY’s latest requests for comment about the FBI’s involvement.
The federal interest follows months of questions about exactly what Kozikowski offered Tackett and whether the proposed county job could legally or administratively have existed as described.
The lunch meeting
According to WHYY, Kozikowski invited Tackett to lunch June 24 at Cosmos Restaurant near Newport while Tackett was considering whether to challenge him for recorder of deeds.
Tackett recorded the conversation.
During the meeting, Kozikowski repeatedly discussed a position paying $76,295 annually and suggested Tackett would be well-suited for it because of his experience dealing with the public as a councilman.
WHYY reported in September that Kozikowski described the job as a constituent service outreach position that he said he created by upgrading a vacant legal aide position. Kozikowski acknowledged making the offer but disputed that he had done anything improper.
His position was that Tackett had not yet filed as a candidate and therefore remained free either to consider the job or enter the race.
“He still had that choice,” Kozikowski told WHYY in September.
Tackett ultimately did not accept the offer. Instead, he went to the county elections office after the meeting and filed to challenge Kozikowski.
He later submitted a complaint to the Delaware Department of Justice’s Division of Civil Rights and Public Trust, accompanied by the recording and a transcript. Copies were also provided to the Department of Elections and New Castle County Ethics Commission.
The Department of Elections said the issues raised were outside its jurisdiction.
What Hartley-Nagle found
While WHYY’s reporting revealed the recorded conversation and the complaint, Hartley-Nagle subsequently examined county budgets, pay schedules, vacancy records and legislation to determine whether the position described during the lunch could be found in the county’s official records.
Her Sept. 15 report, “The Job That Was Not There,” raised several questions about the offer.
Hartley-Nagle reported that the Recorder of Deeds Office had identified five vacancies in a May 4 presentation to County Council. Three were funded positions carrying salaries of $37,593, $38,533 and $47,979.
None carried a salary of $76,295.
The position Kozikowski later told WHYY had been upgraded was identified in county records as Position Control Number 102453, a Row Office Legal Aide position carrying an anticipated salary of $38,533.
According to Hartley-Nagle’s review of the county documents, that position had been vacant since May 2022 and the Recorder of Deeds Office told council in May that it planned to fill it during the second quarter of fiscal 2027 — beginning Oct. 1, months after the June lunch and after the September primary.
Hartley-Nagle also highlighted the unusually precise salary Kozikowski quoted.
The $76,295 figure did appear on a New Castle County pay schedule, she reported, but that schedule did not take effect until July 1 — seven days after the meeting.
On June 24, according to her review, the corresponding salary on the pay schedule then in effect was $74,434.
Hartley-Nagle also reported that she could find no county classification carrying the title Kozikowski described and no ordinance creating that position.
Those findings do not, by themselves, establish that a crime occurred. They do provide additional context for investigators examining what was offered, whether there was an authorized position behind the offer and whether the proposal complied with county and state law.
A legal complication
There was another significant issue with the proposal: Tackett was already an elected New Castle County councilman.
Delaware law prohibits a County Council member from simultaneously holding another county office. WHYY reported that Kozikowski was aware lawyers would have to examine whether Tackett could hold both positions.
Hartley-Nagle’s review went further, pointing to Delaware law providing for forfeiture of a council seat when a member accepts another county office.
That means the questions surrounding the meeting extend beyond whether Kozikowski verbally offered Tackett a job. The recording and public records raise questions about what job was actually being offered, how it would have been created and funded, and whether Tackett could legally have accepted it while remaining on County Council.
From complaint to FBI review
Tackett and his campaign did not ask prosecutors to assume a crime had occurred. The complaint requested that authorities determine whether Kozikowski’s actions violated Delaware criminal law, election law or county ethics rules.
Kozikowski has consistently defended his conduct.
He told WHYY in September that because Tackett had not yet filed as a candidate, he believed there was nothing improper about offering him employment. After Tackett filed, Kozikowski said, the decision had been made.
The political question was subsequently settled by voters.
Tackett defeated Kozikowski in the Sept. 15 Democratic primary with 52.2% of the vote, ending Kozikowski’s 24 years as recorder of deeds. No Republican filed for the office, leaving Tackett unopposed in the Nov. 3 general election.
The legal questions remain unresolved.
WHYY reported that an FBI agent specifically requested the recording after reviewing information concerning the complaint. Tackett’s campaign provided it.
Neither Tackett nor his campaign manager said they know how far the FBI review has progressed, and WHYY reported that the agent has not subsequently requested an interview or additional information from them.
The involvement of the FBI does not establish that Kozikowski committed a crime. It does mean federal law enforcement has obtained evidence concerning a matter that began as an unusual conversation between two Delaware elected officials and subsequently became the subject of complaints, investigative reporting and questions about how a public job could be created and offered.
For Delaware taxpayers, the broader issue is also one of government accountability: Public positions, salaries and hiring authority generally leave a paper trail.
Hartley-Nagle’s investigation sought to find that trail.
The FBI is now examining the recording at the center of the dispute.

LATEST DEVELOPMENT: WHYY News reported Oct. 24 that an FBI agent requested and received Tackett’s recording of the meeting.
BACKGROUND: Karen Hartley-Nagle’s Sept. 15 report, “The Job That Was Not There,” examines county budgets, vacancy records, pay schedules and legislation related to the position Kozikowski described.
STATUS: No criminal charges have been filed. Federal authorities have not publicly disclosed the scope or status of their review.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Democratic US senators considering presidential runs rally party faithful at New Mexico matanza
text:
U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and his wife, former U.S. Rep. Gabby Giffords (D-Ariz.), addressed Democrats gathered Oct. 24, 2026, for the "4th in the Nation Matanza." (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Hundreds of enthusiastic Democrats gathered at Balloon Fiesta Park in Albuquerque on Saturday to hear from two United States senators who are considering runs for president, marking New Mexico’s first step into the 2028 Democratic presidential primary as a newly crowned early primary state. 
The Democratic National Committee in August moved New Mexico’s Democratic presidential primary to Feb. 15, 2028, making it the fourth primary to be held in the country. Previous New Mexico primaries took place in June, often well after the party’s nominee had emerged.
U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) convened the inaugural “4th in the Nation Matanza,” which served as both a political rally with just over a week until the Nov. 3 general election and an informal kickoff to a long presidential campaign. 
Between performances by local mariachi bands and other performers, U.S. Sens. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), who both have said they are considering runs for president, gave stump speeches laying out the stakes of the upcoming mid-term elections and recounting their own high-profile fights with President Donald Trump.
U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) organized a "4th in the Nation Matanza" to celebrate New Mexico's new date in the presidential primary, a change Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham helped lobby national Democrats to make. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Crowds of Democrats cheer Oct. 24, 2026, during New Mexico U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján's “4th in the Nation Matanza" in Albuquerque. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) speaks Oct. 24, 2026, at Sen. Ben Ray Luján's “4th in the Nation Matanza" in Albuquerque. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Young hoop dancers perform between speeches Oct. 24, 2026, during the "4th in the Nation Matanza" rally in Albuquerque. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
“People from all over the country now have a chance to see the beauty and everything that New Mexico has to offer,” Van Hollen told attendees Saturday. “And you, the people of New Mexico, will have a really key role in shaping the future direction of the Democratic Party, and you’ll have an essential role in selecting the next president of the United States of America.”
Van Hollen, a U.S. senator since 2017, told Source NM after his speech that he visited New Mexico to help campaign for Luján, who is running for reelection against Republican opponent Larry Marker, and to listen to New Mexicans while he “kicks the tires” on 2028.
“There’s no better way to kick the tires than talk to people in New Mexico, give them my vision of where the Democratic Party needs to go, but also get input and feedback from them,” he said. 
Both Kelly and Van Hollen, in interviews after their speeches, said they are embracing New Mexico’s new prominence in the presidential race. They cited the state’s high population of Native American, Hispanic and rural voters, as well as its proximity to the U.S. Mexico-border as reasons the state should be more prominent in the campaign.
NM governor, Democratic leaders make case to national party for earlier 2028 presidential primary

 
“I think it’s significant not only for New Mexico but for the West,” Kelly said. “I think it means that the Democratic Party is prioritizing, you know, what happens out here.”
Kelly, in his speech, criticized the Trump administration for rising prices, healthcare cuts and the ongoing war in Iran and urged New Mexico Democrats to head to the polls.
“I’ve been traveling all over the country campaigning for Democrats in some of the most competitive races because so much is on the line for families here in New Mexico and across our nation,” Kelly said. “Everything, everything comes down to the work we do between now and election day.”
Kelly was joined on stage by his wife, former U.S. Rep. Gabby Giffords (D-Ariz.), who has advocated for an end to gun violence since she was severely injured in an assassination attempt in 2010. Giffords described her difficult recovery from the gunshot wound that nearly killed her. 
“Words once came easily to say I struggle to speak, but I’ve not lost my voice,” she said. “America needs all of us to speak out, even when you have to fight to find the words.”
Van Hollen and Kelly are just the latest potential Democratic presidential candidates visiting New Mexico in recent weeks. Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg campaigned for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland and incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) in Las Cruces in September. 
U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) joined Haaland on Oct. 19 to tout the state’s universal childcare program. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker visited the state and filmed a campaign video endorsing Haaland, and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear is slated to join Haaland for a healthcare event Tuesday in Española. 
In her speech Saturday, U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) celebrated the visits of the high-profile Democrats and predicted that more are on their way. 
“Every single Democrat who wants to run for president has to come to New Mexico. It means they have to talk to you,” she said, pointing to the crowd. “It means they have to look you in the eye and ask you what you care about, your hopes, your dreams, your vision for the future of this country.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Community organizations ask candidates for governor to expand work opportunity programs
text:
Transitional jobs in Milwaukee include construction positions that pay $12.53 per hour (Photo courtesy Milwaukee Department of Public Works)A coalition of community and faith groups are calling on both the Republican and Democratic candidates for governor to expand a transitional jobs program.  In an open letter the groups state that the program provides short-term jobs “aimed at getting people who are isolated from economic opportunity into the productive workforce.” 
The letter, from WISDOM, MICAH, Guest House of Milwaukee, the Wisconsin Council of Churches and UMOS among other groups — asks Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley to expand transitional jobs programs support funding for the programs and expand the Earn & Learn summer youth employment program in Milwaukee so that all of its 3,700 applicants can work in 2027. 
The letter is signed by Pastor Joseph Ellwanger, a longtime grassroots activist who has been an organizer in Milwaukee since the civil rights movement. 
“These programs are very effective in getting participants into regular unsubsidized employment once the period of subsidy ends,” the letter states. “Many participants have significant barriers to employment such as being long term unemployed and having criminal justice system involvement. The Department of Children and Families’ own data analysis of thousands of transitional job participants over a five-year period shows that approximately two thirds of participants go on to secure and maintain long term unsubsidized employment.”
Transitional jobs programs are important because, the letter states, while “the unemployment rate is historically low in Wisconsin at present there are parts of our communities that suffer from high rates of joblessness.” It notes that the DCF’s Transform Milwaukee and transitional jobs programs help people who are “largely not counted in the narrow official definition of the unemployment rate,” including  “such groups as the previously incarcerated and people who have historically been only marginally attached to the labor force.”
The letter argues that ensuring that these programs are protected helps the people they serve earn money, pay taxes, receive insurance and live better lives. “They earn money in law abiding ways and are less inclined to seek money in informal or illegal activities,” it states. “They grow the labor force which is an important social and economic objective in a time of tight labor markets. They participate in the dignity of work which provides purpose and contributes to the economic well-being and strength of the community.”
DCF data shows that over 60% of transitional job participants go on to secure long-term, unsubsidized employment. 
The program also supports an estimated 16,000 young people between the ages of 16 and 24. 
The community organizations that signed on to the letter are asking both Tiffany and Crowley to expand the Transitional Jobs and Transform Milwaukee Jobs programs to serve all 72 Wisconsin counties and  commit to providing $5 million annually in state funds, along with another  $8.2 million to expand the Earn & Learn summer youth employment program to support all 3,700 applicants in 2027.

name: VTDigger
title: Teen food pantry tackles food insecurity
text:
Stock photo by Antoni Shkraba via Pexels

This story by Sophia Keshmiri was first published in the Addison Independent on Oct. 22, 2026.
VERGENNES — Just under a year since Martha DeGraaf and her Commodore Club participants launched a teen food pantry, what was intended to be a supplement for kids in the after-school program has grown into a resource run by those very students for their peers throughout the community. 
As the cost of food and other basic needs rises, wages fail to keep up with inflation, summer food aid benefits end, changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program continue to strain families and states and just over a year since President Donald Trump’s Department of Agriculture ceased an annual decades-old food insecurity survey, the issue is clear to see at the year-old food shelf. 
DeGraaf, who has spent years in the education and childcare sector — most recently heading the Vergennes Recreation Department — and is a lifelong Vermonter, said she hasn’t witnessed food insecurity at this scale in her decades-long career. 
The 20-plus kids, in grades six through 12, who participate in the free department-run after-school program — plus any others who need something — clean out the 20 Armory Lane shelves and fridge, stocked with meals, snacks, fresh fruit and hygiene products. 
“It was a really big eye-opener to me — really big eye-opener to me,” DeGraaf emphasized. 
“I really thought, ‘Wow, where have I been?’ And then I wonder also, the struggles may not have been so much when I was growing up, or I just wasn’t aware of them, but I really realize it now. It doesn’t matter who you are or what you do. A child, a teen, or a youth in that environment may just be hungry.” 
While food insecurity is an ever-present problem, it wasn’t just flying under DeGraaf’s radar all these years — the demand for food assistance is growing in real time, as evidenced by data from the Vermont Foodbank. 
Across the organization’s roughly 215 network shelves and meal sites — of which there are 10 in Addison County — traffic in the last year has gone up roughly 30%, according to spokesperson Carrie Stahler.
“That is a steep increase in need for food access and support,” she said. “That is a trend we do not see changing, unfortunately, in this time of high costs, high inflation, and reductions in federal benefits like SNAP/3SquaresVT and other key programs to help people meet their basic needs.” 
She also commended the Commodore Club effort to help participants. 
“Honestly, it is a complicated time for families. With costs going up for everything, grocery budgets are often the only place where a family can find a way to supplement,” she said.
“You can’t stop paying rent or putting gas in the car to get to work or school, but you can use a food pantry or food shelf to get supplemental food when you need it, and a lot more families are having to make that choice.” 
Project genesis
The teen food pantry got its start immediately after DeGraaf was approached by a child stuck between a rock and a hard place. 
Before heading into a Commodore Club business meeting one night last fall, she was approached by one of her program participants. Described by DeGraaf as riddled with guilt, the child confessed he had taken a sleeve of ramen noodles from the kitchen on site. 
“He said, ‘I really wanted to bring it home and share it with my family,’” DeGraaf recalled. “I was devastated for him. … I just was thinking how that child felt, and my heart was broken.”
DeGraaf sent him home with the food, a compassionate reprimand and the promise that the following day they’d tackle a bigger issue — “figure out some sort of plan as to how to … find out things that maybe some people would need,” she told him. 
DeGraaf went into her meeting, but her mind was still on that interaction. Rather than push it aside, she brought up what had just happened, which led another attendee to suggest a teen food pantry. She and her Commodore Club participants got to work the following day. 
“The focus wasn’t a teen food pantry for the community. It really was a teen food pantry, sort of for the kids that were attending the club,” DeGraaf said. 
“It started to take off right away and evolved into something more than I had imagined, but manageable.”
What started as an empty bookshelf and a wish list — heavy in hygiene products — became a way to fill a gap in the community. 
An initial Front Porch Forum post from DeGraaf asking the public for donations made an impression, which inspired Commodore Club participants to expand the pantry’s capacity. 
In the days that followed, the kids added more shelves and were eager to keep track of inventory and donors. 
“The kids really started to take ownership of it,” DeGraaf said. “It really became a kid-led program.”
Just two and a half weeks after going public with the concept, DeGraaf took to Front Porch Forum again, but to share a statistic. 
“Because of you, since Sunday, 52 teens have been able to shop in our pantry,” DeGraaf wrote on Nov. 28. 
“Because of all of you, 52 teens will not go hungry for the remainder of the Thanksgiving break.” 
High demand
The teen food pantry had its shelves stocked for the first time just as Trump was threatening to — and in some cases did — withhold SNAP benefits amid last fall’s record-breaking government shutdown. At the same time, his administration’s sweeping tariffs were putting pressure on prices. 
Since then, grocery store aisles, and the economy generally, have only gotten gloomier, especially for those on the margins. 
More SNAP changes initiated by the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” signed in July 2025, went into effect earlier this month; Trump’s trade war with Canada has jeopardized the Green Mountain State’s most prominent international trade partner; and the ongoing Iran war has caused gas and diesel prices to spike and stay elevated. 
Rising diesel prices have put even more pressure on the cost of necessities such as food because transporting and fueling farm machinery is pricier for producers. 
“People are having to choose — are we going to put gas in our car? Or are we going to put food on our table? Now those are tough choices to make,” DeGraaf said. “Are we going to pay for fuel, or are we going to pay for toiletries?” 
In early March, just as some of the Big Beautiful Bill’s SNAP eligibility changes went into effect, DeGraaf took to Front Porch Forum and reported a marked increase in traffic at the teen food pantry and wrote that “we are in need of a healthy restock to keep supporting the teens who rely on it.” 
At the start of the school year, DeGraaf was again struck by the quantity of food and other items the pantry was going through. 
“With school back in session, the Teen Food Pantry at 20 Armory Lane in Vergennes is getting visits every day, and our back stock has dwindled much faster than we expected,” she wrote on Sept. 8. 
While DeGraaf wonders if the trend she’s observed has to do with her own awareness or if it’s the economic context, and she thinks “it’s a mixture of both,” the cost of food is glaring. 
“I’m leaning towards the way the food prices have gone,” she said. “I’m experiencing that shock at the store myself.”
As food prices rise, not as many Vermonters are receiving assistance, according to data from the Public Assets Institute. 
SNAP benefits ceased for roughly 5,332 Vermonters — over a third of whom are children — from summer 2025 to summer 2026. In Addison County, the number of SNAP recipients dropped 7%, or by 179 people, in that time. Just over 60 of those recipients were children.
“We know that when families no longer get federal benefits to support grocery purchases, they often have very few other resources and turn to food shelves to help put food on the table,” the Vermont Foodbank spokesperson said. 
“We and our partners hear from neighbors that food they buy has become more expensive while the amount they have to spend on food has not kept up.” 
The organization is also repeatedly being told by those it serves that fuel prices are of big concern. 
“This year is especially difficult because of the high cost of heating fuels. This is a concern for neighbors, and also for the organizations serving them as their costs go up, making it more difficult to continue to serve the increasing needs of households,” she said.
While the Commodore Club teen food pantry is helping those who are facing financial stress, the pantry — which DeGraaf emphasized is nonjudgmental, a key tenet of the program that she said makes it a success — is available to any kid for any reason. 
“There’s all the different needs from all the different walks of life,” she said. 
DeGraaf doesn’t turn away a teen who might have forgotten a stick of deodorant, for example. 
She said she’s used to hearing kids say they have to “fend for themselves” for meals, whether that’s because their parents are busy with work or shepherding a younger sibling to activities. 
“That’s a quote I hear a lot,” DeGraaf said. “‘Oh, Mom said I can fend for myself for dinner, so that’s why I’m here.’”
For DeGraaf, this trend has been another eye-opener. 
“What I didn’t anticipate was it doesn’t matter if you have food stamps or not,” DeGraaf said.
“It doesn’t matter if your parents can eat out six times a week. It doesn’t matter. Some of these kids are just plain hungry, and they need to be fed.” 
Not a junk food pantry
When DeGraaf and the Commodore Club participants were getting the food pantry organized, and the kids were scouring the building for useful infrastructure, they claimed an unused refrigerator they felt would best serve the food pantry and moved it to the space.
“I turned around, and there are these kids at this refrigerator in the open space of the club,” DeGraaf recalled with a slight chuckle. 
The pantry is going beyond making sure stomachs are full; it’s making sure they’re full of nutritious food, some of which requires a fridge and which DeGraaf said her students crave. 
“It’s not a junk food pantry, and that’s really what the kids — they feel … they’re associated with not having any money and eating junk. They’ll tell you that,” DeGraaf said.
“They really do long for the crisp fruits. The yogurts, the vegetables and things like that.” 
It’s a similar story when it comes to hygiene products. DeGraaf said one of the most highly sought items is deodorant, specifically Old Spice. 
“Biggest request that I have. I just got it again yesterday. Old Spice deodorant and body wash.”
Hearing the request for the first time sticks with DeGraaf. 
“They didn’t want the generic (brand) all the time. They want Old Spice,” she said. “They want to smell like their peers or the people they look up to.” 
Name brand toothpaste is another hot commodity. “Colgate or Crest, and they get so excited, and it’s great,” DeGraaf said. 
Another big hit among the kids is when donations allow them to make a meal. One that came to DeGraaf’s mind was a chicken and dumplings kit that somebody donated, complete with the pan, the needed ingredients and instructions. 
Not unlike the very first student she had wanting to take home ramen for his family, the kids have their loved ones at heart when opportunities such as this one arise.
“Some of the kids that took it or that got it and brought it home were so thrilled that they made this chicken and biscuits for their whole family,” DeGraaf said. 
“The kids really — I really feel the self-satisfaction when they do something for others.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Former President Obama rallies with Ohio Democratic ticket in Cleveland
text:
Former President Barack Obama rallying in Cleveland. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)Several thousand Ohioans packed the Cleveland Public Auditorium Saturday for a rally featuring former President Barack Obama. Several Ohio Democratic officials and allies warmed up the crowd and the party’s entire down ballot slate appeared on stage briefly to wave at the crowd.
But the main focus of the event was Democratic nominee for governor Dr. Amy Acton and the party’s pick for U.S. Senate, Sherrod Brown.
Both candidates are offering a working class, populist message, aiming to win back voters who have strayed closer to the Republican party in recent elections. They’re also painting their opponents as out of touch and more aligned with wealthy Americans and special interests.
Entering the final days of the race, both candidates hold a narrow advantage in public polling and have significantly out-raised their Republican counterparts. As in many other states around the country, a flood of Republican Super PAC money has doused that advantage.
Former President Barack Obama speaking at a Cleveland rally. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)
Former President Obama
Obama made a pitch for basic decency in the face of leadership he dismissed as “unserious.” Between building a White House ballroom, paving the rose garden and installing a helipad, Obama quipped that Trump ought to be on HGTV.
“What’s up with the gold?” Obama asked. “Everything more gold. He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The former president acknowledged the economy isn’t working for a lot of people, and that, speaking for experience, there are limits to a what a leader can accomplish from the White House. But between the Iran war and Trump’s tariffs against allies like Canada, “That is not the case here.”
“In this case, he said, “this administration’s actions are directly responsible for rising costs.”
Still, Obama reached for something deeper than just affordability. He pointed to examples of the president’s family or inner circle leveraging their positions for profit and insisted you can’t “unrig” an economy when its leaders “think it’s OK to lie and cheat and bully.”
“Yes, we need to lower costs. We need to put money in people’s pockets,” he said. “Yes, we need to end this war and the corruption in Washington. But we don’t do any of those things if we don’t fix our moral compass as a nation.”
Obama also spoke about the controversial ad Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy has begun running against Acton. The ad features Acton’s mother Donna Arthur claiming Acton “has a serious problem: she is a liar. She lies about her past.”
That past includes Arthur’s husband, Cledith Arthur, raping Acton when she was a child. Mahoning County officials brought charges in 1978, but Donna sided with her husband and fled the state once he was out on bail.
Arthur doesn’t bring that history up in the ad, but does claim that she worked on sexual abuse programs to attempt to establish her credibility, and says Acton’s claim of living in a tent at one point isn’t true. The 1978 arrest warrant for Cledith Arthur lists his residence as a campground called Terrace Lake Park with no specific address.
“There’s a decency that we should expect out of our public officials,” Obama said of the ad. “And I don’t know what’s happened where the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody can run and ad like that.”
“There’s got to be something inside you where you just say, you know, no office is worth stooping that low,” he said.
Democratic nominee for governor Amy Acton speaking at a Cleveland rally. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)
Dr. Amy Acton
On stage, Acton told the crowd she wished they could see what she was seeing. Growing up as a “a scrappy kid from Youngstown,” she said, neighbors knew more about a person’s union or church than their political party. She credited that community for supporting her when she needed it.
Acton acknowledged the abuse she and her brother suffered and criticized her opponent for attempting to “exploit” her childhood to “save his struggling campaign.”
“But it’s not going to work,” she said. “It’s not going to work, because compassion and decency still matter.”
Acton told the crowd those experiences drove her to become a doctor. And, taking a page from the former president’s book, they have a lot to say about hope.
“Hope is what got me through sexual abuse,” she said, “living through cold nights where all I could think about was how to keep my brother safe and warm.”
It drove her to work three jobs to get through medical school, Acton said, and to keep going when she was juggling a young child and working the night shift during her residency.
Acton promised a “working families tax cut”— pairing a child tax credit and an earned income credit — and committed to bringing down the cost of childcare and utility bills, as well as introducing a program to alleviate medical debt.
“All of this, Ohio, is my promise,” she said, “I’m going to make it all cost less.”
In a statement ahead of Saturday’s rally, Ramaswamy campaign spokesperson Connie Luck criticized Acton for campaigning with Obama and went all the way back to the earliest days of the Affordable Care Act.
“Obamacare was a broken promise from day one,” she said. “The website crashed, people lost the plans they were told they could keep, premiums skyrocketed, and Ohio’s own Obamacare co-op collapsed and left families scrambling.”
“Ohioans can’t afford a liberal governor who shows up for Obama but never shows up for them,” Luck added.
The ACA reduced the overall U.S. uninsured rate by half, from around 16.3%, or about 49.9 million uninsured people before the ACA was passed, down to around 8.8%, with an estimated 21.8 million adults newly gaining health insurance directly because of the law, according to a 2020 study in Health Affairs.
More recently, the Trump administration and Republican-controlled Congress allowed Affordable Care Act subsidies to expire, which led to nearly 114,000 Ohioans going without health insurance under the ACA.
Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate. Sherrod Brown speaking at a Cleveland rally. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)
Sherrod Brown
Obama praised Sherrod Brown’s record of “looking out for folks who are doing an honest day’s work.”
“And by the way, you can tell by how he’s dressed,” Obama teased Ohio’s famously rumpled former senator. “I mean, this is not a guy who enriched himself cozying up to corporations.”
In a white dress shirt under a blue quarter zip sweater, Brown’s appearance didn’t quite match his reputation, but his message was the same as it ever was. Corporate profits are soaring and workers are more productive than ever, he said, but CEOs earn 300 times what the average worker does.
“You work harder than ever, but no matter how hard you work, your pay doesn’t keep up,” Brown said. “Too often you simply can’t get ahead. Families see more money going out the door, not enough money coming in to pay for utilities and healthcare and groceries — everything.”
Instead of lowering costs, Brown said, Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted has cozied up to utility executives and big tech. Brown pointed to the more than $300 million Super PACs funded by Elon Musk, Donald Trump, and others have poured into the race to defeat him.
“They know that John Husted’s their boy,” he said. “They know he will do whatever they want. They know I will stand up to them and make them accountable.”
“The billionaires, the trillionaires, and shady corporations all know John Husted is for sale,” Brown added.
And he took Husted to task for saying Americans who are struggling to make ends meet don’t know how to budget and that the country’s “work ethic is broken.” Brown encouraged him to get out of Washington and visit any public school in Ohio.
“Talk to the teacher who dips into her own pocket and look that teacher in the eye and say your work ethic is broken,” Brown said. “Or talk to the custodian cleaning the hallways long after everyone has gone home and tell them your work ethic is broken. Or go to Dominion Middle School in Columbus, Ohio and talk to a cafeteria worker who serves hundreds of kids a day. Look her in the eye and tell her your work ethic is broken.”
Brown also hammered Husted on two of the most radioactive issues in American politics: the Epstein files and data centers. Husted voted against a Senate motion in 2025 that would have ordered the release of files; legislation directing the Department of Justice to release its files later passed the U.S. Senate by unanimous consent, so there was no roll call vote.
Even Republican leaders have acknowledged data centers are a millstone around Husted’s neck. Husted even introduced legislation. His Ratepayer Protection Act encourages states to come up with plans to ensure data centers pay their own way. Brown dismissed it as “toothless,” and insisted Husted is “the face of data centers.”
“He led the charge to bring 226 data centers to our state, to our community — 226.” Brown said of Husted. “Then he gave these corporations $2.5 billion of our tax dollars. And now we pay thousands of dollars more on our utility bills.”
Following the event, Donovan O’Neil, from the Koch-backed nonprofit Americans for Progress, said Brown is “relying on Ohioans to forget the economic hardship that his shared record with Barack Obama imposed on them.”
Like Ramaswamy’s campaign he pointed to Obamacare — deriding it as the “Unaffordable Care Act” — and he criticized Brown for votes he took during the Biden administration as well.
“He also consistently cast votes for the reckless spending that set off record inflation, and Ohio families are still feeling it every time they fill a grocery cart or pay a medical bill,” O’Neil said. “Now he’s sharing a stage with Obama to prove he would do it all again.”

title: Second-home taxes aren’t fair
text:
Dear Editor,
In our state, we care deeply about community and equity. There is now a clear battle over state identity when it comes to proposals to create a second-home tax. Is Vermont still Vermont if we remove the incentive for second homes? 
There seems to be a prevailing notion that most second homes belong to wealthy out-of-staters, driving up housing prices and pushing out Vermonters from Vermont. The emotional truth of this tax is to remove these out-of-staters so we can lower costs. 

READ MORE

This ignores the reality that second homes are part of the economic story that pushes Vermont forward. Tourism created partly by these second homes accounts for 9% of our state’s total GDP. If we create a negative incentive on second homes, we could drive away those valuable out-of-state dollars. The U.S. Supreme Court restricts states’ ability to levy property taxes that discriminate against out-of-staters. This will force legislators to levy this tax on all second homes, defeating the emotional purpose of this tax.
If we want to tax our tourism sector more heavily, other taxes can meet the moment. Higher dining taxes, city taxes and even tolls on interstates begin to make sense. Vermont cannot lean on a second-home tax to effectively target wealthy out-of-staters. 
Dan Kronlund
South Burlington, Vt.

title: What’s behind the Vermont Catholic Church’s ever-evolving bankruptcy case — and what’s next
text:
St. Charles Church in Bellows Falls is one of more than 60 Catholic parishes in Vermont. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger
Leaders of the Vermont Roman Catholic Diocese said filing for Chapter 11 financial protection in the fall of 2024 promised the church stability amid a rising number of payouts to resolve priest misconduct lawsuits.
So why, two years later, is the state’s largest religious denomination seeking to withdraw its request?
The church’s explanation remains the same: escalating costs — this time, to pay for all the wrangling the Chapter 11 process was supposed to resolve.
“The diocese does not believe it can afford to incur even greater legal bills,” Bishop John McDermott wrote in a recent statement about attorney fees that have hit $2 million and counting.
The church has repeatedly declined to comment further when asked about the case. But as its operating funds continue to dwindle, others in the know are speculating about what’s ahead for its leaders, more than 100 claimants of child sexual abuse and the state’s 100,000 Catholics.
The diocese isn’t the first to enter U.S. Bankruptcy Court and then request to exit, according to Marie Reilly, a retired Penn State law professor who has researched and kept records on the 44 U.S. Catholic entities with Chapter 11 experience. Although most debtors threaten to pull out as a way to pressure creditors to settle, the Vermont church has several incentives to stay.
Ending the proceedings would revive dozens of individual misconduct lawsuits now on pause, the professor said, leading to the church having to defend itself in as many as 120 civil trials. 

READ MORE

The diocese also would lose its chance to ask the bankruptcy court for a “discharge” order that would release the church from future liability for any more past claims — the only way to end such litigation once and for all.
Under federal law, Burlington-based Judge Heather Cooper must weigh “the best interests of creditors” when deciding whether to approve the withdrawal request. Then again, no court facing similar calls by other dioceses has ever granted a dismissal. Instead, they’ve often postponed rulings so all sides could keep negotiating.
Reilly sees a similar possibility in Vermont, since the judge isn’t set to consider the issue until Dec. 8.
“The bankruptcy court scheduled the hearing,” the professor said of the date six weeks from now, “with the hope that the parties will continue to mediate.”
The delay also gives everyone time to decipher all the plot twists. For people with questions, here are some answers.
Why did the Vermont Catholic Church file for Chapter 11 protection?
The statewide diocese asked for help in reorganizing its finances on Sept. 30, 2024, after facing yet another wave of costly lawsuits alleging past clergy misconduct.
The diocese began in 1853 with five priests, 10 parishes and 20,000 members, according to its online history, and grew to highs of 275 priests, 130 parishes and 160,000 members in the baby boom decades after World War II. That success came with a secret: The church hid records for a half-century that showed at least 40 Vermont clergy had faced accusations of sexually abusing children.
Then in 2002, the Boston Globe published an investigation about Massachusetts priest misconduct that was later dramatized in the Academy Award-winning film “Spotlight.” Sparked by similar complaints, the Vermont attorney general’s office reviewed allegations against 10% of the 400 clergymen serving in the Green Mountain State since 1950.
In the end, local and state authorities didn’t charge any priests because the claims found credible were too old to prosecute under criminal statutes of limitations. 
Accusers, however, were free to sue in civil court. The diocese spent more than $30 million to settle nearly 70 cases up to a 2012 state deadline for filing. Then the Vermont Legislature adopted laws in 2019 and 2021 repealing that statute of limitations, leading to a new wave of lawsuits.
By 2024, the diocese reported settlements had drained its monetary holdings by half — to about $35 million — with a rising number of abuse cases yet to be resolved. 
The church filed for Chapter 11 protection that fall, knowing bankruptcy court offered three benefits:

It placed the plethora of individual civil lawsuits on hold and required accusers to file claims as a single group of creditors, potentially reducing legal costs.
It presented the diocese a way to develop a financial reorganization plan (although one that requires approval by the court and creditors). 
And it promised the church the possibility of receiving a bankruptcy court discharge order that would permanently release it from liability for any future claims of past abuse.

So why is the church seeking to change course?
The diocese may have hoped the bankruptcy filing would save time and money, but it’s only eaten up more: specifically, two years that have required the church to pay $2 million for its attorneys and, as stipulated by federal law, counsel for creditors.
It’s also seen the number of abuse claimants increase nearly fourfold from 31 at the start of the process to 119 after the court put out a call in 2025 for anyone else seeking compensation.
In a mediation session last month, the diocese proposed a $29.4 million collective settlement that would average $247,000 per person, according to a court filing.
An official committee representing creditors rejected the offer. It said the diocese’s assets weren’t limited to the $30 million in state-level holdings listed in a recent public financial statement, but also included an estimated $500 million in local parish property and possessions sheltered in trusts since 2006.
Creditors have asked the court for permission to seek the local parish assets. They argue the trusts are illegal under Vermont’s fraudulent deeds law, which bars any move “with intent to avoid a right, debt or duty.” 
On Sept. 27, Judge Cooper told everyone she was ready to consider the trust question. Reilly called that simple notice a “significant win” for abuse claimants because it raised pressure for the diocese to increase its settlement offer and for the parishes to add some of their own money to avoid the risk of losing more.
But the bankruptcy judge can rule on the local trusts only if the larger Chapter 11 case remains in her hands. On Sept. 30 — the second anniversary of the diocese seeking the court’s help — the church filed a motion to end the financial reorganization process, leading to the current state of limbo.
“The diocese played its own big card,” Reilly said.
Not privy to the next hand, the professor has only one conclusion about the future: “We shall see.”

name: California
title: A last-minute voter guide to all 14 propositions on the California ballot
text:
In summary
Californians are voting on 14 ballot measures, including propositions on taxes, voting, healthcare, housing and the environment. It’s a lot to take in, but we’re here to help.


Yes, the much talked-about billionaire tax is on the ballot this November, but it’s just one of 14 statewide propositions. 
If you’re not a policy wonk who knows the ins and outs of state election, tax or environmental law, don’t worry — you’re not alone, and we’re here to help. The CalMatters voter guide has full explainers, videos and even quizzes to help you decide how these measures line up with your values and priorities.
But if you do want the tl;dr on who is supporting what, here’s an even shorter, last-minute summary.
Taxes: Props. 2, 3, 40, 41, 42 and 43
If it seems like this year’s ballot has an unusually high number of tax-related ballot propositions, well, you’re right. It does. 
Prop. 2 would allow the state to deposit more money into its reserves, otherwise known as the rainy day fund. The state has strict rules about how much money it can save for lean times in part because of limits imposed during the state’s 1970s taxpayer revolt. But California also has a fairly volatile tax system that rises and falls with the incomes of its highest earners. Democrats want more flexibility to sock money away for downturns. Many Republicans say leftover money should go to taxpayers, rather than sit in state coffers. 
Prop. 3 would turn a temporary income tax for high earners into a permanent law. The tax, which hits those with individual income over $360,000, was enacted as a quick fix in 2012, with most of the money going to support K-12 education and community colleges. Now the state’s largest teachers union wants to make the tax permanent, but opponents say California already has some of the highest taxes in the country.  
Prop. 40, otherwise known as the billionaire tax, is hands-down the highest profile and the most expensive proposition campaign this year. It would enact a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth, raising roughly $100 billion over five years, according to the healthcare workers union that put the measure on the ballot. Proponents argue that these ultra-wealthy Californians are already getting federal tax cuts and that the money will help healthcare programs that face state and federal funding cuts. But business leaders point out that California relies on these billionaires for tax revenue, and if they leave, the state could suffer. Even some healthcare organizations, such as Planned Parenthood, oppose Prop. 40, because they are concerned the money won’t actually help stave off state and federal funding cuts. 
Prop. 40 is so controversial that its opponents have two rival ballot measures, Prop. 41 and Prop. 42, which, if approved, would thwart the billionaire tax. A yes vote for either of these two ballot measures would invalidate the billionaire tax. 
Prop. 43 would make it harder for local citizen-driven tax referenda to pass. Currently, these local tax measures only need a majority to win. If Prop. 43 passes, they would need two-thirds of the vote. Proponents say Prop. 43 closes a loophole in election tax law. Opponents say it’s anti-democratic.
Should California borrow money for housing and medical research?
The state can quickly raise lots of cash by selling bonds to investors, but selling too many bonds risks saddling the state with debt. 
Prop. 1 would authorize the state to borrow up to $11.25 billion toward housing construction and renovations, mostly for rental units. Many developers and local governments that receive the money would have to reserve a portion of it for affordable housing for low-income renters or for specialized housing that serves the homeless. Some money would also be earmarked to support first-time homebuyers, veterans, farmworkers, students and California’s tribal communities. 
Prop. 37 would create a loan fund that helps middle-class homebuyers with their down payment. It’s technically a $25 billion bond, though the money would get paid back slowly by homebuyers rather than from taxpayers. If passed, most California renters would qualify. Proponents, including unions, real estate developers and the Democratic Party, say the proposition could make homebuying accessible, but opponents say it has a number of problems that could prevent the program from actually happening, or worse, that it could put homebuyers in greater debt.
Prop. 38 would pump $8.4 billion in state funding to immunology research — but with a catch. About half the money would go to one nonprofit organization, most likely the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. Gary K. Michelson, the institute’s co-founder, put this proposition on the ballot.
Changing election laws
These ballot propositions could shape how the candidates raise money and how recall elections operate. Voters will also weigh in on a voter ID proposal. 
Prop. 4 would allow the state and local governments to create public financing for political campaigns. Proponents, including the California Democratic Party, argue it could help cap political spending because candidates usually have to accept certain spending limits in exchange for access to public money. Opponents say the proposal could force taxpayers to chip in money for candidates they don’t support. Research on the effectiveness of public financing for political campaigns is mixed. 
Prop. 5 would modify the rules surrounding California’s recall elections. Currently, a recall election asks voters whether they want to oust the officeholder and who they want instead. A yes vote on Prop. 5 would make it so that recall elections only ask whether voters want to remove the elected official from office. If recalled, another election would determine who should replace the officeholder. The Democratic Party supports this proposition. Republicans oppose it. 
Prop. 39 would increase identification requirements for California voters. To register, voters are already required to provide proof of citizenship, such as their Social Security number. This proposition would require voters to reaffirm their citizenship again before casting their vote. Republicans argue the proposition would put California in line with many other states and that it will crack down on voter fraud, which is rare. They’ve spent over $36 million supporting the proposition, almost half of it from Illinois billionaire Richard Uihlein. Democrats say Prop. 39 could create “unnecessary barriers,” especially for immigrants and low-income Californians who lack a driver’s license. 
Other stuff: Healthcare and the environment
Anyone can place a proposition on California ballots if they follow the right procedures and get enough signatures, but special interest groups, such as unions and pro-business organizations, do it more often than most.  
Prop. 44 comes from the same healthcare workers union that put the billionaire tax on the ballot. It would force health clinics to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The union, Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, argues Prop. 44 is needed to keep CEO salaries in check and ensure clinics are spending money on patients. The Democratic Party and healthcare associations oppose it, saying it will create unnecessary regulation at a time when clinics are already facing financial pressures from federal budget cuts. 
Prop. 45, sponsored by the pro-business California Chamber of Commerce, could pare down California’s landmark environmental review law, known as CEQA. The 1970 law requires agencies to consider environmental harm before building, but developers say the law is often a tool to delay much-needed affordable housing and infrastructure projects. Environmentalists say approving Prop. 45 could be “disastrous” for communities that live near industrial pollution.
If you want more information, remember that all of this information, and much more, is available in the CalMatters voter guide.

title: ‘Anti-homelessness landscaping’ in Middlebury raises questions over approaches to rural encampments
text:
Middlebury officials placed a layer of uneven rock beneath a bridge where unhoused residents used to camp. Photo by Theo Wells-Spackman/VTDigger
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
For Josh Simon, who lived outdoors in Middlebury for a time until finding a new place to stay last fall, a spot under the large concrete supports of the town’s Cross Street Bridge had been a frequent resting place. 
A combination of relative quiet, shelter from the elements — bar the wind, he said — and the presence of others hanging out, smoking or watching the water there too made the site appealing.
“It was certainly helpful to people in our position, you know, that were outdoors and wanted some company,” said Simon, a 40-year-old who grew up in Hinesburg and other nearby towns. “There’s blue herons that come through there. It’s really quite nice.”
Now, the spot is uninhabitable by design. 
This summer, town officials layered large, uneven rocks across the area where tents used to pop up, and built a new chain-link fence blocking a space where residents sometimes struck small fires. Town Manager Mark Pruhenski said the decision stemmed from public safety concerns for local residents and businesses.
The move has drawn a conflicted reaction from local service providers, who said affected unhoused residents often have nowhere else to turn. As cold weather approaches and debates rage in Montpelier over the state’s approach to homelessness, the small municipality faces a difficult balance between the competing needs of its constituents.
Town staff decided to move ahead with the landscaping move in July, Pruhenski said earlier this month, after a period in which the bridge had become “a really difficult area to manage.” Staff gave the small handful of residents several weeks’ notice of the change, he said, and tried to connect them with local service providers. 
“We just didn’t see this situation ever ending again. It was a revolving door of tents coming in,” Pruhenski said in an interview.
It’s a prohibited location under the town’s encampment policy, he added, and activity in the area had elicited a number of complaints from adjacent businesses. But the town’s process for removing those living in tents from such a location is time-intensive, Pruhenski said, and the repeated need to do so had required significant resources and police time.
Rick Buck, who owns the nearby pub Mister Up’s, said customers reported being disturbed by the camp’s residents, and recalled reports of vandalism to cars in the adjacent parking lot several years ago. Those factors likely influenced traffic into the restaurant, he said.
Buck expressed support for the town’s approach to the problem, saying he only wished it had come sooner.
Simon said the town’s argument struck him as “completely reasonable.” But he knows that for others, the forced move was deeply upsetting. 

READ MORE

“There could be a gentler solution,” Simon said, but “it’s not an easy problem.”
The behavior of a couple of individuals impacted the town’s approach to the whole group, he added.
“Problems are caused, and then everybody gets booted,” he said. “It’s kind of a thing that happens on repeat with homeless people.”
A number of Vermont towns have long struggled to address encampments, with Montpelier, Burlington and Middlebury all evicting gatherings of unhoused residents in recent years.
Middlebury area service providers agreed that the town faced a tricky situation, and said officials and local police have consistently approached the issue thoughtfully. But several expressed concern about the move’s impact on the area’s unhoused population. 
“We keep moving people away from places and saying ‘get out, get out, get out,’ but where are they supposed to go?” said Jeanne Montross, who leads Helping Overcome Poverty’s Effects, a social services nonprofit in Middlebury.
Local shelters aren’t just full, according to Susan Whitmore, executive director of the nearby John Graham Shelter in Vergennes — they’re dramatically overflowing. Whitmore’s organization, which can hold nine households at a time, has a 23-household waitlist. Middlebury’s Charter House, which can house 25 people and did not respond to requests for comment, has a waitlist of 47 individuals, according to Whitmore. 
Andy Hooper, who chairs the Middlebury Selectboard, called the landscaping decision effective in its purpose, but said whether or not he agrees with the move is a “very tough question.”
There’s a delicate balance between keeping vulnerable people as safe as possible and not creating such a hospitable environment that people with complex psychological or substance use treatment needs are drawn to the area from elsewhere, Hooper said. Fundamentally, he added, homelessness is “really hard to deal with at the municipal level.”
“And as the federal and state spigots are increasingly running thinner, I don’t know where those resources come from,” Hooper said. Advocates have criticized recent changes to Vermont’s homelessness response, including reduced emergency housing intake hours and changes to the program’s eligibility assessment process, as misguided and restrictive.
Montross is all too familiar with budgetary limitations. Her efforts last month to try and create a seasonal emergency shelter in Addison County fell through after it became clear that no local provider had sufficient resources to oversee the project, she said.
This kind of “anti-homelessness landscaping” can also cause unhoused people to settle in more dispersed, remote locations, according to state Rep. Jubilee McGill, D-Bridport, who sits on the House Human Services Committee and works at Addison County’s Peer Recovery Center. That can make it more difficult to connect them with services, she said.
Simon says he knows several small camps which have sprung up in hidden or remote areas of town, including in the woods.
Several former residents of the bridge encampment have gone north to Burlington, according to Trevor Burton, who conducts regular street outreach in Middlebury with McGill’s organization. He hasn’t seen a third in several months, he said.
Burton said his work has become harder as the town’s unhoused population becomes more dispersed. He’s also worried about how people will fare without assistance as harsh weather draws closer. He doesn’t feel that he can direct people to any specific place in town where they are allowed to camp, he added.
“It’s really just pushing people further out of town,” Burton said of Middlebury’s approach to its unhoused population.
