name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia draws high-profile boosters to the campaign trail as candidates enter the homestretch
authors: Jill Nolin, Ross Williams, Maya Homan
text:
It's been a busy October, and the last week of early voting promises to bring more big names to Georgia, with former President Barack Obama and former vice president and 2024 presidential candidate Kamala Harris. Georgia Recorder photos Several big names are hitting the campaign trail in Georgia in hopes of driving up turnout on their side as voters choose their next governor and decide whether to send Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff back to Washington. 
Congressman Mike Collins, who is challenging Ossoff, and gubernatorial candidate and healthcare executive Rick Jackson joined President Donald Trump on the stage Saturday in middle Georgia. Both candidates also appeared on stage at Trump’s recent rally in Dalton. Jackson initially said he would skip Saturday’s rally to campaign in the northern Atlanta suburbs before reversing course Friday and saying he would do both events. 
President Donald Trump gestures to the crowd at a rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Three GOP congressional candidates – John Cowan, Jim Kingston and Houston Gaines – joined Congressman Austin Scott in warming up the crowd in Perry. Some speakers referred to Georgia as “Trump country.” 
“What I’m asking you to do is pretend that I’m on the ballot. You got to get out and you got to vote,” Trump said to the crowd at Guardian Centers in Perry. 
Back in Atlanta, Ossoff campaigned Saturday with Pete Buttigieg, the former secretary of transportation under President Joe Biden, who is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate. And the Democratic nominee for governor, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, stumped in Savannah as part of a swing through south Georgia. 
Both Ossoff and Bottoms are set to join former President Barack Obama at an Atlanta rally Wednesday, and former vice president and 2024 presidential candidate Kamala Harris is set to be here Friday. 
“Look, we’ve got 10 days left,” Buttigieg said Saturday. “And we’re ready to use every one of those 10 days to get every possible vote out, right?”
Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg speak at a Saturday canvassing event at the Atlanta Carpenters Training Center. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
While Republicans look to fire up the base, Buttigieg urged Ossoff’s supporters to try to persuade disaffected right-leaning voters to support Democratic candidates during this year’s midterms. He argued that the current climate presents an opportunity to build “a bigger, better coalition.” 
“There’s a lot of our friends and neighbors who, let’s face it, believed Republicans when they said they were going to come in and cut costs on day one,” Buttigieg said. “Now they’re looking for a different direction.”
About 1.6 million people have already cast a ballot in Georgia, with one more week of early voting and Election Day on Nov. 3. 
Trump returns to Georgia for second rally in about a week
Trump’s call to pretend he is on the ballot is one he has been repeating at stops all across the country as he tries to rally his supporters to the polls at a time when Republicans are at risk of losing control of Congress. 
“You think this is easy on my voice? It’s not,” Trump said at one point Saturday, referring to the number of rallies he has been doing lately. He’ll head to Michigan next after taking aim at Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed at Saturday’s rally in Georgia. 
Collins heaped praise on the president at the rally.
Congressman Mike Collins speaks at a rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“On behalf of what was the forgotten men and women in this country, because of your bold leadership, your steady hand at the wheel, these men and women are not forgotten anymore,” he said.
With Trump’s approval ratings underwater, Democrats have pounced on his plea to pretend he is on the ballot and say they hope voters will be thinking of the president when they cast their ballots. According to a recent poll from the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, about 55% of likely Georgia voters disapprove of the president’s job performance. 
As he has in other states, Trump used the rally to make an announcement: Audi AG will start construction next month on a new Audi plant that will produce 200,000 vehicles a year, he said. Gov. Brian Kemp announced later that the project, which will be Audi’s first U.S. manufacturing facility, is a $4 billion investment that will create about 4,500 jobs in middle Georgia. 
Trump also blasted Bottoms and Ossoff from the stage and touted his economic policies at a time when the cost of living regularly ranks as a top concern for voters. 
“Before you go and vote, take a look at your 401(k),” he said. 
The president argued that Georgia’s economy would “boom like never ever before” if Collins and Jackson are elected, saying he would “help them make it boom.” And he signaled that Georgia would have more success accessing aid, such as help for farmers, if Collins and Jackson were the ones asking for it, noting that the “president has a lot of power.”
“People don’t realize what a big difference it makes, and probably I shouldn’t say that because they’ll say this is not appropriate. But no, it makes a big difference – the difference between having people, even beyond the party, having people that you like call you as opposed to people that you can’t stand.” 
Trump said he believed he would be “the first call they make when they get to be governor and senator,” referring specifically to National Guard reinforcements. 
Sen. Jon Ossoff speaks with reporters after a Saturday canvassing event at the Atlanta Carpenters Training Center. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
A Democrat running for his second term, Ossoff slammed Trump’s economic policies earlier in the day, arguing that they have hurt Georgia residents struggling to afford basic necessities.
“Under the failed president Donald J. Trump, it costs more than ever in American history to fill up your truck, to stock your fridge, to power your home or to go to a doctor,” Ossoff told the crowd gathered Saturday for the campaign stop with Buttigieg. “That’s Donald Trump’s legacy of failure as president of the United States.”
Jackson stumps in conservative strongholds as Republicans express turnout worries
Before joining Trump on stage in Perry Saturday evening, Jackson made stops in Fannin and Cherokee counties alongside Gov. Brian Kemp, who initially did not support Jackson but who has been featured in his ads and often campaigns alongside the Republican nominee. 
Fannin County is a Republican stronghold, giving over 82% of its votes to President Donald Trump in 2024. Cherokee County in the northern Atlanta suburbs is not quite as ruby red – about 69% of voters there cast a ballot for Trump in 2024 – but the strong conservative lean and its size makes it a vital source of votes for Republican candidates.
Kemp, who is term-limited, tried to fire up the Cherokee crowd to head to the polls by comparing the upcoming election with his first victory over Democrat Stacey Abrams. Kemp, then Georgia’s secretary of state, defeated Abrams by less than 55,000 votes out of 3.9 million ballots cast.
“This is 2018 all over again,” he said. “Everything is on the line for our state, and we know the other side is very motivated. Like was mentioned earlier, they want Georgia to go the way of New York or California. Well, I say not on our watch, y’all.”
The visit comes as Jackson and other Republican candidates are expressing unease with the early voting turnout. 
“A lot of rural Georgia, because you go to church and places with people, you think it’s red. It is not,” Jackson said at an earlier stop in Perry this Thursday. “It is right down the middle, and if people stay home in rural Georgia, there’s nothing that we can do to win this race. I’m just telling you, it is that close.”
Speaking at the same event, former Republican Georgia governor and U.S. Agriculture Secretary Sonny Perdue was even more blunt.
“If you saw the vote total statewide, that’d scare you right now too,” he said. “Guess what? They’re up in early voting. You know what that means? If we stay home in middle Georgia – not you, you’re gonna go vote – but if we stay home as a group in middle Georgia, in south Georgia, they win.”
At a separate Friday event in Henry County, Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz, who campaigned with Jackson, lamented that the governor’s race in Georgia was “basically tied.”
“It shouldn’t be, but it is,” he said.
Recent polls show the race razor-close, including a recent Atlanta Journal-Constitution poll putting Jackson at 46% and Bottoms at 45% with a 3.1% margin of error. Polling averages have Ossoff in the lead in Georgia’s U.S. Senate race.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Obama on attacks against El-Sayed: ‘We have seen this movie before. I starred in it.’
text:
Former President Barack Obama addresses supporters and Democrats at a rally featuring at Cass Technical High School on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — As pundits and commentators question whether Michigan’s Democratic Party base is unified ahead of the Nov. 3 general election, the party brought one of its most formidable communicators — former President Barack Obama — into the Great Lakes state on Saturday to energize voters for Abdul El-Sayed, Jocelyn Benson and the party’s entire 2026 slate.
El-Sayed, the nominee for the U.S. Senate, is in a tight battle against Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers. Meanwhile, Benson, the current secretary of state, is up against Republican U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township, a race in which several polls show Benson ahead.
The Senate race, however, has become contentious and a bellwether contest for Democrats, who must hold the seat this November if the party wants to take back control of the upper chamber of Congress. 
The former president called for Detroit to hold strong, to vote for the Democratic ticket — including El-Sayed — despite calls from some in the Black and Jewish community to leave the U.S. Senate section blank.
“Abdul and Jocelyn understand that this election is not about them or you, but about we,” Obama said. “It’s not just about economics. It’s not just about inflation. It’s not just about policy. It’s about values. There’s a moral component to the choices that we face right now, and we are not going to fix a system that’s broken, we won’t unrig our economy, so long as we have a culture that anything goes; where what is true and what’s false is poured into social media and money is the measure of our worth. … That’s part of what is going on right now. We have lost touch with those things that really matter in our life.”
Former President Barack Obama shakes hands with U.S. Senate Nominee addresses supporters and Democrats at a rally featuring at Cass Technical High School on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Obama also praised the entire Democratic ticket. Several members of the slate — Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist, Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit and 10th Congressional District nominee Christina Hines — also gave remarks. Gilchrist is seeking Benson’s current post of secretary of state, while Savit seeks the position of attorney general, currently held by Attorney General Dana Nessel. Hines will face Michael Bouchard Jr. in the 10th District, which is James’ current seat.
It would be a significant political and historical signpost if El-Sayed can defeat Rogers in just over a week on Election Day: He would become the first Muslim U.S. senator, but it would also notch a serious victory in the progressive movement led by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, the independent from Vermont, in a state that twice voted for President Donald Trump.
Obama’s presence in Michigan and his interest in the race were telling. El-Sayed has struggled to win decisive support among Black voters in Detroit during his primary race with U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham. Many of them have come back into El-Sayed’s coalition for the general election, but Rogers has said his outreach to Detroit and Black voters is paying off and that his campaign is making inroads among traditionally Democratic voters.
U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) also boosted El-Sayed, telling attendees that they count on him to be a key partner in busting up Trump’s MAGA agenda in Congress.
U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed addresses supporters and Democrats at a rally featuring former President Barack Obama at Cass Technical High School on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Obama said the election was the best chance Americans and Michiganders had to “at least rein some of this in.”
“It is the circuit breaker in the system; we’ve got to flip that circuit breaker, and bring some accountability to this government,” Obama said. “We need to start showing the American people who are hungry for solutions what real leadership looks like, what concrete plans look like that actually lower costs and make health care more affordable, and make housing more affordable, and get utility bills under control.”
Obama said he was tired of the country’s anger and division and urged Americans to look toward the future.
Democratic divisions could hurt El-Sayed, but Trump’s economy may matter more

“We didn’t get into this moment overnight, we didn’t get into it overnight, but this election can be an inflection point, a course correction, in America’s journey to a more perfect union,” Obama said. “Michigan, you and I have proved before to stop change when its time has come.”
Invoking his signature message of change, the former president said that El-Sayed and Benson were both a key part of that future.
On El-Sayed, Obama said that the attacks El-Sayed has faced for advocating progressive policies that Obama said would improve people’s lives, were similar to those he faced in 2008. Obama said that he did not let those attacks on his name and his nationality deter him then, and that El-Sayed would surmount them, as well.
“Abdul is fighting for change,” Obama said. “Some of these folks say, ‘Abdul didn’t like some of the things you did as president.’ Let me tell you something. We are not going to agree on every detail of every issue. … “When people who share your fundamental values are arguing … that’s the kind of disagreement we want in a democracy.”
Democrats and supporters of the party’s 2026 slate wait for a rally featuring former President Barack Obama at Cass Technical High School on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
As Rogers’ campaign surrogates continue to center their attacks against El-Sayed around his Muslim faith, as evidenced by a protest held by white nationalist Jake Lang outside Cass Technical High School, where the rally took place, Obama said that he knows those attacks well.
“Whenever a movement builds to challenge that broken system, the people who benefit from the status quo will say and do anything to stop that train from coming,” Obama said. “They will use lies, and they will use fear, and they will use division, and their name, or your faith, to somehow suggest that you are dangerous and less than trustworthy and less patriotic and less American than they are. We have seen this movie before. I starred in it.”
El-Sayed thanked the former president for his backing, which could be pivotal to solidifying his support in Detroit.
“We shape our own destiny. It’s about building on the foundation of those who have come before us, learning from the lessons they leave us behind,” El-Sayed said. “For me, that foundation was having watched a skinny guy with a funny name do what I had thought was impossible. His legacy continues to offer a guiding light and fitting lessons for the work that is yet to be done. And that work is not just about getting elected, but using your seat to make a difference in the lives of the people you serve. So when they tell me ‘Well his name’s Abdul though,’ I remind them his name was Barack.”
Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who is the Democratic nominee for governor in 2026, addresses supporters and Democrats at a rally featuring former President Barack Obama at Cass Technical High School on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Benson’s race is also important to Democrats, as a victory over James would allow the party to retain the governorship after Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s tenure, and prevent a reversal of state policies if James — who has been a key supporter of Trump’s national agenda — wins and takes office as governor next year.
Benson also thanked Obama for flying in to give her his support, even though it appears that she’s better positioned, at least, for a victory on Nov. 3 than El-Sayed’s toss-up race with Rogers. Still, Benson said voters should not get complacent about either race.
The secretary of state said that she wanted to make sure that until a new president is elected in 2028, a Democrat is in office to ensure there is a continued wall against Trump’s policies in Michigan.
“In 2028, the path of the presidency to the future of our nation runs right through Michigan,” Benson said. “Let me ask you this: Who do you want leading this state when Donald Trump tries to pressure the governor to overturn an election, or to turn over your private voting information in the lead-up to that election? Who do you want? Who do you want leading this state when Trump tries to illegally send ICE agents to our polling places?”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Crowley campaigns with Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock
text:
David Crowley (left) listens to U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia) fire up the crowd at a campaign rally in Madison (Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)“In the history of our country, this is a defining moral moment,” U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia) told a crowd outside Cargo Coffee in downtown Madison Friday, as he stood on stage with Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democratic candidate for governor of Wisconsin. 
Warnock has been traveling across the country to support Democratic candidates as his party tries to flip control of the U.S. House of Representative and Senate. He made a detour to Wisconsin, he told the Examiner, because he believes Crowley is a “good man” and because the stakes are high in Wisconsin, like they are in Georgia, due to both states’ history of Republican gerrymandering. “The next governor will preside over the next reapportionment,” he said, “and I think it’s important to have somebody like David Crowley in office.”
“We are seeing gerrymandering supercharged in the South and all across our country with this latest Callais decision,” he said, referring to a Supreme Court ruling  legal experts have called a severe blow to the Voting Rights Act. 
“Politicians are turning elections on their head, so that rather than the people picking their representatives, the politicians are cherry-picking their voters. It’s clear to me that Tom Tiffany will represent that same kind of approach,” Warnock said. 
Warnock, in addition to serving in the U.S. Senate, is the senior pastor at Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, Georgia – the same pulpit once occupied by Martin Luther King, Jr. On the stage set up outside Cargo Coffee, he praised Crowley as a “man of faith” and a proven leader who has united voters across Milwaukee County. He recounted asking Crowley about his margin of victory in his last election as county executive. “And he answered, with a lot of humility, 85%” 
“Think about how divided our country really is,” Warnock said. “And this man won by 85% because he knows how to bring people together, how to get us to work together, because he understands that at the end of it all, the only way to rise is to rise together.”
He contrasted Crowley’s unifying vision with the divisiveness of the “people at the highest levels of our government.” 
After the event, Warnock told the Examiner he believes that when the midterms are over, after what he expects will be big midterm losses for Republicans, President Donald Trump “will feel the bruises and the humiliation of that,” making him dangerous.  “We need strong governors who will hold the line to protect their people.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Gubernatorial candidates make their pitch at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention
text:
Treg Taylor, Dave Bronson and Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins listen to a question posed by moderator Antonia Gonzalez at a candidate forum at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention on Oct. 23, 2026. Taylor and Bronson, both Republicans, and Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, are three of the four gubernatorial candidates on the general election ballot. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The three gubernatorial candidates who spoke Friday at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention found plenty of common ground on education, fisheries, public safety and other subjects.
But some divides emerged in what was, for the most part, a friendly and collegial panel discussion between Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, Republicans Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor and journalist Antonia Gonzalez, the moderator.
Bernadette Wilson, the Republican endorsed by President Donald Trump and the fourth candidate on the general election ballot, did not participate in the forum, though she visited the convention earlier in the day.
The Alaska Federation of Natives conference is the largest statewide Native organization representing more than 140,000 people, or nearly one in five Alaskans. This year marks the organization’s 60th annual convention. 
For the Alaska Native audience, the most consequential disagreement that emerged between the candidates on stage concerned rights to subsistence, the traditional harvests of food and natural materials for personal and family use.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state lawmaker from Sitka, drew repeated applause, especially for his commitment to respect the rural preference for subsistence food-gathering rights that are enshrined in federal law. That rural preference was affirmed in 1990s-era litigation named for an Ahtna elder who was the lead plaintiff, Katie John.
“It should be the policy of the state of Alaska, in the Department of Law, with the attorney general and the governor, to support subsistence and not undermine the Katie John decision,” Kreiss-Tomkins said.
Left unspoken, but implied, was current Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s unsuccessful legal campaign to overturn the rural subsistence priority and grant all Alaskans subsistence rights. 
Taylor, as Dunleavy’s attorney general, spearheaded that campaign, which centered on federal management of salmon fishing on the Kuskokwim River, a flashpoint for AFN and other Native organizations. He appealed the decision up to the U.S. Supreme Court in 2025.
Another difference emerged among the two Republicans on the stage.
Taylor praised the Community Development Quota system, under which quota shares for federally managed groundfish harvests are allotted to coastal Alaska community cooperatives. The program enables residents of rural coastal villages to conduct trawl harvests of groundfish or contract with trawl companies to do that.
“I love the CDQ program,” Taylor said. Rural communities’ control of the fisheries continues to grow through the program, he noted. “I can’t wait for the day when those communities own the vast majority of the commercial fleet,” he said.
 

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Republican Dave Bronson, both gubernatorial candidates, listen to a question posed by moderator Antonia Gonzalez, a journalist. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	But Bronson, the former Anchorage mayor who has staked out a position opposing large-scale commercial trawling, said CDQ-affiliated trawling is part of the problem affecting Alaska fish.
“If the CDQ program is just going to what the large commercial trawlers are doing . . .I can’t support that program,” he said. “When we don’t have enough fish, we’re not just destroying industry, we’re destroying cultures both coastal and upriver. And we’ve got to have more fish.”
Common themes on salmon, education and more
However, there were broad levels of agreement on other subjects.
All spoke about the importance of salmon and the various factors contributing to run declines in key parts of the state.
Bronson cited a particular area of agreement with Kreiss-Tomkins: a desire to expand the state boards of fisheries and game to ensure that there is a greater diversity of members, including those dependent on subsistence harvests. The boards, which currently have seven members each, should be expanded to 11 each, he said.
In the case of fisheries, there is too much emphasis on large commercial operators, both at the state board and at the North Pacific Fishery Management Council, Bronson said. “They drive the agenda,” he said. That is a large part of the reason why there are too few fish in the rivers, he continued, “because large corporate interests who do not represent Alaska, who are not from Alaska, are catching too many fish in the open seas.”
Kreiss-Tomkins is advocating more diverse representation on the fishery and game boards, including a stronger subsistence emphasis, but he is not advocating specific numbers.
The issue of climate change, which is cited by scientists as a major reason for salmon run problems, got scant mention in the forum.
All three candidates committed to elevating tribal issues in their administrations, whether through special advisors, panels or cabinet appointees.
Bronson, a self-described conservative, gave credit to former Gov. Tony Knowles, the last Democrat to occupy the office. Knowles set a good foundation with an administrative order that established “a framework for tribal governance and communication with tribal governance with the state government,” Bronson said.
 

An audience member at the Alaska Federation of Natives convention wears face makeup and a T-shirt with the symbols protesting the high rates of violent crimes against Native women. Gubernatorial candidates speaking to the convention said they planned to aggressively combat the problem. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	All three candidates said they favored forward funding of education to ensure that school districts’ budgets are not left unresolved until the end of each legislative session.
All said they favored some initiatives to improve the availability and affordability of housing, which is in short supply and, in many cases, poor quality in rural Alaska.
All pledged to rebuild the Alaska Marine Highway System, which has atrophied in recent years after budget cuts that reduced ferry service.
Kreiss-Tomkins, whose hometown is on an island and is one of those dependent on ferries, criticized Dunleavy for  contributing to the condition of the Alaska Marine Highway fleet, which he called “an embarrassment.”
“The ferry system is a shadow of what it used to be in Alaska,” he said. And that is not a coincidence, he said. 
“The lack of investment from this governor and the lack of coordination between this administration and the incredible resources that Senator Murkowski brought to Alaska for the ferry system, it’s been a huge missed opportunity,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. “And I think it’s frustrating to anyone from coastal Alaska who cares about the future of the ferry system.”
Kreiss-Tomkins was referring to federal funds secured by U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, to shore up gaps in state operations and maintenance.
Dunleavy is finishing his second term and is not eligible to run for reelection this year.
All three candidates also spoke about public safety, particularly the crisis of domestic violence and crimes against Indigenous women.
Taylor said that during his tenure as attorney general, crime in Alaska was brought to a 40-year low, with violent crime reduced by 5% and sexual assaults reduced by 26%. “Now we’re still the worst in the nation, even with that reduction,” meaning there is a lot more work to do, Taylor said.
Kreiss-Tomkins said he has “a lot of appreciation for the work that Treg did as attorney general on the subject. And I mean, if this isn’t a bipartisan issue, I don’t know what is.”
Election Day is Nov. 3 and early voting in Alaska began on Oct. 19. Voters in Alaska use a ranked-choice system to select candidates.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: West Susitna’s tab won’t leave office with the governor
text:
This screenshot from a January 2022 Matanuska-Susitna Borough document shows the route of the proposed West Susitna Access Road. (Mat-Su Borough screenshot)At an October 6 public meeting about Alaska’s next transportation plan, a Chilkat Valley resident asked why she couldn’t find projects for the Haines area over the next four years, despite road problems there. A state transportation official acknowledged that funding is limited. Not every community can get what it needs.
Yet the same plan includes nearly $245 million for the first 22 miles of the West Susitna Access Road and a connector. That doesn’t include Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority proposed 78.5-mile industrial road farther west.
I attended the meeting because I wanted to understand why the state was prioritizing a speculative road through an intact watershed I’ve worked for years to protect as an environmental policy and community advocate, and what that decision could mean for other communities.
The document at issue is Alaska’s four-year plan for federal transportation spending, technically the draft 2027–2030 Statewide Transportation Improvement Program, or STIP. It comes just weeks before a new governor takes office.
The West Susitna project raises two questions: How was it chosen, and how will Alaska pay for it?
Many community road projects are nominated publicly and scored against established criteria. West Susitna entered as a departmental priority. When Transportation Commissioner Ryan Anderson announced it in July 2023, an agency email written three weeks earlier said DOT&PF had “not yet committed” to the project and was in “a very early brain-storming stage.” The Susitna River Coalition obtained that email through a public records request.
But at this price, the public should be able to see why it took priority over other needs. Its forecasted cost has risen from roughly $89.6 million in the previous plan to $227.6 million for the 22-mile road and bridge, plus $17.25 million for the connector.
Steve Perrins, owner of Rainy Pass Lodge, Alaska’s oldest hunting lodge, established in 1937, questioned the cost at the October meeting. His wilderness tourism business lies near the proposed industrial road’s western end, amid extensive mining claims and exploration plans. Anderson said the road would open millions of acres of state land for recreation, but residents and businesses along the proposed corridor continue to question its real purpose.
During the presentation, I spotted a footnote about Advance Construction, a financing tool that lets Alaska start projects with nonfederal money and seek federal reimbursement later. The slides didn’t include new Advance Construction funding, which caught my attention. After years of squinting at DOT&PF’s project documents, I knew to look closer. West Susitna was scheduled for construction, but its federal reimbursement was pushed beyond 2030.
Advance Construction allows Alaska to pay for work with state or other nonfederal money, hoping to be reimbursed through future federal highway allocations. But reimbursement isn’t guaranteed. If federal funding falls short, Alaska bears the cost.
What concerns me is how heavily Alaska is relying on this financing tool. The draft programs approximately $770 million in Advance Construction in 2027 alone, nearly an entire year’s worth of Alaska’s expected federal highway funding. Over four years, planned Advance Construction adds up to more than $2.1 billion forcing the state to front vast treasury cash upfront while tying up future federal reimbursement capacity.
For West Susitna, roughly $204 million is programmed this way, with no conversion to federal funding scheduled before 2031. That’s beyond the plan the public is being asked to review.
I asked Deputy Commissioner Katherine Keith what keeps commitments that large from squeezing out other community projects if federal funding falls short.
Keith said the department aims to keep its outstanding Advance Construction balance within about one year of federal highway revenue, roughly $800 million. She said DOT&PF uses the tool “judiciously.” But that guideline doesn’t tell us which projects might have to wait if future federal funding falls short.
Federal regulators have raised similar concerns. In July 2025, the Federal Highway Administration and Federal Transit Administration identified about $783 million in planned Advance Construction conversions after 2027, equal to 87% of Alaska’s anticipated annual federal highway program. They warned that unrealistic funding assumptions could put project delivery at risk.
Advance Construction can keep projects moving. Using it to finance a major new road, years before any planned federal conversion, calls for a fuller explanation of the risks.
Federal fiscal year 2031 begins in October 2030, near the end of the next governor’s term. Legislators elected years from now could be sorting through the consequences of these choices. Meanwhile, Alaska will still have bridges to repair, dangerous roads to improve and emergencies no one can predict.
When communities consider bonds for public investments, people expect to know the price and how repayment will work. Why shouldn’t the same standard apply here?
Alaska has more transportation needs than money. Public comments on the four year transportation plan are due October 29. What’s planned for your community, and just as importantly, what’s missing?

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Many voters can’t name a single major accomplishment of Gov. Healey’s. Here’s one that has flown under the radar: saving public transit.
text:
SOME POLLING HAS suggested that, when asked about Gov. Healey’s record, many voters cannot name a single outstanding accomplishment of her first term.  
For me, there is a clear answer to this question: She has saved public transportation in Massachusetts from imploding. This has gone largely unmentioned and unheralded, but it deserves recognition as a significant accomplishment. 
Part of the reason why this has largely flown under the public radar is that there remains so much to do to bring our transit systems up to the level that users deserve. That makes it hard to necessarily see huge improvements in day-to-day service.  
But Gov. Healey has taken crucial steps to reverse the downward trajectory our transit systems were on. If that course correction is maintained, it will make an enormous difference over the coming years in rider experience and in spillover benefits on roadway congestion. These are critical infrastructure upgrades needed for our regional economy to thrive and grow.  
The Massachusetts Taxpayers Foundation has identified congestion as one of five significant problems hurting the growth of the Massachusetts economy. Better public transportation is the key to giving commuters and other travelers an alternative to some of the worst roadway congestion in the country.
For those who can use it, public transportation offers relief from the frustration and tension of driving in congested conditions. For those who must drive, persuading even a small percentage of other drivers to switch to transit can substantially reduce congestion. 
When Gov. Healey took office, public transportation in Massachusetts was in a very sorry state. 
Decades earlier, two governors who believed strongly in public transportation—Republican Frank Sargent and Democrat Michael Dukakis—provided consistent support for it.  
Gov. Sargent initiated a reorganization of the MBTA and increased its funding. He secured legislation establishing 12 regional transit agencies to improve service in smaller metropolitan areas across the state. He also began the process of taking responsibility for commuter rail service from bankrupt private railroads that had been steadily shrinking it. 
Gov. Dukakis completed the integration of commuter rail funding and oversight into the MBTA. He invested heavily in new equipment, increased service levels, and provided reliable, growing operating support.  
Working with the Massachusetts congressional delegation and the Legislature, he secured major capital investments that extended the Red Line from Harvard Square to Alewife and from Quincy to Braintree, and rebuilt Orange Line and commuter rail infrastructure along the Southwest Corridor through Jamaica Plain, Roxbury, and the South End. He also invested in new equipment for the Red, Orange, Blue, and Green Lines and secured the operating funding needed for more frequent, reliable service. He provided increased funding to the regional transit authorities to support their efforts to increase service. 
When Jim O’Leary became the MBTA’s general manager in 1980, he skillfully used the management tools provided by the reorganization, along with the new capital investment, to deliver better service and carry out major transit expansions. A customer satisfaction survey he initiated at the beginning of his tenure found satisfaction at just 50 percent. Eight years later, when he left the MBTA, that figure had risen to an impressive 80 percent. 
Gov. Dukakis appointed Tom Glynn to succeed him, and Glynn’s sustained focus on customer service helped raise satisfaction to a remarkable 92 percent by the end of the Dukakis administration. 
Unfortunately, subsequent governors did not sustain that commitment to capital investment and operating support. The “forward funding” legislation enacted in 2000 sought to impose budget discipline on the MBTA by dedicating one percentage point of the state’s then-five-percent sales tax to the agency. But it contained two major flaws: 

The arithmetic was wrong: The dedicated sales tax revenue fell far short of expectations. 


Sales tax revenue did not grow fast enough to keep pace with the operating costs of an expanding transit system. 

Although these flaws became apparent within a few years, the legislation was not revised to provide adequate operating funding. The MBTA began deferring essential maintenance as a short-term strategy to avoid service cuts. Gov. Patrick’s effort to raise the gas tax by 19 cents to close the funding gap was blocked by the Legislature, which provided only part of the money needed.
When COVID-19 dramatically reduced ridership and fare revenue, the already weakened MBTA was saved from collapse only by emergency federal funding provided by President Biden. But the inadequate funding structure established in 2000, compounded by two decades of false austerity and deferred maintenance, continued to weaken the system. The MBTA was short at least 1,000 employees and burdened with aging trains, poorly maintained track, and deteriorating infrastructure. 
When Gov. Healey took office, the system was close to collapse. She took decisive action: 

She appointed Tom Glynn, who had served as general manager during the MBTA’s highest levels of customer satisfaction, to chair its board and lead a nationwide search for a new general manager, Phil Eng.  


She provided budget support to fill more than 1,000 positions lost through attrition.  


She worked with the Legislature to secure revenue from the millionaires tax, which she had supported, to help fund the rescue effort. That funding supported an ambitious program, led by Eng, to address deferred maintenance and restore tracks, maintenance facilities, and other essential infrastructure to a state of good repair. 

Gov. Healey also secured legislative support for increased funding for regional transit agencies statewide, allowing them to expand service and eliminate fares. Ridership has since risen well above pre-pandemic levels. 
With support from the congressional delegation, she has also secured federal funding to prepare infrastructure for East–West and Inland Route passenger rail service connecting Boston, Worcester, Springfield, Pittsfield, and Hartford. 
There have been setbacks: 

The purchase of new Red and Orange line cars from a Chinese firm selected through a low-bid procurement has been delayed amid foreign-policy tensions with China and Trump administration tariff policies. Those delays have required additional maintenance to keep antiquated Red Line cars running well beyond their intended replacement dates.  


The Republican Congress has clawed back $327 million in federal grant funding for the replacement of functionally obsolete rail and highway facilities in Allston. The governor has pledged to fight for its restoration. 


Trump’s tariff policies have driven up the cost of imported steel, concrete, and other essential materials for rail renewal and construction, and the inflation in the price of diesel fuel and cost of living is making operating costs rise dramatically. 

Hopefully, the midterm elections will produce a more transit-friendly Democratic House and Senate. There has been bipartisan congressional support for renewing federal authorization for transportation capital grants and operating subsidies.  
Working with our congressional delegation, the governor will need to secure additional funding to offset cost increases driven by Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war, restore the funding clawed back from the Allston project, and continue advancing East–West Rail. 
Commuter rail should be converted to “regional rail,” with more frequent service and lower fares. That would increase ridership, improve access to housing across the state, and encourage economic growth in Gateway Cities. 
The MBTA’s funding formula also needs permanent restructuring to correct the flaws in the 2000 statute and cover the higher operating costs of preventive maintenance and increased service. Similar increased reliable funding is needed to support growth in service provided by the regional transit authorities. Essential funding should not depend on annual budget negotiations.
A significant casualty of the false austerity of the past 25 years has been investment in rapid transit and commuter rail expansion. An ambitious expansion program is needed to make the MBTA a stronger force for reducing congestion and giving people alternatives to driving. 
To paraphrase the ancient Chinese philosopher Lao Tzu, a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step. 
Gov. Healey has taken far more than a single step toward restoring the MBTA and public transportation across Massachusetts. She deserves credit for initiating a significant, and desperately needed, turnaround. 
Fred Salvucci is a senior lecturer and senior research associate in the Department of Urban Studies and Planning at MIT. He served as secretary of transportation for all 12 years under Gov. Michael Dukakis.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Early voting begins in New Jersey
text:
Early voting at Kearny Town Hall in Kearny on Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]More than 170 in-person early polling centers opened across New Jersey Saturday and began accepting machine votes in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Voters can cast in-person machine ballots at any early polling center in their county of residence between the hours of 10 a.m. and 8 p.m., or 6 p.m. on Sundays. Early voting closes on Nov. 1.
All 12 of the state’s seats in the House of Representatives are up for a vote this year, as is the U.S. Senate seat held by Sen. Cory Booker (D), who is seeking a third full term in the chamber and faces a challenge from Republican Justin Murphy.
Eyes are on New Jersey’s House Republicans this year as the party attempts to defend the state’s three GOP-held seats amid a cost-of-living crisis spurred by tariffs and President Donald Trump’s invasion of Iran.
The 7th Congressional District is again expected to host the state’s marquee House race.
Two-term Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R) faces a challenge in the 7th District from former U.S. Navy helicopter pilot Rebecca Bennett in a reelection bid complicated by a monthslong absence from Congress that Kean said was due to depression.
Bennett spent Saturday crisscrossing the district. In the morning, she attended a union rally outside Rahway City Hall where she urged workers to “fire” Kean.
“There is no other alternative than flipping this seat and taking back the House,” she said. “We have to do it. And just like in the military, we are on a no-fail mission and we’ve got to get this done.”
Kean’s campaign declined to make his schedule available.
Hartaj Singh speaks with Democratic House hopeful Rebecca Bennett outside Rahway City Hall on Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by New Jersey Monitor)
The state changed the law to allow early in-person voting in 2021, and its popularity with voters has risen since then.
In 2023, only about 214,000 residents cast early in-person votes. In the following year’s presidential race, nearly 1.2 million New Jerseyans used early voting, and during last year’s election, when voters picked a governor and 80 legislators in the state Assembly, the figure was 741,924.
“Early voting has really become a popular way to vote because it’s easy, it’s accessible,” said Nuzhat Chowdhury, director of the New Jersey Institute for Social Justice’s democracy and justice program. “You can go anytime within that early voting window as long as the polls are open, and it really helps alleviate congestion during Election Day.”
Counties are required by law to host between three and seven early polling places, based on their population, and the state will reimburse them for up to five, seven, or 10 polling sites, again based on a county’s population.
This year, two counties, Essex and Hudson, will stand up polling sites at their own expense. Essex will host a total of 11 sites, while Hudson will host 31. Overall, the 171 early polling centers that opened Saturday mark a small decline from the prior year, which had 173.
See a list of early voting centers
Voters can also cast mail-in ballots ahead of Election Day by mailing them, depositing them in a secure ballot drop box, or hand-delivering the ballot to their county’s Board of Elections.
Some county clerks have nudged mail voters away from the U.S. Postal Service and toward drop boxes after the Postal Service adopted a rule saying it would not deliver ballots in states that refused to upload protected voter data to federal systems. The U.S. Supreme Court blocked that rule last month, but voting rights groups are still advising voters who wish to cast their ballots through the post to do so sooner rather than later.
“You can mail your ballot up to Election Day, but just to be safe and to leave plenty of time for the postal service to do what they need to do, we’re recommending doing so a week in advance,” Chowdhury said. “Mail-in-ballot voters can also drop their ballot off at any authorized drop box.”
See a list of secure ballot drop boxes
Workers with the Essex County Board of Elections set up an early voting banner outside the Wally Choice Community Center in Montclair on Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Under state law, valid mail votes must be accepted so long as they are postmarked by Election Day and reach election officials no more than six days after polls close.
The Postal Service made changes to how it applies postmarks this year. Instead of applying them at post offices, the agency now applies them at regional distribution centers.
It could take days for election mail to reach those distribution centers, and election officials have advised voters returning ballots close to Election Day that they can request post office staff apply a postmark to their mail directly instead of waiting for it to reach a distribution center.
Last year, 20,749 mail ballots cast in the general election reached officials after Election Day, out of the 671,763 tallied in those races.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Candidatos a fiscal general de Kansas debaten sobre acuerdos de culpa y delitos contra inmigrantes
text:
El republicano Kris Kobach, a la izquierda, y el demócrata Chris Mann se enfrentaron en un debate televisivo en Topeka que reunió a los candidatos a fiscal general de Kansas. En esta imagen, tomada el 6 de octubre de 2026, Mann y Kobach se preparan para su debate en el condado de Johnson. (Foto por Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)Traducido por Claudia Amaro.
TOPEKA — Los candidatos a fiscal general de Kansas, Chris Mann y Kris Kobach, aprovecharon un debate televisado para atacarse mutuamente con preguntas delicadas sobre cómo responsabilizar a personas influyentes por conductas criminales y sobre el costo humano de una aplicación laxa de la ley migratoria.
Kobach, fiscal general republicano del estado y exprofesor de derecho constitucional, le pidió a Mann, durante el debate de KTWU la noche del miércoles, que explicara las críticas a las redadas migratorias en el contexto de dos mujeres asesinadas por hombres sin autoridad para estar en Estados Unidos.
Mann, demócrata y exoficial de policía de Lawrence con una práctica legal enfocada en víctimas de conducir ebrio, preguntó a Kobach sobre el acuerdo de culpabilidad que  su equipo ofreció al desacreditado fiscal del condado de Neosho, Linus Thuston.
Mann dijo que la oficina del fiscal general desarrolló un plan para ayudar a Thuston a evitar la cárcel si el fiscal del condado se declaraba culpable de dos delitos menores: uso indebido de una tarjeta de crédito del condado y falsificación de un documento para evadir impuestos en la compra de un vehículo. El personal de Kobach abandonó la idea de acusar a Thuston de supuestamente extorsionar a unas 50 mujeres pidiéndoles fotos desnudas, dijo Mann.
“El juez de ese caso tuvo que anular el acuerdo para dar algo de tiempo en la cárcel”, dijo Mann. “Dices que eres duro con el crimen. ¿Por qué dejarías libres a los poderosos?”
Kobach, quien busca una segunda elección como fiscal general, dijo que él no manejó personalmente el acuerdo de culpabilidad. En el caso de 2024, el equipo de Kobach recomendó a Thuston evitar ir a la cárcel pagando una multa de $10,000.
“En algunas ocasiones, cuando te llevan a procesar un caso, la evidencia que crees que está ahí para meter a alguien tras las rejas o imponer una pena muy significativa no está”, dijo Kobach. “Yo no negocié ese acuerdo. Mi equipo de fiscalía penal sí, pero sintieron que eso era lo máximo que podían obtener, dados los datos limitados que tenían.”
“Vamos por la sanción más severa posible en cada caso, y no creo que nadie que nos vea realmente crea que estaríamos haciendo tratos con alguien que viole la ley”, agregó Kobach.
El juez de distrito retirado Merlin Wheeler aceptó las declaraciones de culpabilidad de Thuston, pero ordenó al fiscal del condado que pagara más de $3,000 y que Thuston cumpliera 120 días de cárcel — 60 días por cada delito menor.
Un fiscal especial acusó posteriormente a Thuston de delitos graves relacionados con su testimonio en un caso de drogas, por trabajar con informantes confidenciales fuera de registro, entre ellos reuniones nocturnas con una mujer que le envió fotos desnudas. Un jurado declaró culpable a Thuston de perjurio en agosto.
“Cuando sea fiscal general, nos aseguraremos de ir tras los delincuentes sin importar cuán poderosos sean”, dijo Mann.
 
Muertes trágicas
Cuando llegó la oportunidad de Kobach para darle la vuelta a la situación, acusó a Mann de decir que Kansas debería esforzarse por evitar que la Oficina de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas de EE. UU. realice redadas para arrestar y deportar a personas sin documentación para vivir en Estados Unidos.
El fiscal general personalizó el tema al abordar el asesinato de María Morfin-Rojas en 2005 en Lenexa y la muerte de Amanda Bixby en 2007 cerca de Basehor.
Rojas, de 30 años, fue apuñalado hasta la muerte por Ángel Herrera, quien huyó de Estados Unidos y no fue arrestado hasta 2023 en El Salvador. De regreso a Kansas, fue sentenciado a 50 años de prisión. Bixby, de 19 años, de Tonganoxie, murió en un choque de tres vehículos provocado cuando Ricardo Flores se saltó una señal de alto. Inicialmente fue acusado de homicidio vehicular, pero el caso fue desestimado.
“Eran inmigrantes ilegales quienes los mataron. Si esos extranjeros hubieran sido deportados, esas personas estarían vivas hoy y sus familias no estarían de luto”, le dijo Kobach a Mann. “Sin embargo, usted dijo: ‘Tenemos que hacer todo lo posible para detener las deportaciones de ICE en Kansas.’ Estoy haciendo todo lo posible para ayudar. ¿Cómo explicaría su posición a esos familiares?”
Mann dijo que el fiscal general estaba difundiendo falsamente una acusación de que proponía el cese de las actividades de aplicación de la ley migratoria.
“Nunca dije eso a ninguna audiencia”, dijo Mann.
Sin embargo, Kobach dijo que tenía una grabación en la que Mann hacía ese comentario.
Mann dijo que los delincuentes violentos, ya sean ciudadanos estadounidenses o no, deben ser retirados de las calles para que las comunidades sean más seguras. Condenó la defensa de Kobach por una ley propuesta que exige que los alguaciles del condado firmen acuerdos 287(g) con ICE. Los acuerdos permiten que las fuerzas del orden locales sean capacitadas y designadas como agentes para asumir funciones federales en materia de inmigración.
“Muchos de ellos no tienen los recursos para aceptar un acuerdo así o simplemente no quieren”, dijo Mann. “Mi oponente nunca ha caminado un solo día en la vida, en los zapatos de los hombres y mujeres que protegen nuestras comunidades. Voy a confiar en las fuerzas del orden locales.”
Kobach dijo que la Oficina de Investigación de Kansas, que está bajo la jurisdicción del fiscal general, y 30 alguaciles de Kansas tenían acuerdos 287(g) con ICE para ayudar en la detención de personas por posible deportación.
“También hemos deportado a muchos inmigrantes ilegales de Kansas”, dijo Kobach, “y eso probablemente terminaría si mi oponente llegara a ser fiscal general.”
 
Estadísticas de criminalidad
El moderador del debate, Bob Beatty, profesor de la Universidad de Washburn, pidió a los candidatos que explicaran qué harían para abordar la delincuencia en Kansas. Dijo que la delincuencia violenta en Kansas aumentó un 7.5%, a pesar de una disminución general del 5% en la tasa de criminalidad del estado en 2025.
“Los delitos contra la propiedad han disminuido de manera constante en los últimos 18 años”, dijo Mann. “Las agresiones agravadas están en su punto más alto en 10 años y los homicidios relacionados con la violencia doméstica aumentaron en un 65%. Mientras mi oponente ha estado colgando su bandera de ‘misión cumplida’ y dando una vuelta de victoria, yo he estado en el terreno, hablando con alguaciles y líderes de las fuerzas del orden en todo el estado. Me han dicho que necesitan un mejor socio en la oficina del fiscal general.”
Kobach dijo que su trabajo como fiscal general fue parcialmente responsable de reducir la tasa de criminalidad del estado al nivel más bajo en 57 años.
“Solo en el último año hubo un ligero aumento de la delincuencia violenta. Pero los delitos contra la propiedad estaban disminuyendo drásticamente. De hecho, el robo está ahora en su punto más bajo en más de 60 años”, dijo Kobach.
Antes de las elecciones del 3 de noviembre, Mann fue respaldado por la Logia Estatal de Kansas de la Orden Fraternal de Policía. Fue la primera vez desde 2002 que el sindicato, que representa a 4,300 agentes de la ley, respaldó a un candidato demócrata para el cargo de fiscal general. Kobach dijo que 53 alguaciles respaldaron su reelección.
Kobach dijo que era importante reconocer que la oficina del fiscal general lideró un esfuerzo para reducir las muertes por fentanilo. Las muertes en Kansas causadas por personas que consumían esta potente droga disminuyeron en un 17%, dijo.
“La disponibilidad de fentanilo en las calles de Kansas era 120 veces mayor que cuando asumí el cargo. Un logro enorme”, dijo el fiscal general.
Mann dijo que Kansas documentó más de 2,000 muertes relacionadas con el fentanilo y que, a principios de este año, Wichita reportó 29 sobredosis de fentanilo en un solo fin de semana.
“La crisis no ha terminado”, dijo.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Omaha among 14 U.S. cities tapped for Bloomberg housing program; a goal is more ‘granny flats’
text:
"An accessory dwelling unit" is a smaller, secondary home on the same property as a single-family residence. They can take a variety of forms, including a detached smaller home such as the one pictured here. (Courtesy of RL Mace Universal Design Institute)OMAHA — Omaha is among 14 cities nationwide selected for a Bloomberg Philanthropies program intended to boost creation of local housing — particularly “accessory dwelling units,” known also as granny flats or in-law suites.
Participation comes with up to $750,000 in grant funding, but local leaders say a key benefit is technical expertise from field-leading specialists and mentoring from cities deemed to have pioneered best strategies.
The Whitney by Straightline Design of Omaha was among the winners of a competition sponsored by AARP Nebraska, the City of Omaha and others in 2023 to try to gain local momentum in a national trend to build “accessory dwelling units.” (Courtesy of Straightline Design)
“We’re excited for the opportunity,” Eric Englund, deputy city planning director, said Friday. He will spearhead Omaha’s role. “We think we can make some great improvements in helping to increase production of ADU units.” 
The team representing Nebraska’s most populous city also hopes to gain insight on innovative building techniques, materials and tips that can help expand affordable housing options. 
Other cities across Nebraska and the nation will have access to strategies and outcomes on Bloomberg’s Idea Exchange site. Potential exists for 16 additional cities to join the program later. 
The initiative comes as the nation confronts a housing shortage the U.S. Chamber of Commerce says has created “cascading economic and social challenges from skyrocketing prices to reduced workforce mobility.” 
Nebraska, meanwhile, continues to pursue goals laid out in an unprecedented strategic housing framework plan in which statewide leaders said Nebraska’s economy depended on solving its “housing crisis.” Cities including Omaha and other Nebraska urban and rural communities have created more tailored roadmaps.
 Looking to Austin, Texas

Seeking to help mayors adopt “proven ways” of getting more housing built, Bloomberg  will partner the 14 participants with certain cities that have successful track records.
 

Bloomberg Philanthropies encompasses the personal and corporate giving of Michael R. Bloomberg, a media and financial data billionaire who founded the parent company of Bloomberg News. He served as mayor of New York City as a Republican and independent, and later registered Democrat and ran for president in 2020. The philanthropies arm distributed $4.3 billion last year, focusing on creating lasting change in the arts, education, environment, government innovation and public health.



The group points to San Diego’s relatively fast and digitized permitting process, Atlanta’s housing “strike force” teams and an accessory dwelling unit increase in Austin, Texas. 
Omaha chose its focus to be on creation of ADUs, which are second or smaller homes on the same lot as a primary house. So city planners will be working with and adapting Austin’s model to meet local demands and rules, Englund said. 
A Pew report earlier this year documented a turnaround in Austin’s housing market, where home sale prices had gone up 82% and rents jumped more than any other major American city in the decade of 2010-2019.
Austin amended its city code in 2015, partly by reducing minimum lot size for building an ADU, Bloomberg said. In 2023 and 2024, the city legalized having up to three homes on most single-family lots and communicated that and various other changes via a live applications dashboard, webinar series and more. ADU permits issued from 2015-2024 reportedly grew to 260 per year in the capital city of Texas, up from an average of 37 annually during the previous decade.
 Affordability, flexibility

Nonprofit Habitat for Humanity in a 2023 report said ADUs are becoming an increasingly popular housing option because of affordability, flexibility and potential for housing stability. 
Bloomberg said Omaha was chosen for reasons including local housing pressures, population size, demonstrated mayoral leadership on the issue and readiness to adapt.
Omaha Mayor John Ewing Jr. (Courtesy of City of Omaha)
“We looked at cities that had already made a commitment to zoning reform, softening the ground for supply,” said Bloomberg’s James Anderson.
Omaha changed its zoning code in 2024 to expand potential for ADU development in Omaha. But city officials said they haven’t seen enough production, likely for lack of builders specializing in the ADU model and barriers from lending institutions.
Englund said 30 to 35 ADUs have been built or approved since the zoning code loosened. “It’s an increase, but it’s not substantial,” he said.
A goal of the program is to at least double annual ADU production, Englund said, and to explore ways to help speed up production of other affordable housing types.
Mayor John Ewing Jr., who has proclaimed housing creation a priority, called the Bloomberg initiative “another critical tool toward achieving that goal.”
Related grant funding is to go toward such things as engaging architects to draft permit-ready ADU plans and adding technology to streamline the permit process.
Travel expenses would be covered by Bloomberg separate from the grant, Bloomberg representatives said.
 Positioned for federal incentives

They said participation also positions Omaha to capitalize on new federal policy, organizers said, as the ROAD to Housing Act created incentives for similar reforms.
Michael R. Bloomberg, founder of Bloomberg Philanthropies, said in a press release that cities have been taking action to ease the housing shortage that is driving up rents and pushing homeownership out of reach.




Quotation







As local governments address this issue, we have a great opportunity to spread the best ideas across the country.


– Michael R. Bloomberg, Bloomberg Philanthropies



“As local governments address this issue, we have a great opportunity to spread the best ideas across the country,” he said. 
Other cities in the Bloomberg initiative: Albuquerque, New Mexico; Alexandria, Virginia; Charleston, South Carolina; Chattanooga, Tennessee; Cleveland, Ohio; Columbia, South Carolina; Durham, North Carolina; Louisville, Kentucky; Miami, Florida; Nashville, Tennessee; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; Providence, Rhode Island; and San Jose, California.
The housing venture is the third “government innovation” effort launched this year between Omaha and Bloomberg. Omaha is participating in the Bloomberg Harvard City Leadership Program, a yearlong effort involving various mayors and senior staff who identify a problem and strategies to address it. Omaha’s subject is street homelessness.
The city also received $50,000 to provide Youth Climate Action Fund microgrants to people ages 15 to 24.
