name: Delaware
title: Newark Charter remains undefeated, defeats Seaford for first district win of the 2026 season
text:
The Newark Charter Patriots gather in front of their fans to celebrate their win over Seaford, Friday night. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
The Newark Charter Patriots defeated the Seaford Blue Jays, 20-0, on Friday, October 23, earning the program’s fourth shutout win this season.
 
NEWARK, DE — Newark Charter’s offense jogged out of the huddle and lined up in the pistol formation. The ball was spotted at the Seaford 43-yard line and the Patriots needed to gain 17 yards for a first down. 
Quarterback Chase Kennedy received the snap, immediately turned to his left and stretched his right arm out to hand the ball off to senior running back Austin Gbadegbe. Gbadegbe took the handoff and ran to his left behind the blocking of junior tight end Austin Ledoshuk and sophomore left tackle Donovan Pray. Gbadegbe ran about five yards down field before being touched by a Blue Jay defender. 
The abundance of space allowed the senior runner to evade a couple hopeful tacklers and rush the full 43 yards into the endzone, giving the Patriots a three score lead with a little over a minute remaining in the first quarter.
Gbadegbe finished the game with over 100 yards rushing and two touchdowns helping the Newark Charter Patriots defeat the Seaford Blue Jays, 20-0, Friday night.
“He’s a special player,” Patriot head coach Jody Russell said postgame. “He’s a really powerful, low to the ground guy and explosive when he gets the chance.” 
Gbadegbe’s game-high 43-yard touchdown run not only showcased his talent as a runner, but the prowess of the offensive line he ran behind. The Patriots’ offensive line played a strong game creating running lanes for their offense — which ran for over 150 yards — and holding the Blue Jays’ defensive pass rush to two sacks. 
Newark Charter’s defensive line created a similar impact on the other side of the ball. 
The Patriots’ defensive line generated multiple pressures throughout the night and earned four sacks as a result of that pressure. Two of those sacks came on Seaford’s second drive of the game and the success of the Patriots’ defensive lineman allowed the rest of the Newark Charter defense to swarm to the ball for quick tackles.
“They just have a motor. They don’t stop,” Russell said about Newark Charter’s offensive and defensive lines. “They play together. They’re not the biggest guys in the world, but they’re fast, they’re quick, their speed really, you know, sets them apart from other teams.”
Newark Charter’s aggressive defense also generated a pair of turnovers that resulted in Gbadegbe’s two touchdowns. Both scores came on runs. The first was a one-yard run up the middle and the second was his 43-yard dash down the left sideline. Newark Charter’s first touchdown was a nine-yard pass from Kennedy to Ledoshuk on the Patriots’ second offensive possession of the game. Ledoshuk leaped over the Blue Jay defender to make the touchdown grab near the front right pylon.
“I’m on the backside and this week they said I was gonna get the ball and I definitely did get the ball,” Ledoshuk said with a smile postgame.
Neither offense could get rolling in the second half, but the Blue Jays moved the ball well with quick throws from senior quarterback Everette Burton. Burton completed six passes in the half for 66 yards through the air. The Patriots run game continued to play well and helped the offense put together time consuming drives that limited the number of possessions the Blue Jays’ offense had. 
Newark Charter’s win improves their record to 7-0 this season and completes an unresolved mission from a year ago. 
The Patriots lost three games in their inaugural varsity season last year. One came against the Odessa Ducks whom the Patriots beat this season, 13-0. The other two were at the hands of the Blue Jays. Seaford defeated Newark Charter, 33-7, during the 2025 regular season and 21-20 in an overtime victory to claim the Class 1A championship title. 
“We’ve been preparing for this game, we’ve had this game marked for like a year now and it just feels great to come out and beat these guys,” Ledoshuk said.
The Patriots seem poised to return to the Class 1A championship game and will try to continue their strong season against Early College School on October 30. The game will be played at Early College and start at 6:00 p.m.
Seaford’s next matchup will be against an out of state opponent — Washington High School from Maryland — and begin at 6:00 p.m. on October 30. The game will be played at Seaford High School.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Enrollment increases at South Dakota technical colleges, despite drops in some programs
text:
Western Dakota Technical College in Rapid City is one of the four technical colleges in South Dakota. (Courtesy of WDTC)Enrollment at South Dakota’s four technical colleges increased, according to the 2026 fall enrollment report.
The state Board of Technical Education reviewed the report Thursday during its Rapid City meeting.
Total enrollment grew by 39 students over last year, reaching a record 7,813 across degree-seeking, dual-credit and non-degree-seeking categories. Dual-credit programs allow high-schoolers to earn both high school and college credit simultaneously.
By contrast, enrollment fell at South Dakota’s public universities by 294 students to 35,797, driven primarily by drops among undergraduate and international students.


Both systems reported a decrease in dual-credit enrollment. Among the public university system, dual-credit enrollment decreased by 10 students. Dual-credit enrollment at technical colleges decreased by 53 students, to 1,421.
Jenna Reis, policy and data analyst for the board, called it a “slight decrease.”
“I think our dual enrollment numbers still remain strong and are a great connection point for high school students to get connected to college coursework and get familiar with our technical colleges,” Reis said.
South Dakota public university enrollment drop includes fewer undergrad and international students

The drop in dual enrollment within the technical education system was entirely attributable to Western Dakota Technical College in Rapid City, where it decreased by 132 students, from 411 to 279. Dual enrollment increased at all other technical colleges.
“We saw that decrease, and we’re trying to diagnose it,” Nick Wendell, executive director of the board, told South Dakota Searchlight after the meeting. “We don’t have absolute certainty this early what led to that.”
Western Dakota Technical College President Kendra Ericson attributed the drop in dual-credit enrollment to “multiple factors,” including students or school districts taking courses through other institutions.
Ericson told Searchlight that the college no longer teaches in-person courses at the Meade School District, decreasing its district involvement from nine to eight districts. Meade School District Superintendent Wayne Wormstadt said students are still able to take courses online at Western Dakota and other higher education institutions across the state.


Dual enrollment at Black Hills State University increased by 48 students over last year and South Dakota Mines increased by six, according to data from the South Dakota Board of Regents.
Ericson also said the number of course sections Western Dakota faculty have taught at schools decreased for some districts. 
Ericson told board members that students who take dual-credit courses are more likely to later enroll full-time at that institution. Dual credits earned at technical colleges or universities can carry directly into a degree program without needing to transfer. That pipeline has resulted in an 8% increase in degree-seeking students at the institution, she said.

Kendra Ericson, president of Western Dakota Technical College, speaks to the media on April 14, 2026, at the college in Rapid City. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)

“From my standpoint, we’re not concerned,” Ericson said to Searchlight about the decrease. “We know we’re meeting the needs of our school districts and our enrolled students.” 
In 2022, the Rapid City School District announced that it would no longer cover the cost of dual-credit enrollment at Western Dakota. The next year, dual enrollment at the college dropped by 38%, to 310 students.
After Western Dakota rebuilt dual enrollment over the next two years, the Legislature passed a bill in 2025 that shifted more of the cost of dual enrollment onto families. Ericson said that recent cost increase could also be a factor in Western Dakota’s decrease.
“Any time we have a change in cost structure that puts more on our students and families, we can always see a potential decrease in our enrollment because they don’t have the financial means to cover that,” Ericson said.
Health sciences remain the most popular programs at technical colleges, with enrollment growing by 147 students systemwide. Information technology enrollment dropped by 90 students systemwide, with 79 of those lost at Southeast Technical College in Sioux Falls.
Southeast Technical College President Cory Clasemann attributed the drop to uncertainty around the rapid growth of artificial intelligence.
“There is just some hesitation among students, particularly in that program, and that’s where we are seeing the drop at the moment,” Clasemann said, adding that he hopes it’s a “one year blip” as the college updates its Information Technology curriculum to align with AI advances.
South Dakota’s four technical colleges are in Sioux Falls, Watertown, Mitchell and Rapid City.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi sculptor comes home to bring Walter Anderson’s art to life
authors: Michelle Pinto, RHCJC, McKenna Klamm, RHCJC, and Justin Glowacki, RHCJC
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
OCEAN SPRINGS — Phil Proctor left South Mississippi to build a career as a professional sculptor, creating large-scale art installations across the country. Two decades later, the Lucedale native has returned to the Mississippi Coast to create sculptures inspired by an artist he has admired since childhood — Walter Anderson. 
“Walter Anderson has been sort of a name I’ve known for many years, going back to being a young child and being one of my favorite artists ever because of the content of the work and the naturalism and just the representation of the animals and the way they are drawn,” Proctor said. 
Proctor was chosen to create two sculptures for the Ocean Springs Gateway Sculpture Project, a shearwater bird and a pelican based on Anderson’s work. 
From South Mississippi to a career in sculpture 
Proctor graduated from the University of Southern Mississippi in 2000 with a bachelor’s degree in fine arts. He later earned a master’s degree in fine arts from East Carolina University before moving to Atlanta. 
His path to becoming a full-time artist was gradual. 
“Being an artist is — sometimes you gotta hold down a couple of jobs,” Proctor said. “I’d say after about ten years or so, I could leave most of my other kind of work behind and just focus on sculpture professionally full time.” 
His work has since taken him across the country, including projects in Arizona, Oklahoma, Florida and Ohio. 
“It was really nice to be able to work where I really know a lot of the people,” Proctor said. 
Bringing Anderson’s work into the third dimension 
The Walter Anderson Museum of Art viewed its collaboration with sculptor Phil Proctor on theGateway Sculpture Project as an opportunity to connect contemporary art with the past.  Credit: Justin Glowacki/RHCJC
The Gateway Sculpture Project took shape through meetings with residents and community leaders about what best represented Ocean Springs. 
Julian Rankin, strategic adviser for the Walter Anderson Museum of Art, said the process led organizers back to Anderson and the city’s artistic tradition. 
Proctor was selected after a public call for artist qualifications from Mississippi and the surrounding region. His task was to transform two-dimensional designs based on Anderson’s work into large-scale sculptures.
“Phil got to collaborate, if you will, with Walter Anderson across time and to turn these into three-dimensional sculptures,” Rankin said. “That, I think, was the magic about it.” 
“It was really kind of a wonderful experience working what I would describe as a collaboration with Walter Anderson in spirit,” Proctor said. 
Design and engineering work began in late 2025, followed by manufacturing around March 2026, Proctor said. The sculptures were unveiled Oct. 1. 
Rankin said the overall project took about two and a half years, including public input, design, funding and manufacturing. 
More than just art 
Pelicans appear throughout Walter Anderson’s artwork. Sculptor Phil Proctor believed the bird’sshape would translate well into a three-dimensional sculpture.  Credit: McKenna Klamm/RHCJC
The Gateway Sculpture Project aims to place public art at entrances to Ocean Springs while helping direct visitors downtown. 
The project was funded through the Gulf Coast Restoration Fund as part of the Mary C. O’Keefe Cultural Center rehabilitation and signage project. 
Rankin said the sculptures are intended to guide visitors toward businesses and bring art into developing areas of the city. 
He said the project could serve as an example for other Mississippi communities. 
“It’s a model for other cities and areas of the state to say, ‘We could do something like this too,’” Rankin said. 
For Proctor, the project also marked a return to his Mississippi roots. 
“Being able to work on a project in Mississippi really meant a lot to us,” he said.

name: California
title: 3 bonds are on the California ballot. Here’s a last-minute voter guide to make sense of them
text:
In summary
Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research.


 Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds.
You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass.
Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 for housing and Proposition 38 for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37, is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly.
Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans.


Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest. The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. 
Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you.
Prop. 1: Affordable housing
If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. 
The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless.The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature.
This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election.
Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans.The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans.Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. 
Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. 
Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1. 
Prop. 37: Help for down payments 
This bond measure is strange, novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns.
Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.”
Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment.
Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. 
Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county.What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments.
How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. 
Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37.
He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. 
Prop. 38: Immunology research
This bond proposal would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. 
The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies.
Previous reporting by CalMatters found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. 
Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year.
The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies.Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: Getting beyond the ideological force behind Michigan’s political and economic woes
text:
The Ford Rouge Plant in Dearborn on July 7, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)The economy consistently ranks among the leading problems cited by voters in Michigan, sentiment that is supported by the evidence. 
Economic indicators show Michigan struggling with very slow growth and falling economic competitiveness. The economic performance rankings in Rich States, Poor States dropped Michigan from 12th place in economic outlook in 2019 to 32nd in 2026. The latest rankings in the  U.S. News & World Report Overall Best States report points to a similar conclusion.  
After eight years of Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s administration, Michigan stands among the worst states (43rd) in the nation in economic vitality and performance.
The state’s economy is exacerbating the affordability crisis for lower-and middle-income Michigan residents. A September report from the Georgetown Center on Poverty and Inequality found nearly two-thirds of Michigan families were in a cost-of-living squeeze, as stubbornly high prices for essential goods continue to strain household budgets.  Families increasingly rely on credit cards and loans to cover basic living expenses, pushing household debt to unprecedented heights.
Michigan’s economic problems are decades in the making. The state’s shrinking manufacturing sector has caused the Michigan unemployment rate  to be  mostly higher than the national average since the 1980s. Per capita income has been generally lower than the national average since 1980, and the gap between the state and national median incomes has more than doubled since 2014, Income inequality also has worsened since the 1970s.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Michiganders worry about their economic future but also about the threats to democracy. They are particularly concerned with how wealthy special interests influence political leadership. According to a poll released by Progress Michigan, there is strong bipartisan support for Proposal 2, a ballot initiative that aims to ban utility monopolies from donating to state officeholders and that prohibits corporations with government contracts from making certain kinds of political contributions.
Today’s political upheaval and economic challenges are driving the resurgence of democratic socialism, a broad political ideology that combines a democratically-elected government with a collective arrangement of the economy. Millennials and Gen Z, particularly, display a significant tolerance of socialist concepts. According to a recent survey, 62% of American adults under 30 say they hold favorable views of socialism. Their support for candidates who embrace its core principles has made these candidates a viable political force that is challenging the right-of-center candidates for the future direction of the Democratic Party.
This is not the first time that the form capitalism has taken has been brought into question. In fact, capitalism has taken different forms in times of political and economic upheaval. 
To survive the Great Depression, for example, Franklin Roosevelt abandoned the federal government’s hands-off approach to the economy that had dominated since the country’s founding in favor of a more regulated form of state-assisted capitalism. Similarly, the economic trauma of high inflation and high unemployment of the 1970s prompted the Carter administration to replace government management of the economy with neoliberalism, a doctrine that shifted the locus of power to central banks and Wall Street.
Franklin D. Roosevelt Memorial, Washington, D.C. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)
This form of capitalism, which now reigns over much of the world, is anti-union and advocates open markets, global free trade, less regulations, less government spending, and an enhanced role of the private sector in the economy.
While positive changes have taken place under neoliberalism, its chief policy prescription, that financial markets and central bankers manage the economy, has failed mightily. So is the conclusion of many critics of neoliberalism, both on the left as well as in the mainstream.
Neoliberalism has effectively created a plutocracy, corrupting American democracy in the process. It is the ideological force behind the rise in severe inequality and aggravated racial disparities. Its stance on the role of government in the economy explains why the United States is the only developed country that does not have universal health care, why the homeless problem has become a crisis, and why children in many states do not get free meals at school. 
However, despite the growing criticism and visible damaging impacts on our politics and our economy, this reigning ideological force continues to be upheld in the name of freedom, individualism, and economic growth.
The negative impacts of neoliberalism are particularly evident in Michigan, a state that has served as a laboratory for neoliberal experiments. The state’s decline in industrial capacity, for example, can be traced to neoliberal policies enacted in the 80s that incentivized major auto companies to restructure their operations and supply chains to leverage cheaper labor markets and fewer regulations outside the United States. 
Once an industrial powerhouse, Michigan is now the epicenter of deindustrialization, a process that strips high-wage jobs from the state and strains local economies. Even Gov. Whitmer, who does not explicitly use the term neoliberal to define her political ideology, has drawn criticism from both the left and the right for favoring corporate favoritism over free market restraint.  
Beyond favoring corporate America, neoliberal policies have led to significant reductions in state funding to municipalities, as state leaders prioritized cutting corporate and individual income taxes to attract business. The emergency manager laws of 2012, passed in the interest of neoliberal fiscal responsibility, enabled state-appointed unelected managers to run financially distressed predominantly Black cities. In practice, these managers prioritized corporate creditor payouts and fiscal austerity over local democratic control.
The Flint Water Crisis of 2014 is similarly seen as a direct consequence of neoliberal policies that prioritized fiscal austerity and market-based logic over public health. Neoliberal ideas also have sought to restructure state public education, causing the state’s public-school systems to contend with market-based reforms, charter school expansion, and district takeovers.
Residents held a rally in 2019 to draw attention to the Flint Water Crisis. (Photo by Nick Manes/Michigan Advance)
Some political and economic experts also assert that Donald Trump’s 2016 victory was a direct result of decades of inequality and other failures of neoliberalism. The results of his presidency have been devastating to democracy. The 2026 Democracy Report notes that democracy in the United States has fallen back to the same level as in 1965. The country lost its long-term status as a liberal democracy for the first time in 2025.
Importantly, the backsliding of American democracy is part of a broader global decline in democracy that is occurring under neoliberalism. Over the past two decades, both the number of autocratic regimes and the share of the global population living under authoritarian rule have increased significantly. Today, autocratic countries not only outnumber democracies globally, but they rule over most of the world’s population. Roughly 7 in 10 people in the world live under autocratic rule.
The failures of neoliberal capitalism has led to calls for its reform and for the need to chart a new vision for society. 
I am not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, but I do favor a change in today’s economic arrangements that channel the country’s wealth into the hands of the few. The emergence of democratic socialism as a political force offers the opportunity to discuss its merits in reforming our current economic system to create a more just society. 
Rather than debating its virtues in terms of socialism vs capitalism, it is more productive to focus on what this philosophy means for deepening our democracy, stabilizing the economy, and reducing economic inequality, the latter being the main source of today’s political divisions.

name: California
title: LA chemical plant on short leash from state regulators as neighbors continue to protest its operations
text:
For nearly 30 years, an electronic waste processor in Los Angeles County has operated on a permit that expired in 1996 while neighbors, some living 550 feet away, say it harms their community.
On Thursday, a state oversight board faulted the Department of Toxic Substances Control for how it renewed that permit, but stopped short of revoking it. It was the first time in the board’s five-year history that residents asked it to pull a facility’s permit.
The Board of Environmental Safety granted separate appeals by community members and the company, Phibro-Tech. But it voted to allow the facility to continue operating while state regulators reassess the permit, which they renewed for the first time in the facility’s history last year. 
Environmental advocates say the case is a test of whether the board, created in 2022 to address the Department of Toxic Substances Control’s  history of flawed oversight, would put communities first. Its mandate is to protect public health, particularly in communities most burdened by pollution.  But the decision shows the board and the community disagree about how the board uses its authority, and how far that authority goes.
The department recorded 29 violations at Phibro-Tech between 2013 and 2022 for actions such as failing to clean up leaks and treating waste its permit doesn’t allow. Officials say the facility has since improved, but the state is still suing over alleged violations of hazardous waste laws. Phibro-Tech maintains that DTSC inspected it more often than other facilities and cited it disproportionately as a result.
Neighbors Against Phibro-Tech, a community group represented by Earthjustice, argued that state regulators renewed the permit without accounting for that violation history, failed to provide the public with a complete record on the decision and relied on health and cumulative impact analyses that didn’t properly evaluate the risk to nearby residents. 
“It’s important to acknowledge the victory that happened today,” said Esme Levy, Earthjustice attorney. “But the board has the opportunity or had the opportunity to go further.” 
The board granted Phibro-Tech’s two appeals and ordered the department to remove some rules from the permit that don’t apply to them. Robert Martin, an attorney for the company , said he appreciated the board’s consideration, but declined to comment on the decision before reviewing the board’s official order. 
CalMatters provided questions to the board about its performance in its first five years. In an emailed statement, Andrew Rakestraw, board chair, said the board has made the department “more fiscally stable, more transparent, and more accountable to the public, particularly those communities across California dealing with the burdens of toxic waste. 
The board debates
On Wednesday, lawyers for the community argued that the Department of Toxic Substances Control illegally renewed Phibro-Tech’s permit because it did not consider the company’s longstanding history of serious violations in the decision. 
The department “didn’t think that Phibro-Tech was able or willing to comply with its permit, and yet it went ahead and granted a permit that significantly expands Phibro-Tech’s operations without an explanation,” Earthjustice attorney Esme Levy told the board.
Earthjustice Attorney Esme Levy speaking at the City of Montebello Council Chambers  in Montebello on Oct. 21, 2026. Photo by Ariana Drehsler for CalMatters
Earthjustice also said the department’s public record was incomplete. Levy told board members that Earthjustice representatives had to request specific documents and that the department asked for more time to prepare them after the permit decision.  
Wayne Lorentzen, head of the department’s permitting division, said the complete record “was accessible to the public and contained the documents that permitting relied on and considered when making its permit decision.”
“That same administrative record provides specific evidence to refute the allegation that (the department) did not consider Phibro-Tech’s complete compliance history,” he told the board.
The board ultimately agreed with Neighbors Against Phibro-Tech that the record was incomplete and that the department didn’t show it completely reviewed the company’s compliance history. 
The department itself “recognizes that there’s a significant concern for (Phibro-Tech’s) ability or willingness to comply,” board chair Andrew Rakestraw said. “Those are two issues that really get at the core of the permit decision, and so what I would have expected to see here is some connection between this significant concern … and their subsequent decision to grant this permit.” 
Byron Chan, an Earthjustice attorney, said he appreciated the board’s willingness to identify problems in the department’s process, but hoped for stronger action. 
“They agreed with us that permitting violated the law in three different ways in issuing this permit,” Chan said. “How many illegal acts does permitting have to do until (the board denies) the permit?” 
Greg Forest, the board’s attorney, said it has authority to ask the department to deny permits. But the board didn’t discuss that option. 
Phibro-Tech’s appeal 
The board also heard a separate appeal from Phibro-Tech. The company argued the department should have issued a permit for 10 years instead of five and that the department wrongly imposed waste-treatment rules that shouldn’t apply. 
The board agreed that the department didn’t adequately explain why the permit was issued for five years and required the department to reconsider the permit and justify its term limit. The board also asked the department to remove the waste-treatment rules. 
“What we’re asking for is not a specific term, but to show the work,” said board member Rhys Williams. 
Phibro-Tech had also asked the board to review the department’s decision to certify its tanks for three years instead of five. But a week before the hearing, the company and state regulators settled that issue, with regulators agreeing to extend the tank certification to five years.
Chan said the settlement undermined the appeal process. 
“You can see an effort from permitting and Phibro-Tech to try to avoid the public scrutiny of the board and try to resolve as much as they can before they have to go before this public-facing body,” Chan said. “That’s really troubling, especially for what the board is supposed to represent as far as protecting communities.”
Asked about this criticism, the department didn’t comment on it, or the earlier settlement. 
But at the hearing itself, Mandi Bane, a deputy director at the department who oversees its hazardous waste management program, said the board’s independent check on its work has been “a great addition.” The department will wait for written direction from the board before taking its next steps. 
The board has 30 days to finalize its decision.  
Jaime Sanchez, an advocate with Neighbors Against Phibro-Tech, attends a Board of Environmental Safety meeting at the City of Montebello Council Chambers  in Montebello on Oct. 21, 2026. Photo by Ariana Drehsler for CalMatters
In a 2024 cross-complaint, Phibro-Tech alleged the Department of Toxic Substances Control violated its due process rights by inconsistently applying rules to the company.
“DTSC inspected (Phibro-Tech) over the past (10 years) considerably more frequently than other permitted facilities,” the suit states. “Because of this, DTSC has disproportionately cited (the company) for violations.”
Residents living in the nearby Los Nietos neighborhood say the company has impacted their lives for over 30 years. 
“To think that the whole time that I’ve been alive (Phibro-Tech) has been operating kind of under the radar, with little consequences, with very little oversight, it’s just so frustrating and so disheartening,” said resident Jordan Salcido.
The renewed permit is temporarily paused while the appeals process continues, but Phibro-Tech continues to operate under its original permit.
Attorney Zachary Walton representing Phibro-Tech speaks at a Board of Environmental Safety meeting  at the City of Montebello Council Chambers  in Montebello on Oct. 21, 2026. Photo by Ariana Drehsler for CalMatters
The board’s authority
Lawmakers created the board, but some now say it may need more direction. 
A legislative committee reviews the board and the department’s performance in oversight hearings yearly. At this year’s hearing, Rakestraw told legislators it has met its mandate to improve transparency and fiscal responsibility at the department. But it’s still unclear how far the board can go in telling department staff what specific actions to take. 
Rakestraw said the public expects detailed oversight, and that the board will force regulators to take action in a certain way. But, he added, much of the department’s work “occurs outside of the board’s jurisdiction.”
“Many stakeholders view the board as California’s hazardous waste watchdog,” he said. “In reality … we have decision-making authority in a handful of areas.”

name: VTDigger
title: Manchester weighs Flock camera alternatives ahead of Vermont ban on automated license plate readers
text:
A license plate reader camera on VT Route 7A in Manchester seen in June 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

MANCHESTER — At Tuesday night’s selectboard meeting, members heard an update from Chief of Police James Blanchard about the town’s current contract with Flock, maker of the controversial automatic license plate recognition system, set to expire in March and what steps the town should or could reasonably make from a law-enforcement perspective in light of a new state statute. Vermont is set to enact 23 V.S.A. § 1609 on July 1, 2027, which says, “No State agency or department or any political subdivision of the State shall use automated license plate recognition systems or automated traffic law enforcement systems.”
The town had previously paused the use of the Flock system pending a review by the Agency of Transportation since the cameras were initially meant to be used for work-zone traffic safety, not as a policing tool more broadly. The town resumed their use in February of this year after assurances from Transportation Secretary Joe Flynn that the town’s current camera use fell within the existing law, following consultation with the Department of Public Safety confirming that data gathered by such systems is not promulgated. 
The upcoming July legislation, though, means that Manchester will likely lose the ability to use any automated license plate recognition system. Chief Blanchard has publicly expressed concern over the loss of the tool. But given the town’s soon-to-expire Flock contract, the legislation set for July and the possibility of changes to the law before then, Blanchard is trying to navigate a reasonable way forward that is centered on researching possible alternative systems.
In an Oct. 15 email to Town Manager Scott Murphy, Blanchard outlined some of his concerns.
“Before the Town makes a significant investment in any replacement system, I think it would be worthwhile to obtain updated guidance from the State on how they interpret Section 1609 and whether any automated license plate reader system would still be permitted after that date,” he said.
“(M)y preference would be to continue researching alternatives over the next few months so we can make an informed decision before the renewal comes due,” adding that “(m)y concern is simply that we’ve found the automated license plate reader to be a valuable investigative tool, and I’d like to avoid losing that capability altogether if there’s another solution that better fits the Board’s expectations and remains legally viable.”
At Tuesday’s meeting, Blanchard described the current state of his research into possible alternatives. One alternative his team is looking into is the Unify Camera System.
“That’s actually the camera system that we currently use on the public safety building,” he said. “(They’re) the cameras that are around the exterior of our building. So we’re familiar with it. One of the reasons that it’s appealing is that it has the potential to store all of the data locally on town-owned equipment, rather than a vendor-managed cloud, which addresses mainly the primary concern that we had heard.”
Blanchard outlined some of the “hiccups” that would come with adopting the Unify system, including potential cost, how data would be transmitted to the in-house server and whether the system could offer the capability Blanchard is seeking. A second challenge would be how the cameras are powered. Currently, Flock cameras use solar power. Blanchard expressed a preference for a system that was hardwired and would need additional research to know if that would be possible with Unify.
Whatever the town decides to do, Blanchard reiterated his desire to find a tool that would approximate the same policing capabilities within the expected legislative changes.
“We’re certainly not looking to continue our relationship with Flock past March, but I would like to focus on finding an alternative because it is an extremely valuable resource from a public safety standpoint,” he said.
“I think it’s just trying to find the fine line and the balance between the concerns that we’ve heard as far as respecting privacy, and focusing on public safety,” said Blanchard, “and I’m hopeful that there is another option out there, such as Unify.”
Following Chief Blanchard’s update, the board heard from Peter Campbell of The Crooked Ram restaurant.
“I’d like to share, being a small town, how shocked a lot of people were when I would bring up (the town’s use of surveillance technology), and this sort of immediate loss of trust that was felt with law enforcement and the town government, which is disappointing, because a lot of us have moved to this area precisely to be in a community where there is trust with the police department and trust with the people on the selectboard who are running the government. That’s why I moved here from New York City.”
Board member Jonathan West broadened the discussion when he expressed concern over proceeding to a solution without necessary caution given the current state of artificial intelligence technology and the corrosive effect it can have on the political process and the possibility of its nefarious use even in a law enforcement context.
“There are concrete examples of, not necessarily an entire police department, but individuals within the department, who are savvy about the workarounds within the system, which oftentimes just require a few keywords and then you can access different parts of the system that are supposedly ring-fenced,” he said.
“I think anytime you pass (technology) over to a centralized corporate entity that we don’t have control or access to, or to put our town’s safety in their hands and take them at their word for it, is dangerous,” West warned. 
“It’s not to say that there aren’t good uses … but I think the sort of fears and concerns everybody would have could be assuaged, if we are in control of our own data, we’re being very transparent about what we’re doing with this surveillance, why we’re using it and giving examples about what it does to keep the community safe,” he said. 
Select Board Vice Chair Heidi Chamberlain emphasized the need to educate the public about the thinking behind the town’s adoption of the technology and that it was important to draw the distinction between the town’s initial intent and the current negative examples of AI and surveillance cameras given the rapid evolution of the technology, subject of public discourse at home and across the country.
“I think that’s worth noting, when you talk to people that think that we set this up to do something deceitful, that was certainly not the intention,” she said “and that we (are) respond(ing) in real time. This is our second or third meeting about (the use of Flock and associated technologies), so we recognize that it’s problematic.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Online sports betting supporters, opponents clash before Nebraskans get final say Nov. 3
text:
Officials celebrated the launch of Maryland’s legal sports betting market at MGM National Harbor in December 2021 in Oxon Hill, Md. As many states legalize sports betting, officials are increasingly eyeing a certain type of wager known as a prop bet for increased regulation. (Photo by Shannon Finney/Getty Images for MGM National Harbor)LINCOLN — Nebraskans will have the final say Nov. 3 on whether to legalize and regulate online sports betting as advocates and opponents clash in the final days of the 2026 race.
Initiative Measures 440 and 441 would together amend the Nebraska Constitution and state law, respectively, to legalize and regulate online sports wagers. In 2020, Nebraskans authorized casino gambling at the state’s existing five racetracks. Under current state law, annual gaming revenue is taxed at 20%, and 70% of that amount is directed to property tax relief credits.
An opposing group, Save Nebraska Sports, has stepped up opposition in the final two-week stretch, including an ad from State Treasurer Joey Spellerberg and State Auditor Mike Foley and an opposing letter from 45 current and former Huskers student-athletes and coaches.
“Husker athletics is about teamwork, discipline, competition and pride in our state,” the Huskers’  letter, led by legendary coach Tom Osborne, states. “We cannot allow it to be used as a vehicle to enrich out-of-state gambling interests at the expense of Nebraska families.”
Regulating the ‘status quo’
Jordan McGrain, a sponsor of the ballot measure campaign, which is known as Tax Relief Nebraska, said the integrity and safety of student-athletes and coaches have a meaningful place in the debate. But he noted that state law and regulations offer protections for players and that sports bets placed in person at casinos are already legal.
Under state law, Nebraskans cannot bet on the Huskers or other collegiate teams when they are playing at home. The State Racing and Gaming Commission can add other restrictions.
“Without legalizing and regulating the marketplace, we just get the status quo, which not only provides none of these protections but sees millions of dollars in revenue going across state lines,” McGrain said.


Gaming tax distribution
Annual gross gaming proceeds (including all games of chance at casinos) are taxed at 20%.
The tax revenue is then distributed as follows:

70% — Property Tax Credit Cash Fund.
25% — The county where a racetrack is located (if located at least partially in a city or village, the proceeds are split between the county and city or village).
2.5% — Compulsive Gamblers Assistance Fund.
2.5% — State of Nebraska General Fund (main state checking account).

If online sports wagers are legalized, the new revenue would be taxed, and the revenue distributed, in the same manner, unless determined otherwise by the Legislature. Voter-approved laws can only be changed by at least two-thirds of lawmakers (33 of 49).
Source: Nebraska Revised Statute 9-1204


McGrain said Nebraskans are already participating in unregulated, illegal platforms on their phones through loopholes, such as “prediction markets” like Kalshi or Polymarket, or they’re crossing borders to all but one of Nebraska’s six neighboring states to place bets: Iowa, Missouri, Kansas, Colorado or Wyoming. 
He and other supporters, such as state Sen. Jason Prokop of Lincoln, have said Nebraska has the ills but none of the possible revenue that could help with taxes or problem gambling. 
“There’s no question to me that Nebraska is just better served by legalizing it, regulating it and instilling these consumer protections and guardrails that have been effective in other states,” McGrain said.
Prokop noted that under Nebraska’s prohibition, Iowa benefits from the “country’s busiest cornfield right across the river” as people cross over, place bets on their cellphones and then return.
Safety of student-athletes, coaches
The Huskers’ letter states that game manipulation, relentless gambling ads and the harassment of athletes over losing bets are dangers in the sports world, and that student-athletes should be able to compete without worrying that every play, mistake or outcome could affect someone’s financial well-being.
“When fans begin questioning whether the outcome of a game is determined by honest competition, the integrity of the entire sport is at risk,” the letter states.
Prokop said he sees two separate issues this year: whether Nebraska has a well-regulated, legal sports betting system instead of the unregulated networks where “anything goes,” and protections for players and consumers.
“I would work with anyone on a bill, whether it’s to look at if we need to increase penalties or anything like that if people are harassing student-athletes,” Prokop said. “That absolutely should not happen.”
Executive branch divided
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, who is running for reelection this fall, repeatedly said in 2024 that he supported the legalization of online sports betting. In summer 2024, he called a special session specifically on property taxes, including possible new revenue sources. At the time, he said he was an “advocate” and would not “stand in the way” if lawmakers sought legalization.
Pillen played for Osborne in the 1970s as a defensive back.
“The governor is going to respect the will of the voters,” Pillen spokesperson Laura Strimple said in an email Friday when asked if Pillen supports Initiative Measures 440 and 441.
The Nebraska Board of State Canvassers, composed of State Treasurer Joey Spellerberg, Secretary of State Bob Evnen, Gov. Jim Pillen, Attorney General Mike Hilgers and Auditor of Public Accounts Mike Foley, meets to certify Nebraska’s May 12 primary election. At the podium, speaking to the board, is Deputy Secretary of State Wayne Bena. June 8, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Foley and Spellerberg, in the Spellerberg-paid-for ad, say the sports betting industry is “lying” about property tax relief and that advocates are making the “same false promises” as casino supporters did in 2020.
“And our property taxes aren’t lower,” Foley says in the ad. “… Don’t believe the lies.”
Foley, a former state senator and lieutenant governor, is running for a fourth nonconsecutive term as state auditor. Spellerberg, the former Fremont mayor, is seeking a full term after Pillen appointed him treasurer last year.
Candidates can purchase cheaper ads in competitive ad markets than can ballot question committees, such as Tax Relief Nebraska. Lawmakers declined to close that loophole this year.
FanDuel Inc. and DK Crown Holdings Inc. (the parent company of DraftKings) are the primary donors of the Tax Relief Nebraska campaign, each contributing more than $7 million. Through Sept. 29, the campaign raised $14.65 million and spent $9.22 million.
Pat Loontjer, executive director of Gambling with the Good Life, left, watches Les Bernal, national director of Stop Predatory Gambling, speak to reporters before a Nebraska hearing to expand gambling, such as to online sports betting, in-state collegiate sports and fantasy sports. March 10, 2025.(Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Save Nebraska Sports has taken a more front-facing role than another longtime anti-gambling group: Gambling with the Good Life. The leader, Pat Loontjer, is still speaking out, and last week, she joined with Open Door Mission in Omaha. The nonprofit has helped people facing homelessness and poverty for more than 70 years.
“For those struggling with addiction and homelessness, lottery tickets, gambling machines and betting apps put false hope within easy reach,” said Steven Frazee of Open Door Mission. 
Providing property tax relief
The Tax Relief Nebraska campaign commissioned a study estimating $166 million in possible revenue over the next 10 years. Adding in expected casino gambling revenue, McGrain said gaming taxes could be about $500 million, on a conservative estimate, over the next decade.
State Sen. Jason Prokop of Lincoln, left, talks with State Sen. Christy Armendariz of Omaha on the floor of the Nebraska Legislature. March 10, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The campaign has at least seven different video ads, according to the Google Ads Transparency Center. In one, multiple Nebraskans say they support the measures to take property taxes into their own hands. In another, a woman states: “It’s time for the relief we deserve.”
Prokop, a member of the Legislature’s Appropriations Committee, said lawmakers’ hands could be more tied next year without the revenue to provide continued tax relief as they work to close a budget deficit that could be as high as $847 million if left unchecked by mid-2029.
If policymakers can find revenue from untaxed activities that Nebraskans are already participating in, Prokop said: “I think we need to seriously consider it.”
“Our revenue options right now are minimal,” Prokop said.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, right, leads a ceremony after a Huskers football game honoring legendary former football coach and former Huskers athletic director Tom Osborne, left, as the newest and first living inductee into the Nebraska Hall of Fame on Sept. 19, 2026, at Memorial Stadium. (Photo by Zach Wendling)
McGrain said he respectfully disagrees that the new revenue isn’t relevant. He agreed with Prokop that, given Nebraska’s budget situation and schools raising property tax rates or property valuations skyrocketing, online sports betting is a valid option for revenue.
“It’s really one of the only options we have, especially in this economic environment,” McGrain said.
In 2025, multiple state senators proposed regulations to accompany online sports betting, had voters later decided to legalize the wagers. State Sen. Stan Clouse of Kearney, for instance, proposed diverting 90% of the new tax revenue toward property tax relief, instead of 70%.
“It’s not the gaming industry’s job to deliver property tax relief. It’s the politicians’ job,” he added. “This is just one part of the revenue that Nebraskans approved in 2020 and are on track to approve in 2026.”
The general election is Nov. 3. If the measures pass, Initiative Measure 441 gives the Racing and Gaming Commission a June 1 deadline to adopt any necessary regulatory changes.



Huskers joining opposing letter
In addition to former Huskers football coach Tom Osborne, who would go on to represent Nebraska’s 3rd Congressional District for six years, Wrestling head coach Mark Manning also signed the letter, as did four other athletic staff or coaches and 39 current or former players:

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland members of Congress, elections officials targeted by suspicious letters
text:
Almost every member of Maryland's congressional delegation has received ominous letters filled with what turned out to be a nontoxic powder in the last week, part of a string of such attacks nationwide. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Almost every member of Congress from Maryland, as well as the state’s elections office, received ominous letters filled with what turned out to be a nontoxic powder at one of their offices in the last week.
It makes Maryland offices the latest in a string of such attacks nationwide, just weeks before the Nov. 3 elections. Dozens of congressional lawmakers, election officials and secretaries of state across the U.S. reported receiving similar letters, that were first sent to Louisiana and Oklahoma representatives early last week.
The incidents are being jointly investigated by the FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service.
Maryland Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis described the situation as “pure madness” in a Thursday interview. The letter sent to his office was intercepted by law enforcement officials, following enhanced mail and inspection procedures, he said, after authorities flagged officials to be on the lookout for any letter similar to the ones sent early last week.
On Capitol Hill, both of Maryland’s senators and at least five of the state’s eight House members confirmed that they had received such letters.
Only Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st) said the office had not been targeted, a spokesperson for the office said. An aide to Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-4th) declined to comment Thursday, and Rep. April McClain Delaney (D-6th) did not respond to a request for comment on the subject.
Every other member confirmed or announced receiving a letter, with almost all arriving last Friday.

Rep. Kweisi Mfume (D-7th) received a letter at his Baltimore office, according to his press team. 
Mfume sent a letter last Friday to postal inspection service leaders requesting a briefing on the mailings for all congressional and elections officials, with information detailing how many letters have been identified, how many were intercepted, and how postal services communicate with other agencies regarding similar security situations.
“I take the recent mail threat against our office with the utmost seriousness. The safety of my staff, constituents and all who enter our doors remains my highest priority,” Mfume said in a Thursday statement. “In this political climate, I will not be intimidated, silenced, or frightened from the call to serve.”
Office staff for Rep. Johnny Olszewski (D-2nd) discovered the letter and isolated it immediately before notifying law enforcement, his spokesperson wrote in a statement. 
“Political violence, intimidation and threats are never acceptable. Public servants should be able to do their jobs and serve their communities without fear,” the statement read. “We are grateful to our team for responding quickly, to the first responders who keep us safe, and to the investigators working to hold those responsible for these crimes accountable.”
Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-5th) also received a letter to his district office in Greenbelt on Monday, after the FBI and postal inspection services had already announced an investigation. Hoyer issued a statement on Monday calling the efforts to intimidate staff and officials across the country “un-American” and saying similar actions pose a threat to democracy.
The FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service would not confirm specific instances of letters being received, the FBI said an a statement Thursday. The agency did say that investigators have yet to identify who sent the letters, why they were sent or what the powdered substance is, except that it is nontoxic. The agencies are working closely with law enforcement to respond to each incident, the FBI added.
“This FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens,” the Thursday statement reads.
DeMarinis said the incident has not intimidated him or his staff, but that it has strengthened his motivation to lead a safe election.
“It’s a cowardly act … the goal of this person is to disenfranchise Marylanders,” DeMarinis said. “It’s just a pure coward that wants to undermine American democracy in its foundations, starting with elections.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Offering cash for votes is quite common throughout history — but here’s why it doesn’t work
text:
President Donald Trump speaks during an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)Politics is about the distribution of power and money. So it comes as little surprise that many politicians campaign on the material benefits that citizens can expect if those candidates win.
President Donald Trump has been no different in this respect. He has promised voters, among other things, a “DOGE dividend” using money saved by cutting federal jobs, rebates from tariff revenues, and a diversion of money currently used to subsidize health insurance companies directly to Americans.
But his pledge to give $5,000 to every U.S. citizen if Republicans retain majorities in the House and Senate in the November 2026 midterm elections had a different dimension. This offer wasn’t a rebate for taxes paid or a subsidy for an impacted constituency. Instead, it was tied to an electoral outcome. That brings it closer to vote buying, which raises concerns from a legal point of view.
For this to actually happen, it needs congressional approval — and Republican legislators haven’t taken action. But Trump has yet to rescind the idea, which could cost over $1 trillion. So it’s time to ask whether it could make a difference in the midterms, where margins are tight in key races.
I’m a political scientist who has studied for the past decade vote buying in countries around the world. Cash for votes may seem like a straightforward way to win support, but my research shows that offering people money rarely changes their vote.
 
Why vote buying rarely works
The practice dates back to ancient Rome and was a staple of American political machines from the 19th century to the mid-20th century in New York City, Chicago and states including Georgia, Missouri, New Jersey, Ohio and Virginia.
By diverting public money for partisan purposes, local power brokers cultivated relationships with particular constituencies, such as newly arrived immigrants. Institutional reforms, including the professionalization of government bureaucracies at the federal and local levels, slowly constricted these political machines until the last holdout in Chicago succumbed by the late 1970s.
But in recent decades, vote buying has surged in new democracies, with politicians in at least 73 countries offering cash, food, clothes, building supplies, medical care or legal advice for votes.
If vote buying is so common, it stands to reason that it must work. But a survey of recent research shows otherwise. On average, I have found that the vote-buying attempts across 10 countries and 57 elections around the world have had no detectable influence.
Why are the electoral returns so poor? For vote buying to work, the value of the benefits people receive has to outweigh the factors pushing them toward an opposing party. As in the U.S., voters around the world make their choices based on considerations such as their own partisanship; issue preferences; the performance of the incumbent party; the perceived competence of the candidates; and more. Very few voters in any electorate are truly indifferent.
As long as those factors together outweigh the value of the benefits that people would receive to switch, vote buying fails. And that’s what typically happens, as I explain in my new book, “Against the Machine.”
 
The importance of competition
There are three specific reasons why vote buying usually flops.
First, local competition creates vigorous campaigns that amp up partisan sentiments. These sentiments influence voters’ responses to electoral gifts. If you already like the political machine, you interpret its gifts as a sign that it cares about your welfare. But if you strongly identify with an opposing party — and therefore are a potential target of vote-buying efforts — you interpret gifts as an attempt to manipulate your vote and deprive you of basic political rights.
This calculation is one reason why vote-buying attempts can backfire, as a vivid example from Mexico shows. In 2018, two vote brokers working for Mexico’s conservative National Action Party were accosted by local voters in Nuevo Laredo. Angry residents stripped the brokers down to their underwear and painted them with the party’s blue color from head to toe, decorating them with the words “Vote for the PAN for 500 pesos.”

The second reason vote buying often fails is that competitive elections make it difficult for party machines to identify the best voters to target. Strong opposition identifiers react negatively, but weakly opposed voters might trade their vote for a payday. The trouble is that even if local vote brokers can pinpoint these voters before the election, they’re also among the most susceptible to the influence of standard campaigning. That makes them moving targets: Their changing preferences mean that machines end up inadvertently paying voters who either don’t need gifts to vote for them or would need more to actually change their decision.
Finally, even when voters who are good targets get these benefits, they often look for an escape hatch to vote their sincere preferences anyway. The secret ballot provides one if they trust that it’s truly secret.
It turns out that people are acutely aware of who’s watching them vote. When they see poll watchers only from the party machine, they worry that their votes could be discovered by spies, cameras or by other means. But when they also see poll watchers from an opposing party, they believe that ballot secrecy is preserved and that they can vote sincerely without punishment.
Taken together, these reasons have led me to optimistically conclude that the effectiveness of vote buying depends not on the party machine’s prowess but on the strength of the parties that oppose it.
 
Bringing it home
Vote buying has a checkered recent history in elections around the world, but could the “Trump dividend” swing the midterms? I see that scenario as unlikely.
Partisanship, a core element that makes people resistant to vote buying, is very strong in the U.S. electorate. There’s no need to pay committed Republicans, while committed Democrats will see the offer as a bald monetization of politics that can deepen their antagonism.
The design of Trump’s offer also makes it likely to flounder. Promising to pay everyone gets around the targeting challenge, but it also creates what social scientists call a “free-rider problem.”
At issue is that people tend to behave in selfish ways. If they expect a certain outcome anyway, they’ll make a decision based on self-interest. For example, independents and less committed Democrats who could be swayed by a $5,000 check might think they can avoid feeling like a sellout if they vote sincerely but they will still get paid as long as others switch their vote to Republican.
In theory, there is one way Trump’s offer could succeed. Research shows that buying turnout, rather than trying to change vote choices, is routinely effective. But all the examples come from countries where party officials actively monitor who comes to the polls. Without that surveillance, which is illegal in the U.S., the free-rider problem could bedevil turnout as well.
But whether enacted or not, the promise of cash for votes has a big downside for democracy. It means that no one will know whether victorious Republican candidates won this November because Americans preferred their policies and gave them a mandate — or because they expected to get paid.

Kenneth Greene is a professor of government at the University of Texas at Austin. name: Maryland Matters
title: Judge orders Harford school board to put banned book back on library shelves
text:
A Harford County Circuit judge this week ordered the county school board to restore a graphic novel it had ordered removed from school system library shelves in the first test of the Freedom to Read Act, which targets school book bans. (Photo by Getty Images)Lawmakers and educators Friday hailed a Harford County Circuit Court judge’s ruling reversing the county school board’s decision to pull a graphic novel from school system library shelves, after a panel of teachers and students had voted to keep it.
The ruling by Circuit Judge Yolanda Curtin was the first legal test of the state’s Freedom to Read Act, a 2024 law that sought to prevent the removal of materials from school libraries because of their authors’ backgrounds or because of “partisan, ideological or religious disapproval.”
Curtin, who ruled from the bench Thursday after a hearing on the dispute, upheld a 2025 decision by the state Board of Education that said the local board was wrong to remove the young-adult graphic novel “Flamer” from school libraries.
Del. Dana Jones (D-Anne Arundel), the lead sponsor of the 2024 law, said Curtin’s ruling shows the law is “doing exactly what it was intended to do: protecting our libraries, librarians, and the fundamental freedom to read.”
“When we passed this landmark law, we made a commitment that books would not be removed from our libraries simply because of partisan, ideological, or religious objections,” Jones said in a statement released by the House speaker’s office. “Parents have every right to make decisions about what their own children read, but no single individual or school board should be able to make that decision for every family.”
Somerset County schools book policy faces new State Board challenge

A request for comment from the Harford Board of Education was not immediately returned Friday.
The case involved the county school board’s attempt to remove “Flamer,” Mike Curato’s semi-autobiographical novel about a boy at camp the summer before he enters high school, struggling with his sexuality and his religion, bullying by other boys at camp and thoughts of suicide.
The book was the subject of a complaint from a parent in November 2024 who said that, while she had not read the book in its entirety, she was concerned that the parts she had reviewed did not “meet the values of the community … and plants seeds in the heads of children that not only are trying to find themselves but could also be experiencing mental health challenges.”
The parent worried that the book “does not reveal local resources that may be out there for those struggling
with their identity,” according to state school board documents in the case.
Under the Freedom to Read Act, the county had created a process for reviewing requests for “reconsideration” of library materials. It called for the creation of a nine-member Reconsideration Subcommittee made up of a community member, two parents, two eighth- to 12th grade students, a teacher, an administrator, a librarian and a curriculum specialist.
Committee members are charged with reading the entire work in question and required to “read copies of professionally prepared reviews and list of awards, and review the HCPS Evaluation Procedure before voting whether to retain, move the material to a different level, or remove the material altogether,” according to the state board. That recommendation is sent to the county superintendent, who makes the call.
The committee met in March 2025 and considered the book, which includes “scenes with partial nudity, use of profanity, exploration of sexual identity and homosexuality, instances of bullying, suicidal ideation, and masturbation.” Committee members found those scenes were not excessive and were “contextually appropriate,” and found the overall literary and artistic merits of the book would appeal to students.
The sub-committee ultimately voted to keep “Flamer” in high school libraries, including in schools with middle and high school grades combined. The superintendent accepted the recommendation on May 15, 2025, telling the complaining parent that the book had “literary and artistic merit, educational and community value, and professional recognition” and that, read in its entirety, it had value to the community.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The parent appealed to the Harford County Board of Education.
The board met in private and announced on July 1, 2025, that it had voted 5-3, with one abstention, to reverse the subcommittee and the superintendent and order “Flamer” removed from school libraries. It said school administrators failed to consider the age-appropriateness of the book as well as its “extensive profanity, sexual situations and demeaning observations of females.” The local board said it based its decision “on the pervasive vulgarity and the novels’ absence of educational suitability.”
That decision sparked an appeal to the state board of education by a group of parents, a local advocacy group and the Harford County Education Association. The state board reversed the local board, saying it failed to show that the superintendent’s and the subcommittee’s decisions were improper or did not follow the review procedure required.
“Where the Reconsideration Sub-committee received training and took detailed notes on a book that all members were required to read in full, there is nothing in the record that indicates the local board members even read the book beyond some choice passages, which were not identified,” the state board said in its Nov. 4, 2025, opinion. “Nor did the local board provide any evidence of how the Reconsideration Sub-committee’s review was inconsistent with the Evaluation Procedure.”
The state board’s opinion, in turn, sparked a legal challenge by the local board, which lost Thursday in Curtin’s court.
Sonia Kumar, the senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union of Maryland, called Curtin’s ruling “a victory for the freedom to read.” ACLU of Maryland argued the case.
“This historic decision affirms the promise of Maryland’s Freedom to Read Act and the First Amendment: students deserve access to books that reflect the richness of our experiences, identities, and perspectives, free from censorship,” Kumar said in a statement released Friday by the ACLU of Maryland.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Judge dismisses DOJ lawsuit against Utah lieutenant governor demanding private voter information
text:
Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson speaks during a press conference at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on the final night of the legislative session, Friday, March 6, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A federal judge has dismissed a lawsuit filed by the Trump administration against Utah’s top election official, Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, that sought Utah voters’ sensitive private information. 
Henderson announced the ruling on social media, writing “0-27” with a heart emoji, referring to the number of times the U.S. Department of Justice has lost similar lawsuits.  
Trump’s Department of Justice sues Utah to force it to hand over sensitive voter information

U.S. District Court Judge David Barlow issued the order Friday, determining Henderson does not need to make voters’ private information available for the Department of Justice. 
“We appreciate Judge Barlow’s ruling dismissing the Department of Justice’s lawsuit that sought to force us to disclose the private data of every Utah voter,” Henderson said in a prepared statement. “Our office will continue to uphold the rule of law and safeguard the fundamental right to free, fair, and secure elections for the people of Utah.”
Since the lawsuit against her was filed in February, Henderson has argued that neither state nor federal law entitles the Department of Justice to private voter information. 
Henderson has repeatedly pledged to protect the sensitive information, which includes voters’ full names, dates of birth, residential addresses, state driver’s license numbers and Social Security numbers.
