name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Reconstruction of affordable housing complex in Stamford enters 2nd phase
text:
The affordable housing complex Oak Park, in Stamford, was never meant to be permanent housing.
Constructed in the 1940s, Oak Park was intended for veterans returning from World War II to live with their families. Eighty years later, the complex is in the middle of a full reconstruction.
The original complex consisted of 166 townhomes spread among 27 buildings on Ursula Place. Once completed, the new complex will have a total of 161 units, the majority of which will be townhomes, with a handful of apartments in one multifamily building.
Oak Park is fully affordable, according to Connecticut Department of Housing (DOH) Deputy Commissioner Julian Pierce.
“This redevelopment involved replacing outdated buildings with modern, energy-efficient townhomes and multifamily buildings that will serve residents at or below 60% of the area median income,” Pierce said.
Families can earn between 25% and 60% of the Area Median Income (AMI). In Stamford, that amounts to an annual income of no more than about $82,300 for a family of two, according to the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).
“Thank you to the residents of this community whose voices and needs continue to guide this work,” Pierce said. “Today is ultimately about them, about ensuring that every family has the foundation they need to thrive.”
The first phase of the redevelopment, completed in February, consists of 61 units, 35 of which are townhomes, according to Karen Coquillon, with Stamford’s housing authority, Charter Oak Communities.
The second phase, which began in August, is still in the demolition process, removing the existing townhomes. Forty-three units will be constructed in their places.
Phase two is expected to be completed late next year, with the third and final phase beginning shortly after, in early 2028.
In all, the project will cost an estimated $120 million, with funds coming from a range of sources, including Stamford’s Affordable Housing Trust Fund, HUD and DOH.
Charter Oak Communities Advisory Board member Bianca Shinn-Desras grew up in Oak Park and said while she enjoyed her childhood, the apartments were often lacking, with mold, mice and shoddy heating. Now, she works in public health.
“Where we live profoundly influences how we live,” Shinn-Desras said. “Housing is a fundamental social determinant of health. These conditions, the conditions of our homes, our neighborhood, safety, access to green spaces, educational opportunities are all interconnected, and have the ability to determine the trajectory of a generation.”
This story was first published Oct. 22, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: California
title: What will Becerra and Hilton do on climate?
text:
Gubernatorial candidates Xavier Becerra (left) and Steve Hilton. Photos by Fred Greaves and Rahul Lal for CalMatters




California’s carbon market was supposed to help the state cut pollution and reach its ambitious zero-emissions climate goals. But 20 years after its creation, some environmental advocates argue recent changes to the program will greatly diminish its effectiveness, and the fallout could land at the feet of the next governor. 
As Emma Foehringer Merchant explains for CalMatters, the landmark program aims to lower greenhouse gas emissions by enabling companies to buy and sell carbon pollution allowances at a marketplace managed by the state. It also provides billions of dollars in funding for climate projects.
But amid pressure from Gov. Gavin Newsom’s administration to keep oil refineries in California, state regulators in May approved changes to the program, providing major companies with as much as $4 billion in new free emission permits. The changes also halved annual auction revenue, generating about $2 billion less in funding for environmental programs.
Critics said the move was a giveaway to Big Oil, and that it would put California even more out of reach of hitting carbon neutrality by 2045. The candidates running to replace Newsom also have environmentalists doubting whether the state will continue to lead on climate.
Neither Democrat Xavier Becerra nor Republican Steve Hilton centered climate in their campaigns. In their one debate last month, both steered a question about climate change’s impacts toward affordability concerns, offering little detail on the climate policies they favor. 
The Becerra campaign also did not respond to CalMatters’ multiple requests for comment. Meanwhile, Hilton called the cap-and-trade program “a disaster” and told CalMatters he would move to suspend the carbon market — something a governor does not have the power to do alone.
The uncertainty is leading experts to warn that California has little time left to act on climate change before its consequences come for us all.

Danny Cullenward, an economist who focuses on energy policy: “There’s not many more governors left we can kick the can to before that bill comes due.”

CA counties leader under investigation


The state Capitol in Sacramento on April 29, 2024. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




From CalMatters’ Kate Wolffe and Jeanne Kuang:
The CEO of California’s State Association of Counties, Graham Knaus, has been placed on administrative leave while attorneys investigate “various confidential personnel-related issues,” the nonprofit’s president Susan Ellenberg wrote in a letter obtained by CalMatters. 
The association is a well-known presence in Sacramento, where it lobbies on behalf of the state’s 58 county governments. 
It’s unclear when CSAC placed Knaus on leave but one board member reached for comment said he got the letter last week. Ellenberg, a Santa Clara County supervisor, confirmed the investigation but declined to comment further. 
Knaus has been a vocal advocate for counties, occasionally calling out Newsom directly for not providing them enough financial support on state mandates. He declined to comment Thursday afternoon.
Knaus was paid more than $468,000 in the 2024 fiscal year, according to the organization’s latest available tax filing. He has worked at the association since 2015 and became chief executive in 2018.



Saving for a rainy day? ☔


Newsom unveiling his revised 2025-26 budget proposal at the Capitol Annex Swing Space in Sacramento on May 14, 2025. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




When the economy is booming, should California stow away more money for lean times? 
That’s the crux of Proposition 2, which would boost the cap on how much of the state’s general fund tax revenue lawmakers are allowed to save — raising it from the current 10% to 20%, writes CalMatters’ Yue Stella Yu.
Prop. 2 proponents say it’s a commonsense solution, one that has been long recommended by the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. Newsom, Democratic lawmakers and a bipartisan coalition of groups including labor unions and chambers of commerce, support it.
But GOP lawmakers and critics argue that expanding the pot of savings would incentivize future governors and lawmakers to dip into the reserves rather than cut spending. Instead, they want excess money to go back to taxpayers.

California congressional candidate Mai Vang (right) meets with canvass volunteers from SEIU in South Sacramento on Oct. 17, 2026. Photo by José Luis Villegas for CalMatters

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Advocates rally, seek records on ICE access at Tweed Airport
text:
Immigrant rights advocates rallied outside Tweed New Haven Airport Wednesday afternoon and filed a public records request demanding proof that federal immigration agents with access to the airport have been properly vetted, trained, and tracked.
The New Haven Immigrants Coalition organized the press conference at the corner of Fort Hale Road and Burr Street, then brought its demands inside to the monthly meeting of the Tweed New Haven Airport Authority board.
“Sacred principles cannot end where the airport property lines begin,” said Rev. Scott Marks of New Haven Rising. “No agency is above the rule of law, and no agent walks through these doors without accountability.”
The coalition says Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has detained four people at Tweed in the past two months, including two students. At least two arrests there have been publicly confirmed, including that of Deng Deng, a 19-year-old Southern Connecticut State University basketball player arrested on Sept. 4. A federal judge later ordered Deng’s release.
Kiana Cintron of the New Haven Immigrants Coalition, who co-hosted the event, said the detentions have shaken the community.
“We’re talking about real people, real neighbors, real families, real students, real coworkers, our friends,” she said, “and they deserve to feel safe in the communities they call home.” 
Cintron also read a statement from Kica Matos, president of the National Immigration Law Center.
“The airport authority says it has no visibility into or influence over what ICE does here. We strongly disagree,” Matos wrote. “Tweed Airport is not a hunting ground.” 
Through Yale Law School’s Worker and Immigrant Rights Advocacy Clinic, the coalition filed a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request with the airport authority Wednesday morning. 
The request seeks records showing that ICE agents with airport access have undergone criminal background checks, meet federal identification standards, and have been trained on federal rules — as well as records of all ICE arrests at Tweed since 2025, maps of the areas ICE can access, and the names of agents with airport credentials.
“If Tweed New Haven Airport Authority has nothing to hide, it should disclose the records NHIC has requested,” said Trinh Truong, a law student intern with the clinic.
The coalition is also asking the authority to train staff on a new state law, Public Act 26-14, which took effect Oct. 1. Advocates and Mayor Justin Elicker argue that the law bars ICE from making civil immigration arrests at Tweed without a judicial warrant, since the airport sits on city-owned land.
Under state law, the authority has four business days — until Tuesday — to provide the records or deny the request, according to the clinic. If it doesn’t, the coalition could appeal to the state Freedom of Information Commission.
Wednesday’s rally followed a September letter from Elicker to the authority’s board chair, Robert Reed, asking the airport to stop giving ICE agents “preferential parking” and to “not exceed any federal requirements by extending additional assistance to ICE.” Reed responded on Sept. 18, promising a thorough analysis of federal regulations.
At Wednesday’s board meeting, Reed said the authority’s next steps “are being actively pursued,” but declined to offer specifics.
“I cannot get into detail because of legal reasons, but I can tell you that all parties are actively, aggressively, thoughtfully looking at the request from the mayor,” Reed said, as well as the policies that “come from the FAA and law enforcement officers’ partners.”
Avports, the private company that runs Tweed day to day, has said that federal rules require airports to grant unescorted access to federal law enforcement officers, and that Tweed “has no visibility into or influence over enforcement activity.”
Speaking during public comment at Wednesday’s board meeting, Truong argued that federal rules only require such access for officers who have passed criminal records checks, so the authority is not obligated to admit agents who haven’t. 
She also said the community “has seen photos of ICE agents wearing Tweed-issued access badges and using special parking privileges.”
Rose Murphy, a teacher at Hill Regional Career High School, told the board that about a year ago she brought a group of students to Tweed on a career field trip. They left talking about becoming pilots, she said.
Last month, Murphy said, she was at the airport when an ICE agent “shoved past” her at the arrivals doors as a 19-year-old student was detained. She said the agent looked at her and said, “Ha ha, too late.”
Murphy asked board members whether she could still, in good conscience, bring students to the airport on a field trip.
“Could I do that in good faith?” she asked. “No.”
Leslie Blatteau, president of the New Haven Federation of Teachers, said public schools are open to all children regardless of immigration status.
“The same should go for Tweed,” she said.
Anne Watkins of the New Haven Immigrants Coalition urged board members to use the authority they have.
“Don’t underestimate your power,” she said.
Paul North, a Yale professor of German and philosophy who formerly led Jonathan Edwards College, told the board that families are left traumatized when a student “who is here on good faith, who’s been doing everything they should do, who has no criminal record” is “ripped out of the airport.”
Speaking as a scholar of German history and the Nazi era, North urged board members to act. 
“It is bodies like these who can use every bit of their moral fiber and every bit of the law to put in obstacles in the way of what can only be described as ethnic cleansing,” he said.
This story was first published Oct. 22, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: ‘Not only convenient, but necessary’: Voices of mail-in voters
authors: Meghan O'Brien, Makenzie Huber, Seth Tupper
text:
Election workers use a machine to process absentee ballot envelopes for Minnehaha County, South Dakota, on Nov. 5, 2024, in the county administration building. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Byron Sutter has been voting by mail for years, ever since he worked in healthcare and couldn’t leave his patients to vote in person.
Mary Ann Klarenbeek votes by mail because she has breathing problems and can’t stand in line at a polling place.
John Jeratowski travels for work as a journeyman electrician and would have to surrender pay to go home and cast his ballot if he couldn’t vote by mail.
Trump drops longtime aversion to mail-in voting with GOP trailing in polls

Dorian Miller has been spending more time with grandkids in Texas than she expected, leaving mail-in voting as her only option to cast a ballot in South Dakota when she’s 1,100 miles from home.
They’re some of about 5,700 people who have voted by mail so far in the runup to South Dakota’s Nov. 3 general election. Mail-in voters account for 13% of advance ballots cast in the state at this point, with the rest coming through in-person voting, authorized messengers, or special accommodations for overseas and military voters.
President Donald Trump has alleged “mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt,” despite voting by mail himself. He tried to impose new regulations on mail-in voting, but the U.S. Supreme Court blocked him last month.
South Dakota Searchlight recently purchased a list of advance voters from the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office and used it to locate and interview those who cast ballots by mail, including some who agreed to have their voices recorded and posted on Searchlight’s website. Searchlight asked why they vote by mail, why it’s important to them, and what it would mean if mailing their ballots were no longer an option.
Physical limitations, but a sharp mind for voting

https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Eva-Rawerts-vignette.wav
 Eva Rawerts in her own words.

Eva Rawerts, age 90, voted by mail from a nursing home in Aberdeen.
The registered Republican can’t make it to the voting booth, but said she wants to support the candidates of her choice. Rawerts said she’d be “very despondent” if she were no longer able to vote by mail.
“My mind is very sharp,” Rawerts said, “and I want to vote, and I care what happens to our country.”
Voting by mail for 28 years: ‘It is safe and secure’
When Jeff Odell lived in California, he stood in line for two hours to cast a ballot, he said. He’s been voting by mail ever since.
Odell moved to Lemmon, South Dakota, in 2021. The 58-year-old who’s registered as an independent works in technology sales and isn’t always able to make it to the polls on Election Day.
“I’ve been voting by mail since I was 30, and it’s so much more convenient,” Odell said. “Regardless of what the president rambles about, it is safe and secure. In South Dakota, you have to provide so much documentation to even register to vote.”
If voting by mail was restricted to some degree, Odell said, “it would be a shame.”
“I could see it happen for pure political reasons, but I think it’d be a bad move overall,” Odell said. “South Dakota has enough rules and regulations around what it takes to mail-in vote. I think there’s plenty of safety in there.”
More time to digest a long ballot

https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Alexander-Campbell-Vignette.wav
 Alexander Campbell in his own words.

Alexander Campbell is 21 years old and said he’s only ever voted by mail. Originally from Virginia, the registered Democrat moved to South Dakota this year to live and teach in Mission.
“Voting by mail is important to me because it allows you to sit at home and digest the long ballot,” Campbell said. “It also allows you to make sure that your vote is in early, so that way you don’t have to deal with an emergency on Election Day.”
But South Dakota has many barriers that can make it difficult to vote in rural and tribal areas of the state, Campbell said. South Dakota does not have online voter registration, for example, like Virginia does.
“I was pretty shocked at the level of difficulty,” Campbell said.
In healthcare, ‘you can’t just walk away from your job’ to vote

https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/byron-sutter-vignette.wav
 Byron Sutter in his own words.

Byron Sutter of Rapid City said he started voting by mail about two decades ago when he and his wife worked at a Rapid City hospital and struggled to step away to vote on Election Day. Sutter said he worked mostly in intensive care units caring for ventilator patients.
“We were in direct patient care. You can’t just walk away from your job, and oftentimes we were short-staffed,” Sutter said. “I know employers are supposed to allow employees to go vote, but the reality of it is that it just does not work out sometimes, especially in acute healthcare.”
Sutter has continued to use mail voting at 81 years old, rather than going to a polling place.
“A lot of times, we’d be standing in line for a relatively long period of time,” Sutter said, adding that while filling out his ballot at home, he doesn’t “feel pressured to hurry up” so someone else can vote behind him at a polling place.
In recent years, though, after receiving his ballot by mail, Sutter has chosen to drop his completed ballot off at his county auditor’s office rather than rely on the Postal Service to return it.
“I feel like it’s a little more secure — a little less chance of somehow the ballot being misplaced or whatever,” Sutter said.
1,100 miles from a polling place

https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/dorian-miller-vignette.wav
 Dorian Miller in her own words.

On Election Day, said Dorian Miller, she will be 1,100 miles from her South Dakota polling place.
The 78-year-old registered Democrat was born and raised in Marion, but said she spends a lot of time in Texas to be close to her children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
She said traveling back to South Dakota to vote, especially in the winter, would be difficult, so she votes by mail.
“I started out as a winter Texan and had no intention of being here this much, but as time went by, things happened,” Miller said. “I’m a resident of South Dakota, and I have a lot of family there.”
Voting by mail saves journeyman electrician from missing pay

https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/john-jeratowski-vignette.wav
 John Jeratowski in his own words.

John Jeratowski never knows where he’ll be on Election Day. The 44-year-old Republican from Egan works as a journeyman electrician, often working away from home.
He votes by mail because he isn’t typically home for in-person advance voting on weekdays when the county auditor’s office is open.
“It’s not only convenient, but necessary for me,” he said.
If he wasn’t able to vote by mail, he said, he’d have to take unpaid time off work.
“I would end up having to lose a good amount of money just to come back on Election Day to vote in person,” he said.
Disabilities keep couple from the polls

https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Mary-Klarenbeek.wav
 Mary Ann Klarenbeek in her own words.

Mary Ann Klarenbeek and her husband can’t stand in line to vote at the polls, she said. The 84-year-old registered Republican lives in Harrisburg.
“We’ve got breathing problems, and our legs don’t move like they used to,” Klarenbeek said. “And my husband has heart problems, so that’s why it’s important for us to vote by mail.”
If the two lost the ability to vote by mail, she would “feel really bad.”
“I feel it’s important for everybody to vote, and I feel if you don’t vote, you don’t have any say in anything,” Klarenbeek said.
Snowbirds get ballots before heading south

https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/jess-hall-vignette-FINAL.wav
 Jess Hall in his own words.

Jess Hall won’t be in South Dakota on Election Day. He’ll be at his second home in south Georgia, escaping the northern Great Plains weather.
The 63-year-old Republican is a resident of Winner. He and his wife request mailed absentee ballots before they head south for the winter.
Hall served 20 years in the military and 20 years as a government contractor, so it’s important to him to “take care of our country and make sure it’s going in the right direction that I would like to see happen,” he said. Hall drops his ballot off at the auditor’s office before leaving town, but his wife mails hers.
Hall added that even though he and his wife participate in the mail voting system, he thinks it is “susceptible to fraud.”
“I mean mine’s, you know, legit, but I mean, some of those people, yeah, they’re not,” Hall said. “They’re not legit. So that’s the only part that I don’t like.”
Disabled veteran relies on mail-in voting

https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/greg-adams-vignette.wav
 Greg Adams in his own words.

Greg Adams said he has voted by mail for as long as he can remember — since he served in the military during the Vietnam War, through decades of work travel, and into retirement as a disability has made leaving the house difficult.
The 80-year-old non-politically affiliated voter from Sioux Falls said if he couldn’t vote by mail, he’d figure out how to vote “somehow.” He was not aware that South Dakota allows authorized messengers to deliver ballots for voters if they can’t make it to the polling place.
While he’s heard reports about election “hanky panky” across the country, he said, South Dakota “has safeguards” to ensure elections are secure and that only U.S. citizens can vote.
“I hope that people that have valid reasons for voting absentee get to continue voting absentee,” Adams said. “In South Dakota, it seems safe and like everything is on the up and up, and it’s easy for me to do.”
Would need a ‘carrier pigeon’ without mail-in voting in rural area

https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Nicholas-Janis-vignette.wav
 Nick Janis in his own words.

Nick Janis is 69 years old, is a registered Republican and lives north of Kyle, which is on the Pine Ridge Reservation. He’s disabled, he said, doesn’t have a driver’s license and doesn’t have a ride to the polls on Election Day.
“I don’t know how I could get to the polls to vote, because I live in the country. I’ve got to drive on a dirt road for 7 miles, or 5 miles of gravel before I even see pavement,” said Janis, a member of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
He added that November weather in south-central South Dakota can be unpredictable. He’ll sometimes be snowed in for weeks at a time or lose electricity.
Janis joked that he’d need a “carrier pigeon” if mail-in voting wasn’t an option. He did not know some voters can use authorized messengers if they’re unable to vote in person, but he said it wouldn’t be realistic for him.
“Nobody would know where to find me out here,” he said. “They’d get lost.”
He dismissed concerns about mail-in voting fraud as “dumb,” citing South Dakota’s safeguards.
“You have to be a citizen, you have to be that to get signed up to vote by mail,” Janis said. “You have to show your picture ID and describe where you live and all that just to vote by mail.”
Trucker says voting by mail is convenient for work schedule

https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ted-otten-vignette.wav
 Ted Otten in his own words.

Ted Otten, 64, is a Democrat. He lives in Aberdeen, but is often on the road as a long-haul truck driver. Otten has been voting by mail for decades, he said, because it gives him time to review what’s on the ballot.
“If I lost the ability to mail in my vote, first of all, then there’s something wrong with our system, and there would be a type of suppression going on,” he said. “I would be, also, very restricted in my time to vote, though I will still vote.”
Disability limits travel to polls: ‘What other alternative do many of us have?’

https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/jacki-omland-vignette.wav
 Jacki Omland in her own words.

Jacki Omland, a 70-year-old Democrat, had a fall in 2022 that left her unable to leave her home in Aberdeen.
She’s been voting by mail since then, with help from her husband, who makes sure her ballot gets returned.
“Some of us have to do it,” Omland said. “I mean, what other alternative do many of us have?”
If she lost the ability to vote by mail, Omland said, “it would be devastating.”
“For other things for handicapped people, they make arrangements for us,” Omland said. “One of the primary things we have in our life is voting. And so why take that away from me just because I’m handicapped?”
Former election worker receives ballot by mail

https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Shaun-Feilmeier-vignette.wav
 Shaun Feilmeier in his own words.

Shaun Feilmeier, 42, is registered as an independent and lives in Sioux Falls. He used to serve as a deputy auditor in Lincoln County, a job that included helping to run elections. Because he was always busy on Election Day, the job “necessitated” voting early.
His time in the office was stressful because it overlapped with “the election-denying craze,” Feilmeier said, referring to people who agitated for election policy changes in the wake of President Trump’s false claim that he won the 2020 presidential election.
“I was literally followed home and threatened by some of these election deniers,” Feilmeier said. “That’s what really started a lot of this stress, was the insanity of that time, and I don’t really see it going away. It’s just changing its face.”
Feilmeier receives his ballot by mail but returns it to the county auditor’s office himself to make sure it gets counted.
He said all forms of mail-in voting are secure, though, and “should be encouraged.”
“A lot of people that couldn’t or wouldn’t otherwise get to the polls can vote or will vote, and we need more people to vote,” he said. “Making it easier and more convenient to vote is a good thing, especially since we know how to do it in a secure way.”
Retiree says winter travel shouldn’t restrict his vote
Wayne Halma travels from Sioux Falls to Arizona to escape the Midwest winters. But the 78-year-old Republican still votes in South Dakota elections by mail. Without that opportunity, he said, “then my voice is not heard.”
“My home base is South Dakota, so I would expect to vote as a South Dakotan,” Halma said.
It’s “hard to believe” accusations that mailed-in votes in South Dakota could be fraudulent, he said, because of state laws that require a photocopied ID or notary seal for mail-in voting.
“The safeguards they have in place, just the type of people that we are here, I don’t see a push for any of that type of election fraud,” Halma said. “I think South Dakota in general is above board on everything as far as voting.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: Michigan must meet this moment to pass critical innocence reform legislation
authors: Olivia Viglietti, Jessa Webber, Eric Anderson
text:
Getty ImagesWhen Michigan passed the Wrongful Imprisonment Compensation Act (WICA) in 2016, the intent was clear: provide support to those who have lost years, even decades, of their lives to wrongful convictions. Over a decade later, experience has revealed the many flaws in the statute. As a result, decisions made a decade ago continue to prevent exonerees from receiving the compensation they deserve.
Alongside WICA reform, Michigan has the opportunity to improve upon another critical tool for the wrongfully convicted by passing legislation this session to expand access to post-conviction DNA testing.
Senate Bill 909, introduced by state Sen. Stephanie Chang (D-Detroit), and cosponsored by senators from both parties, aims to fix the current flaws in WICA, making it more accessible to those the state has wronged. One significant obstacle standing between innocent Michiganders and the money they are owed is the statute’s current standard of proof.
To receive compensation, exonerees must demonstrate their innocence by “clear and convincing evidence” – a standard more demanding than the default standard of proof in most civil claims.
In addition, exonerees face unequal bargaining power throughout the WICA process. Because exonerees frequently walk out of prison with absolutely nothing, obtaining safe housing, employment, and healthcare after years behind bars is an extremely difficult task. These significant hardships often pressure exonerees to take a reduced WICA settlement in order to get at least some funds to afford basic needs.
The amendments proposed in SB909 would change the standard of proof to “a preponderance of evidence,” which is the same threshold used for most civil cases. Far from a radical change, this would simply bring WICA in alignment with the majority of Michigan’s civil legal system. Additionally, SB909 critically clarifies what new evidence of innocence is sufficient for relief – a point of confusion that has posed a barrier to relief for a number of exonerees. Administrative technicalities should not stand between innocent Michiganders and compensation.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Compensation reform is not enough – wrongfully convicted individuals must have access to forensic science to prove their innocence. Michigan has an opportunity to do this by passing Senate Bill 1035 sponsored by state Sen. Jeff Irwin (D-Ann Arbor), and House Bill 6092, introduced by state Rep. Kara Hope (D-Holt), which expands access to post-conviction DNA testing.
The amendment removes antiquated technological restrictions and updates the standard of review, making post-conviction review easier.
Last session, similar legislation received strong bipartisan support in committee before ultimately running out of time before session adjourned. The legislation introduced this session again has broad support and will improve processes for individuals, including those who pleaded guilty, petitioning for DNA testing to prove their innocence.
It would also remove outdated restrictions, and change the standard of proof warranting relief from “clear and convincing” to “a reasonable probability of a different outcome” – bringing this statute in line with the standard for winning all other post-conviction claims.
 SB909 along with SB1035 and HB6092 are opportunities for Michigan to improve access to critical support for those wrongfully convicted. Wrongful conviction is one of the worst misfortunes that can befall someone. No amount of money could ever make up for the loss of their freedom.
The financial redress that WICA provides is the bare minimum, and exonerees should not have to worry that they may not even receive it. Similarly, those still in prison who may be exonerated by DNA evidence should not face unjust barriers to accessing the critical forensic testing needed to prove their innocence.
Michigan already demonstrated a commitment to the wrongfully convicted when they passed these statutes, and can now honor that commitment by improving access to the relief they provide.

name: California
title: Californians’ support for cutting carbon emissions wanes as new climate warnings arrive
text:
Earlier this month, Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger staged a low-key celebration marking the 20th anniversary of Assembly Bill 32, the landmark legislation committing California to immense reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.
It was the most notable achievement of Schwarzenegger’s governorship, not only setting a series of deadlines for emissions reductions, but creating as one of its major tools a system for industry buy-in known as “cap-and-trade.”
Environmental groups were opposed, favoring direct regulations, but Schwarzenegger insisted. Since then, the state has auctioned off a gradually diminishing number of emissions permits, thus, in theory, incentivizing industries to reduce greenhouse gases.
The Los Angeles Times has calculated that early goals were met. But in recent years reductions have slowed, and the 2030 goal of being 40% lower than 1990 emissions levels is highly unlikely.
Popular and political support for the state’s commitment to reach virtual zero emissions by 2045 also has been waning.
Public Policy Institute of California pollsters found that while Californians still support emissions reductions in concept, views on specific programs have slipped. That’s particularly true of Newsom’s desire to ban the sale of new gasoline-powered vehicles by 2035. Support for that has dropped from 49% in 2021 to just 32%.
“Affordability has become a dominant theme in public discourse today — and it’s affecting the public’s views on the environment,” the PPIC says. “Most Californians choose cost of living as the top issue facing the people of California today; few name environmental concerns.”
The declining popularity of climate change programs is visible in the political arena.
Newsom spent months portraying gasoline refiners as price gougers and polluters, but when two refineries announced plans to shut down in 2025, raising the possibility of fuel shortages, he quickly changed his tune.
“We are all the beneficiaries of oil and gas. No one’s naive about that,” Newsom said at a press conference. “So it’s always been about finding a just transition, a pragmatism in terms of that process.”

Defying environmental groups, he and the Legislature passed bills designed to increase oil production, and this year the state even redesigned the cap-and-trade program to provide no-cost emissions permits to refineries.
The flip side of declining popular and political support for emissions reduction policies is a new warning from Newsom’s administration that California faces a slow-motion apocalypse.
“Climate change is increasing the frequency, intensity, duration, and impacts of climate related events in California, including short- or long-term hazard events like wildfire, extreme heat, drought, flooding, and sea level rise,” the administration’s 109-page Fifth Climate Change Assessment declares.

It is the latest in a series of such reports issued since AB 32 passed. Newsom endorsed its findings while, as might be expected from a likely presidential candidate, taking a shot at President Donald Trump.
 “As the Trump administration turns its back on science, California is doubling down on climate action, on protecting our communities, and on building a safer future,” Newsom said in a statement.
Meanwhile, the climate assessment report’s warning of potentially catastrophic effects is re-energizing those who prescribe aggressive actions.
UC Berkeley’s Center for Law, Energy and the Environment issued what it describes as a “roadmap” of steps that must be taken.
“California is at a critical moment in its efforts to protect residents from the extreme weather caused by climate change,” Louise Bedsworth, the center’s exective director, said. “The next governor will need to demonstrate strong leadership to help the state navigate the intersecting challenges of worsening climate impacts, affordability, and federal hostility to the state’s goals.”
Xavier Becerra, the former attorney general almost certain to succeed Newsom, has been noncommittal about the issue, especially about the 2035 halt on sales of gas-powered vehicles. It’s smart politics given the reversal of popular support.

name: California
title: California’s carbon market changed this year, and the next governor will inherit the fallout
text:
In summary
Steve Hilton would suspend California’s carbon market. Xavier Becerra’s campaign hasn’t said what it would do.




In September, Gov. Gavin Newsom unveiled what is likely one of the last large climate announcements of his tenure: California will move forward with linking its decade-old carbon market with a newly formed market in Washington state, aiming to merge it with the market California already shares with Quebec. 
Newsom said California was “choosing certainty, partnership, and clean energy” amid a stream of federal climate policy rollbacks. 
But the announcement didn’t distract environmental advocates from the sting of a challenging year back home for the so-called “cap-and-invest” program. As Newsom leaves his post, many policy and climate experts say the adjustments to the program put California’s climate goals further out of reach. The program provides billions of dollars in funding for climate and other programs.
Yet with little talk of climate policy in the governor’s race, Californians are largely left guessing about how Steve Hilton or Xavier Becerra would handle the program or California’s broader climate ambitions. The Becerra campaign did not respond to multiple emailed requests for comment. Hilton told CalMatters he would move to suspend the carbon market — which he called “a disaster of a program” — entirely.
Twenty years ago, lawmakers made California the first state to mandate broad cuts in greenhouse gas emissions with AB 32, the landmark carbon emissions reduction law, which authorized the subsequent creation of a market. The law requires the program to be as cost-effective as possible while maximizing benefits to the state’s economy. 
Whoever wins in November can appoint a handful of new members to the California Air Resources Board, which has to finish writing the linkage rules and will propose the budget that leans on carbon market revenue. The next governor will also help decide how aggressively California leads on climate, after a year of mixed signals about where the program is headed.
“It’s really set up the politics of these issues to get worse and not better over time, and that is the problem that is being tossed like a live grenade into the lap of the next governor,” said Danny Cullenward, an economist who sits on an advisory committee focused on the carbon market. 
A question of climate leadership
In May, a process to reauthorize the keystone climate program ended with a controversial agreement that the Legislative Analyst’s Office projects will roughly halve annual auction revenue, offering about $2 billion less in funding for priority environmental programs while opening a separate pool of free permits for polluters that pledge to invest in decarbonization, valued at as much as $4 billion. 
Oil companies fought the initial cap-and-invest reauthorization proposal, arguing it would encourage companies to leave the state or further increase fuel prices. The California Air Resources Board, which manages the program, said the increased allowances it eventually approved were meant to balance affordability and economic uncertainty alongside emissions targets. In an email, a board spokesperson said the new incentives would not have any impact on the market’s auction revenue. (The Western States Petroleum Association, which represents refiners in the state, declined an interview for this story.)
The concern comes as California prepares to elect its next governor and nears its own 2030 target to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 40% below 1990 levels, on its way to zeroing out emissions by 2045.
“This is not a question anymore of whether or not we’ll reach the target. This is a guarantee that we won’t,” said Katie Valenzuela, a consultant for Communities for a Better Environment who previously co-chaired an environmental justice committee that advised regulators on the state’s program. 
State officials have long framed cap-and-invest as a backstop, keeping the state on track for its climate targets by ratcheting down the emissions limit even if other programs fall short. Advocates worry the changes will have a chilling effect rather than signal the market’s long-term strength, just as California loses ground to federal rollbacks.
“It is going to become very difficult for us to say we are a climate leader when we are visibly missing our targets,” Cullenward said. 
Others remain more optimistic. Cap-and-invest is one tool in California’s toolbox, even if this year dulled it. Meredith Fowlie, an economist at the University of California, Berkeley, said the program is not optimal but has done the basics of its job: sending a price signal to drive down emissions while raising revenues for important programs. 
Linking with Washington’s market will strengthen California’s program overall, air board Chair Lauren Sanchez wrote to Newsom in September. In addition to creating a larger market with more credits available to industries in both states, the link is expected to raise carbon credit prices in California, where recent auctions have yielded prices at state minimums. A connected market could also lower prices in Washington, making the state’s more stringent program less lucrative. Low prices reduce the program’s revenues and starve polluting industries’ incentive to invest in lowering emissions. 
Regulators have not yet established a rulemaking timeline for the linkage process, a spokesperson for the board told CalMatters, but the board expects the joint market to begin operating next year. 
Chloe Ames, policy adviser at NextGen Policy, an organization founded by former gubernatorial candidate Tom Steyer, called linkage a strong step forward. The group is disappointed by the other changes made to cap-and-invest this year, she said, and will keep urging the legislature to adjust the industry incentives and California’s next governor to take climate seriously. 
“It’s been more challenging for us to say that we’re a climate leader, and that’s why we need to step up,” Ames said. “In this work, what are you going to do other than to be hopeful?” 
Kicking the can
Since the market began, revenue has funded a wide range of priorities, including job training, clean energy and affordable housing. Managing those investments, alongside costs to Californians and emissions cuts, has been a balancing act — one the next governor will inherit, Fowlie said. “Some of those objectives are potentially in tension,” she said. “A sole focus on designing the program to meet our greenhouse gas reductions misses this really important larger picture that this program is about more than that.”
The legislature approved the program’s reauthorization and the state’s air regulators lay out its rules, but a governor has influence over how that process plays out and can exert his own priorities, Cullenward said. 
Beyond the carbon market, governors have wider latitude: Newsom has used his executive authority on wildfires, water shortages and clean energy. 
In the governor’s race, neither candidate has centered climate in his campaign. In their one debate, both candidates steered a question about climate change’s impacts toward affordability concerns, offering little detail on the actual climate policies they favor. 
“I think it’s fair to say that climate probably isn’t the top priority of either one,” said Barry Vesser, the chief operating officer at the Climate Center, a California environmental group that opposed this year’s changes to the carbon market.  
Becerra’s campaign website emphasizes affordability in climate policy. He has faced criticism for defending Chevron and for accepting large oil and gas donations. As attorney general, though, he defended the state’s carbon program in court, arguing that “carbon pollution knows no borders” and promising that California would fight the first Trump administration’s rollbacks. 
Hilton has rallied against California’s Democratic establishment, and he told CalMatters he would aim to de-bloat the bureaucracy guiding the state’s climate policies. He likened the market’s recent programmatic changes  to “rearranging deck chairs on the Titanic.” Hilton, who considers himself an environmentalist, has argued for redirecting resources from current climate programs and wildfire mitigation toward management of the state’s natural lands. He also wants to rework renewable incentives to create “a level playing field” for technologies like rooftop solar, hydropower and geothermal energy. His strategy, he claims, will reduce economic burdens for Californians while exceeding the state’s climate targets.  
The relative lack of attention to climate policy is a missed opportunity, according to Valenzuela and Vesser. They see a chance for the next governor  to more directly and publicly connect climate programs to affordability, a key concern for likely voters and an issue on which Becerra and Hilton agree. 
Ultimately, the race’s rhetoric has advocates like Valenzuela “freaked out.” She points to a “huge chasm” between present reality and the policies that would put California on the right track. The state has little time left for the aggressive action its climate ambitions require, she and other advocates say, and it’s time to start dealing in reality. 
“There’s not many more governors left we can kick the can to before that bill comes due,” Cullenward said.

name: California
title: A ‘battle of the ages’ in a California House race: Matsui, 82, faces a 41-year-old challenger
text:
In summary
The race for Sacramento’s seat in Congress hinges on what kind of “experience” voters value most — seniority and familiarity with Capitol Hill, or first-hand knowledge of the struggles today’s workers face?


Rep. Doris Matsui and Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang are locked in an intergenerational “battle of the ages” in the 7th Congressional District. 
Matsui, 82, touts her experience securing federal funding for local projects and her ability to work across party lines, such as a 2022 law she co-authored to boost domestic semiconductor manufacturing, despite a largely gridlocked Congress. Her massive fundraising advantage has enabled her to flood the airwaves and voters’ mailboxes with millions of dollars in traditional television ads and mailers. 
Vang, 41, wants to prove that money and seniority aren’t enough anymore to win a seat in Congress. She has relied on door-to-door canvassing, in-person events and an active social media presence to introduce herself to voters. 
The race, a more intense iteration of their June primary contest, ends a nearly 50-year span without a competitive congressional race in the district. Matsui has held office since 2005 after succeeding her late husband, former Rep. Robert Matsui, who was first elected in 1979. 
At its heart is the question of which candidate’s “experience” in politics voters care about more — Matsui’s seniority and experience in the U.S. Capitol, or Vang’s lived experience of being a working-age person in the 21st century?
Democrats in the left wing of the party, who support policies championed by national figures like Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, are betting it’s the latter. 
They’re bullish on candidates like Vang, whose campaign signs appear to outnumber Matsui’s in Sacramento front yards, especially as voters sour on career politicians from both parties and lawmakers who they see as rubber stamps for party leadership or monied special interests. 
While races featuring two Democrats won’t change the math for which party controls the U.S. House, they will likely play a crucial role in deciding the future of the Democratic Party after a highly anticipated Election Day rout of Republicans. 
Vang said she speaks frequently with other young, progressive candidates around the country seeking to unseat longtime Democrats about how to support each other and they are making plans to stick together if they get to Congress.
California congressional candidate Mai Vang at a Youth Civic Engagement event at the Reason Center in Sacramento on Oct. 17, 2026. Vang is running to represent California’s 7th Congressional District. Photo by José Luis Villegas for CalMatters
“I always have said that this race is more than just about one congressional seat,” Vang said. “It is truly about the future of this country.”
A similar dynamic is unfolding in the 34th Congressional District in Los Angeles, where community organizer Angela Gonzales-Torres, 30, hopes to unseat Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez, 50. Gonzales-Torres is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. 
Unlike Matsui though, Gomez belongs to the Congressional Progressive Caucus and has vocally supported progressive policies such as the Green New Deal, Medicare for All and abolishing the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency.
Still, Gonzales-Torres has criticized Gomez for not being progressive enough, particularly for continuing to accept campaign contributions from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, which has systematically targeted progressives it views as too sympathetic to the Palestinian cause. AIPAC bankrolled successful efforts in 2024 to oust members of the left-leaning “Squad” for being too outspoken on the war in Gaza.
Political relationships
Matsui argues that her more than two decades of experience in Congress have allowed her to build the trust and lasting relationships with colleagues required to produce results.
“I really feel that it is important to have somebody there who understands how to get things done,” Matsui told CalMatters. “In a world like we have in Congress today, with the administration that we have today, we cannot afford to not have enough people there who understand that.”
She points to her role authoring a law to boost domestic production of semiconductor chips and strengthen workforce training programs to create a labor and talent pipeline. 
“Legislating is really about relationships,” Matsui said. “That might be in an elevator, just talking about your kids or the last football game.” 
Matsui has painted Vang as a young, naive newcomer to national politics who is “more focused on making political statements on social media than doing the hard work of getting things done,” according to one recent Matsui campaign mailer that also criticizes Vang for voting against city budgets and missing meetings on local boards. 
Vang points out that she is two years older than Bob Matsui was when he first ran for Congress. When Matsui won the special election to succeed her late husband, she had even less governing experience than Vang, a city council member for six years and a school board member for four years prior to that. 
U.S. Rep. Doris Matsui, a Democrat from Sacramento, speaks during a news conference in Sacramento on Oct. 29, 2024. Photo by Rich Pedroncelli, AP Photo
Vang contends that Matsui is offended by her decision to eschew the “unspoken rule” in Democratic Party politics that younger elected officials should pay their dues and wait in the wings until more senior members are ready to leave.
“I don’t have the luxury of waiting on the sidelines when our democracy is under attack. When I have family members who wake up every morning afraid that they’re going to be separated by ICE,” Vang said.
Matsui argues that her close relationships with Democratic Party leaders who will wield outsized power if Democrats win back control of the House gives her greater leverage to deliver more federal funding to Sacramento-area projects. She frequently highlights the more than $4 billion in flood prevention funding she has secured, including nearly $1 billion for improvements to Folsom Dam to prevent water from rising too quickly in Folsom Lake.
But much of Matsui’s flood prevention work has targeted levee projects in West Sacramento and Natomas, which are no longer part of the 7th Congressional District after voters approved Proposition 50 last year. The district now encompasses downtown and southeast Sacramento along with more conservative portions of El Dorado and San Joaquin counties.
Money and power take center stage
Vang has excoriated Matsui for accepting campaign contributions from companies that contract with ICE and the Department of Homeland Security, including Lockheed Martin, which has contributed $3,000 this election cycle, and AT&T, which has contributed $10,000, according to campaign filings. 
During a candidate forum earlier this year, Matsui declined to return those contributions, saying, “I’m not for sale at all.”
With a warchest built up over years without a competitive challenger, Matsui was able to spend more than $1.3 million between July 1 and Sept. 30, according to the latest financial filing, while Vang only spent about $192,000. 
“We always knew that we were never going to outspend the incumbent, but the only way to beat the money is to have the many,” Vang said, touting the more than 900 volunteers who have signed up to knock doors and make phone calls for her campaign in the final weeks.
She also criticized Matsui for lending her own campaign $1.4 million for the June primary and another $1.5 million for the general election.
Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang, a candidate for California’s 7th Congressional District, right, and U.S. Rep. Doris Matsui, center, attend a caucus meeting during the California Democratic Party convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jungho Kim for CalMatters
“I just never thought about myself as being someone who is characterized as this wealthy person. That’s not who I started out with, and not who I am now,” Matsui said.
She is married to billionaire philanthropist and Applied Energy Services co-founder Roger Sant, whom she married in April 2020.
The two candidates are also leaning heavily into their Asian and immigrant roots. Vang is the daughter of Hmong refugees and Matsui was born to Japanese Americans while they were incarcerated at an Arizona relocation camp during World War II.
One area they have clashed on is immigration enforcement. Vang supports completely abolishing ICE. Matsui has denounced ICE’s raids and hosted several news conferences outside detention facilities where she has been denied entry, but she has stopped short of calling for the agency’s dissolution. 
A similar debate is happening in the Los Angeles race, where ICE has become a key element of Gomez’s pitch. 
“When ICE blocked congressional oversight of detention centers, I personally sued them and won,” Gomez wrote in a statement shared with CalMatters by his campaign, which did not make him available for an interview. “When Trump started his ICE raids in LA, I went straight from the plane to Chinatown, demanded that federal agents leave, and de-escalated the situation.”
Gomez’s district is a heavily Democratic, urban tapestry of neighborhoods that cut across racial, ethnic, economic and educational attainment lines. It spans from Koreatown and Downtown Los Angeles, including Skid Row, through Little Tokyo and Chinatown into the heavily Latino Boyle Heights and East Los Angeles.
His success in suing ICE doesn’t make up for what his opponents view as an unforgivable act: accepting more than $2.6 million from AIPAC. 
That spending, some of which went directly to Gomez’s campaign and some through super PACs, helped Gomez fend off challenges from progressive Democrat David Kim in 2020, 2022 and 2024. 
“Too many of us are struggling while our current congressmember is in the pockets of those perpetuating and profiting off of our pain. And I just think it’s unacceptable,” Gonzales-Torres said following the June primary. 
Gonzalez-Torres’ campaign told CalMatters she was unavailable for an interview.
Connecting with young voters
Vang campaigned last week alongside Hogg, the co-founder of Leaders We Deserve, who rose to prominence as a co-founder of March for Our Lives after surviving the 2018 shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida.
At a leadership forum for local high school students, Hogg stressed the importance of electing leaders who have lived through the affordability crisis that has saddled them with student debt and unable to afford homes — “people who understand what it’s like to pay rent in the 21st century.” 
From right, California congressional candidate Mai Vang and David Hogg take a selfie after meeting with SEIU volunteers and joining the “No Kings: Vote Early” rally in Elk Grove on Oct. 17, 2026. Vang is running to represent California’s 7th Congressional District. Photo by José Luis Villegas for CalMatters
Vang pointed to her own experience struggling to pay off student loans and afford childcare while also covering her family’s everyday expenses.
“Younger people feel like the system is rigged against them,” Hogg said in an interview with CalMatters. “Gen Z, which has really grown up under Trump’s presidencies, they’re much more hopeless, and they don’t have any real faith that anything is going to get better.”
Matsui challenged the idea that young people today face greater challenges than previous generations. When asked how she planned to persuade 20-and-30-somethings that she understands the financial obstacles they face, such as high housing and childcare costs, Matsui said young people were too short-sighted and needed to hold out hope that costs will come down eventually.
“I mean, all of us struggled at some point in time, and I’m not going to say that it was any easier or harder or anything like that, because you have to take it at the moment you’re at,” Matsui said. 
“I’ve gone through enough to know that these kinds of things — and I know I sound Polyanna-ish — we’re going to get out of this.”

name: California
title: California has more revenue than expected thanks to AI. Should the state save it?
text:
In summary
Proponents say Prop. 2 would allow the state to shore up its reserves for an economic downturn. Critics say it would only allow state leaders to spend more in the future.


The question Proposition 2 poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming?
The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act, seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. 
It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. 
Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. 
Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. 
Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups, including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce.
“It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover, a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure.
Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend.
“When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican.
How long have we had a rainy day fund?
Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst.
In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. 
But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees and delayed payments to schools and local governments. 
In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it.
“When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed stumping for the reform.
The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. 
Under the law, state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. 
A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for.
Bigger reserve = more to spend?
Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending.
“The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane, a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse that aims to “counter special interest influence.” 
“Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”
In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times.
“I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.”

name: California
title: Latino voters backed Karen Bass in June. Will she maintain their vote for LA mayor in November?
text:
There is a defining question in the Los Angeles mayoral election that perhaps only the ballot count can answer: Which candidate do the city’s Latinos, the largest ethnic group in this multicultural metropolis, prefer?
Polling points in all directions. Just before ballots were mailed this month, a poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies found that Councilmember Nithya Raman had a commanding, 24-point advantage among Latinos in her bid to unseat Mayor Karen Bass.
That took both camps by surprise. The Bass campaign dismissed it outright, and even some Raman operatives acknowledged that it was a bigger margin than their own surveys suggested. The picture was clouded further a week later when a Bass-backed poll reported that Latinos favored her by 12 points. That, too, seems unlikely since citywide polls consistently show Raman leading, and it would be hard to build much of a lead in L.A. without significant support from Latinos, who account for more than a third of the city’s voters.
That leaves analysts to search for other ways to measure the leanings of Latinos in this campaign. One place to look is actual results.
An analysis by CalMatters of the votes cast in June, when Bass, Raman and Spencer Pratt all were on the ballot, found Bass vastly outperformed her opponents in precincts where Latinos accounted for at least half of the vote. About 1 out of 5 precincts in the city are majority Latino, based on data from the state’s official redistricting database.

Bass carried 120 of these 144 precincts, compared to just 16 for Raman. Combined, Bass won those precincts by securing 37.5% of their votes, exceeding Raman and Pratt’s vote share by 11 and 16 percentage points, respectively.
The geographic distribution of those precincts also is significant. The precincts that Bass won stretch from the heavily Latino bedroom communities of the South Bay, through the center of the city and up into the Northeast Valley, where neighborhoods of single-family homes in Sunland and Pacoima include many longtime residents and homeowners.
Meanwhile, those that Raman carried were concentrated in the communities in and around her city council district — Hollywood, Silver Lake, Los Feliz, Highland Park — home to younger Angelenos and many others who are newer to L.A. Those are densely populated communities, with fewer single-family homes and more apartments.
Pratt’s Latino support was minimal and scattered, a passing reminder of why a Trump-backed Republican was a non-starter in a liberal city.
What the June votes illustrate, then, is that Latino supporters mirror the larger electorate, with homeowners and longtime residents more inclined to support Bass, while renters and newcomers find Raman more appealing.
The strength of this data is that it is not subject to the preconceptions or interpretations of pollsters. It represents actual votes cast, and supporters of a candidate who vote for that candidate are unlikely to change sides in a runoff. As a result, it provides evidence that Bass enters the fall with a broad band of Latino support, drawn mainly from middle-class communities where Latino voters are plentiful.
That said, this by no means guarantees Bass a victory among Latinos — any more than it suggests she’ll be reelected. Raman’s support may be less concentrated but greater overall, less visible on a map but more powerful in the end. The shock Berkeley IGS poll from earlier this month indicates that could be happening.
From left: Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and mayoral candidate and councilmember Nithya Raman. Photos by Damian Dovarganes, AP Photo and Vivien Killilea, Getty Images
That was underscored when I reviewed the CalMatters analysis with strategists for the two campaigns. A representative of the Raman camp, for instance, said the character of Latino-majority precincts for Bass is not reflective of the larger Latino electorate, which is spread across the city and more heavily tilted toward newer arrivals and renters — the core of Raman’s support. 
“Many Latinos live in younger, renter-heavy communities where Nithya has built strong support,” said campaign spokesperson Lauren Perez-Rangel. “They’re ready for change, and they’re choosing Nithya.”
The citywide surveys reinforce that argument. All of the credible ones show Raman with at least a modest lead, and since Latinos are the city’s largest voting demographic, it’s hard to see how Raman could be ahead without them, Perez-Rangel noted. The LA Times poll, she added, showed Raman with an overwhelming advantage among Latinos under age 50. 
The Bass campaign, by contrast, sees those Latino-majority precincts as a reliable core of support and a base from which to build. Julie Rodríguez, who manages the Bass campaign, said she regards homeowners as a natural constituency for the mayor in a race against a challenger long supported by the Democratic Socialists of America. Homeowners are more likely to rate public safety as a high priority, and Bass’ record gives her important bragging points, with incidents of violent and property crime at generational lows.
The two campaigns agree that winning support from relative newcomers to the city — those who have lived here for five years or less — is likely to turn on which candidate can make the city more affordable.
There, Raman has the edge. Her affordability credentials start with her record as the member of the city council who spearheaded the city’s rent stabilization ordinance, a measure that limits annual rent hikes by Los Angeles landlords. Bass signed that ordinance, so both candidates can claim some responsibility for it, though it is correctly more associated with Raman.
Beyond that, Bass has proposed expanding city-backed day care, and Raman has offered a host of ideas for expediting the construction of rental housing, trusting that a boost in supply will produce discernable downward pressure on rents. Both candidates promise to reduce City Hall impediments to new construction.
Affordability is not only popular with Latinos, of course, but it is at the top of the list of most surveys that ask renters what matters most to them. Since many Latinos are renters, those two demographics overlap.
One other dynamic lurks within the June election results and their window into the inclinations of Latino voters in Los Angeles: Although both campaigns recognize the importance of appealing to Latino voters overall, they are reaching out to different parts of the community.
Raman’s campaign has a youthful cast, positioning the candidate as a fresh antidote to the stultifying practices of City Hall. She speaks fluent Spanish, and her messaging is intended to draw Latinos into a multi-ethnic coalition that unites young people and renters across onetime divides of race. In her coalition, it matters less whether the voter is white, Black or Latino, and more that the voter is fed up with conventional Los Angeles politics.
Bass, meanwhile, draws upon more institutional bases of support. A longtime liberal Democrat and native of the city, Bass enjoys endorsements from major civil rights and immigrant rights groups, unions and respected leaders such as state Sen. María Elena Durazo, a stalwart of the city’s labor movement.
In the end, elections turn on who turns out. Mashing together the June election results and the polling done since then suggests that Raman probably has broader backing among Latinos in Los Angeles, but Bass probably has stronger support among more consistent voters. 
Will younger Latinos turn out for Raman in sufficient numbers to overcome Bass’ strength among Latinos who own homes and have lived here longer? The June election captures a moment in time and reveals actual voter behavior, but the November election will attract new voters and reflect the campaign itself.
In the end, those are the results that will matter. 
Data reporters Mohamed Al Elew and Jeremia Kimelman contributed to this story.

name: Nevada Current
title: Out of the Flock and into the Axon: Asked to dump license plate readers, Reno just switches brands
text:
"Axon Outpost combines ALPR, livestreaming, and vehicle attribute recognition in one fixed device," the company advertises. (Axon promotional photo)Amid growing public scrutiny of automated license plate readers and citywide protests decrying privacy concerns prompted by surveillance technologies, the City of Reno announced this month it would end its contract with Flock cameras. 
Instead of discontinuing the use of the technology, the Reno City Council voted 5-2 to expand its existing contract Axon Enterprise to include ALPRs and other artificial intelligence tools.
“Announcing the end of Flock just to switch to another intrusive tech surveillance company is an insult to our community,” Democratic Assemblymember Selena La Rue Hatch said in a statement. “Our constituents have been loud and clear that they do not want the government spying on them, end of story.” 
La Rue Hatch, a Reno-based lawmaker, announced in September she plans to bring a bill during the 2027 Legislative Session to ban the technology.
Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve and Reno City Councilwoman Meghan Ebert voted against the $22 million, eight-year contract citing privacy concerns and anger from the community. 
Schieve said the outrage wasn’t about Axon or Flock and was frustrated that the conversation “put protection and privacy against each other.”
“Let’s be honest, people, this is about trusting your government with the technology,” she said. “We had the opportunity to get this right, and I think we stepped in this.”
The Reno Police Department already contracts with Axon for use of body worn cameras, tasers, and interview room recordings. It had entered into a separate contract with Flock in 2024 to use license plate readers, which it decided not to renew.
The new contract with Axon approved Wednesday adds automated license plate readers, drones, and artificial intelligence report drafting. The contract also requires quarterly audits and that data not tied to an investigation be deleted after 15 days. 
Reno Police Chief Corey Solferino argued the use of surveillance technologies, like ALPRs, was needed to reduce crime and enhance public safety. 
“As these calls for service continue to explode, we continue to ask our officers to do more with less,” he said. “At some point, we’re going to reach a critical mass or a tipping point, where we can’t answer all those calls for service. And these efficiency tools that are part of this program are going to free up our officers.”
One of the many points driving apprehension of the technology was ample reporting across the country showing cases of law enforcement using technology to track the whereabouts of significant others, exes, and even random strangers.  
The technology, Solfrino said, was not being misused in Reno and he believed the city already had existing guardrails and parameters. 
“Any notion that the City of Reno can effectively oversee private surveillance technology is fictitious,” Athar Haseebullah, the executive director of the ACLU of Nevada, said in a statement. “Nobody with any semblance of intellectual honesty actually thinks that the Reno Police Department has more technology savvy than a private surveillance technology company it obtains its surveillance tools from. Reno should not be misspending tax dollars for surveillance expansion programs, including the acquisition of ALPRs and drones.”
Many opposed to the technology implored the city on Wednesday to instead invest in affordable housing, social services, or other resources that target root causes of crimes.
The lengthy contract left many, including some of the council members who voted in favor, with lingering questions about transparency, reporting requirements, and accountability.
Amid unanswered questions around the technology as well as the prospect of the state enacting regulations – if not an outright ban – on ALPRs, many opposed to the contract asked the council to at least consider postponing a vote. 
In addition to La Rue Hatch’s proposal to prohibit the use of APLRs in Nevada, the legislative Judiciary Committee voted this summer to bring forward a separate bill to regulate the use of ALPRs. 
Solfrino said he didn’t believe the city needed “to wait to determine what is and isn’t going to happen during the Legislative session.”
“We have the opportunity right now to be bold,” he said. “We have the opportunity now to make sure we have a model policy moving forward that protects the community interest.” 
Backlash to ALPRs has swept the country this year and prompted bipartisan outrage. 
Many cities, like Reno, have similarly ended contracts with Flock in response only to enter new or expansive contracts with other vendors like Axon. 
In a letter submitted to the council prior to the vote, the ACLU of Nevada called Reno’s proposal “a bait-and-switch tactic.”
“People in Reno and throughout Nevada have demonstrated time and again that they oppose warrantless mass surveillance,” Haseebullah said. “ACLU of Nevada has consistently made clear that ALPR surveillance technology is deeply invasive and incredibly dangerous.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: ‘We need help’: Homeless cleanup nonprofit furloughs employees, faces full shutdown
text:
Advantage Services employees Max Loveridge and Anthony Tarchick, left to right, clean up abandoned property called in by a police officer in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A longtime Utah social enterprise nonprofit that employs more than 100 people experiencing homelessness and other challenges has furloughed almost all of its staff — and it’s days away from shutting down completely if it doesn’t get an infusion of cash by the end of the month. 
“We’re going to drown unless somebody jumps in and saves us,” Advantage Services CEO Rob Ferris said. 
Advantage Services — which has a variety of service contracts with the state, Salt Lake City, homeless service providers and other organizations — had recently employed about 125 people. But starting on Oct. 12, Ferris said he had to furlough 110 employees for three weeks as a last-ditch effort to keep the company afloat after not being able to make payroll. 
Longtime Utah homeless cleanup nonprofit on brink of bankruptcy, issues ‘urgent’ call for help

“We’re operating with a skeleton crew of about 15 people,” he said. 
Utah News Dispatch reported in August that Advantage Services had been financially struggling due to several issues: unexpected cost increases, higher insurance premiums, and scaled back contracts from various customers.
