But one of the biggest reasons was its largest contract with Salt Lake City’s Urban Services Division was slashed in half from roughly $2 million to less than $1 million. 
Since then Ferris has been trying to expand Advantage Services’ contracts or merge with another nonprofit to preserve its jobs so that the people who rely on the nonprofit for work aren’t left unemployed. 
“What keeps me up at night is knowing that there’s no place for these people to go if we are not here,” Ferris said. “We’re the largest employer of people in this population — the homeless, people coming out of jail or prison — in the whole state. … Where are they going to go? There is no other company that does what we do.”

Since it was formed more than 34 years ago in 1992, Advantage Services has employed people who are disadvantaged — whether they have disabilities, are currently or formerly homeless, leaving jail or prison, are refugees, or are living in poverty. 
The nonprofit doesn’t function like a typical employer, but rather provides “supportive employment,” offering job coaching, mentoring, and other resources to help meet employees’ needs so they can not only work, but thrive.
Rob Ferris, CEO of Advantage Services, Inc., poses for a photograph at their facility in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Advantage Services employee Trevor Howell drops off a trailer of garbage at the landfill in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
The work Advantage Services employees do isn’t glamorous. They pick up garbage, clean up homeless encampments, power wash streets of biohazards, shuttle people to and from homeless shelters, and more, depending on the contract. But the opportunity to work can be life-changing for people building their resumes and developing life skills to turn their lives around. 
Earlier this month, Ferris sent a notice to Advantage Services’ more than a dozen customers notifying them of the looming furlough and how it would impact their services. 
He said the team would cease all services for Salt Lake City except for emergency biohazard cleanup. Shuttle services for Shelter the Homeless — the owner of several homeless resource centers in Salt Lake County — would pause for a week from Oct. 12 to Oct. 17, while other landscaping, grounds cleanup and janitorial services would cease until Nov. 1. The nonprofit’s highway cleanup contract with the Utah Department of Transportation — and other services for a variety of other organizations — would continue. 
But come Nov. 1, Ferris said if Advantage Services isn’t able to find a path to secure about $750,000 to make payroll until Jan. 1, the nonprofit will be forced to shut down. 
“If nothing changes, if we don’t receive any funding from anywhere, we will be forced to shut down or merge with another nonprofit,” he said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ferris said he’s been conversing with other nonprofits about a potential merger, but those talks hadn’t produced anything firm as of last week. 
“We may or may not come back online if we don’t get any help,” he said. “We need help to stay in business.” 
The situation has caught the attention of the Utah Homeless Services Board, the powerful body that oversees the state’s homeless system and distributes state funding to homeless service providers. 
During the board’s last meeting on Oct. 6, the board’s chair, Randy Shumway, raised the issue and questioned if there was anything the board or the state Office of Homeless Services could do to help. 
Shumway said from what he’s heard, Advantage Services has “done a tremendous job at helping people reskill, develop a job history post recovery … then find other employment that continues to propel their recovery.” 
“From my vantage point, it appears like they’re having tremendous impact. Is that accurate? And if so, then what can we, as a state, do to provide help and support for them to continue their efforts?” Shumway said. 
State Homeless Coordinator Tyler Clancy told Shumway his office would be willing to “engage.” 
Utah Homeless Coordinator Tyler Clancy speaks during a news conference announcing the Recovery Utah Initiative at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 21, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
“I don’t have an answer for you today,” Clancy said in that Oct. 6 meeting. “It certainly has been on our radar in different conversations with community partners, but we’d be more than happy to jump on this and make it a priority.” 
Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall, who sits on the Homeless Services Board, noted that that board doesn’t contract directly with Advantage Services — and she questioned that if the board waded into this issue, are there other organizations the board should also consider helping. 
“I think then the question would need to be broadened to what other organizations are also advancing the path to thriving for individuals in recovery,” she said. “It’s a big funding question without an answer on it just yet. But if we are going to ask that question about organizations that help that path, then we might want to broaden it to look at others, and I would guess many of them are struggling.” 
Shumway said as the “keeper” of the state’s homeless system, he worried that the loss of Advantage Services would have a ripple effect on the system as a whole. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“This is a loss that is going to be felt, and we’re going to pay for it in spades, both economically and socially elsewhere,” he said. 
Josh Romney, board chair of Shelter the Homeless, said Advantage Services “provides a significant amount of our transportation to and from the shelters, and so we are very nervous” about the nonprofit potentially shutting down. 
“It creates a real concern for us about getting people to and from shelter,” Romney said, noting Avantage Services also owns the vans it uses. “There’s a lot of assets there that would be difficult to replace.”
Since Advantage Services also provides transportation for emergency “code blue” shelters during the winter time, Mendenhall wondered if Clancy could look into whether it would be possible to use emergency funding to help. 
“I think it would be an incredible detriment to this winter system if we lose Advantage Services based on the transportation needs,” she said. “So could we look at the potential for matching funding or some kind of financial assistance. Maybe you can help guide us to which funds to look at.” 
Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall speaks during a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Aug. 18, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)Shumway encouraged the Office of Homeless Services “to think about this at a system level and come back to us” during the board’s next meeting with ideas on possible solutions. 
The Utah Homeless Services Board isn’t scheduled to meet again until Nov. 12, after Ferris’ Nov. 1 deadline. Ferris said he spoke with Clancy earlier this month about the issue, but hasn’t heard of any solid solutions yet. 
Ferris stressed that he’s open to any ideas that preserve Advantage Services’ jobs for people who need them most — more so than the company itself. So if that means merging with another nonprofit or service provider, he’s open to that. 
“We’re not looking for handouts. We’re looking to change people’s lives, but do it in a way that doesn’t affect the cost to the taxpayer,” he said. “So whatever that’s going to look like, if it looks like a loan, if it looks like a bailout, we just need $750,000 to come in before next Friday, or at least know that it’s going to be there.” 
Talks are ongoing over if anything can be done to keep Advantage Services alive. 
“We are continuing to review the situation involving Advantage Services and gathering information to better understand the circumstances,” Clancy said in a prepared statement issued to Utah News Dispatch. “Our goal is to ensure state funding supports a sustainable homeless services system that serves Utahns, uses public resources responsibly and focuses on measurable outcomes. We will continue to assess the situation as we determine the next steps.”
Advantage Services employees Max Loveridge, Trevor Howell and Anthony Tarchick, left to right, clean out bins of abandoned property at the Transitional Storage Program  in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Advantage Services employees Anthony Tarchick and Trevor Howell, left to right, drop off a trailer of garbage at the landfill in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Advantage Services employees Anthony Tarchick and Max Loveridge, left to right, clean up abandoned property called in by a police officer in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A camcorder is among abandoned property being cleaned up by Advantage Services employees in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Advantage Services employees Anthony Tarchick and Max Loveridge, left to right, drop off a trailer of garbage at the landfill in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Trevor Howell drives a truck to a cleanup site while working for Advantage Services in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA officials urge leaders not to spend $51 million Meta fine yet
text:
Facebook parent company Meta recently paid Washington state $51 million in penalties for violations of campaign finance law. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Meta has paid Washington state a record-setting fine of more than $51 million for violating campaign finance laws, but lawmakers are being cautioned not to get too excited about the money. 
The Facebook and Instagram parent company is expected to appeal the fine that the state Supreme Court upheld this year in a split decision to the nation’s highest court.
Meta has until Nov. 15 to file an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.
“I’d be shocked if they didn’t,” said Peter Frey Lavallee, the state Public Disclosure Commission’s executive director, in a commission meeting Thursday.
The case that led to the Meta penalty deals with the social media conglomerate not providing records about digital political advertisements hosted on its platforms in violation of state law.
Meta recently transferred more than $51 million to the state to pay the fine, which started at $24.6 million in 2022 but has been rising with interest. 
The state Public Disclosure Commission has urged Gov. Bob Ferguson’s office to not propose sweeping the funding from the agency’s transparency account for other uses. If the governor and lawmakers decide to do so anyway, they could have to pay Meta back if the company ultimately prevails.
“We’ve been shouting from the rooftops to the Legislature and anybody else who will listen,” Lavallee said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Commission leaders met with staff from the state attorney general’s office to discuss their concerns Sept. 25, said commission spokesperson Natalie Johnson. 
The attorney general’s chief financial officer sent a letter this month to legislative budget writers and the director of the state Office of Financial Management warning them that the state could potentially have to return the $51 million to Meta, plus interest and attorney fees.
A decision might not be made for a while.
The U.S. Supreme Court will likely decide whether to review Meta’s appeal before the end of June, according to the attorney general’s office. If the justices take it up, a decision could come a year later, by the end of June 2028.
Just before taking office in 2025, Ferguson proposed sweeping $35 million from the attorney general’s office, his old agency, to use for the state’s general fund amid a massive budget gap. Ferguson expected the then-pending Meta fine would make up for this. His successor, Attorney General Nick Brown, fiercely opposed the idea.
The money in the transparency account goes toward improving public access to political campaign finance information, including website upgrades.
But the state has instead been spending that money on staff, “which we argue is not sustainable since it’s not guaranteed money,” Johnson said. 
Of nearly $4.8 million over two years that lawmakers set aside for the transparency account and general commission expenses, almost all went toward paying for staff, and just over a half-million dollars was left for the initial purpose. 
Lawmakers this year revised the state law underlying the transparency account to allow for this redirecting of funds during the current budget cycle that runs through next June.
Commission leaders fear the tens of millions of dollars from Meta could be swept to cover other government expenses given the state’s budget shortfall.
Still, Lavallee said “we’ve done a pretty good job so far playing defense” in staving off budget cuts.
Meta’s hefty payment comes a few months after six state Supreme Court justices sided with the state and upheld state campaign finance law underpinning the lower court fine against Meta.
But the justices didn’t reach a consensus on whether the penalty was excessive. Three agreed with it, three ruled it was calculated incorrectly, and three others said it may have been determined correctly, but is still excessive. 
Without a majority view, the penalty was affirmed.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Sports Hall of Fame Class of ’27 is most diverse in the museum’s history
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
The Mississippi Sports Hall of Fame announced its 2027 class on Thursday, the most diverse group of inductees in the history of the Magnolia State sports shrine.
The class, which will be inducted in ceremonies next July, includes three women, three football greats and two Major League Baseball standouts.
In alphabetical order, they are: Mississippi State football great John Bond, Jackson State and Major League Baseball standout Dave Clark, Southern Miss and professional football linebacker Rod Davis, Pearl native and Olympic gold medalist sprinter Bianca Knight, Ole Miss All American and 10-year NFL veteran Kris Mangum, Ole Miss and Major League Baseball star Seth Smith, Mississippi State and WNBA basketball great LaToya Thomas and Shirley Gibbs Walker, who coached Alcorn State to 493 victories and 12 SWAC basketball championships.
A brief bio of each:
John Bond
Few athletes in Mississippi State history made such an immediate impact as John Bond did on Bulldog football. The Bulldogs were 3-8 in 1979, Emory Bellard’s first season as the coach. In 1980, with Bond running Bellard’s Wishbone offense, the Bulldogs won nine games, including a historic 6-3 victory over Bear Bryant’s No. 1 ranked Alabama Crimson Tide. Bond, who ran for more than 2,000 yards and passed for more than 4,000, remains the only State quarterback to defeat LSU four times.
Dave Clark
Clark, from the northeast Mississippi town of Shannon, was the 11th overall pick in the first round of the 1983 Major League draft. Clark, an outfielder, played 13 Major League seasons before embarking on a long coaching and managerial career in baseball. Currently a coach for the Houston Astros, he has managed, coached and won championships at the Minor League and Major League level.
Rod Davis
Davis won the C Spire Conerly Trophy, for Mississippi’s top college football player, in 2002 when he was the nation’s leading tackler for Southern Miss. He is the answer to an interesting trivia question: Eli Manning won the Conerly Trophy as a sophomore and a senior. Who won it Manning’s junior season? Davis, a three-time all-conference player at USM, is the school’s all-time leading tackler and was the Conference USA Defensive Player of the Year in 2003. The Gulfport native is currently the athletic director and head football coach at Florence.
Bianca Knight
Knight, a Pearl native, won Olympic gold, running a world record time in the 4×100-meter relay at the 2012 London Games. She was also a 2011 world champion in the same event. She won the 2008 NCAA indoor 200-meter championship, running for the Texas Longhorns after a remarkable high school career at Ridgeland High, where she captured 23 state championships.
Kris Mangum
Kris Mangum follows his older brother, John Mangum, into the Mississippi Sports Hall of Fame. Mangum won All-SEC and All-American honors as an Ole Miss tight end and then played 10 seasons for the Carolina Panthers, excelling as a blocker and catching nine touchdown passes. He helped Carolina reach the 2004 Super Bowl. As a freshman in 1992, he helped Alabama to a national championship before transferring to Ole Miss, where he was a three-year starter and standout.
Seth Smith
Smith, a Jackson native, will be remembered as one of the greatest hitters in Ole Miss baseball history, who wasted no time making his presence known. He was the SEC Freshman of the Year, hitting .402, while also serving as the backup to football quarterback Eli Manning. In three seasons at Ole Miss, he recorded an on-base percentage of .410 and a slugging percentage of .473. He played 11 Major League seasons with five ball clubs and hit 126 home runs. In 2007, he helped the Colorado Rockies reach the World Series.
LaToya Thomas
Thomas, a Greenville native, was a four-time All American and two-time SEC Player of the Year in women’s basketball at Mississippi State. She finished her State career with 2,981 points and an average of 23.8 points per game. Her jersey, No. 32, is retired and hangs in Humphrey Coliseum. She was selected first overall in the 2003 WNBA draft and played professionally in the WNBA for six seasons and internationally for 11 seasons.
Shirley Gibbs Walker
The basketball floor at Alcorn State was named in Gibbs Walker’s honor in 2015 after her 30-year coaching tenure that included 493 victories, 12 SWAC regular season championships, six SWAC Tournament titles and three NCAA Tournament bids. The Bude native was inducted into the SWAC Hall of Fame in 2010.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi declared infant mortality a public health emergency a year ago. What have officials done since then?
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
More than a year after state officials declared a public health emergency over rising infant mortality rates, eyes are on Mississippi, and Dr. Dan Edney, state health officer, said the national media attention has helped the cause. 
“The narrative switched from ‘Poor old Mississippi, they’re so pitiful, they can’t keep their babies alive’ to ‘Oh my goodness, look what Mississippi is doing,’” Edney said. “We’re the only state that’s ever declared one.”
In 2025, an infant mortality report showed Mississippi’s infant mortality rate rose from 8.9 in 2023 to 9.7 in 2024 – nearly twice the national average. Edney then declared the emergency status, which he said has helped his agency cut through red tape to roll out new programs. But state and national stakeholders say more could be done when it comes to transparency and solutions. 
In an interview with Mississippi Today, Edney outlined four initiatives he said his department launched or expanded since the declaration:

In December 2025, the state Health Department launched the Saving the Smallest campaign around safe sleep. To date, Edney said department employees have distributed 680 cribs and taught hundreds of families safe sleep practices during home visits. 
In May, the Legislature approved the creation of a Fetal-Infant Mortality Review Committee, which first met in August and needs about $150,000 annually to keep running, Edney said. 
The state Health Department continues to build its obstetric system of care, designed to streamline hospital transfers for high-risk pregnancies by modeling the trauma system. Hospitals are currently being surveyed and will receive designations in the coming months for the level of care they’re equipped to handle, Edney said. 
The agency is restructuring its county health departments. In 2025, Edney cut services at some county clinics following insufficient funding from the Legislature. Now, Edney said he is working to offer perinatal care at some of those clinics. He said the agency would start with four or five counties, but did not say which ones. 

Some public health researchers in the state were surprised to learn that the state Health Department characterized its response to the emergency as this four-pronged approach. Mitchell Adcock, executive director at the Center for Mississippi Health Policy, said his team had heard about these initiatives, but didn’t know their status. 
“With a public health emergency, I just thought we would know a bit more about what’s been going on,” he said. 
Meanwhile, provisional numbers for 2025 from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show infant mortality in Mississippi went down from 9.7 in 2024 to 8.4. Most of the department’s new initiatives don’t overlap with those 2025 numbers. The crib distribution began in December 2025. Edney said he couldn’t take credit for that decrease and can’t say what accounts for it, but called it a “substantial reduction.” 
“It’s about 40, 45 babies who survived 2025 who would not have survived 2024,” Edney said.
Once the official data is released, Adcock said his team will start digging into what’s driving those numbers. 
The Fetal-Infant Mortality Review Committee has already shed light on hidden problems, Edney said. Within a couple of meetings, the committee identified several infant deaths resulting from one twin rolling over the other while sleeping, Edney said.
“The pediatricians hadn’t thought about it, the neonatalogists hadn’t thought about it. But the FIMR identified it,” Edney said. “So right there, boom, in just a few months, it was a gamechanger.”
‘counties where there is nothing’
Jonathan Webb, CEO of the national Association of Women’s Health, Obstetric and Neonatal Nurses, said he believes the emergency designation was appropriate “given where Mississippi ranks.” He thinks states with similar rankings could collectively prioritize the challenge and share what works. 
“It creates awareness and brings some visibility to the issue,” Webb said. “But it also makes it easier to direct funds to programs.” 
Webb said while the declaration is commendable, Mississippi’s plan lacks certain elements he would hope to see in an emergency response, such as a focus on equity. In 2024, nearly twice as many Black infants as white ones died in Mississippi. 
Data from Mississippi’s most recent infant mortality report shows the death rate for white infants in 2024 was one of the lowest over the last decade. But during that same period, the number of deaths among Black infants reached its highest rate. 
“I really think that an honest assessment of our biases individually and as a system has to happen,” Webb said.
Solutions could include the health department partnering with community organizations that serve women of color, creating patient advisory committees and embedding accountability offices into health spaces, he said. 
Webb also highlighted the importance of providing resources and training to clinicians who might be left picking up the slack when hospitals shutter their labor and delivery units. 
“When you have these maternity care deserts and services leave communities, people are still having babies in these communities,” Webb said. “It just falls to the EMS team or the emergency room teams or critical care units, nurses who are in those environments.”
The University of Mississippi Medical Center has a program called STORK, which trains first responders and emergency room clinicians to better respond to obstetric emergencies. In 2022, UMMC doctors launched the program in response to the dwindling options for obstetric care and the concern that a growing number of women would be delivering babies outside dedicated labor and delivery units. Part of the obstetric system of care involves amplifying that effort, Edney said. 
That’s not a bad thing to do, but it’s not a comprehensive approach, said Getty Israel, founder of a Jackson-based women’s health clinic called Sisters in Birth. 
“Is the state doing enough? No,” Israel said, adding that she doesn’t believe the department can shore up meaningful improvements without more funding.  
For the third consecutive year, the health department requested no increase in funding from lawmakers during legislative budget hearings earlier this month. 
On Tuesday, the Commonwealth Fund released a new report highlighting the importance of midwifery-led birth centers, cost-effective clinical spaces outside hospitals where low-risk women can safely give birth with fewer interventions and more hands-on support. Mississippi has none.
Israel has been trying to open the state’s first birth center for nearly six years. Several state laws have stood in her way, she said, including expensive monthly fees certified nurse midwives are required to pay physicians to practice within their scope. 
A willingness from lawmakers to break the status quo, and to fund the construction of more community health spaces, “could reduce so much of the risk that women experience that leads to death,” she said. 
Nearly half the state’s counties are maternity care deserts, where there are no obstetric clinicians or birthing facilities, according to the March of Dimes. There should be more of a focus on shrinking those deserts by offering more reproductive health services, Israel said, than on routing women out of those deserts. 
“We need to build infrastructure in those counties where there is nothing,” Israel said. “You’re relying on an EMS system to drive how many minutes, how many miles, to get to a woman’s house in a rural place?”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Harm reduction workers demand oversight of opioid settlement fund spending
text:
Arron Wheeler of the Newark Community Street Team testifies during a public hearing on opioid settlement fund spending on Oct. 22, 2026, at the Statehouse in Trenton. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor) People like Arron Wheeler, Precious Kirby, and Jenna Mellor are usually out on the streets, helping those struggling with addiction by getting them into housing and treatment, providing clean syringes and hygiene kits, and saving lives by administering the overdose-reversing drug Narcan.
Thursday, they crowded into a standing-room-only meeting room at the Statehouse, fueled by anger and anguish, for a three-hour public hearing on how counties and towns have spent national opioid settlement funds that drug manufacturers, distributors, and pharmacies have been required to pay to resolve lawsuits.
The money is meant to directly help those harmed by addiction, but local officials in New Jersey and elsewhere have squandered millions since disbursement began in 2022 on concerts and other festival-like events billed as “public awareness” initiatives, police surveillance equipment and fitness gear, and more.
Advocates demanded oversight and urged lawmakers to set stricter guardrails on spending, with the state and local governments set to receive $1.1 billion through 2038.
“People died for that money!” said Wheeler, a harm reduction worker with the Newark Community Street Team. “Let’s get the money to where it belongs. My mother suffered from opioid use. My uncle died in an abandoned building because of prescription drugs. Let’s get this money to the people that it belongs to.”
Kirby, director of community engagement at Black Lives Matter Paterson, told legislators that people sometimes seek help from her group when someone overdoses.
“I’m not sure here who’s ever witnessed an overdose in person, but it’s pretty terrifying,” said Kirby. “When people are asking for our staff, they aren’t asking us if we have popcorn, cotton candy, or a nice $600,000 concert. They’re asking: ‘Who has Narcan?’ Because when someone is dying from an overdose, we don’t need a concert to remind us that overdoses exist.”
Assemblymen Avi Schnall (D-Ocean) and Cody Miller (D-Gloucester), the committee’s chair and co-chair, introduced legislation earlier this month that would expand oversight and transparency of opioid settlement funds.
But Schnall said they wanted to hear from people on all sides of the issue first and would use the testimony to improve the legislation, so the committee did not vote on the bill.
Miller, whose older brother and sister have struggled with addiction, said he found towns’ spending on things like police surveillance cameras and vehicles “abhorrent.”
“This is blood money. It’s for people that have lost their lives, and that’s what we need to spend it for: for treatment, for recovery, for prevention, for families, for individuals who have been impacted, Black and brown communities, everyone who has been impacted by this crisis,” Miller said. “We want to make sure the funds go to the people who need it the most, and we are going to fix this.”
Assemblyman Cody Miller (D-Gloucester) talks during an Assembly oversight committee hearing on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Schnall called it “disgraceful” that many local officials have hoarded and not spent the money, even as the opioid crisis continues.
Overdose fatalities in New Jersey have declined in recent years, from 3,171 confirmed drug deaths in 2022 to just under 800 suspected drug deaths so far this year, state data shows. But racial disparities persist and thousands of people continue to overdose, with emergency responders preventing further deaths by administering naloxone in more than 9,500 incidents last year, data shows.
“People died for that money, and we are not enforcing and obligating and requiring that every dollar is planned,” Schnall said. “It’s disgraceful that we’re letting this happen, and we can’t.”
Their bill would require fund recipients to spend the money within 18 months, unless it’s for a multi-year project or they get approval from the state Department of Human Services to hold the money longer. Money unused within 18 months otherwise would be redistributed to jurisdictions that will spend it.
But advocates said requiring more thoughtful plans for the money would be better than setting a deadline for it to be spent.
A few mayors and county administrators seconded that sentiment, testifying that they welcome more guidance and examples of “good” spending to guide their decision-making. They urged legislators to create a position or commission where they could ask questions about planned spending.
Some of that already exists. A state panel issued a five-year strategic plan last year that advised officials to focus funds on treatment, housing, harm reduction services such as safe syringe sites and testing, and wraparound services that address other barriers to recovery like employment, education, food insecurity, and more. Fund recipients are required to publicly report their spending every fall, and some advocates seeking fuller transparency have investigated and reported on spending themselves.
Several public health officials alerted lawmakers that many towns exclude them from spending decisions and implored them to ensure they get a seat at the table.
Linda Brown is executive director of the New Jersey Association of County and City Health Officials, which represents 104 local health departments. She told lawmakers her group surveyed 25 departments and found that more than half of them reported that they weren’t consulted at all when their towns decided how to spend funds, with police, finance, or human services departments instead deciding.
Others asked lawmakers to make sure local officials stop using opioid settlement money as a “slush fund” to close budget gaps as the economy worsens and to prioritize community-led solutions.
“We want everyday residents, business owners, family members, and neighbors to have the tools to respond when these seconds matter. We are working every day to turn everyday community members into life-saving first responders. This is what meaningful investment looks like. It is practical, it is accessible, and it’s replicatable. It is rooted in public health, and most importantly, it has the potential to save lives,” Kirby said. “But organizations doing this work should not have to compete with publicity campaigns, entertainment expenses, or initiatives that lack any clear connection to evidence-based overdose prevention.”
Jenna Mellor, executive director of the New Jersey Harm Reduction Coalition, testifies during a public hearing on opioid settlement fund spending on Oct. 22, 2026, at the Statehouse in Trenton. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Jenna Mellor, executive director of the New Jersey Harm Reduction Coalition, shared a lengthy petition she sent Thursday to Stephen Cha, commissioner of the state Department of Human Services, seeking new rules to ensure settlement funds are spent wisely.
“It’s time for the Department of Human Services to step up into that authority,” Mellor said. “It is a moral responsibility to do so.”
However lawmakers eventually amend the bill, Raquel Romans-Henry of Salvation and Social Justice urged them to prioritize in policymaking racial disparities seen in the opioid crisis and the recognition that addiction is a disease and not a crime.
“For decades, when addiction devastated Black communities, government responded with arrests, prosecution, incarceration, and surveillance. Today, we rightly speak about addiction through the lens of treatment, recovery, harm reduction, housing, and public health. And while that shift is welcomed, we have to tell the truth. When addiction showed up in Black communities, the state built prisons. When addiction showed up in white communities, the state built treatment systems,” Romans-Henry said.
She added: “Black communities endured the war on drugs, and now they are disproportionately bearing the burden of the opioid crisis itself. That reality should shape every single conversation about opioid settlement dollars here in the governor’s office, in the state, in county, and in local offices.”
Raquel Romans-Henry, policy director of Salvation and Social Justice, testifies during a public hearing on opioid settlement fund spending on Oct. 22, 2026, at the Statehouse in Trenton. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: My sentence isn’t the end of my story
text:
(Getty Images).When I was pregnant, my ex-husband pinned me against a wall. I was afraid he would kill me.
I survived that violence. I also have a felony conviction. And those two parts of my life cannot be separated.
My ex-husband and I often used methamphetamine together. Our drug use led to countless arguments, and I endured repeated physical and emotional abuse. When I tried to stay sober, he pressured me to use drugs with him.
Once, while I was sober and he had relapsed, he trapped me in the bedroom of our trailer. For hours, he paced back and forth with a bat, screaming in my face and threatening me.
When someone has that much power over your life, saying no doesn’t always feel safe. At times, I believed my choices were to use drugs or face more violence. I made decisions I regret, but I made them while living in fear.
My methamphetamine use eventually led to my arrest and felony conviction.
I understand that I should be held accountable for the crimes I committed. But accountability and understanding are not mutually exclusive. When the court system ignores the circumstances surrounding a crime, it fails to recognize the full story.
In court, I tried to explain how domestic violence had influenced my decisions. But I felt the judge gave little consideration to what I had endured. I believe that if my abuse had been taken seriously, I might have had a better chance to enter a treatment program, get away from my husband and find sobriety sooner.
Today, I celebrate eight years of sobriety and a home free from abuse. I have earned credentials in addiction counseling and peer support. My life is very different from what it was then, but my conviction remains part of my story.
And my experience is not unique.
Missouri Appleseed, a nonprofit advocating for criminal justice reform, has documented the experiences of women whose abuse and coercion contributed to crimes that led to incarceration.
The organization is championing the Missouri Survivors’ Justice Act, which would give survivors a meaningful opportunity to present evidence of domestic violence or coercion during sentencing.
If abuse contributed to someone’s crime, judges should be required to take those circumstances into account when determining an appropriate sentence.
A version of the legislation advanced out of a Missouri House committee earlier this year but did not become law. Advocates plan to renew the effort during the 2027 legislative session.
This proposal isn’t about allowing survivors to escape accountability. It’s about recognizing that someone can be responsible for a crime while also having been a victim of violence that influenced their actions.
Domestic violence can affect every part of a person’s life, including their ability to make choices, seek help and escape dangerous situations. The justice system should recognize that reality rather than treating every crime as though it occurred in a vacuum.
As we observe Domestic Violence Awareness Month, I hope Missouri lawmakers will listen to people who have experienced both abuse and the criminal justice system.
I am not asking for my past to be erased. I am asking for the circumstances that shaped it to be understood.
My felony conviction is part of my story. It should never be the only part that matters.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Republicans call Annie Andrews ‘anti-gun.’ She explains her platform to end gun violence.
text:
Senate candidate Annie Andrews, a Democrat, speaks at a town hall in Winnsboro, South Carolina, on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)WINNSBORO — The Democrat running for Senate in South Carolina responded Thursday to President Donald Trump painting her as an “anti-gun extremist.”
Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, said her experiences caring for children who unintentionally shot themselves after finding an unsecured gun prompted her into activism.

For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.

“It takes one of those experiences to make you want to do something about that,” Andrews said.
Andrews’ former job with Everytown for Gun Safety involved creating a pilot program to train medical students on how to talk to parents about safe gun storage to prevent shootings, according to her campaign.
Her explanations came a day after Trump told rallygoers in Anderson County that “she wants to take your guns away,” and hours before her opponent, GOP Sen. Darline Graham, summed up Andrews’ role with the nation’s largest gun violence prevention group as a “paid anti-gun activist.”
With polls showing an unexpectedly tight race less than two weeks before Election Day, Republicans are putting a spotlight on Andrews’ positions for ending gun violence.
“Andrews has made a living working for a gun control group, hell-bent on gutting the Second Amendment and taking your guns,” Graham told reporters in Columbia.
That’s a serious accusation in South Carolina, where legislators passed the “constitutional carry” law two years ago allowing adults to carry a handgun without a permit.
But Andrews said she respects the Second Amendment; she just wants to protect children.
“I don’t want to take anyone’s guns,” she said after a town hall meeting with voters in rural Fairfield County. It marked the completion of her campaign goal to visit with voters in all 46 counties.
“My platform to address the public health crisis of gun violence does not infringe on the Second Amendment,” Andrews said. “I support the Second Amendment, law-abiding citizens’ rights to own firearms, but I know we need to do something about this public health crisis.”
On Wednesday night, Trump said she wants to ban “the most popular firearms in America.”
Andrews has advocated in the past for banning AR-15-style rifles.
And her website says she wants to ban “weapons of war on our streets.” Asked Thursday to be specific, Andrews said she “believes military-grade machine guns and weapons of mass destruction should remain limited under existing law.”
Everytown and the NRA
At her news conference in Columbia, Graham put Andrews’ earnings from Everytown for Gun Safety on a posterboard as a backdrop.
In her candidate financial disclosure, Andrews reported receiving more than $130,000 total from Everytown in 2024 and 2025: about $96,000 from the nonprofit and $35,000 from its political lobbying arm.
She worked for them from May 2023 to May 2025. Though paid separately, her roles for both entities involved “gun violence prevention in medical education and media appearances,” reads her December 2025 filing. She also reported a salary of $97,000 from the Children’s National Medical Center in Washington, D.C., a job her campaign has said involved conducting research and teaching, in addition to seeing patients.
Trump pointed to Andrews’ “F” rating from the National Rifle Association as evidence of her extremism. But an F for a Democrat is standard for the gun rights group.
Graham has an “A” rating and an endorsement from the NRA.
“To me, gun control is how steady you hold your weapon,” she said on stage Wednesday night.
Andrews’ endorsers include her former employer, Everytown for Gun Safety Action Fund; and Giffords, the anti-gun-violence lobbying nonprofit led by former U.S. Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, who was shot in the head in 2011 while meeting with constituents in Tucson, Arizona.
Asked about Trump’s rally in the Upstate, Andrews said it shows “the weakness” of her opponent.
“This race is very close,” Andrews said. “He stood on that stage and said horrible things about me, dishonest things about me. If doing that was going to lower gas prices and grocery prices and keep our rural hospitals open, he can say whatever he wants to say. But we know that’s not a path to solving the problems South Carolinians are facing.”
Andrews is scheduled to hold a news conference Friday in Orangeburg County with “more than 10 South Carolina sheriffs” endorsing her, according to her campaign announcement. It comes a week after Graham held a “back the blue” news conference in Greenville to tout endorsements from sheriffs.
The Senate race in South Carolina was upended when Graham’s older brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, died of a ruptured aorta July 11, a month after defeating five GOP opponents toward a fifth term.
Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to fill the remainder of the term ending in January. She advanced to the contest with Andrews after winning a 10-way GOP special primary in August.

title: The mountain elite: A Teton guide worries about Wyoming’s future
text:
On the way down from the summit of the Grand Teton, some Exum mountain guides point their clients to a helpful granite knob, shaped like a well-fitting ski pole grip, that they call “the world’s best handhold.”
When guide Jessica Baker led a blind woman up the peak — the first blind woman to climb the 13,775-foot-high mountain — the client discovered a mountainside of the best handholds.
Baker had climbed the Grand Teton route numerous times and figured she knew where all the good grips were. But Nancy, her blind client, found more.
“She found a bunch of them,” Baker said. “She found ones that I didn’t even know about.”
Nancy employed “an echolocation style way of finding things for herself,” Baker said. “Oh wow,” Baker recalls saying. “I’ve never even seen that hold. That looks like a great hold.”
To guide Nancy, Baker had to learn about her client’s sensory abilities and also build a system among other guides. “She did it through good communication,” Baker said of her client’s summit climb, “essentially on her own.
“For years after that experience, I was still in awe. To do it without sight just blew my mind. That will always stand out in my career as something very, very special.”
“A good guide can read people. They have a sense of how people are acting.”Jessica Baker
The extraordinary climb proved that a mountain guide needs more than fitness and climbing chops, Baker said.
“It takes a lot of patience. You have to be willing to work with people through their process, and you can’t expect immediate results.
“You have to empathize with where people are coming from and what their experience is. You have to be pretty socially adept. You have to entertain.
“You have to be able to talk about things, be interested in topics. You have to be intellectually, like, interesting.
“A good guide knows how to pace,” Baker said. “They know how to pace the day, the objectives, the climb, the conversation. A good guide can read people. They have a sense of how people are acting, reacting, how to adjust according to their emotions.”
Mountain sense
“The more obvious side of it,” Baker said, “is a good guide is very skilled in the mountains. They have extremely high, like high-level mountain sense. Very, very tuned into their environment.”
Baker began acquiring that sense as the oldest of four daughters raised on a farm — collecting eggs and everything else — in northern Idaho. “My grandparents were skiers, my parents were skiers, and then I’m a skier and my kids are skiers.”
After a successful high school racing career, she chose college and went to Bates College in Lewiston, Maine, an institution with top academic and ski-team credentials. A geology degree seemed to connect her to land, earth and nature, she said. Her first job out of school landed her in Jackson Hole, where she worked as a hydrologist for the Bridger-Teton National Forest.
“I moved to Jackson to ski for sure,” she said. “That was probably goal number one. But it was under the guise of I’m also going to be a geologist.
“It’s kind of a pinnacle place to be a skier,” Baker said. For the Forest Service, she studied the health of rivers and compared untouched waterways with those that had been degraded by grazing, roads and other things. She also coached young ski racers and gave lessons.
Budget cuts under the George W. Bush administration started affecting the Forest Service program, and Baker moved on from river health to ski instruction at the Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, building a list of enduring clients. Associates goaded her into competing on the Freeride World Tour, where in the early 2000s she became the U.S. and North American women’s free skiing champion.
“The prize money was much less for women,” she said, “with the exception of one competition in Crested Butte. They had it right from the beginning.
“I just wanted to prove myself,” Baker said about the pay disparity and why she focused on skiing. “Once I’m good,” she said of her thoughts, “then I can speak up a little bit more.”
“I don’t think I was wise enough nor bold enough to stand up for my rights,” Baker said. I was just trying to prove that we were good enough in the first place, before even asking for anything else.”
Guide qualities
A trip with the late, legendary skier Doug Coombs to the testing ground of La Grave, France, brought Baker into the alpine realm. “I came out of that trip knowing that I wanted to delve deeper into these higher technical things,” like how to be a rock climber and alpinist.
She began helicopter ski guiding in Alaska and also skiing “all sorts of crazy lines” in the Tetons, including down the Grand Teton. An owner of Exum Mountain Guides in 2006 invited her to train with the guides.
“They want you to come well prepared,” she said. “You have to come with an excellent resume. They want you to be at the top of your game.”
That included time spent climbing in Yosemite. “It’s just one of those rites of passage,” she said of the crack climbing on towering walls in the landmark valley.
“Mountain guiding requires an extremely high level of fitness. If I get hurt, who’s helping my clients? And if they get hurt, how much stronger do I need to be to help them … to lift them, to raise them, lower them, scoop them, whatever it would take?
Baker lifts weights, climbs hills and cycles. At work, “we do 20,000 vertical feet commonly in a week up and down mountains.”
She established The Ski Diva, a guiding, ski-camp service and online community for women that’s going on its 20th year. She’s the executive producer of “Going Greenland,” a film about pioneering steep ski lines.
She wants a feeder system that will bring more women into the guiding profession in the Tetons. “People now recognize that not only are women guides very desirable but also just having that balance in the decision-making spaces is really important,” she said.
“We might tune into something just a little more subtle that cues our hackles, that cues our hazard rating, that cues our decision-making,” she said. “I like to discuss it more,” she said of a risk or hazard. “The conversations start to get more varied and diverse, and more voices get heard. I think that difference can actually save you in the balance.”
Kids and Wyoming’s future
If Baker needs patience to be a guide, she also needs it to raise her two daughters, even when teaching about the concept itself.
“They’re like, ‘What do you mean patience? That’s like not in my vocabulary, nor do I understand that concept.’”
“I think they’ve taught me a lot of patience,” Baker said. “I am certain at some point that I will have taught them about patience, but I’m not sure I’ve seen the full fruit of my labor.”
“I think we’re already falling, and we need the net. We need the net sooner than later.”Jessica Baker
Young women in Wyoming may need a mountain guide’s fortitude when facing their future in the Equality State.
“Wyoming has always been or has tried to be rooted in freedom — freedom of choice … freedom to be in your space, freedom to have space. I have always appreciated that about Wyoming. It’s not so much that Wyoming is rooting for women, but rather Wyoming is rooting for the freedom of humans.
“We’re kind of in free fall right now,” she said of women’s lot in Wyoming. “Women’s healthcare is extremely compromised … not being supported the way it should be in Wyoming.”
Some groups are trying to take away women’s freedoms, she said. That’s “completely backwards … and completely against what Wyoming should stand for.
“Wyoming is on the edge right now, and I think we can recover, but we better do it quickly because I think we’re already falling, and we need the net. We need the net sooner than later.”

name: WyoFile
title: Inside Yellowstone National Park’s historic gift from data center developers
text:
A company behind Wyoming’s artificial intelligence data-center boom has launched a $105 million fund for Yellowstone National Park. In a Monday announcement, officials touted the donation as the largest private gift in National Park Service history. But the contribution is also raising questions about the role of private philanthropy as data-center development transforms the rural West.
Funneled through the official nonprofit partner of the park, Yellowstone Forever, the donation from energy giant Tallgrass, a Blackstone Inc. portfolio company, is intended to fund research and conservation; develop a new visitor education center at Norris Geyser Basin; and expand opportunities for students and families to experience and learn about Yellowstone, according to Yellowstone Forever CEO and President Lisa Diekmann.
As U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum posed for pictures at Yellowstone’s Old Faithful Inn on Oct. 16 alongside Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon and representatives of Tallgrass and Blackstone, officials didn’t discuss the environmental impact of AI data centers. Instead, they touted what the donation would do for the park.
Crystal Heter, president and CEO of Tallgrass; Gov. Mark Gordon; Interior Secretary Doug Burgum; Sean Klimczak of Blackstone and Lisa Diekmann, president and CEO of Yellowstone Forever, sign an agreement Friday establishing the conservation and stewardship fund at the Old Faithful Inn at Yellowstone National Park. (Yellowstone National Park)
“More than 120 years ago, President Theodore Roosevelt laid the cornerstone of Yellowstone’s iconic gateway, enshrining the promise that our National Parks exist for the benefit and enjoyment of the American people,” Burgum said in a press release. “This historic $105 million investment honors that legacy, bringing together the best of American enterprise and conservation to expand access to Yellowstone and inspire the next generation to experience America’s great outdoors.” 
But across the country, only about 11% of Americans support the construction of an AI data center in their communities, according to recent polling from the University of Massachusetts Amherst.
Brian Childers lives about three-and-a-half miles from a Microsoft AI data center south of Cheyenne — near the separate Tallgrass facility that’s under construction. He’s hard of hearing, he says, but he still can’t escape a constant, overwhelming hum. Birds have left his property, he said, and at night the sky never quite gets dark. He said the gift to Yellowstone feels like the companies are trying to buy goodwill from politicians and the public. 
“I’m glad (the park) got the money, but if these things are going to impact the people around southeast Wyoming, (the corporations) need to be paying a premium on the electricity they use so that the people don’t have to pay extra,” Childers told Mountain Journal in an interview.
Colorado-based Tallgrass manages more than 10,000 miles of pipelines and, with Google as a partner, is developing a 2.7 gigawatt AI data center near Cheyenne, Wyoming. Matt Sheehy, brother of Montana Republican U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy, led the company from 2019 until earlier this year. Tallgrass is also a subsidiary of Blackstone, the largest financier of data centers in the world and major financial backer of Tim Sheehy’s former company Bridger Aerospace. 
The National Parks Conservation Association, Park County Environmental Council, Wild Montana and the Greater Yellowstone Coalition all declined to comment on the donation.
On social media, however, an uproar ensued. 
“Putting the wolves in charge of the sheep,” one person commented on Yellowstone’s Instagram post, joining a slew of detractors. 
Yellowstone National Park’s new bridge near Tower Junction opened in 2025, replacing a 60-year-old structure over the river at a cost of about $118 million. The new 1,285-foot long, 175-foot high steel girder bridge received funding from the 2020 Great American Outdoors Act. (Rebecca Huntington/WyoFile)
Tax dollars only cover the basics of Yellowstone National Park’s operations, according to Yellowstone Forever’s Diekmann, who said she hopes the gift will inspire further donations. America’s first national park still has a large need, she added: Yellowstone has a $1.2 billion backlog of maintenance that this donation will not address. 
In an interview, Mountain Journal asked Diekmann about how closely Yellowstone Forever examined the public pushback to data centers and their ecological consequences elsewhere in Wyoming and across the country in their decision to move forward with the donation.
“We are focused on mission-aligned programs,” she said. “I think that the business of Blackstone and Tallgrass and their commitment to the communities in which they work is very important. And this is reflected in this donation.”
Tallgrass officials declined an interview. But in an emailed statement, the company touted its contributions to the Wyoming economy, including some of the nation’s largest carbon sequestration technology.
“We’ve always believed that energy from Wyoming should create opportunities for Wyoming, and that means more than the jobs we provide and the taxes we pay,” the company said. “It means being a force for good across the entire state, not just in the specific communities where we operate. Our investment in Yellowstone is one way we’re acting on that belief.”
Blackstone also declined to comment. In the Yellowstone press release, however, the company lauded its donation.
“This historic gift reflects our belief that infrastructure investment can and should be a force for good, helping us invest in Yellowstone’s future and the growth of the communities that surround it,” Sean Klimczak, global head of infrastructure for Blackstone, said in the statement.
Experts say there might be more at play.
“This falls right into that category of philanthropy designed to win over stakeholders who might be unhappy with you,” Thomas Lyon, a professor of business and sustainability at the University of Michigan who focuses on greenwashing, told Mountain Journal.
Donations from data centers across the country are increasingly common, according to reporting from Spotlight PA. They often run in the millions of dollars. In one instance, locals pushed back on a proposal to give every household in Hazle Township, Pennsylvania, $10,000 if officials approve an Amazon data center. Some called it a bribe.
Southeast Wyoming, like Phoenix and Northern Virginia, is rapidly becoming a hub of data-center development. As of May 2026, the area is home to at least 10 up-and-running data centers, according to the city government. At least five more are under construction and another nine are in the planning phase. 
In the case of Blackstone, Lyon pointed specifically to Stephen Schwarzmann, the company’s CEO. According to OpenSecrets, an organization that tracks money in U.S. politics, Schwarzmann was the 12th largest donor in the country during the 2024 election cycle. Nearly all of his $40 million in contributions went to Republican candidates. 
“I’d like to see those kinds of contributions expanded to directly support the counties, cities and towns where these facilities are located.”Rick Keslar, ranch owner near Cheyenne, Wyoming
Last year, Lyon said, many of those same candidates voted to cut $267 million of NPS funding in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. At the same time, the agency has lost about 24% of its permanent workforce since January 2025, according to the National Parks Conservation Association. The Trump administration’s 2027 budget proposes cutting the agency’s budget by 32%.
“Here’s the guy pouring his personal cash into electing people that will systematically undermine the national parks,” Lyon said of Schwarzmann. “And then he wants to turn around and give money to Yellowstone to look like a good guy.”
Philanthropic gifts are a common tactic for companies that want to curry political favor or shift public sentiment away from a negative track record, according to Lyon. Up against the ropes from federal cuts, Lyon said the park was likely forced into an awkward position when Blackstone and Tallgrass offered the donation.
Aaron Murphy, a former Yellowstone ranger now with the Bozeman, Montana-based conservation group American Hunters and Anglers, expressed concern about the companies’ motives.
“One of the world’s largest private equity firms stepping in to fill the gaps is a pathetic solution to something that should have never been a problem,” Murphy said, referencing the park’s need for more funding. “This particular ‘gift’ raises all sorts of questions about the motives of the billionaires behind it, and who’s really going to owe who in the future.”
Around Cheyenne, Childers and his neighbors want to see developers do more for the community. Rick Keslar, who lives near a large historic ranch west of Cheyenne that was annexed for a separate data-center campus, was supportive of Tallgrass making the donation to Yellowstone. But he says that alone isn’t enough. 
“I’d like to see those kinds of contributions expanded to directly support the counties, cities and towns where these facilities are located,” he said.
Childers feels differently. Along with the disturbance at his home, he’s worried about water use and pollution, utility bills and the imbalance of power between people and the corporations behind the developments. 
“I’d like to see them stop building the damn things,” Childers said. “My concern is once they’re all built here and they figure out it’s messing up the environment, it’s going to be too late.”

title: Social Security’s math problem is not going away
text:
Opinion

Last week, the Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living raise for 2027, about $75 more per month for the average retiree. In Wyoming, where roughly 130,000 people (more than one in five residents) receive benefits, that money matters. If you paid in, you deserve it. It also does nothing about the much larger problem ahead.
According to the 2026 Trustees Report, the retirement and survivors trust fund can pay full benefits only through late 2032. After that, incoming payroll taxes are projected to cover about 78% of scheduled benefits. Unless Congress acts, that is a 22% cut across the board, which is roughly $475 per month off today’s average check. That reduces monthly checks by about six times last week’s increase. The cause is largely demographic: The country went from 16 workers per retiree in 1950 to 2.7 today, as Americans have fewer children and live longer.
Someone who is already retired or approaching retirement might ask, “Why should I care? I already paid in.” Because under current law, waiting means taking that sudden 22% cut when you have the least room to financially absorb it. People who have paid in for decades deserve better than a last-minute surprise. Acting early is the only reliable way to keep the promise that was made to them.
I’m 35. Like most Wyoming workers, I pay 6.2% of every paycheck into the system, and my employer matches it. I turn 67 in 2058. A Cato Institute poll found that seven in 10 Americans expect benefit cuts, and 78% of Gen Z expects less than their full benefits. Young families are paying full freight while planning as if the benefit may not be there. That arrangement is neither fair nor honest. 
My neighbor, Travis, an engineer with two kids under 5, pays into Social Security every paycheck and has stopped counting on it. “I’m saving for retirement like it won’t be there,” he tells me, “and I still have to pay for it.”
Social Security was created in 1935 as a basic floor against poverty in old age, not a full pension. That original purpose remains the right test for any reform. Four principles should guide the work:

Protect those closest to retirement. Anyone already retired or within roughly 20 years of full retirement age should keep every benefit they were promised. They planned their lives around that commitment and should not have the rules changed late in the game.


Share the burden. Protecting the safety net has a real cost, and no serious reform is painless. The cost should be distributed across generations rather than dropped entirely on the young. Delays only make the eventual adjustment steeper and less fair.


Make changes gradual and early. Adjustments that affect younger workers should be phased in over decades with clear notice. Small, predictable changes made now are far preferable to a large, sudden cut forced by crisis.


Preserve the floor. Whatever else changes, we must protect the core mission of keeping older Americans and surviving families out of poverty, including disability and survivor benefits.

The specifics of what changes, for whom, and how fast deserve a longer debate than one op-ed allows, and I don’t claim to have settled them. Nearly 70% of Americans support empowering an independent, nonpartisan commission to develop options. It has worked before: A bipartisan commission helped Congress avert a similar crisis in 1983. Congress should pursue a similar effort now and give it a hard one-year deadline so that concrete proposals are public before the 2028 elections.
Wyoming has a long record of living within its means and keeping its word. Both habits are needed here. A cliff that is clearly visible can still be avoided, but only if the country is willing to face the numbers while there is still time to act.
