name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas manufacturing business responds to candidates’ conflicting accounts of tariff effects
text:
Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, right, and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Adam Hamilton participate in a debate at WDAF TV in Kansas City, Mo., Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Pool photo by Charlie Riedel/Associated Press)KANSAS CITY, Mo. — The two major party candidates for U.S. Senate diverged in a debate Wednesday night on whether tariffs were helping or hurting a Salina manufacturing business they both visited. 
A spokesperson for the business, however, denied U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall’s claim that tariffs were contributing to its growth.
Tim Henry, chief financial officer of Great Plains Manufacturing, said tariffs have constrained some of its competition related to one product area.
“That positive aspect, though, is not enough to offset the other burdens coming with tariffs today,” he told Kansas Reflector.
Marshall, a Republican, and the Rev. Adam Hamilton, a Democrat, highlighted their differences during their final debate before Election Day, offering conflicting views on multiple issues, including tariffs.
The two candidates viewed solutions to illegal immigration differently. They didn’t agree on the root cause of higher fuel prices. They favored different stretches of Kansas highway. They differed in opinion on food assistance funding, healthcare benefits, public safety and approaches to good governance.
John Holt, who moderated the debate for FOX4, asked the candidates about halfway through the event to name businesses they spoke with that had direct knowledge of the impact of President Donald Trump’s tariff policies. Both candidates referenced Great Plains Manufacturing, a subsidiary of Kubota, in Salina. Marshall said Kubota was growing, and Hamilton said Great Plains Manufacturing employees were worried about keeping their jobs.
Republican Sen. Roger Marshall participates in a debate with Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Adam Hamilton at WDAF TV in Kansas City, Mo., Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Pool photo by Charlie Riedel/Associated Press)
Marshall said Kubota was one of three manufacturers he visited in Kansas that were positively impacted by tariffs.
“We’re seeing a manufacturing renaissance because we’re bringing these jobs back home,” Marshall said. “So the tariffs are working.”
Henry, who confirmed both the candidates’ visits, said it’s very possible that when Marshall visited, he witnessed growth at Great Plains Manufacturing.
“But that growth was not because of tariffs,” he said.
Henry said tariffs have had the most significant effect on steel and imported components, leading to higher costs for the business, the dealers it sells to and customers such as landscapers, construction companies and farmers who buy Great Plains products from dealers.
Steel prices have exceeded $1,000 per ton for the past six months. Henry said it used to be a rarity.
Great Plains Manufacturing has undergone building expansion and additions in recent months and years, Henry said, but those arose because of capacity needs and market growth, not tariffs.
Hamilton pushed back during the debate, accusing Marshall of enabling the negative effects of tariffs, particularly at Great Plains Manufacturing, where they are charging $2,000 in tariffs for one of their leading pieces of equipment.
“I did sit down with them,” Hamilton said. “You said you’ve listened in 300 campaign stops. You did not listen in 300 campaign stops. You had 300 photo ops.”
Hamilton said he spoke with Great Plains employees who were concerned about job loss, but Henry said he couldn’t speak to individuals’ concerns.
Holt, a veteran TV journalist, was a strict moderator, reigning in candidates when they exceeded their time allotments and pressing them when they strayed from the question at hand. He also asked the candidates about attack ads, foreign policy, artificial intelligence, gender politics, and social security.
 
 
Both favored
The libertarian candidate in the race, David Graham of Overland Park, was excluded from the debate. He told Kansas Reflector on Monday he is focused on issues like criminal justice reform, government transparency and running a positive campaign.
“My percentage of the electorate is greater than the difference between my two opponents,” he said. “Most of my support comes from voters who simply cannot vote for either of the other candidates.”
Marshall and Hamilton are trying to appeal to voters they are at risk of neglecting. Hamilton is courting Democrats who have become discouraged by the party, independents who aren’t sure where to turn and Republicans fed up with Trump, while Marshall must retain Republican support and curry favor among unaffiliated voters and Republicans who are dissatisfied with Trump policies.
Marshall has made a more concerted effort to campaign following the state fair debate in early September. That’s also when the race attracted an influx of outside spending and national attention. Marshall focused his attacks on Hamilton’s affiliations with national Democrats: Hamilton donated to former presidential candidate and Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Joe Biden, and also served on an advisory council during President Barack Obama’s second term. 
“Adam Hamilton wants Kansans to repent for eating beef, thinks there are 125 different genders, and is a pedophile protector who would vote with Democrats like Chuck Schumer. He will never step foot in the U.S. Senate,” said Samantha Cantrell, regional press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Committee. 
Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Adam Hamilton participates in a debate with Republican Sen. Roger Marshall at WDAF TV in Kansas City, Mo., Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Pool photo by Charlie Riedel/Associated Press)
Both candidates said at the debate there are two genders. Hamilton faced a question about his handling of child abuse incidents in 2005 and 2006 at a church sponsored youth camp, to which he said he used the church’s policies at the time and revised subsequent policies to better screen and train church staff and volunteers.
Marshall repeatedly sought to tie Hamilton to Schumer, D-New York, as he did at a Trump rally Monday in Park City, and said Kansas will determine control of the Senate.
Hamilton told reporters after the debate it seemed as if Marshall thought he was running against Schumer. Marshall mentioned Schumer 17 times during the debate.
Marshall left the debate immediately after its close, forgoing the TV station’s offer to appear on its post-debate show and answer questions from other reporters.
 
Docs on Doc
Before the debate, a handful of medical professionals in white coats demonstrated outside of FOX4’s Kansas City, Missouri, studio, holding signs that said “Kansas patients can’t afford Roger Marshall,” eliciting honks from passing cars. They were organized by a national advocacy group, the Committee to Protect Health Care.
Gary Morsch, a Kansan and former family physician and ER doctor in the Kansas City area, said he felt compelled to stand on a corner of 31st and Summit because of Marshall’s record as a doctor. 
“Roger has a bad name as a doctor — not in his skill but in his M.O.,” Morsch said.
He didn’t buy Marshall’s defense of his debt collection practices. The New York Times reported in September that Roger Marshall had a years-long history of suing patients for medical debt while he was a practicing OB-GYN in central Kansas. At least 81 of those medical debt collection cases involved the arrests of former patients.
“We did the same procedures as every other doctor,” Marshall said. “This was such a small fraction of people that ever went. This is such a gross mischaracterization of the compassion and love and care that the other doctors and the nurses and I, patient after patient, we gave free care to.”
Morsch, who cofounded an international medical aid group and started a regional rural hospital staffing agency, said his personal practice was to forgive patients’ debts if they hadn’t paid within a year, and then ask them to pay as they go in subsequent visits.
“Kind, compassionate doctors write off their debt because they’re rich already,” Morsch said.
Morsch became a member of Hamilton’s church, Resurrection, one year ago. Morsch also ran for Congress as a Republican in 2000 against Phill Kline, who later became the state’s attorney general. Morsch attended the state fair debate in Hutchinson and was one of a half-dozen people thrown out of the Trump rally on Monday.
Gary Morsch, a doctor in the Kansas City-area, is escorted from President Donald Trump’s rally Oct. 19, 2026, in Park City, Kansas, after an outburst. He says fellow attendees threw punches and spat on him when he started shouting at the president. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
He said he hadn’t planned to protest at the Trump rally and went because he “just wanted to hear what he had to say.” He wanted to see the president for himself. It was when Trump started talking about Hamilton that Morsch stood up and began shouting. 
“I was nervous as anything because I didn’t know if I would get arrested,” he said.
He confirmed he was neither arrested after being removed from the rally nor paid to be there, as Trump claimed.
“I’m glad I did it,” he said.
 
The lighter side
Finishing the night on a lighter note, Holt asked the candidates which streaming show they were currently watching and their favorite stretch of highway in Kansas.
Hamilton said he didn’t have the spare time to watch TV but favored sci-fi. Marshall seemed confused by streaming services and said: “I don’t know what you’re talking about,” adding he prefers to watch the Kansas City Chiefs, Kansas State University football and University of Kansas basketball.
Marshall’s favorite stretch of blacktop is Kansas Highway 177 between Manhattan and Cassoday, which includes the Flint Hills National Scenic Byway, and Hamilton’s was Interstate 35 through the Flint Hills.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: One man’s story of supporting the wrong side — and how it applies to the Kansas midterms
text:
Columnist Eric Thomas draws a correlation between sports fans and voters switching teams. (Illustration by Eric Thomas for Kansas Reflector)Here’s my confession: After years of rooting for the wrong side, I am making a change this election season.
For the past decade, in one vital contest after another, I’ve made the wrong choice. Over and over, I have supported a corrupt and evasive cabal. Today, in this column, I come clean with my personal failures.
I admit it. I supported the wrong side, regardless of its dominance.
I write this confession not to congratulate myself for some newfound virtue. It shouldn’t have taken me this long to walk away from this flawed conspiracy of billionaires. The last few years provided dozens of moments when my side acted horribly. I should have long ago abandoned them. So, please don’t mistake this column for self-righteousness. 
Instead, I write it with shame and confusion.
How could I have supported this side for so long — and at so many consequential moments? 
Of course, I am talking about the disgraced downfall of my favorite English soccer club, Manchester City. 
What else could I have been talking about? Certainly nothing in American politics.
I know Kansas Reflector isn’t the place that you come for international soccer news. Bear with me though. Manchester City’s monumental soccer deception contains a lesson in blind allegiance — my blind allegiance — but also a lesson about what happens when that irrational loyalty breaks.
For me, at least, it has morphed into a backlash against the team I once loved.
That dynamic — will rabid fans break away from their chosen team? — pervades Kansas politics right now. In the final weeks before a midterm election, as a deeply unpopular president fumbles and as his flagging conservative party pleads for support, Kansas conservatives must decide: “Is this still my team?”
You don’t need to understand everything about Manchester City’s elaborate and brazen $1 billion cheating scheme. (But maybe you want to.)
To track this analogy, all you need to know is this overly simplified shorthand: Manchester City is MAGA.
And former Manchester City fans like me represent disaffected former Trump voters looking back in regret at our former favorite team.
Here’s the backstory: Since my son and I adopted Man City about a decade ago, the team has risen from mediocrity to dominance. They won tournament championships, league championships, continental championships and world championships with crushing excellence.
However, a recent verdict confirmed the team’s unprecedented run was fueled by a sustained series of sham financial deals. The club’s leadership illegally siphoned the oil wealth of their ownership group into accounts that paid for the best soccer players in the world.
Don’t look for an American sports comparison. It doesn’t exist. Manchester City cheated the system so extravagantly season after season, winning overwhelmingly and performing umbrage at anyone who doubted their purity.
And I cheered along.
When you compare the Man City blue to the MAGA red over the past decade, the similarities are obvious.
Both groups have been routinely threatened by legal proceedings that threatened their legitimacy. Trump supporters had to stomach their president living under indictment and nearly had to reckon with an impeachment (twice). He was never convicted, they reassured themselves.
Man City fans like me similarly could shrug off a 2020 UEFA ban on the team playing matches in Europe. We rationalized: “An arbitration court eventually vacated that penalty,” not because of Man City’s innocence but because of a statute of limitations. (Never mind that those earlier charges mirrored the team’s 114-charge conviction this month.)
Man City and MAGA also share common playbooks in their financial misdealings. Both have pushed money shamelessly from the shadowy authoritative underbelly of worldwide finance into restricted places.
Even their origin stories rhyme. Before its recent supremacy over English football, Manchester City delighted in mocking themselves as hapless failures. They celebrated their clown persona, inflating plastic bananas in the stadium stands to remind their opponents of the club’s perverse pride in slipping clumsily on metaphorical banana peels at every key moment.
Back in America, rewind to 2015. The same Man City jester persona could easily apply to Donald Trump, the reality TV star who surrounded himself with a sideshow cast and delighted in the specter of embarrassment on “The Apprentice.” His signature line, “You’re fired,” was delivered with the faux bravado of a CEO who couldn’t recognize his own silliness.
And yet both MAGA and Man City rose to peak power and popularity, nearly on the same timeline.
I repeatedly have used my weekly column to assail Trump and the MAGA sycophants. At the same time though, I spent my weekends watching (and even a vacation visiting) a sham football team whose winning was based on financial cheatery and evasion.
Yes, I see the hypocrisy.
That’s why, during a recent car ride with my son, I announced that my Man City days were over. No more rooting for lovable Erling Haaland, who charmed America during the World Cup. No more wearing my baby blue Man City team shirt. No more score alerts for the team pinging my phone on Saturdays.
It’s a stretch, you say, to compare leaving an English soccer club to changing your political party allegiance. But maybe not.
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall waves to the crowd at an Oct. 19, 2026, rally headlined by President Donald Trump at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Consider our tribal identity to both political parties and sports teams. Passed down through generations, we often choose both based on what our parents and grandparents selected. The family tailgate signals allegiance to a team. The weeknight kitchen table indoctrinates your political ideology.
At this time of year, politics and sports mix in our neighborhoods as college football flags hang on front porches just a few yards away from political yard signs. Our bumpers boast both our teams and our parties: “Vote Kamala” and “Go Chiefs.”
We fill stadiums for both sports contests and political rallies, often cueing up the same songs to pump up the crowds, either for kickoff or the stump speech.
Note also how the red hats of MAGA serve as a team uniform. After all, they are literally baseball caps.
Both in sports and politics, nothing matters more than the win. In winner-take-all America, a thrilling 51-49 nail-biter grips us in both midterm results and basketball. Prediction markets have recently conflated these twin American obsessions, allowing us to bet on politics and sports on the same platforms.
The day after Trump’s 2016 presidential election win felt just like my team being upset by a renegade playoff underdog. “How could we lose to them?” I wondered out loud during my drive to work, like an obsessed sports fan.
If sports and politics aren’t that different, then maybe the anguish of leaving a sports team resembles the conflicted feeling of sadly shuffling away from your lifelong political party, if even for one vote of discontent in this election.
Polling suggests that conservatives are looking back at the Republican party in anger.
Nationwide, voters favor Democratic candidates by 11 points over Republican ones, according to a poll from the New York Times and Siena University. The polling also suggests the Republican party is having trouble convincing voters that it understands and can fix the problems that define voters’ everyday lives.
To my dear wavering Kansas Republicans as we approach Election Day, after my past few weeks of soccer news, I get the pain of not just leaving a team, but actively resenting it. I feel foolish and misled for my allegiance to Man City.
My soccer solution has been simple: Find a new team. That is Aston Villa, one of many teams that was decimated by Man City’s financial misdealings. I figured there was a bit of poetry in supporting my former team’s punching bag, and they have rewarded me with some great recent victories.
For Kansans who want to show their disenchantment with MAGA, there are two political solutions. The easiest would be simply to stay home, holding out their vote for Republican candidates who are in danger of losing previously safe seats. (Yes, I am talking about you, Roger.)
The other possibility is to vote for an independent, Democrat or third-party candidate.
In my current season of sports fan reckoning, I can offer this to MAGA voters who vote blue in November: “Changing your mind feels unexpectedly great.”
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Bottoms is vowing to expand Medicaid. But has the longtime Democratic priority lost its zip?
text:
Democratic nominee for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, speaks at a press conference with U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock in DeKalb County on the first day of early voting on Oct. 13, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderKeisha Lance Bottoms stood outside the DeKalb County elections headquarters facing more than 20 reporters and news cameras as early voting got underway earlier this month. Flanked by U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock, who had just voted for her, Bottoms rattled off the reasons Georgians should vote for her, too. She didn’t mention Medicaid expansion, the driving force for Democrats in Georgia state races since 2010.
Under questioning by a reporter, Bottoms quickly retrieved the issue, reiterating what she’s said before on the campaign trail: Medicaid expansion is a core issue of hers. But the moment was telling. Has Medicaid expansion lost its fire as a Democratic campaign issue?
“Medicaid still remains a top priority in this state,” Bottoms insisted. “It continues to be a priority and will be a day-one priority for me to prepare our state agencies for that expansion.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
More than 1 million Georgia adults lack health insurance as of the latest data in 2024. Of those, more than 300,000 are in poor or low income groups and many more lack health insurance and have too little income to buy it themselves, according Georgia Budget and Policy Institute researcher Leah Chan. Giving them Medicaid, the government health insurance program for poor and low-income children and some elderly and disabled adults, is a solution proposed under the Affordable Care Act.
But Medicaid expansion as an issue has become more complicated following the passage of President Donald Trump’s One Big, Beautiful Bill Act in the summer of 2025. That law took the Georgia concept of work and activity requirements and mandated them nationwide for all states with Medicaid expansion.
To complicate matters more, Bottoms’ opponent, Rick Jackson, says he, too will expand Medicaid – but calls it “intelligent Medicaid expansion.” By that, part of what he meant is that he would not expand it as fully as other states, or as Bottoms says she would.
The lure of Medicaid expansion
The basics remain: Full Medicaid expansion would still insure more people, even under the new federal law. Studies are under way to estimate how many more people, but the numbers remain substantial. 
To boot, 90% of the bill would be paid by the federal government, bringing in billions of dollars to the state health industry – a point that cheers Democrats, and that gives conservatives mixed feelings.
“Every time we ask the question about Medicaid expansion, a majority of respondents say they favor it,” said Trey Hood, a University of Georgia professor of political science who polls Georgians for the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. 
At the same time, those voters have not held the lack of Medicaid expansion against Gov. Brian Kemp, a Republican who stood firm against expanding it and instead created the Pathways to Coverage Program that has never lived up to his expectations. 
“He has like a 69% approval rating,” Hood says, “That’s phenomenal in this day and age … They’re probably thinking more about the economy in Georgia, and the tax rebates and the tax cuts and all that kind of stuff” that Kemp has implemented as governor.
Then and now
Medicaid expansion was the signature issue of Stacey Abrams, a Democrat who ran unsuccessfully for governor twice, and it helped propel her to within 55,000 votes of beating Kemp in their first contest in 2018.
Since then, Georgia’s uninsured rate remains nearly the worst in the nation. This year that’s even more important to elections, as the price of healthcare piles on to the affordability crisis. Medicaid expansion – giving Medicaid to everyone in a state who is below the poverty line and just above it – would solve a big chunk of that uninsured coverage gap. 
Under Rick Jackson, a big difference would be what happens to the several hundred thousand Georgians who are just above the poverty line. Under Kemp, they are eligible for subsidized private plans on the Affordable Care Act exchange. Jackson said he doesn’t want to take those plans away.
However, it appears that large numbers of those low-income ACA policyholders can’t afford even the tiny co-pays and cost-sharing that hit them after Trump and Congress allowed pandemic-era subsidies to expire. With the subsidies gone, several hundred thousand Georgians dropped their plans. Many of those might remain uninsured under Jackson.  
And where Jackson relies on the longheld reputation of private insurance as better than Medicaid, that’s not always how patients see it.  
Private insurance is losing its luster: In a 2023 survey by the health research nonprofit KFF, 83% of Medicaid enrollees rated the overall performance of their health insurance as excellent or good. In contrast, only 73% of those with ACA plans and 80% of those with employer health insurance had the same feeling.
And for those just above the federal poverty line, the paperwork requirements to show they qualify for Medicaid expansion might not be that bad. Under the new federal law, all it would take for those people to get healthcare is showing they make more than $580 per month – which they do because they’re above the poverty line. 
Working across the aisle
The thornier issue, experts say, is whether Bottoms would be able to enact her health promises with a Republican-controlled Legislature.
Jackson and Bottoms are running neck-and-neck, according to recent polls. The Georgia Legislature, though, is likely to stay in the GOP’s hands.  
No Georgia governor can fully expand Medicaid without a vote from the General Assembly. And priorities that need to be funded through the budget require their cooperation, too.
Bottoms has a detailed six-page wish list of healthcare priorities if she becomes governor. A lot of them take money. They include targeted premium support for ACA premiums, investing in enrollment assistance, increasing reimbursements for rural healthcare, expanding health availability from perinatal care to food assistance and more.
Andra Gillespie, associate professor of political science at Emory University, called it a “a reasonable assumption” to expect Republicans to retain control of the Legislature.  
In that case, Gillespie said, “I think what Bottoms should expect if she is elected governor … is that she’s going to have to work across the aisle in order to achieve healthcare. And that there will probably be some compromises involved in terms of policy.”
But a doctor who is also a health policy professor noted that the political uncertainty cuts both ways. 
Dr. Stephen Patrick, who’s both a practicing doctor and chair of health policy and management at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health, took time away from treating premature babies in the ICU this week to address the Georgia Recorder’s question on that issue.
“There is still a strong incentive to expand Medicaid,” Patrick said. Yes, there’s the increased federal dollars to the state, as well as the possibility of covering more people. 
But he noted that the complications voted in by the Trump administration and its allies also might not last. That One Big, Beautiful Bill law slashed Medicaid spending nationwide by $1 trillion, and that’s going to start being felt very soon by lawmakers and the at-risk hospitals, clinics, doctors and patients that they represent.
“I wouldn’t predict a full repeal anytime soon,” Patrick said. “I also think we should be cautious about assuming the federal changes to Medicaid are permanent.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Commentary: What are the Uihleins getting for their massive investment in Tom Tiffany?
text:
Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein (Screenshot from the New York Times YouTube video 
"Meet the Billionaire Couple Trying to Reshape the Republican Party") For years, billionaire Republican donors Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein have given a lot of money to right-wing causes and Republican politicians. The Washington Post recently reported they rank second only to Elon Musk among the biggest donors in the current election cycle. While they live across the border in Lake Forest, Illinois, they take a special interest in Wisconsin. Yet the millions of dollars in donations they’ve given to the Wisconsin Republican Party look like chump change compared to the massive amount of money they’ve showered on the state since Tom Tiffany announced his run for governor.
The Uihliens upped their contributions to the state party from $20,000 in 2014 to $500,000 in 2017 and more than $1 million in 2018, according to campaign finance data published on the Wisconsin Ethics Commission’s Sunshine website.  Altogether, they gave about $3.6 million to the party between 2016 and 2024. But in 2025 and 2026, as Tiffany launched his campaign for governor, the Uihleins gave exponentially more —  about $34.8 million. 
Thanks to a loophole created under former Republican Gov. Scott Walker, donors can sidestep limits on their contributions to particular candidates by giving unlimited money to political parties, which can then pass the money directly to the candidates. And the Republican Party of Wisconsin has funneled the Uihleins’ money directly to Tiffany. Almost all of the money Tiffany raised in the most recent reporting period came from the Uihleins and one other billionaire, Diane Hendricks.
The Uihleins support a lot of Republican candidates and causes, and would likely have supported the Republican no matter who was running for governor this year. But they have a special relationship with Tiffany. 
Back when he was serving in the Wisconsin state Senate, Tiffany’s district included Manitowish Waters, the small town where the Uihleins opened a resort, restaurant, spa, condominium complex and other businesses, turning the sleepy, lakeside community into a fancy tourist destination. 
Tiffany, who lived 30 miles away in Hazelhurst, was very helpful to the Uihleins when some local residents and environmentalists asked the DNR to study the damage caused by a dam on Rest Lake in Manitowish Waters. The dam kept water levels low in the fall so lakeshore property owners didn’t have to take out their piers and high in the spring, just in time for them to take out their boats. According to the River Alliance of Wisconsin, partially closing the dam’s gates in the spring, “to raise the levels back up in time for boating season” meant ”starving the Manitowish River of water at a time when fish spawn. Downstream river property owners would find mud flats where water had been the day before.”
A 2015 article, “Requiem for a River,” posted by the River Alliance, describes how Tiffany slipped a few sentences into the 2015-17 state budget undercutting regulation of the dam and pronouncing a “death sentence” for the Manitowish River, essentially turning Rest Lake, where the Uihliens owned a condominium complex, into a private lake. 
The tiny provision Tiffany added to the budget (#49 in a long list of last-minute budget tweaks), is titled “Dam Water Level Orders” and specifies that the Legislature must approve changes to a dam in Vilas County. With that deft maneuver, Tiffany killed a years-long effort by citizens to save the Manitowish River and rendered moot an environmental study by the DNR.
“What happened to the Manitowish River is a case study of how far we have fallen in resource conservation,” the River Alliance article concludes. “The Manitowish River now has upstream winners – well-connected and wealthy people who know how to use their influence to get what they want – and downstream losers without the same clout. Tiffany’s bill practically makes the Rest Lake chain a private waterway, in a state that prides itself on managing water in the public interest.”
“My constituents elected me to get results,” Tiffany said by way of explanation, in a Milwaukee Journal Sentinel report on his budget maneuver.
Tiffany’s constituents, of course, included the Uihleins.
His intervention in the matter of the Rest Lake dam was no small favor to the most well-connected and wealthy of all the constituents in his northern Wisconsin district. For the Uihleins, the transformation of Manitowish Waters was a special, personal cause.
Elizabeth Uihlein’s intense focus on funding improvements and reshaping even tiny aesthetic details of Manitowish Waters to her liking divided residents, according to a 2015 article in the Journal Sentinel. Some people appreciated the big investment in the community. Others did not like being left out of decisions about public spaces and objected to how their community was forced to conform to one wealthy woman’s tastes. 
Elizabeth Uihlein herself told the Journal Sentinel, “It’s like a little Aspen. It’s beautiful, but it’s dying.” She suggested that local residents should be grateful for her generosity in providing for them, since they would never make it on their own. “The whole thing is dying up there,” she said. “The money had to come from elsewhere.”
The Uilheins, founders of the packing supply company Uline, are among the richest people in the U.S. They were also some of former Gov. Walker’s biggest donors, a fact that was mentioned in news coverage of the sweetheart deal they got on a swath of lakefront property in Manitowish Waters in 2016. Walker’s DNR gave the Uihliens a stretch of Rest Lake shoreline in exchange for a parcel of state forest land the couple owned in a different part of the state. DNR officials came up with the land swap, the AP reported, after critics objected to the state’s proposal to sell the lakeshore property to Elizabeth Uihlein for more than $100,000 less than its appraised value. 
Long before the deal went through, the Uihleins started making unauthorized improvements on the public land they planned to buy. Some local officials were shocked to discover the extensive paths along the shoreline. Elizabeth Uihlein waved away their concerns. Later, with Walker’s help, she was able to claim the property as her own.
The section of Rest Lake shoreline the Uihliens received from the state gave lake access to their condominium complex. Tiffany’s deft tweak to the state budget ensured that boating conditions remained perfect in the spring, and in the fall the Uihleins and residents of their condo complex never had to go through the hassle of taking in their docks. 
It’s worth asking what kind of return on investment the Uihliens expect to receive from their hyperscale donations to Wisconsin Republicans this year.
“The Uihleins wanted to take over a city. Tom Tiffany gave them their law change,” says Democratic analyst Scot Ross. “A decade later the Uihleins give his campaign $35 million. The dam man wouldn’t have a damn campaign without the Uihleins’ millions.”
In addition to the $34.8 million they funneled to Tiffany through the state party, The Uihleins have also given millions of dollars this cycle to try to elect Republican majorities in the state Legislature. In some cases, they’ve provided almost all of the campaign cash those Republican candidates have raised. 
As the progressive group A Better Wisconsin Together put it in a statement on those donations, “it certainly raises questions about who they’re really looking out for.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: The Ohio Secretary of State’s race in the 2026 November midterm election is a battle of priorities
text:
(Photo by Jim Neuger/ )The Ohio Secretary of State oversees elections and sits on the Ohio Redistricting Commission and Ohio Ballot Board. The seat is up for open election in November, with state lawmaker Allison Russo as the Democratic nominee and current state of Ohio Treasurer Robert Sprague as the Republican nominee.
With such a powerful and important role over Ohio election administration at stake, the two candidates have outlined a significant number of contrasts between each other.
Sprague has made the keystone of his campaign his pledge to keep ineligible voters out of the ballot box, aligning himself with other Republicans including President Donald Trump, who has stood against mail-in voting and in support of strict photo identification requirements for voters.
“Our strategy is simply to get out and talk to voters, and make sure they understand the differences in the office between me and my opponent, Allison Russo, and give people a choice,” Republican candidate Robert Sprague told the Capital Journal.
For Russo, currently the Democratic state representative for the 7th District, her role as secretary of state would be to make voting accessible through all legal methods, including early voting, mail-in voting, and ballot drop boxes.
“Voting should be convenient for our eligible citizens and voters,” Russo told the Capital Journal. “There is no evidence of any voter fraud related to mail-in voting or ballot drop boxes, that access should be protected, and our rules around that work.”
Current Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose is term-limited and running for Ohio Auditor, another statewide position that sits on the Ohio Redistricting Commission.
LaRose has consistently said fraud is rare and that the office’s processes in Ohio are working to keep it that way. Sprague said it’s a system that needs consistent enforcement and continuous improvement. He said voters on the campaign trail agree.
“People feel like the elections are good in the state of Ohio, but obviously it’s because we take fraud seriously,” Sprague told the Capital Journal. “We should require a photo ID for every ballot that’s cast, in person, or by mail.”
Ohio does require a valid form of photo ID by law, which is verified both at the time a voter registers to vote and at polling locations while voting.
Ohio Treasurer Robert Sprague.(Photo courtesy of Sprague for Ohio)
Sprague said he supports an effort spearheaded by Republican lawmakers earlier this year to make photo ID requirements part of the Ohio Constitution, a measure voters will decide on in the November general election as Issue 3.
He said voters he’s talked with in the months leading up the election “overwhelmingly” say they support adding the measure to the constitution.
Opponents of the constitutional amendment note that photo ID requirements already exist in state law, and say these efforts would only make it harder to make changes in the future, as well as open the door to further restrictions on voters.
Russo emphasized the importance of keeping voting convenient and accessible and safe for eligible voters, including options such a drop-boxes and voting by mail.
She pointed to Trump’s history of voting by mail himself in Florida as reason enough that the type of voting is appropriate for anyone who chooses.
“If it is good enough for him, it’s good enough for Ohioans,” she said.
Russo also said she plans to be a “guardrail to overreach that we see, whether it comes from this legislature or the president himself,” referencing private voter data turned over to the U.S. Department of Justice by LaRose as part of a federal demand to all states for voter registration information.
“This is about how am I going to advocate for correct information and push back against that misinformation, and how am I going to advocate for our local elections workers so that they have the resources and the training that they need to do this work,” Russo said.
Sprague and Russo also disagree on the reasons the two haven’t been seen across the stage from one another at a debate since the election season began.
One particular event to be hosted by Spectrum News 1 Ohio was set to put the two together, but while Sprague said he agreed, he said Russo wouldn’t partake.
“It’s a shame, because I don’t see how you can ask people to increase their civic participation when you won’t even talk about your ideas in conjunction with your opponent, in front of the media,” Sprague said.
Ohio House Democratic state Rep. Allison Russo, of Upper Arlington. (Ohio House photo.)
In September, a spokesperson for the Russo campaign released a statement about the idea of a potential debate between Russo and Sprague, saying she “honors and values allowing voters an opportunity to hear directly from the candidates.”
“But before agreeing to a debate with Bob Sprague, we need him to stop spreading lies and half-truths and level-set on reality,” spokesperson Dennis Willard stated.
Following that comment, Russo said the team provided dates to Spectrum for a debate, but the date that was eventually chosen was a day on which Russo was unavailable. She pointed to other events, like media endorsement forums in which Sprague was unavailable.
“I don’t think he actually wants to debate, I think it’s just a political stunt,” Russo told the Capital Journal.
Sprague called Russo’s comments “a cop out.”
With the full heat of campaign season and political advertising upon them, both candidates said they’ve heard from voters about the ugliness that comes out of political campaigns, from the governor’s race to the rest of the ballot of candidates.
Russo attributes a lot of the “nastiness” to rhetoric from Trump and other Republicans.
“People are exhausted by the sort of common, fall-back lines of attacks, and people are looking at what these attacks are, attacking trans athletes, saying immigrants are overrunning our borders, and all of this nonsense,” Russo said. “They’re looking at their day-to-day lives … and it just feels very disconnected from what people are actually experiencing.”
Sprague said the current environment means polarization has led to a smaller amount of undecided voters.
“I think the change this time is there are fewer people that are undecided, but it makes it all the more important to be able to talk to them and address some of their pain points.”
Those pain points include the price of gas and property taxes, along with affordability on a general level, Russo and Sprague said.
What agreement there is between the candidates lies in a pledge to lead the office of secretary of state with qualified individuals, and with the public in mind, even if the candidates may disagree on the priorities that will drive it.
“As the chief elections officer, I think people very much understand that you can only hold elected leadership accountable and transparent for their decisions and about their decisions if you have the power of your vote, and if we maintain fair, free, and secure elections,” Russo said.
Sprague pointed to the necessity of professionalism.
“I think the most challenging thing is you want to run the office professionally,” Sprague said. “You want to have competent people running these offices.”
Early voting, military, overseas, and absentee voting have already begun in Ohio, ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
The last day for early in-person voting is Nov. 1, and absentee ballots must be received by local boards of elections by Nov. 3. In-person voting on election day begins at 6:30 a.m. and ends at 7:30 p.m.

title: Ohio policymakers wrestle with prediction markets as wagers on sports and politics explode
text:
A casino sports book. Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images.People wanting to know who will win a contest before it’s over isn’t new, but as Ohioans head to the polls this year, there’s a bit more prognostication than in recent elections. Political polling has been around for nearly a century, but in the past several years prediction markets have muscled in as another way to tap the wisdom of crowds.
Instead of surveying opinion, prediction markets let users put their money where their mouth is — placing bets on not just political contests, but sporting events, commodity prices, even the weather.
And bet they have.
On Polymarket as of Oct. 21, users had staked $1.4 million on the outcome Ohio’s U.S. Senate race and another $603,000 on the governor’s race. On Kalshi, users had bet $8.1 million on the Senate race and $3.6 million for governor.
Game six of Major League Baseball’s American League Championship Series between the Cleveland Guardians and the Tampa Bay Rays produced $22.1 million in bets on Kalshi. The National Football League matchup between the Cleveland Browns and the Pittsburg Steelers earlier this month? $119.5 million.
Those dollar figures are fueling anxiety among policymakers in Ohio and around the country. Ohio state Sen. Bill DeMora, D-Columbus, has filed legislation to treat sports transactions on prediction markets like gambling at any other sports book, and to ban bets on politics outright.
Kalshi and Polymarket are also the subject of dozens of federal lawsuits around the country, primarily for their role in sports betting. States typically regulate sports gambling and they stand to lose out on significant tax revenue if prediction markets can avoid oversight.
Cases have made their way up to eight different appeals courts, including the Sixth Circuit which covers Ohio. Opinions among those appellate courts don’t quite line up, though. So, earlier this month, Ohio Republican Interim Attorney General Andy Wilson led a coalition of 38 states urging the Supreme Court to settle the matter.
The litigation
The Sixth Circuit case dealt with a disagreement between district courts in Ohio and Tennessee. Prediction markets like Kalshi contend their customers aren’t so much betting as buying “swaps” — a financial derivative where two parties agree to exchange payments based on a real-world outcome. They’re typically used as way to hedge against financial risk, and they’re overseen by The Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
Kalshi argued the federal law granting the CFTC authority over event contracts like swaps means states can’t regulate its sports offerings. A federal court in Tennessee agreed, but another in Ohio rejected that argument.
Late last month, a unanimous Sixth Circuit panel sided with Ohio. The judges didn’t buy that Kalshi’s argument that their contracts meet the statutory definition of swaps, and even if they did, the CFTC’s jurisdiction doesn’t preempt state gaming laws.
“The States’ gaming laws do not directly target the licensing and operation of (prediction markets),” the court wrote. “They are thus not the sorts of laws that Congress sought to preempt, and their application to Kalshi does not subvert Congress’s goals.”
The Third Circuit, however, came to the exact opposite conclusion.
Wilson’s amicus brief in that case insists the courts are “hopelessly confused and divided,” and urges the Supreme Court to settle the matter. He cited conflicting appellate decisions in three circuits as well as an “incomplete sample” of more than two dozen lower court cases involving prediction markets.
“Like the circuits, these courts disagree not only about whether state law is preempted, but why — and how,” Wilson wrote.
The courts have previously determined regulating gambling is a core element of a state’s police powers. And while federal authorities regulate derivatives like swaps, Wilson contends, that doesn’t mean prediction markets should be able to sidestep state oversight.
“They cannot strip the states of their core sovereign power through relabeling and window-dressing,” Wilson wrote.
Wilson added that state restrictions like licensing, minimum age requirements and spending limits have been put in place to protect citizens. The prediction markets’ reading of federal law, he wrote, “threatens to wipe out all those critical protections.”
Prediction market platforms ignoring Ohio’s legal threats

Ohio Capital Journal reached out to Kalshi and Polymarket for this story. Kalshi did not respond. In a written statement, a Polymarket spokesperson said simply, “Prediction markets are regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission under a federal framework, not a patchwork of state rules.”
Ohio proposals
Following the Sixth Circuit decision, Ohio’s Casino Control Commission issued cease and desist orders to prediction markets operating in the state. The companies largely ignored them.
While market operators continue to insist on a distinction between their services and gambling, Ohio state Sen. Bill DeMora, D-Columbus, has introduced legislation to explicitly define their sports contracts as gaming.
“(The Sixth Circuit) decision solidifies that prediction markets are not exempt from Ohio law,” DeMora said in a statement, “and that they need to be regulated the same way other sports betting companies are.”
“Ohio is losing out on tens of millions of dollars every month by not regulating these sites,” he added.
In addition to Ohio Senate Bill 430, which brings prediction markets within the scope of sports gaming, DeMora has introduced Ohio Senate Bill 479 which prohibits betting on elections.
In the Ohio House, state Rep. Sean Brennan, D-Parma, has filed Ohio House Bill 887 which bars public officials and employees from participating in prediction markets, or disclosing privileged information relevant to a prediction market contract.
“With the rise of prediction markets in Ohio and across the country,” DeMora said, “this is not a partisan issue; it is one that needs to be addressed immediately.”

title: Commentary: Vice President JD Vance: The Ohio ‘hillbilly’ who learned to punch down
text:
SHARONVILLE, OHIO - OCTOBER 21:  Vice President JD Vance speaks during a campaign rally at the Sharonville Convention Center on October 21, 2026 in Sharonville, Ohio.  Vance traveled to Ohio to campaign for local Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections. (Photo by Jacquelyn Martin-Pool/Getty Images)JD Vance built a national career as the Ohio hillbilly who could explain what it felt like to be looked down on. Now, as vice president, he is inviting Americans to look and punch down on others.
I am a gay man in Sandusky, Ohio. When the vice president uses the suggestion that a man is gay to get a laugh, I recognize the move. A powerful man is reminding people like me that our dignity is available for his entertainment.
Campaigning in Texas on Oct. 13 for Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, Vance answered a man who shouted that he loved him. He returned the sentiment, made clear it was platonic, and added: “I’m the vice president, not James Talarico.” Talarico is Paxton’s Democratic opponent.
The joke only works if being gay would make Talarico ridiculous. Without that assumption, there is no punchline. That is homophobia, delivered with the authority of the vice presidency.
Vance went further. Attacking Talarico’s statements about transgender children, he cast suspicion on Talarico’s internet search history — then admitted he was “just guessing.”
One statement he invoked came from a 2023 interview in which Talarico praised transgender children who had come to the Texas Capitol to advocate for themselves. Vance offered no evidence of misconduct.
Consider what that asks an audience to believe. A public official expresses care for children who feel threatened, and the vice president invites people to imagine something sinister. The children vanish as human beings. Their vulnerability becomes ammunition against the adult who spoke up for them.
Adults can disagree about laws affecting transgender young people. Those disagreements deserve serious arguments. Suggesting that compassion hides predatory intent poisons the debate before it starts — and warns everyone watching that defending these kids may get their own name dragged through the mud.
Ohioans are watching the same tactic on our own televisions. A Senate Leadership Fund ad attacking Sherrod Brown features a young woman who detransitioned, describing “irreversible surgery on kids like me.”
Court records show she had that surgery at 19, in Texas. Ohio has banned the procedure for minors since 2024. Whoever made that ad assumed Ohio voters wouldn’t check. We should prove them wrong.
Vance’s Ohio story makes this especially galling. He grew up in Middletown, served in the Marines, went to Ohio State and Yale Law, and wrote “Hillbilly Elegy.” Few people have had more opportunity to learn how one label can flatten a whole human life.
There are gay hillbillies, too, Mr. Vice President. They have families and hometowns. Their claim to belonging is every bit as real as yours.
Vance chose “hillbilly” as the defining word of his public introduction. People from poor and Appalachian families have the same capacity for generosity as anyone else. His conduct belongs to him, and Ohioans should refuse to let him pass it off as our regional character.
In 2016, writing in The Atlantic, Vance warned that Donald Trump offered struggling communities emotional relief without solutions. He called Trump “cultural heroin.” He understood how grievance makes people feel powerful while leaving their problems intact. That warning now describes the politics its author practices.
I have spent more than 30 years in communications. I know why this tactic works. An insinuation forces an opponent to defend his character. An anti-gay joke gives an audience permission to feel superior. The argument that follows eats the attention that should go to what candidates intend to do with power. The people being demeaned pay for the distraction.
Vance owes Talarico a withdrawal of the unsupported insinuation. He owes gay and transgender Americans a plain acknowledgment that our lives deserve respect.
Republican officials who say they welcome gay voters should say whether they accept a vice president using those voters’ identity as a punchline.
Ohioans should demand an answer, too. Vance carried our state’s name into national office. A man with his platform can afford to make an argument and stand behind the evidence.
He wrote a book about the people he came from. Ohio should judge him by the people he is willing to step on.

 Catching Our Eye

• Domestic violence. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Sarah Donaldson reports, “Ohio saw the second-highest domestic violence fatalities in a decade.”
Domestic violence fatalities in Ohio fell about 15% since last year, according to the annual fatality count released Wednesday morning by the Ohio Domestic Violence Network.
But the decrease followed a 37% surge last year, and the number of deaths was still the second-highest recorded in the last decade.
• Vance’s Trump politics. Axios reports, ““Stop whining”: What Vance’s take on Ohio ad controversy means for 2028.”
Vice President Vance’s call for fellow Republicans to “stop whining” about Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial attack ad in Ohio’s race for governor showed a key part of his political mindset ahead of his expected run for president in 2028: Never back down.
Why it matters: Channeling President Trump, Vance has shown contempt for what he sees as the old-guard GOP’s reflex to cave under pressure from Democrats and the media.
• Breaking Eisenhower’s globe. The Washington Post reports, “Hegseth wanted Eisenhower’s globe for his office. His staff broke it.”
Ordinarily, moving historical items within the building is a deliberate process overseen by trained curators. Instead, Hegseth’s staff dispatched its own team to relocate an Eisenhower globe. They lost control of the artifact and dropped it, sending the globe crashing onto its base and impaling the fragile shell near Antarctica, according to those familiar with the incident. The resulting gash appears to be several inches wide.

name: Maryland Matters
title: On a quiet first day of early voting, officials make a lot of noise about Question 3
text:
Voters line up to cast their ballots several minutes after doors opened Thursday at Honeygo Community Center in Baltimore County on the first day of early voting in Maryland. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Inside the centers on the first day of early voting Thursday, the process appeared smooth and largely calm as voters lined up in relatively short lines to cast their ballots. Outside, it was a slightly different story at select centers.
At the Silver Spring Civic Building, Democratic elected federal, state and local officials gathered to argue for Question 3, the proposed constitutional amendment that would loosen rules on how lawmakers draw congressional districts. The argument was simplified on signs that sprouted up next to the center: “Stop Trump. Votes Yes on 3.”
“Question 3 is about making sure that Marylanders are in charge of our democracy and not Washington, D.C. and not [Republican President] Donald Trump,” Gov. Wes Moore (D) said Thursday at the Silver Spring center, standing alongside Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-8th) and other Democratic officials.
“What Donald Trump has been doing for the past year is trying to manipulate elections. He’s been trying to cancel mail-in balloting. He’s trying to do middecade redistricting in Republican states, but not Democratic states. He is making this systemic,” said Moore, who’s also on the ballot for reelection.
About 48 miles north, the vibe outside the Honeygo Run Regional Park in Baltimore County was different, and so were the signs. Instead of “stop Trump,” the signs urged voters to cast their ballots against Question 3 to “stop gerrymandering. Save our voice.”
Gov. Wes Moore (D) and Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-8th) share a laugh for early voting at the Silver Spring Civic Center, as Scott Goldberg, left, and  Montgomery County Councilmembers Kate Stewart and Will Jawando look on. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Voters cast their ballots Thursday at Honeygo Community Center in Baltimore County. Voting was smooth and quiet for the most part. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Del. Kathy Szeliga (R-Baltimore County) chats with a voter outside Honeygo Community Center on the first day of early voting in Maryland. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Signs for candidates for state and local offices greet voters on the first day of early voting Thursday at the Mechanicsville Fire House in St. Mary's County. (Photo by Angela Breck)Del. Jheanelle Wilkins (D-Montgomery) puts her ballot in a drop box in Silver Spring on Thursday, the first day of early voting. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
“I think you need a law degree because the smartest lawyers in Maryland wrote the question,” Del. Kathy Szeliga (R-Baltimore County) said outside the Honeygo Community Center. “It’s unfortunate, but we hope people will know that if you don’t want partisan, political gerrymandering, you need to say no.”
With few major contests on the ballot this fall, and few seats in doubt, Question 3 is expected to grab most of the attention over the next few weeks. It’s the continuation of a fight that has gone on for a year, as Maryland lawmakers debated mid-decade congressional redistricting to counter Republican-led states that had redrawn their maps for partisan advantage, at Trump’s urging, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Szeliga’s point about lawyers refers to the involvement of the Supreme Court of Maryland, which rewrote the ballot question that was passed during a two-day special session of the General Assembly in August.
Two circuit court judges, in Anne Arundel and Dorchester counties struck down the bill. The Supreme Court agreed with the lower courts that the question was misleading as written. But rather than trick it down, a divided court decided in early September to rewrite the question and let it go before voters.




Ballot Question 3
“FOR the purpose of clarifying that certain requirements apply only to districts for the election of members of the Senate of Maryland and the House of Delegates; authorizing the General Assembly to grant original jurisdiction to the Supreme Court of Maryland to review the congressional districting plan of the State; and providing that nothing in the Maryland Constitution provides applicable criteria for the boundaries of a congressional districting plan.”




If approved by voters, Question 3 would amend the Maryland Constitution to change the rules applying to the ways congressional districts are drawn, making it easier for the party in control to draw a map that favors it. Currently, seven of Maryland’s eight congressional districts are held by Democrats — the only Republican seat is held by eight-term Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st), representing the Eastern Shore-centered First District.
The changes would not take effect until the 2027 legislative session, and would not affect congressional races until 2028 at the earliest.
A poll released earlier this month showed a more people opposed to the question than in support of it. But some voters interviewed Thursday morning backed Question 3, and Moore’s explanation that it goes against the Trump administration.
“I support him [Moore] totally,” said Lee Holland, a Democrat from Baltimore County, one of the first voters to cast a ballot at Honeygo Community Center.
Vanessa Davis, a Democrat from Montgomery County, was more blunt.
“I want every Republican running to lose,” Davis, 71, said outside the Silver Spring Civic Building. “Donald Trump is trying to make everything for the Republicans … We got to fight back some kind of way, and if Republicans are going to back every single thing Donald Trump wants to do, we have to at least make [an] attempt to slow it down.”
In addition to Question 3, voters this fall are faced with a choice between reelecting Moore or backing Republican nominee Dan Cox in a rematch of the 2022 race between the two that Moore won easily. Voters will also weigh in on other contests, including the race for attorney general, state comptroller, the state’s eight U.S. House members and all 188 members of the General Assembly.
Voters who didn’t vote by mail, and don’t want to wait until Election Day on Nov. 3 can cast their ballots at one of 94 early voting centers around the state. State law allows counties to open one additional early voting location: Anne Arundel, Calvert, Garrett, Harford, Montgomery, Queen Anne’s, St. Mary’s and Washington counties did so this year.
Turnout for the first day was not immediately available Thursday evening, but was expected to be posted some overnight. Four years ago, nearly 45,000 voters cast ballots on the first day of early voting. Maryland State Elections Administrator said Thursday that it had been a “smooth first day [of] voting.”
Early voting runs through Oct. 29 with polls open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Polls open at the same time on Election Day.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s new money curriculum should start at the check cashing counter
text:
Starting with the class of 2027, my class, every public high school student in Connecticut has to pass a half credit course in personal financial management before they can graduate. It is a good law, and I say that as someone who once wrote a financial literacy curriculum so bad I had to throw it out after one class.
It was a slide deck about budgeting, built for kids in Bridgeport through a program I started called Bridges 2 Business, and it assumed everyone in the room had a checking account. Nobody did.
What most of them had was years of experience reading their parents’ bank statements and filling out insurance forms for them, and it took me about 20 minutes to figure out they understood how money moves through a poor household a lot better than I did. I rewrote the curriculum after that class and kept rewriting it, and it’s now 25 lessons taught by more than 30 volunteers to over 100 students at three schools.
The thing they taught me has a name. Economists call it the poverty premium, which is a polite way of saying it costs more to be poor. A family without a bank account pays a fee to cash a paycheck and pays again to buy a money order for rent. If they send money to relatives abroad, as a lot of Bridgeport families do, they’ve paid a 1% federal tax since January that applies only to transfers paid in cash or money orders, while transfers from a bank account are exempt. 
Washington looked at the unbanked and decided they weren’t paying enough.
This is not a small group. The FDIC’s most recent survey found 9.5% of Hispanic households and 10.6% of Black households had no bank account, more than double the national rate, and the most common reason was that they couldn’t meet a minimum balance. 
I used to think the fix was to tell people to open an account, which is roughly what my first slide said. I remember a father at a check-cashing counter in Bridgeport splitting his paycheck on a Friday, part for rent and part wired to his mother in Guatemala, and thinking he was making a mistake, and only later understanding that the counter was open when he got off work, didn’t ask for a minimum balance, didn’t hold his check for days, and spoke Spanish, which is more than I could say for the bank. So the mistake was mine, and it was the same mistake my slide deck made, which is assuming the expensive choice is an uninformed one.
So here’s my ask for the State Department of Education as schools build out the new course. Put a unit in it on the poverty premium, including how to find accounts certified by the national Bank On program, which have low monthly fees and no overdraft charges and are offered by several of the biggest banks in the country. The standard version of this course teaches credit scores and compound interest. Those matter, but a kid in Bridgeport who’s been managing a household’s cash since sixth grade needs to know what the cash is costing.
I don’t know whether a class fixes any of this. A student who learns what a minimum balance is still can’t make one appear, and some of the kids I teach will graduate knowing exactly how the poverty premium works and keep paying it anyway, because the counter is still the only thing open at 7 p.m. I haven’t figured out what to do about that part.
My first curriculum had a slide titled “Opening Your First Checking Account.” I still have it. It’s a very nice slide.
Marcos Cruz is a senior at Fairfield College Preparatory School in Fairfield and the founder of Bridges 2 Business, a financial literacy program for immigrant students in Bridgeport.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Trump calls for Omar to resign, defends Ramaswamy campaign ad at Iowa rally
text:
President Donald Trump waived to supporters gathered at the Sioux Gateway Airport in Sioux City Oct. 22, 2026 for a rally supporting Iowa Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)SIOUX CITY — While President Donald Trump came to Sioux City Thursday to rally with Iowa Republicans facing contentious elections in November, he spent a portion of his speech defending Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and criticizing Minnesota U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar.
Iowa currently has an all-GOP federal delegation. This could change in the 2026 midterms — polls and political forecasters predict the U.S. Senate race and three of the four House races in Iowa will be highly competitive in the Nov. 3, 2026 election. State and federal leaders have said Iowans could play a decisive role in determining which party controls Congress for the remainder of Trump’s second term.
Trump came to Iowa as part of a larger tour to support Republicans across the country. While he did speak in favor of U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, running for the U.S. Senate, as well as Iowa Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn at the event, he also took time to talk about recent campaign developments in other states.
He brought up a “breaking news” report that Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, had not used her “real name” when she was to elected and sworn into Congress. The president was referencing reports published Thursday about an ongoing investigation into Omar and claims that the representative’s full name was “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi.”
“It’s not looking good because she used a fake name to be sworn in, I assume she must immediately have to resign from Congress,” Trump said.
The president also said to “please inform our great speaker of the House of Representatives … Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, her real name, has openly admitted to fraud, and she will not be legally allowed to be a member of that august body. If you get sworn in with a false name, I would imagine that’s pretty tough.”
In a response to Fox News Digital earlier Thursday, a spokesperson for Omar said, “This is completely false. Ilhan Omar is her real name.”
Earlier in October, Homeland Security Investigations conducted an early morning raid of Omar’s home in the District of Columbia, which a Department of Justice official told States Newsroom was “part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation” regarding her immigration paperwork. The president called Omar a “scammer” and said she comes from a “non-country” as a Somali refugee.
Additionally, he defended Vivek Ramaswamy as the Republican candidate has faced significant backlash for a campaign advertisement in the Ohio gubernatorial race. Ramaswamy’s campaign released an ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, who called her daughter a “liar” and urged Ohio voters to not support her in the election.
Court documents show Acton’s mother lost custody of Amy Acton and her brother after Acton’s stepfather was charged and arrested for sexually abusing her when she was 12 years old. The stepfather pleaded not guilty and fled the state after posting bond, becoming a fugitive until his death in 2004.
The advertisement has drawn bipartisan criticism. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, called for Ramaswamy to pull down the ad Thursday, saying, “it’s just wrong to continue to run it.” But Trump said when Ramaswamy called him to consult on the ad, he told the Republican gubernatorial candidate to keep the ad up.
“The mother is calling the daughter a terrible person and a liar, everybody should be so lucky,” Trump said. “Why would you shield somebody from that? Why would we do that? So I told them, leave it up and look upstairs and say, ‘thank you, God, very much. I appreciate it.’ But that’s a hot story for me. They wanted to take down an ad. I only wish I could have had an ad like that against somebody. But as it turned out, we didn’t need it.”
Trump, Hinson criticize Turek on Statehouse votes
Hinson, who is running to fill Republican U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst’s seat in 2026, repeated comments on the important role Iowa plays in 2026 at the Trump rally.
“The stakes here are pretty high, right? That’s why you’re all here today,” Hinson said. “Iowa could very well be the majority-making seat in the United States Senate. If we lose this seat here in Iowa, the Democrats will control the U.S. Senate, mark my words. And that is why Chuck Schumer is spending over $50 million dollars here in Iowa to try to buy this seat.”
Hinson is running against Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, a Democrat, in the upcoming election. The U.S. Senate race has brought a massive amount of outside spending into the state. According to Open Secrets’ analysis of recent Federal Election Commission disclosures, Turek has brought in slightly more than Hinson in outside spending at $59.85 million to the Republican’s $51.67 million.
The Republican claimed her opponent was receiving support from groups affiliated with Senate Democratic leadership because Schumer, Senate minority leader, “knows that he would have a reliable and very liberal vote in Josh Turek.”
Trump called Turek a “woke far-left radical.”
He claimed the Council Bluffs Democrat had voted to “allow schools to turn your children transgender without informing the parents” and that “he wants men in girls’ bathrooms.”
These claims are reference Turek’s vote against a Republican-led measure banning transgender students from using school restrooms that conflict with their assigned sex at birth. He also voted against a measure that requires parental consent if a child requests gender-related accommodations like the use of  different name or pronouns at school — a law that is currently being challenged in court for banning books that contain depictions of sexual acts from being available in K-12 school libraries.
Trump also criticized Turek’s votes related to several immigration measures. Turek has campaigned as a Democrat who supports strengthening border security and improving the immigration system, saying in a campaign ad, “I’ll work with anyone to fix it, including President Trump.”
Hinson said Turek’s voting record showed he was “too liberal for Iowa.”
“There’s never a good time to elect a ‘tax and spend’ liberal to the U.S. Senate. Now would be the worst time,” Hinson said. “We’re going to keep Iowa red and keep Iowa, Iowa.”
A Turek campaign spokesperson emphasized the Democrat’s bipartisanship in the Iowa House.
“Josh Turek is a common-sense prairie populist who has always done what’s right for Iowans, even when it meant breaking with his party. Josh voted with Republicans more than 700 times to lower prices, cut taxes, address immigration, and keep Iowans safe – that’s why he is independently recognized as one of Iowa’s most bipartisan and effective legislators, and it’s why Iowans will send him to the Senate in 12 days.”
Hinson pushes back on campaign attack ad claims
Hinson also took time to address “two of the lies that are really starting to irk me” in campaign attack ads.
She said Turek and Democrats were lying about her by saying she trades stocks “and got rich off my public service.” In statements and campaign ads, Turek has criticized Hinson for retaining private stock in Elliott Hartman Agency, an insurance company founded and sold by her husband, despite speaking and voting on banning members of Congress from stock trading.
Hinson told the crowd her husband “sold his business, and now he has a private stake in that business, but not public stock — it’s as simple as that.” She said she and her husband sold all of their publicly traded stocks when she was elected to Congress in 2021.
“Nothing could be further from the truth, and Josh Turek knows that, so shame on him for lying about this,” Hinson said. “But it’s been very clear, and I’ve made it very clear that I am fighting to actually root out the corruption in both parties in Washington D.C. — career politicians need to be held accountable, and so I want to clear the air on this vote. I actually voted to ban members of Congress from trading stocks. The only reason that’s not a law is because Chuck Schumer and the Democrats blocked it in the Senate.”
Hinson said “the other lie that he’s pushing is that I tried to vote to block the release of the Epstein files.”
“Can you believe that? I think, as a woman, I find that one especially offensive. Right? It’s disgusting. It’s completely made-up nonsense,” Hinson said.
As a member of the U.S. House, Hinson voted, alongside all members of the state delegation, to pass the “Epstein Files Transparency Act” in 2025. But Democrats have cited her vote against an amendment compelling the release of the Epstein files, and her decision to not sign off on the initial discharge petition to override leadership and force a vote in the House on the bill as proof that she did not support releasing the information about the Florida financier and convicted sex offender. In July 2025, Hinson stated she disagreed with the approach of U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky, to compel the release of the files while saying she supporting Americans pursuing justice against Epstein’s crimes.
“I will say this: of course, I voted to release the Epstein files, and I think every single creep who actually did something wrong should be held accountable for that, and I think there’s a special place in hell for those people,” Hinson said.
A Turek campaign spokesperson disputed Hinson’s characterization of her stock holdings:
“Ashley Hinson is lying to Iowans – she still owns up to $5 million in private insurance stock and made as much as $1 million off it last year alone, despite telling Iowans she sold all her stock. Iowans are sick and tired of corrupt politicians like Hinson who sell out Iowans to enrich themselves and their donors.”
Republicans urge voters to stay enthusiastic
Trump urged voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and vote for Republicans in the election to ensure his administration’s work on issues from immigration law enforcement to tax cuts stay in place.
“If (Democrats) win the midterms … it’s the start of something very bad, very dark, very horrible for our country,” Trump said. “They will do it again. They’re going to open up the borders. They’re going to have men playing in women’s sports. … But the proud people of Iowa will never let that happen.”
He also repeated claims that he will provide $5,000 to every American if Republicans win the U.S. House and Senate in the midterms. Even if Republicans retain majorities in both chambers, there is no certainty that the appropriations proposal would be passed through both chambers.
“If the Republicans win, you’ll each have $5,000 in your pocket and economic success for our country like we have never ever seen before,” Trump said.
Iowa GOP Chair Jeff Kaufmann told the crowd to not let reports about Democrats’ chances in the upcoming midterms dampen their spirits.
“I need you to ignore the polls. I need you to ignore the media. And I want you to do one simple thing: Follow your heart and follow this process that has done so much for this state historically,” Kaufmann said. “Iowa loves Ashley Hinson. Iowa loves Ashley, and Iowa will forever love Donald Trump.”
Iowa Rep. J.D. Scholten, D-Sioux City, attended the rally to observe — and said he believed Democrats may be in a stronger position in 2026 than in the last Trump midterm election cycle in 2018. In 2018, he was the Democratic nominee for Iowa’s 4th District, when he lost to former U.S. Rep. Steve King by a 47% to 50.3% margin — a much tighter race than typically seen in the longtime conservative stronghold.
He said he believed there was less GOP enthusiasm in 2026 than in 2018, because more Iowans are frustrated with Trump and Republicans for high gas costs, the ongoing war in Iran and the impacts of tariffs on Iowa’s economy.
“I don’t think any pollster, anybody can really predict who’s going to be turning out or who doesn’t turn out,” Scholten said. “The one big thing that I notice is — I lived 2018, and we pulled out, Democrats pulled out a ton of votes. … What I don’t think we anticipated was Republicans were just as excited, and turned out a lot of people too. I don’t feel that this time.”
