name: Daily Montanan
title: Valley County says train shooting was actually varmint hunting
text:
Train cars on a BNSF line sit in Helena, Montana, on Aug. 12, 2025. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)Two people who spoke to law enforcement after a suspected train shooting near Glasgow were, in fact, using a spotlight to find “varmints” and shoot them.
No shots were directed at the train, the Valley County Sheriff’s Department said in a press release on Thursday.
“This was a misunderstanding on the part of the BNSF crew, who reasonably but incorrectly believed they were being targeted,” a press release from Valley County said. “No malicious intent was established. No charges will be filed.”
Valley County on Wednesday morning sent out a press release after BNSF Railway employees reported a gunshot on Tuesday evening around 10. Investigators at the scene recovered a shell casing and the Valley County Sheriff’s Office issued a description of the truck in a press release.
According to the Valley County release, two people voluntarily spoke with law enforcement on Wednesday and cleared up the misunderstanding.
“Both individuals came forward promptly and voluntarily following the initial press release, cooperated fully with investigators, and were forthright throughout the process,” the press release said. “Their cooperation is acknowledged and appreciated.”
BNSF Police and Valley County both consider the matter closed. In Thursday’s release, the Sheriff’s Office reminded the public of firearm safety.
“Shooters have a responsibility to be conscientious of their surroundings, including proximity to public areas, roadways, rail corridors, and locations where other people may be present. The basic rules of firearm safety exist for good reason and apply in every situation,” the press release said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: DOJ sending election observers to Indianapolis, Lake County
text:
Voters head into a polling site at Grand Park in Westfield, Indiana, on Tuesday, May 5, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Federal observers are coming to Indiana’s Marion and Lake counties on Election Day as voters in the two heavily Democratic areas cast their votes.
A U.S. Department of Justice email addressed to the Marion County Election Board didn’t indicate why the counties were selected for monitoring.
“Out of 92 counties in Indiana, Trump’s DOJ has chosen two counties with the largest populations of Democratic voters and Black and Hispanic voters to subject to ‘election monitoring.’ It’s no coincidence,” said U.S. Rep. André Carson, who represents most of Indianapolis, in a news release.
Candidate signs staked outside the City-County Building, a vote center, in Indianapolis on Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“It’s also no coincidence that it comes just weeks before an election, when Trump has record low poll numbers. It follows multiple, illegal attempts to change election procedures for his benefit, from a president who still maintains the 2020 election was stolen,” continued Carson, who urged residents to vote early.
Marion County Clerk’s Office spokesman Dan Goldblatt said the choice comes off as partisan, but that the election board is “very curious to learn more.” The election board’s attorneys are scheduled to meet with DOJ representatives Oct. 28, he told the Capital Chronicle.
Lake County Election Board Director Michelle Fajman said she’d only “heard speculation” as to why the two counties were selected.
The DOJ, meanwhile, assured officials that the monitors “only observe.”
“They do not intrude or interfere in any way in the voting process,” the Marion County letter reads, signed by DOJ Civil Rights Division Trial Attorney Hwui Lee.
The monitors will look for compliance with a range of federal voting rights laws, plus the Americans with Disabilities Act, according to the letter.
The email was sent Tuesday afternoon to a general inbox at the Marion County Clerk’s Office that residents typically use for questions about child support or ticket payments, Goldblatt said. Election board members didn’t receive word until Wednesday.
Guidance to poll workers
Marion County election board members have already approved a “poll worker response protocol.” The document offers step-by-step guidance for several hypothetical scenarios involving DOJ monitors and other federal representatives.
Lake County’s Fajman said guidance to poll workers will depend on whether the monitors stay outside or have credentials authorizing them to enter polling places.
“We’re waiting more information from the state,” said Fajman, who reported being notified Wednesday by the Indiana Election Division. “… That’s how we’ll determine the notification for our poll workers that either one: you may see these individuals outside the polling place, or two: these individuals may have credentials that would look like this, and hopefully give them a copy of what to be aware of.” 	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US




Communicating that to Lake County poll workers won’t be difficult, Fajman said. The election board has their email addresses, and they’re picking up their Election Day supplies next Saturday.
“So, (we) appreciate, you know, the heads-up notice that they are trying to provide, so that way we can inform our poll workers of expectations and what they may or may not see on Election Day,” she said.
Local officials in other states have reported receiving similar notifications from the DOJ. Some had observers for primary elections in the spring.
The DOJ in August announced plans to dispatch 1,000 election monitors to midterm election polling places nationwide, according to comments made to Bloomberg.
That’s significantly more than the 289 observers sent out for the 2022 midterm elections, and above the 714 involved in the 2024 presidential election, CBS News reported.

name: VTDigger
title: Could nuclear power return to Vernon?
text:
Spent nuclear fuel casks are stored at the Vermont Yankee nuclear power plant in Vernon in July 2019. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Susan Smallheer was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on Oct. 22, 2026. 
VERNON — There could be another nuclear reactor in Vernon’s future.
Vermont Public Service Commissioner Kerrick Johnson told the Vernon Selectboard on Tuesday evening that a new, small modular nuclear reactor might be a good fit at the Vermont Yankee site, which is almost cleared of the former 600-megawatt reactor that shut down in 2014.
Johnson said the Vernon site is very valuable not just to Vernon, but to Vermont and the New England power grid because of the transmission infrastructure located next to the reactor site. The switchyards and transformer belong to the Vermont Electric Company, known as VELCO, a consortium of Vermont’s electric utilities that owns the state’s transmission lines and infrastructure.
Johnson said affordability and climate change are behind Vermont’s interest in new nuclear technology. But he said a new, small modular reactor is years away — seven or eight was his estimate.
Small modular reactors are in development in the U.S., but one was recently approved for use in Ontario, Johnson said. The small reactors are in use in Russia and China.
When Yankee shut down, the town lost hundreds of well-paying jobs and a substantial tax customer, and it’s been watching reuse of the site closely.
Electricity demand in Vermont is high and growing, and was behind the consumers’ electric bills, which have climbed substantially in the past four years and are expected to grow 40% in coming years, he said in an earlier interview.
The interest in the Vernon site is part of a New England-wide renewed interest in nuclear power as the region grapples with increasing demand, Johnson said, and a move away from fossil fuels.
He said the modular reactor could work well with the battery storage facility that is under consideration by a Texas company, PowerTransitions, which has been holding public meetings in Vernon to introduce the company and its potential plans for the site.
NorthStar Group Services, which has owned Vermont Yankee since 2019 and is rapidly completing its $602 million demolition and cleanup, has signed a lease agreement with PowerTransitions.
But Johnson said the state of Vermont actually has the right of first refusal on the Yankee site and is evaluating what its role should be. The state option is included in the small print in the 2018 memorandum of understanding the state signed with Entergy Nuclear and NorthStar when Yankee changed hands.
Johnson said there is strong support among New England’s governors for nuclear power, and all six governors signed a letter of support in March. There are two remaining nuclear reactors in New England — the Seabrook station in New Hampshire and Millstone 2 in Connecticut.
Together, the two nuclear stations produce about a third of the electricity consumed in New England, according to recent reports.
Vernon officials and townspeople listened intently to Johnson, who himself is a former Vermont utility executive with VELCO and the former Central Vermont Public Service Corp., which was purchased by Green Mountain Power’s corporate owner.
Johnson acknowledged that support or opposition to nuclear power appears generational — with younger people supporting nuclear power as it is viewed as “cleaner” and not contributing to climate change and has a low-carbon footprint. Older generations, he said, remain skeptical.
Vernon resident Maddy Arms, who is a member of the Vermont Nuclear Decommissioning Citizens Advisory Panel, which coincidentally met Monday night to get an update on decommissioning, predicted there would be continued opposition from anti-nuclear activists who campaigned for decades against Vermont Yankee’s operation.
Selectboard members voiced neither support nor opposition, but thanked Johnson for coming to Vernon and speaking directly to them.
Johnson said Gov. Phil Scott has long been a supporter of nuclear power, and in fact Scott reiterated that support during a gubernatorial debate on Vermont Public Wednesday evening.
“I don’t think we should close the door on nuclear,” Scott said, saying he was interested in “small-scale nuclear.”
In contrast, his Democratic challenger, Amanda Janoo, said she was not a supporter of nuclear power, and she pointed to the high-level radioactive waste still stored in Vernon from Yankee’s 42 years of operation.
There are 57 large steel and concrete casks at the Vermont Yankee site, which contain the spent fuel and will remain in Vermont until the federal government builds a storage facility.
A small modular reactor would still produce high-level radioactive waste, but some of the reactors are being designed with re-processing of its fuel, which reduces but does not eliminate the amount of waste.
Johnson said that modular nuclear reactors would be about half the size of Vermont Yankee in terms of generation, but would create more jobs than a battery storage or solar facility. A data center has been all but ruled out for the Vernon site due to local opposition.
“Vernon will always have a say,” he said. “The department would never support” a project opposed by Vernon, he said.
Johnson took pains to reassure the Vernon board and townspeople that a new nuclear reactor wouldn’t be installed in their town without their support and approval, not to mention state approval. Johnson said the majority of Vermonters would support the return of nuclear generation to the state, claiming the figure was 63% according to a recent survey.
Vermont electric customers receive about 28% of their power needs from Seabrook, which is largely owned by a Florida-based power company, NextEra Energy.
Vermont Yankee and its sister plant, the Pilgrim reactor in Massachusetts, were shut down by its then-owner Entergy Nuclear because its power was too expensive compared to natural gas, not because of environmental concerns or political opposition. In fact, in the weeks leading up to Entergy’s announcement, the company had won a major court case against the state of Vermont in a federal appeals court about the future operation of Vermont Yankee.
Johnson said the state was looking at other options to increase power availability, including a “resizing” of the wind facility in Searsburg and an off-shore wind project proposed by a Canadian province, as well as upgrading a key transmission facility in Highgate, which brings Hydro-Quebec electricity to Vermont.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa nursing homes lead the nation in short-staffing violations
text:
Harmony House Health Care Center in Waterloo is one of seven Iowa nursing homes cited three times for insufficient nursing staff during fiscal year 2026. (Photo via Google Earth) Iowa’s nursing home inspectors issued more citations for insufficient staffing last year than regulators in any other state in the nation, an Iowa Capital Dispatch review of federal data shows.
The Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services data show that 66 Iowa nursing homes were cited at least once for insufficient nursing staff during fiscal year 2026. With seven Iowa homes cited for the violation three times, and seven more cited twice, the total number of insufficient staffing citations issued in the state was 87, the data show.
That places Iowa — which has far fewer nursing homes than more populous states — at the top of the rankings for insufficient-staffing citations.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Lack of adequate staffing has long been considered the single biggest contributor to poor quality resident care in nursing homes. Attempts to impose more stringent federal requirements on nursing home staffing have been opposed by the Trump administration, Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, and Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird.
The CMS data shows that the 10 states with the most nursing home citations for insufficient staffing in fiscal year 2026 were:
Iowa: 87 citations in a state with 393 nursing facilities.
Illinois: 85 citations in a state with 669 nursing facilities.
California: 59 citations in a state with 1,169 nursing facilities.
Michigan: 49 citations in a state with 424 nursing facilities.
Pennsylvania: 51 citations in a state with 657 nursing facilities.
New York: 42 citations in a state with 597 nursing facilities.
Ohio: 31 citations in a state with 926 nursing facilities.
Missouri: 23 citations in a state with 489 nursing facilities.
Minnesota: 16 citations in a state with 339 nursing facilities.
Wisconsin: 11 citations in a state with 323 nursing facilities.
The data show that Iowa also ranks high in the number of citations related to a more specific staffing requirement that calls for nursing homes to have at least one registered nurse on duty for at least eight hours each day.
Iowa nursing homes were cited 16 times for that nurse-specific violation. Only the states of Texas, Illinois, Ohio, California, Missouri and Oklahoma had more citations for violating the registered-nurse requirement.
The seven Iowa homes that were each cited three times during the year for insufficient staffing are Accura Healthcare of Carroll; Pinnacle Specialty Care in Cedar Falls; Ravenwood Specialty Care in Waterloo; Foxglove Wellness and Rehabilitation Center,  aka Stone Cottage Care Center, in Sigourney; Harmony House Health Care Center in Waterloo; Iowa City Rehab & Health Care Center, and Southfield Wellness Community in Webster City.
The seven Iowa homes that were each cited twice times during the year for insufficient staffing are Hallmar Village in Cedar Rapids, Harmony Cedar Rapids; Bishop Drumm Retirement Center in Johnston, Exira Care Center, Garden View Care Center in Shenandoah, Parkridge Specialty Care in Pleasant Hill and Pine Acres Rehabilitation and Care Center in West Des Moines.
Typically, violations for short-staffing do not result in fines or any other financial penalties in Iowa, although short-staffing can contribute to issues of safety and neglect that do result in fines.
Trump, Bird fight staffing mandates
In March 2026, an Iowa Capital Dispatch review of the CMS data showed that in 2025, 60 of Iowa’s 397 nursing homes — 15% of all the homes in the state — were cited for insufficient staffing. That represented a rate of staffing-level violations that was two to five times higher than most other nearby states.
In fiscal year 2023, 14% of Iowa’s 422 nursing facilities were cited for insufficient staffing, which was more than double the 5.9% national average at that time. At that time, only five other states had a worse record of compliance with the sufficient-staffing requirement.
Nationally, a 2026 report from the Long-Term Care Community Coalition indicates that in the third quarter of 2025, almost 9 in 10 nursing homes fell below their expected their staffing levels, with the average facility under-staffed by 24% on a daily basis. The report is based on federal data derived from the homes’ self-reported payroll information and assessment of residents’ needs.
In 2023, the Biden administration sought to impose new staffing requirements on all nursing homes that collect taxpayer money through Medicare and Medicaid. The new requirements, which would have allowed rural homes facing workforce shortages to receive a waiver exempting them from the mandate, would have required homes to have a nurse on staff 24 hours per day.
In November 2023, Reynolds and 14 other Republican governors sent Biden a letter objecting to the new rule and predicting it would “force over 80% of facilities nationwide to hire more staff,” which would result in many of them closing.
In 2024, Bird, along with other Republican attorneys general and industry representatives, sued the Biden administration to block implementation of the rule, with Bird calling it an “attack on senior care that will force nursing homes out of business, increase costs for families, and remove access to senior care altogether.”
The Trump administration eventually dropped the federal government’s legal defense of the rule, effectively killing most of its requirements.
‘Help me, help me!’
Among the specific staffing violations cited by state inspectors this past year — none of which resulted in fines or penalties — at Iowa nursing homes:
Accura Healthcare of Carroll: In October 2025, inspectors noted that the staff took as long as 39 minutes to answer call lights and the facility had no call-light policy in place.
In December 2025, inspectors found there still was no policy in place, and wait times still extended to 39 minutes. The administrator allegedly explained the facility was following “the state standard” which says call lights are “expected” to be answered within 15 minutes.
In April 26, 2026, inspectors noted the issues remained unresolved, with wait times of up to 39 minutes and no call-light policy in place.
Pinnacle Specialty Care in Cedar Falls: In November 2025, inspectors watched as nurses and aides walked past, without entering, rooms where residents’ call lights were activated. Some residents complained of waiting 60 to 90 minutes for their call lights to be answered.
In June 2026, residents reported waiting up to two hours, and the director of nursing acknowledged the home’s policy didn’t include a “targeted time” for responding to a call light.
In September 2026, inspectors reported interviewing seven residents, all of whom expressed concern with staffing levels or waiting up to two hours for a call-light response while missing medications or being left to lie in urine.
Ravenwood Specialty Care in Waterloo: In October 2025, an inspector reported watching as a female resident sat for 55 minutes in her wheelchair, wearing clothing recently soiled with fecal matter, near the nurses’ station, waiting for assistance. Throughout the hour, the inspector reported, employees sat at the nurses’ station doing charting or watching the hallways, while offering no assistance to the woman. One resident complained of waiting up to an hour for a call light to be answered.
In May 2026, one resident complained of waiting four hours for a call-light response, while another said he didn’t bother with the call lights since the staff takes too long to respond. One resident complained of being forgotten and left on the toilet, saying she eventually grew physically numb. No penalties were imposed, although fines were proposed for violations related to untreated injuries and resident assessments.
In August 2026, a resident reported she had her call light on from 3 a.m. to  6:45 a.m., at which point she got out her cellphone and called the facility to inform the staff she needed assistance in her room. The facility staff told inspectors the resident’s call light was switched on at 5:21 a.m., not 3 a.m., but acknowledged the staff didn’t respond until 6:45 a.m. when the phone call was made.
Foxglove Wellness and Rehabilitation Center, aka Stone Cottage Care Center, in Sigourney: In December 2025, a resident reported he repeatedly had to use his cell phone to contact the staff after they failed to respond to his call light. A registered nurse at the home reported she was concerned with staffing levels due to the high acuity levels of residents who were totally dependent on the staff or had behavioral issues.
In May 2026, residents complained of waiting up to four and a half hours for assistance. A quadriplegic resident said he sometimes had to use Siri to activate his cell phone and call the facility’s front desk to reach a staff member. When he needed assistance, he said, it could take more than 30 minutes for the staff to respond. The delays, he alleged, resulted in several instances in which he wasn’t repositioned for more than two hours – putting him at risk of pressure sores.
In September 2026, inspectors reviewed the care of 16 residents and found that in all 16 cases, the home had failed to provide sufficient staffing to ensure timely assistance with medications, showers and daily activities. One resident reported waiting up to three hours for a call-light response.
Harmony House Health Care Center in Waterloo: In March 2026, inspectors reported that the staff failed to answer residents’ calls for assistance in a timely manner, with logged wait times sometimes extending to 90 minutes or more. “The failure persisted despite residents reporting concerns through interviews and the facility’s own grievance logs and after staff were reportedly re-educated,” inspectors stated. “Staff, including the director of nursing, failed to respond to a prolonged audible alarm indicating an issue with a resident’s essential feeding-tube pump, and the facility did not have a written policy to ensure timely call-light response.”
In June 2026, residents told inspector wait times were sometimes close to an hour and complained that workers would sometimes enter their room, shut off the lights so the electronic monitoring system would indicate a staff response, and then leave the room, not returning to provide any assistance for up to 45 minutes. According to inspectors, the home’s written policy authorized that sort of response to call lights in nonemergency cases.
In September 2026, the home was cited again for insufficient staffing, noting that in 24 instances over a 25-day period, one resident had to wait more than 15 minutes for a call-light response. Some of the responses were logged as taking 40 minutes, 51 minutes, 58 minutes and two hours and 16 minutes.
Iowa City Rehab & Health Care Center: In December 2025, inspectors alleged the home failed to have sufficient staff to meet residents’ needs, with employees taking up to an hour to answer call lights.
In August 2026, the facility was cited for the same violation with the director of nursing telling inspectors the facility was “aways working on staffing.”
A few week later, in September 2026, the facility was cited again, with inspectors stating the home “failed to have an adequate number of staff to assist residents” with daily activities such as bathing or to answer call lights. At the time, the call-light system wasn’t working so residents were given bells to summon the staff.
While one inspector watched, a resident’s bell rang at 9:26 a.m. At 9:31 a.m. the bell continued to sound and the resident began yelling, “Help me!”  At 9:34 a.m., the resident could be heard yelling, “Help me, help me!” One minute later, with the bell still ringing, the same resident was yelling for help in a louder voice. At 9:37 a.m., the inspector reported, a certified nursing assistant “walked down the hall as (the resident) yelled, “Help me!” According to the inspector a registered nurse later explained that the home needed more staff, saying it was hard to care for 53 residents with only one nurse working.
One worker reportedly told inspectors that with the call lights not working, the staff was “supposed to check on residents that are paralyzed and not able to yell for help.” When asked how she would know whether a resident rang their bell, the worker stated if she heard a bell, she’d walk the halls and find out who had rung it. “When asked how staffing was at the facility, she stated, ‘It’s horrible,’” the inspector reported.
A quadriplegic resident said he was left on the toilet for about three hours because the staff couldn’t hear his bell ringing. The home’s administrator told inspectors the home was not short-staffed. When told what inspectors had observed, the administrator said she’d “look into it.”
Southfield Wellness Community in Webster City: In November 2025, the facility was cited for taking up to 22 minutes to respond to call lights.
In July 2026, residents complained of waiting an hour or more for assistance. While an inspector watched, one resident was in bed with their call light activated at 7:46 a.m. and was yelling for help. At 8 a.m. and the call light remained activated, and the resident continued to shout for help. At 8:21 a.m., more than a half-hour after the initial call for help, a worker responded.
A certified medication aide complained that management was instructing the staff to answer the call lights due to the inspectors’ presence in the building, adding that she felt responses should happen even without the inspectors being there.
In August 2026, inspectors again cited the home for failing to provide sufficient to meet residents’ needs. One of the home’s licensed practical nurses told inspectors she ran call-light reports periodically to check on response times and had spoken to management about residents’ long waits for assistance. No penalties were imposed.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Medicaid cuts could cost NJ $3.7B annually, NJ officials say
text:
Medicaid funding shifts will cost New Jersey up to $3.7 billion dollars in federal funding annually, state officials said Thursday. (iStock / Getty Images Plus)By the end of the decade, New Jersey stands to lose up to $3.7 billion dollars in federal healthcare funding each year under the Trump administration’s changes to Medicaid, much of it in cuts to state-directed aid for hospitals and doctors, state officials warned lawmakers Thursday.
The shifts in Medicaid, the state and federally funded program known here as NJ Family Care, are also expected to force up to 330,000 people off their existing health plans, a change that Human Services Commissioner Stephen Cha said could reduce payments through the program to Garden State doctors and hospitals by an additional $2 billion to $3 billion annually.
“Behind every number is a person: someone who needs a checkup, a parent managing a chronic condition,” Cha told legislators during a hearing at the Trenton Statehouse.
Cha joined Health Department Commissioner Raynard Washington and Susan Ochs, head of the Department of Banking and Insurance, Thursday to brief the Senate’s health committee on the likely impacts of the changes to Medicaid and other social service programs triggered by a law Trump signed in July 2025.
Some of the changes, like tighter restrictions on which groups of legal immigrants can qualify for Medicaid, have already taken effect, while cuts to hospital funding will be phased in over the years to come.
The biggest change comes in January, when 540,000 low-income adults on NJ Family Care will need to start submitting documents to prove they are working, volunteering, or in school at least 20 hours a week to still get benefits. Limited exemptions are available for people who are disabled or have a chronic health condition that makes them unable to work, rules New Jersey and other states are challenging in court.
Cha said his department is working with county welfare agencies, the insurance companies that provide NJ Family Care plans, community groups, and others to inform people about the pending changes and help them navigate the additional bureaucracy involved. Members facing the new work requirements will also be forced to enroll in Medicaid every six months, instead of once a year like now.
“New Jersey cannot fully offset every federal reduction, but we can invest thoughtfully, reduce administrative complexity, and work with the Legislature, providers, counties, and community organizations to build a system that can withstand change,” Cha said.
Even if the state succeeds in limiting the impact of the new law, Cha’s office predicted it will cost New Jersey at least $1.8 billion annually and leave at least 165,000 additional adults uninsured. NJ Family Care currently covers 1.8 million residents.
Sen. Holly Schepisi (R-Bergen) pressed Cha on the potential funding gap, noting that the state spent more than $250 million less on Medicaid last year than it had anticipated, a savings she said could offset future funding loss. Cha said the decline reflected actual costs that were lower than expected, noting that the Treasury Department allotted the extra money to other programs.
Sen. Owen Henry (R-Middlesex) lamented the Democratic majority’s use of funds for pet projects.
“The priorities need to change. The money is here,” he said.
The loss of federal Medicaid dollars will result in cuts to state-run programs that fund hospital outpatient services, something New Jersey has relied on heavily in recent years, but shrinking insurance coverage also means fewer reimbursements for doctors who treat these patients. Even if it’s not reflected in the state budget, the cuts will impact healthcare in New Jersey, Cha explained.
“We are going to see those cuts in different ways. It’s not going to show up as a $1.3 billion to $3 billion deficit, but it’s $1.3 billion to $3 billion less from the federal government,” he said.
Trump said the changes he approved to Medicaid aim to reduce costs to the federal government, which pays for roughly two-thirds of all Medicaid expenses nationwide.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Work begins on spendiest bridge project in South Dakota history
text:
The South Dakota Highway 44 Platte-Winner Bridge, which crosses the Missouri River in the southeast part of the state. (Photo courtesy of the South Dakota Department of Transportation)State and federal officials on Thursday heralded the start of a yearslong, $290 million project to replace the “vital lifeline” that is South Dakota’s longest bridge.
State Highway 44’s Platte-Winner Bridge, which opened in 1966, is more than a mile long and crosses the Missouri River in the southeastern part of the state. The new bridge will be 115 feet longer, built just to the north of the existing bridge, which will remain open through the anticipated June 2030 completion date for the new crossing. Removal of the old bridge is scheduled to run through November 2031.
The new bridge is the most expensive undertaking in South Dakota Department of Transportation history, Secretary Joel Jundt told the state’s Transportation Commission two months ago.
On Thursday, Gov. Larry Rhoden spoke at the groundbreaking, alongside South Dakota’s U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson and its senators, John Thune and Mike Rounds.
State commission accepts $290 million bid for Platte-Winner Bridge, $40 million above estimate

The new bridge, with its anticipated 100-year service life, “is a responsible investment in South Dakota’s transportation infrastructure,” the governor said in a press release about the event.
Federal Highway Administrator Sean McMaster was also on hand for the groundbreaking. The federal government has pitched in $65 million for the project through the Federal Highway Administration Competitive Highway Bridge Program grant, and the state’s congressional delegation secured another $25 million in federal funds.
“For rural communities across south-central South Dakota, this Missouri River crossing is a vital lifeline that keeps supply chains moving, connects local producers to markets, and ensures families can safely reach key recreational areas,” McMaster said in the Rhoden press release, in which McMaster pointed to the project as evidence that President Donald Trump’s administration is “putting federal dollars to work to rebuild America’s infrastructure.”
Other federal grant applications for the project were pending as of August, when Jundt spoke about the project to the Transportation Commission. Those applications were still pending as of Thursday, Department spokeswoman Julie Stevenson told South Dakota Searchlight.
Burnsville, Minnesota-based Ames Construction got the contract for the bridge work through a bid $39.25 million higher than the state’s estimate.
The estimate came in high based on complexities of building in deep water, specialized equipment, the bridge’s size, market conditions and the remote location, which creates logistical costs, Jundt said in August.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Much of southern New Mexico a designated screwworm ‘infested zone’ as USDA reopens cattle imports
text:
Three confirmed New World screwworm cases detected the week of Oct. 16, 2026, have left much of southern New Mexico in an “infected zone” as designated by the New Mexico Livestock Board. (Photo courtesy of Michael Miller/Texas A&M AgriLife)Three confirmed New World screwworm cases in recent weeks in New Mexico have left swathes of the state’s southern border under a state-designated “infested zone,” which demarcates where ranchers must receive state Livestock Board authorization before moving their cattle. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The zones span much of southern New Mexico, according to an interactive map the state publishes online, including the bootheel in southwest New Mexico and an area east of Las Cruces. The zones are aimed at preventing further spread of the New World screwworm, a parasitic fly whose maggots feed on live tissue.
The discovery last year of the screwworm’s reemergence has raised widespread concerns for the cattle industry across much of Mexico, along with New Mexico, Texas and Arizona.The fly advanced northward through Mexico after being mainly contained in Central America for several decades. 
Over the last week, the state Livestock Board has announced three confirmed infections, including of a calf and horse in Grant County on Oct. 16, followed by an Otero County cow on Wednesday. 
“We are working closely with our state and federal partners to investigate these cases, increase surveillance and monitor for additional infestations,” State Veterinarian Samantha Holeck said in a statement Wednesday.
Holeck’s announcement notes that incoming cold weather may slow the screwworm’s spread but not completely eliminate it, so she and other state officials urged livestock owners to remain vigilant and keep an eye out for infections in their animals. 
The reported infections come days before the United States Agriculture Department has authorized two New Mexico ports of entry along the state’s shared border with Mexico to resume accepting some livestock imports.
The ports at Columbus and Santa Teresa accepted approximately one-third of all the nation’s cattle imports until screwworm concerns prompted their closure last July. 
New Mexico border officials say New World screwworm outbreak hitting state hard

The prohibition on cattle imports meant a halt to a $1.3 billion industry, according to authority officials, and is hitting the Columbus, N.M. port of entry particularly hard. Mexican cattle growers ship approximately 300,000 cattle through Columbus and Santa Teresa ports of entry each year, according to the New Mexico Border Authority.
On Tuesday, USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins visited Columbus to announce the Columbus port would resume accepting cattle Oct. 26 and that the Santa Teresa would resume accepting horse imports that same day. 
In a statement touting its “phased” reopening, the USDA said it would consider reopening another port of entry in Nogales, Ariz., “if conditions continue to support safe trade and all required inspection arrangements and infrastructure are in place.”

name: VTDigger
title: Separate ballot asks voters to decide $54.9 million career center bond
text:
An architect’s drawing shows the proposed site plan for the new facility on the U-32 campus. Image courtesy of CVCC

A version of this story by Lisa Scagliotti was published in the Waterbury Roundabout on Oct. 17, 2026.
For the second year in a row, voters in 18 Washington County communities are being asked to consider supporting a bond to pay for a new Central Vermont Career Center.
But this year’s $54.9 million proposal is dramatically different — and a fraction of the cost — from the $149 million bond that voters rejected in 2025.
There’s one catch, however: Voters will need to seek out the ballot with the bond question, because it is not being automatically delivered in the mail.
First, the proposal.
Creating a second campus at U-32
The revised plan for expanding the Central Vermont Career Center is substantially different from the initial plan the district put to voters a year ago. In 2025, the district proposed purchasing a 27-acre property in the Graniteville section of Barre Town with a plan to construct a 167,000-square-foot facility that would have replaced the center that’s been operating at Spaulding High School in Barre since 1969.
Cost, location and site issues such as traffic and wetlands all contributed to the resounding rejection at the ballot box in a special vote last November, when 60% of the voters opposed the plan.
Demand from interested students and space constraints at the existing center motivated district leaders to go back to the drawing board. For example, the center had 443 applications for the 2025-26 school year compared with just 134 applicants for the 2020-21 school year. That’s an increase of 230% in five years. School officials say the current center can accommodate approximately 245 students, with more than 100 qualified students waitlisted or turned away each year.
With 39 students attending the career center this year, Harwood Union High School is the third-largest sending school to the center after Spaulding and U-32, according to district data.
After the bond failure last fall, career center school district officials said they were determined to put together another proposal. They carefully reviewed voter feedback across many platforms, examined the demand for their programs, looked at the current facility’s constraints, and considered multiple alternatives before landing on the latest project plans.
CVCC Superintendent and School Director Jody Emerson said district leaders decided to take a different approach to considering the size, structure and cost of the project.
The new plan calls for keeping the Spaulding career center in operation and building a free-standing, two-story, 61,000-square-foot facility at U-32 High School. Together, the two career center locations will be able to enroll approximately 450 students.
The new configuration would not only open up CVCC programs to more students, Emerson said, but it would make greater use of both campuses and shared resources, creating more opportunities for students to pursue academic and career education together.
Emerson said that today’s career and technical education programs have evolved to combine both technical skills and academic focus. Students may be working toward entering the workforce in specific technical careers, but they also may be preparing to pursue higher education in their chosen fields.
“Every program at CVCC has college credits, industry-recognized credentials, or both. Students don’t need to choose between career or college; they need to be provided opportunities to explore both,” Emerson said.
The two-campus approach would give CVCC the ability to expand its offerings while making good use of the facilities and resources in both locations, she said. The additional location would also allow the center to expand its offerings in fields including healthcare, early childhood education, construction, automotive/diesel, hospitality, arts and business.
For example, the site plan for the new center at U-32 designates an “animal area.” Asked about that, Emerson said the spot is a placeholder for space that could be used for a future veterinary technician program. “Animal science is likely to be a new program by the time the building opens,” she said.
The spot chosen for the new career center facility at U-32 is now a playing field. School officials say the site can accommodate creating a replacement field elsewhere on the school’s campus.
On the ballot
For the project to be approved, voters across the 18 municipalities of the career center school district need to vote in favor collectively. After Election Day, ballots are tallied in a single combined count. Specific city and town results are not determined.
The career center district includes all the communities across six central Vermont school districts: Barre, Montpelier Roxbury, Washington Central, Harwood, Twinfield and Cabot.
The CVCC ballot that all voters will use has two questions: one asking voters whether they approve of the $54.9 million bond, and another asking voters to approve a 30-year lease with the Washington Central Unified Union School District, which owns the U-32 property.
In addition, voters in the Washington Central district, which covers East Montpelier, Middlesex, Worcester, Berlin and Calais, will have their own local ballot with a single question pertaining to the career center project. They are being asked to approve their school district entering the 30-year land lease with the career center school district.
Bond vote ballots won’t be mailed automatically
It’s important for voters to know that ballots for the CVCC project are not being automatically mailed to all registered voters across the district with their general election ballots. The decision to hold the bond vote for the November election was made too late for those ballots to have been printed and ready to be mailed with the general election ballots for Washington County voters.
In Vermont, general election ballots have been mailed to all registered voters. Those ballots contain all the elections from Congress and statewide offices such as governor and lieutenant governor, to state House and Senate seats, regional judges and justices of the peace. Voters are encouraged to vote using the ballot they receive by mail and return it by dropping it off at their municipal clerk’s office or at the polls on Election Day.
However, to weigh in on the Central Vermont Career Center bond (and the lease question in Washington Central), voters will need to either vote in person on Election Day, Nov. 3, or seek out the career center ballot ahead of time.
Career center ballots are now available from city and town clerks in the 18 communities. To vote on the bond before Nov. 3, voters may request a ballot by mail from their local clerk. They also can visit their municipal clerk’s office in person to cast their ballot on the bond (and in Washington Central towns, the additional ballot on the lease question).
Voters can direct questions to their local town and city clerks.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Administrative judge sides with Florida instructor regarding Charlie Kirk post
text:
Tyler Robinson, left, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, sits while Judge Tony Graf conferences with attorneys during a preliminary hearing at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah on July 9, 2026. (Pool photo by Spenser Heaps for the Associated Press)The Florida Department of Education failed to prove its allegations that a Clay County public school instructor violated state laws and rules when she posted about conservative activist Charlie Kirk after he was killed, a state administrative judge has ruled.
The case involves Kelly Brock-Sanchez, an Exceptional Student Education facilitator at Ridgeview Elementary in Orange Park when Kirk was shot and killed in Utah in September 2025.
“This might not be the obituary we were hoping to wake up to, but this is a close second to me,” she initially posted on her private Facebook page under the pseudonym “Kelly Steele Magnolia” that Sept. 10.
She wrote a second post about Kirk the next day, Sept. 11: “Charlie Kirk had 2 kids and STILL SAID gun deaths were the cost to keep the 2nd Amendment…this philosophy led to his own death becoming an acceptable cost…one of the top five Trump surrogates. One less evil person on this planet.”
After Brock-Sanchez’ posted privately about Kirk, it was quickly copied and went viral within hours.
Officials at Ridgeview said they received more than 800 emails regarding the post, 300 posts on ts Facebook page, some of which were threatening, and numerous calls and voicemails.
In her ruling on Wednesday, Division of Administrative Hearings Judge Suzanne Van Wyk wrote that that although Brock-Sanchez’ first post “was clearly impulsive, and may have been reckless, thoughtless, offensive, and even callous,” the Department of Education had failed to prove the five specific allegations made against her.
“The allegation that Respondent’s post was made on a public social media account is a threshold allegation from which the rest of the material factual allegations flow — that it constituted grossly immoral conduct, that it caused parents to question her qualifications as an educator, and that the overwhelming response to her post necessitated increased security at Ridgeview which cost the District money,” Van Wyck wrote. “Without establishing that material threshold issue, Petitioner failed to prove all the material allegations in the Administrative Complaint.”
The judge noted that each of the allegations was predicated on Brock-Sanchez having posted her opinion on a “public social media account” for the all the world to see.
“She did not,” she writes. “Though someone decided to more broadly disseminate the post, Respondent did not make that decision, and the consequences of posting to a ‘public’ account cannot be attributed to her.”
Backlash
Brock-Sanchez was one of several Florida educators who posted messages about Kirk immediately following his death that Sept. 10. The next day, then-Education Commissioner Anastasios Kamoutsas sent a public letter informing all school districts that he planned investigations of every educator who “engages in this vile, sanctionable behavior.”
On Sept. 22, 12 days after Kirk’s death and her social media posts, Kamoutsas said he had found “probable cause” to seek the permanent revocation of Brock-Sanchez’ educator’s certificate. He said she had violated three statutes and two rules in the Florida Administrative Code.
“This teacher’s comments were grossly immoral, reduced her effectiveness in the classroom, failed to protect the health, safety and welfare of students, and did not distinguish her personal views from that of a public educational institution,” he wrote. “Accordingly, I am seeking a permanent revocation of this teacher’s license.”
Following an investigation, Clay County Superintendent David S. Broskie that Sept. 25 recommended to the school board that Brock-Sanchez’ contract be terminated effective Oct. 2, which it was.
Brock-Sanchez says her attorney will now go back to the Clay County School Board to see whether members want to come a financial settlement or go back to court.
Brock-Sanchez has also filed a federal lawsuit against Kamoutsas in his official capacity, alleging violation of her First and Fourteenth Amendment rights and that the administrative complaint he filed constituted “governmental retaliation for protected speech.” That case is set to go to trial in November 2027.
Kamoutsas stepped down as education commissioner in July to become president of Polk State College.
600 people
A Reuters investigation last November estimated that 600 people across the country had been terminated, disciplined, investigated, suspended, or otherwise admonished for their Kirk posts, likening the reaction to an ideological purge.
In addition to teachers who have won their cases in Florida after being fired for posting about Kirk’s death, employees with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission have also been successful in fighting for their rights after being terminated for such messages.
Last month, the agency agreed to settle free-speech lawsuits by three employees who’d been fired over posts about Kirk’s death, the Tallahassee Democrat reported.

name: National
title: The percentage of people without health insurance is growing
text:
Dr. Navdeep Lehga sets up equipment in the exam room of a  mobile clinic in Mendota, California in 2025. The percentage of working-age adults without health insurance has grown in the past two years, according to a new report. (Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local) The percentage of working-age adults without health insurance has increased in the past two years, largely because many people can no longer afford Obamacare coverage after Congress allowed federal subsidies to expire at the end of last year.
The uninsured rate for adults ages 19-64 rose to 11.2% this year, up from 8.9% in 2024, according to a new analysis by the Commonwealth Fund, a health policy and philanthropic nonprofit.
Nearly half of the 7,362 working-age adults who participated in the group’s biennial health insurance survey said they were uninsured, underinsured, or experienced a gap in coverage this year. Half said they delayed or avoided getting medical care because of the cost, compared with 46% in 2022.
The subsidies significantly lowered the cost of Obamacare coverage — making it free or nearly free for some people with low incomes. But the aid was designed as a temporary pandemic-era measure, and Congress allowed it to expire at the end of last year.
As a result, the percentage of working-age adults with health insurance from the marketplaces created under Obamacare, officially known as the Affordable Care Act, declined to 6% this year, from 8% in 2024.
The percentage of working-age adults enrolled in Medicaid also declined, to 13% this year from 16% in 2022, as many states removed people from the rolls at the conclusion of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The increase in the uninsured rate almost certainly will accelerate in January, when the Republican tax and spending law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act takes effect. That law will require many Medicaid recipients to prove they are working or engaging in approved community service activities for at least 80 hours a month.
The law also mandates that states verify enrollees’ Medicaid eligibility every six months.
Another factor in the growing percentage of people without coverage is the rising cost of healthcare, which is pushing up premiums for private insurance.
“It’s affecting people’s ability to pay off bills right away, and it’s having an effect on health plans,” said Sara Collins, a senior scholar at the Commonwealth Fund and the lead author of the report.
Almost a third of the survey respondents, whether insured and uninsured, said they currently had medical or dental bills or were paying off medical debt. And more than 70% of uninsured adults said they had cost-related problems getting care.
“I think it’s very concerning,” Collins said. “We know from our survey data that not going to get care isn’t and just generally is not good for people’s health over the long run.”
The rise in the uninsured rate comes after a long period of progress: Between 2010 and 2025, the overall uninsured rate in the United States fell by half, to 8% from nearly 16%, largely because of the Affordable Care Act.
Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida Supreme Court opens door to some lawsuits against insurers
text:
The Florida Supreme Court seal, displayed in front of the chamber. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Florida homeowners got an important ruling Thursday from the Florida Supreme Court.
The high court put to rest a years-long legal controversy over whether a sweeping 2021 law that required policyholders to give their insurance companies 10-days notice before filing a lawsuit applied retroactively or prospectively.
In a unanimous decision, the justices said the law, which took effect July 1, 2021, didn’t apply to a lawsuit initially filed in 2021 over a claim made in 2019.
Florida Justice Reform Institute President William Large said he was disappointed by the ruling but that it should put to rest any future disputes as to whether a law, insurance-related or otherwise, can be applied retroactively.
“This is probably the clearest articulation of what is necessary to make something retroactive,” Large told the Phoenix Thursday. “And if it’s not clearly stated in the legislation, it’s not going to be retroactive. I think that there was a lot that was a gray area that led to a lot of litigation. So, I think the court tried to answer that question once and for all today.”
The underlying case involves a lawsuit Rebecca Hughes filed in August 2021 against her homeowner’s insurance company, Universal Property and Casualty.
The lawsuit involved a 2019 water damage claim Hughes had filed. Universal, Hughes’ insurance carrier from April 24, 2019, through April 24, 2020, reviewed the claim and issued a payment. Hughes, who had gotten three different quotes to repair the damage, sought more.
Unable to reach an accord with her carrier, Hughes on Aug. 4, 2021, sued Universal.
The company, though, moved to dismiss the claim, alleging Hughes hadn’t complied with the new 10-day notice requirement. The provision was included in SB 76, a far-reaching bill passed by the Legislature earlier that year.
The insurer argued that requirement on its face applied to all suits.
The lawsuit
The members of the Florida Supreme Court as of July 2026. Chief Justice John Couriel is seated front, center. (Photo via Florida Supreme Court)
Hughes argued that the pretrial requirement didn’t affect her claim. The trial judge disagreed and dismissed her complaint.
Hughes appealed to the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeal.
While she awaited a ruling on her challenge, the Fourth District Court of Appeal reviewed a similar lawsuit on appeal, Cole v. Universal Property and Casualty Co.
In that case, the Fourth Circuit found that the pre-suit notice requirement applied retroactively to insurance policies in effect at the time the law changed. The court opined that “[i]f the legislature had intended to limit this pre-suit notice provision to policies issued after the statute’s effective date, the legislature would have included language stating so.”
Meanwhile, following the Cole ruling, the Sixth District issued its ruling in the Hughes’ lawsuit, finding that pre-suit notice didn’t apply retroactively.
Following those two rulings the First, Second, and Fifth District courts of appeal issued rulings on the pre-suit requirement, finding it applied prospectively. The Third District Court of Appeal also issued a ruling finding the pre-suit notice applied retroactively.
Given the conflicting opinions, the Florida Supreme Court agreed in January 2024 to hear the case.
Large’s Florida Justice Reform Institute, joined by the American Property Casualty Insurance Association, the National Association of Mutual Insurance Companies, and the Personal Insurance Federation of Florida, filed an amicus brief in support of Universal.
Writing for the court, Justice John D. Couriel relied on precedents establishing that when the Legislature doesn’t say directly how a law should be interpreted, that legislative silence is not “clear evidence of retroactive intent.”
Justice Adam Tanenbaum agreed with the majority that the pre-suit requirement didn’t apply retroactively but wrote a separate opinion explaining how he reached that conclusion.
The precedents are “not needed to answer the question here. The Legislature has told us expressly that “[e]ach amendment” to the insurance code … shall be construed to operate prospectively, unless a contrary legislative intent is specified,” he wrote.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Inflation hits Oklahoma road, bridge construction
text:
Cars travel southbound on North Lincoln Boulevard, east of Interstate 235. (Photo by Mindy Ragan Wood/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Inflation has taken a big bite into the state’s ability to maintain its roads and bridges, a legislative panel was told Thursday.
In what could be one of his last addresses to lawmakers before he gives up the reins at the Oklahoma Department of Transportation, Transportation Secretary Tim Gatz said the state is about $255 million short annually of what it needs to keep the system in the condition it is today.
“We are going to start to see more of the deterioration we have seen in the past,” Gatz said.
Oklahoma in recent years has made some notable progress, he said.
Oklahoma was able to reduce the 1,200 backlog structurally deficient bridges to about 35, he said, adding that it was due to a legislative commitment. Oklahoma has gone from ranking 24th or 25th in pavement condition to 16 or 17th, he said.
But rising inflation has had an impact, he said.
“We’ve seen the highway construction cost index rise as much as 18% in one year and the reduction that causes in your buying power is something that has already knocked us to our knees,” Gatz said.
Highway construction cost inflation is significantly higher than inflation for a loaf of bread and takes into account many factors, such as labor and materials, he said.
In 2021, $245 million would build and put shoulder on 100 miles of two-lane road, but today it would only cover 65 miles, Gatz said.
Transportation Secretary Tim Gatz in 2024 participates in an Oklahoma Turnpike Authority meeting. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)
He said 2021 was an inflection point where everything changed. The state in 2021 and 2022 started to see inflation like it had never experienced, Gatz said.
For fiscal year 2027, the agency’s appropriation was about $837 million, but certain commitments, including a $3 million allocation for a new state plane, reduced that figure to about $778 million, he said.
Oklahoma’s eight-year construction program costs about $7.3 billion, which is less than $1 billion a year, he said, adding that 60% of it comes from federal highway dollars, which are facing a bit of uncertainty.
Oklahoma has 1,100 highway bridges that are 80 years old that need some attention, he said.
“We’re trying to make investments in them, but it’s going to be hard for us to catch up with that kind of deterioration in our infrastructure with flat funding and the longer you wait, the more it costs,” Gatz said.  
The Oklahoma Turnpike Authority, like ODOT, has a number of aging bridges and turnpikes, said Trent January, OTA chief engineer.
The Turnpike Authority is in the midst of an $8.2 billion turnpike improvement and expansion project, financed by bonds which are retired with toll revenues. The original cost was $5 million, but inflation increased the price.
The agency needs to reconstruct 311 miles on the system which are not part of the turnpike expansion and improvement project, January said.
The cost is $1.9 billion in today’s dollars, January said.
Gatz discussed revenue enhancements being considered or implemented by other states.
Twenty-six states index motor fuel taxes to inflation or construction costs, Gatz said.
That is a difficult subject given the price of gas and diesel right now, he said.
Other states are talking about delivery fees on ecommerce, such as Amazon deliveries, he said.
A lot of states are implementing managed lanes, where a driver pays a fee to drive in a less congested and quicker lane, he said.
Some states are looking at a road user charge where a person pays per mile, Gatz said.
“We’re not ready for that yet,” he said.
Oklahoma’s gas tax is 20 cents per gallon, one of the lowest in the nation, Gatz said.
“We’ve got to diversify our funding,” Gatz said. “I promise you, there is no magic bullet that is going to come in and address it.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: DeWine and Vance: A case study of Ohio political reaction to the now-infamous Ramaswamy Acton ad
text:
Then-candidate for U.S. Senate JD Vance stands onstage with Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine at a campaign stop on Nov. 4, 2022 in Moraine, Ohio. (Photo by Drew Angerer/Getty Images)Ohio’s 2026 campaign for governor made history this week with what’s quickly becoming one of the most notorious political advertisements of all time.
Ohio voters can find it airing on all of our screens, with the campaign of Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy putting $4 million behind its promotion.
It features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent Dr. Amy Acton, who Acton says she has not seen since she was 12 years old, leaving a Mahoning County courthouse where her stepfather was charged in 1978 with raping her.
Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, stayed married to the indicted stepfather, Cledith Arthur, until his death in 2004, after they had fled to Pennsylvania to escape the charges. Arthur herself has a record of being convicted for theft by deception in Pennsylvania in 1996, and animal abuse in 2021.
Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother calls her liar in ad; court documents say otherwise

Acton and her brother went to live with their dad.
Despite Arthur not seeing Acton in nearly 50 years, Ramaswamy’s ad features her talking directly to camera and calling Acton a liar.
The ad drew swift bipartisan backlash after it was leaked from a test poll. Acton said she thinks making the ad “was a horrible and hideous thing to do, a sad thing, and I feel like it was an exploitive thing to do. My mother is not well.”
Acton’s brother, who has confirmed the childhood abuse the siblings suffered, took him aim at Ramaswamy: “After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died. This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”
After dodging direct responsibility for the ad during most of the day Tuesday, that evening Ramaswamy confirmed the ad came from his campaign and announced he would double-down with the $4 million ad buy.
JD Vance, Donald Trump, and lying in politics
Vice President JD Vance of Ohio backs Vivek Ramaswamy amid attack ad blowback

On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance of Ohio came to his home town of Cincinnati and tripled down on the ad, directing his ire at fellow Republicans, whom he said “disgusted” him for “whining” about it.
“Disgusting” seems to be one of Vance’s favorite words and he often relates how disgusted he is by one thing or another in speeches, podcast interviews, and social media.
“I have to admit that I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” Vance told his campaign rally crowd Wednesday.
Some Ohioans might be surprised to see this closing argument from Ramaswamy, Vance, and today President Donald Trump, that lying is disqualifying for politicians, given Ramaswamy’s, Vance’s, and Trump’s track records on that matter.
Trump specifically boasts a magnificent historical canon of lying about the most mundane to the most monstrous things.
Trump famously told more than 30,000 lies just in first term alone. It’s been so many lies, in fact, it’s become a subject of academic study.
CNN fact-checker Daniel Dale in September wrote a column on fact-checking 10 years of Trump’s lies.
“His relentless dishonesty has become a central feature of US and world politics. Voters and members of Congress, allies and adversaries, CEOs and investors alike have had to try to figure out how to read a man whose words are so frequently not true,” Dale wrote. “It’s abundantly clear that there is no public official in Washington who lies like Trump — not as constantly, not as obviously, not about as many topics. I’ve heard people dismiss Trump’s mendacity with a shrugging ‘they all lie,’ but we are witnessing a rare, very possibly once-in-a-lifetime political liar.”
Fundamentally it is 100% correct that voters should demand honesty from our politicians, but their glaringly obvious hypocrisy on the issue turns the political play of hyperventilating over lying into just another form of dishonesty and manipulation.
The slime machine in Ohio politics has reached a despicable new low in the 2026 election

Lying has consequences. Policy based on lies have even more dire consequences. We know this in Ohio.
In the 2024 Election, both JD Vance and Trump infamously told the most horrid, blatant, racist lies about the city of Springfield, Ohio. Vance claimed at the time he would create stories for media attention on Americans’ suffering.
Those lies formed the basis of Trump revoking legal status for protected Haitian refugees in Springfield this year as president.
Springfield now leads the state in year-over-year job losses.
Federal job reports show the city’s labor force lost 1,100 manufacturing, leisure and hospitality jobs, contracting 2.2% in 2025 alone.
Trump jumped in on defending Ramaswamy on the anti-Acton ad on Thursday with a lengthy post on his social media site.
Trump took credit for suggesting that Ramaswamy keep the ad up; he attacked the press; ignoring the context of childhood rape; Trump claimed Arthurs words should be disqualifying for Acton; he claimed “artificial” news was trying to demean and embarrass Ramaswamy; he called on the mothers of his opponents to call their children liars; he said Arthur calling Acton a liar “took a lot of courage;” he claimed that the press is trying to convince the public that the ad is bad “because it’s so good;” he asked who wouldn’t use such an ad, and confirmed he would; he alleged that Acton uncontrollably lies, cheats and steals; and he called Ramaswamy brilliant and outstanding.
Through the last 11 years, Trump has warped American politics by practicing an ethos of never adhering to basic public norms of decency and never backing down on that.
‘Never back down’ and other inanities
On Wednesday, Axios reported how this is apparently one of Vance’s favorite things about Trump.
“There is nothing JD has more personal disdain for than weak Republicans who reflexively kowtow every time the Dem-media demands a scalp,” a source close to Vance told Axios. “It drives him crazy to see the cucked reaction from some establishment operatives and politicians in the GOP, who he views as nothing more than useful idiots for the left.”
In recent years, the terminally online right has become somewhat obsessed with the idea of cuckolding, and use the metaphor relentlessly to attempt to mock pretty much anyone or anything they want to try to portray as weak.
They like to refer to themselves as alphas and to use puerile slogans like “live by the sword, die by the sword” to describe their desk jobs.
The standard operating procedure for these emotionally stunted man-children is the acronym DARVO: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender.

Deny all wrongdoing and even deny that reality is reality or fact is fact;
Attack anyone and everyone who pushes back in any way (big points for calling them a cuck or referencing cuckolding);
Reverse Victim and Offender. They are the victim, the true victim, the only victim; never anyone they victimize.

It’s a very adolescent mindset, and shows a severe lack of emotional and mental maturity.
It smacks of 13-year-old-kid-trying-to-show-his-friends-how-tough-he-is.
It’s also fundamentally an anti-social and dehumanizing mindset. It sets out to dehumanize others but really just dehumanizes whomever adopts this mindset.
It’s also, fundamentally, just very pathetic for any grown adult male, and far more revealing of themselves than I suspect they realize.
I suspect they imagine themselves as coming off as tough when really they just come off as childish.
Strength doesn’t come from strutting and peacocking, puffing your chest out and desperately trying to prove to everyone how big and strong and mean and tough you are; strength comes from inner control, discipline, restraint, self-esteem, and having the confidence and power of mind to be wise and gentle, and to serve others instead of serving your own small, selfish, insecure ego.
Mike DeWine
‘Just wrong.’ Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine tells Ramaswamy to immediately take down controversial ad.

Other Ohio Republicans did show maturity and strength of mind.
Most prominent among them was Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, who gathered reporters in the Statehouse rotunda Thursday.
“It’s deeply, deeply, deeply troubling,” DeWine said of the ad. “It needs to come down; it’s just wrong to continue to run it.”
This is the second time that DeWine has had to refute or condemn an ad put out by his would-be Republican successor.
While DeWine did show the strength and maturity of mind to condemn Ramaswamy’s attack ad, he did not rescind his endorsement of Ramaswamy.
DeWine claimed that what he thinks or who he endorses “is pretty irrelevant,” and couched his refusal to rescind his endorsement of Ramaswamy in specific with his support for the entire Republican ticket in general.
“Look, I believe, as I just said, that people I’ve worked with on that ticket are very, very good people,” he responded. “Look, I’m a Republican, and so I did my endorsement a few months ago. What I wanted to talk today about is this ad.”
It’s hard not to get the impression that DeWine feels pretty squeamish and uncomfortable here.
He’s a smart guy. Playing modest about how much his endorsement doesn’t matter as a sitting governor is a political evasion, and somewhere inside he knows that.
This isn’t surprising from DeWine because at the end of the day DeWine is and always has-been Republican-no-matter-what.
Despite whatever’s happening in his stomach, DeWine has repeatedly co-signed the Trump Era of American politics, and his name is on the bill too.
I find that fascinating, because — acceptance, normalization, and rationalization of public corruption notwithstanding — I believe Mike DeWine is fundamentally a decent person in his heart.
I am captivated by what politics does to many decent people: how they will squirm with discomfort but still accept worse and worse and worse out of pure partisan loyalty.
Nevertheless, Trump attacked DeWine nearly as viciously as Acton: “He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn’t want someone who will do a much better job than he’s capable of doing.”
With friends like these, eh? What a time to be alive.
