name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa governor race sees record fundraising
text:
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, left, Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn and U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, the GOP candidate for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat in 2026, waved to the crowd at the Iowa Republican State Convention at Horizon Events Center in Clive June 13, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa’s competitive congressional and statewide races have brought in record high campaign fundraising hauls for the state ahead of the Nov. 3, 2026 election.
Iowa’s race for governor between Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn has shattered the state’s previous fundraising records within a gubernatorial race. According to reports from the Iowa Ethics and Campaign Disclosure Board, Sand and Lahn have raised a combined total of $81 million dollars over the course of the campaign, breaking the previous $36 million combined total record set by current Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds and Democrat Fred Hubbell in the 2018 election.
Sand has raised more than twice as much as Lahn over the course of the 2026 campaign season at nearly $54.15 million to the Republican candidate’s $26.94 million. But Lahn pulled slightly ahead in the campaign finance reporting period from July 15 to Oct. 14. Lahn raised $16.87 million in the most recent period, while Sand raised $16.31 million.
Lahn’s fundraising in the most recent reporting period was more than he had raised in total receipts up to that point. This is in part because Lahn emerged as the Republican nominee following a contentious GOP gubernatorial primary. Lahn defeated U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra, who received President Donald Trump’s endorsement in the primary, by less than a percentage point in the June 2 election, as well as three other Republican candidates. Sand ran unopposed as the Democratic nominee.
The latest campaign finance reports show Lahn received $11.8 million from the Right Direction PAC – the political action committee associated with the Republican Governors Association — in the recent reporting period. He also received $1.7 million from the Republican Party of Iowa.
Sand’s campaign received $5.5 million from the Democratic Governors Association. In a news release, Sand’s campaign emphasized “nearly 95 percent of contributions were $100 or less, and nearly two-thirds of all donors are Iowans,” including Republicans and independents, according to a news release.
In the most recent reporting period, Sand received a total of $1.25 million from his wife, brother-in-law and mother-in law, who are a part of the Lauridsen family. In the previous reporting period, the Sand campaign did not receive any donations from his wife’s family, but Sand faced criticism for receiving millions in campaign contributions from his wife and in-laws earlier in the campaign.
“Hardworking Iowans are supporting Rob because they believe in his vision to lower costs, strengthen public schools, and put people over politics,” Sand’s Deputy Campaign Manager Emma O’Brien said in a statement. “With just over two weeks until Election Day, Iowans are fired up to turn the page on a decade of one-party control that has left them behind, and are ready to elect a governor who will make Iowa not redder or bluer, but better and truer. That leader is Rob Sand.”
Turek outraises Hinson in U.S. Senate race as outside spending surges
Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, running for U.S. Senate in 2026, spoke to Democrats gathered for state Rep. Sean Bagniewski’s annual Fish Fry dinner in Des Moines Oct. 11, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The governor’s race is not the only election drawing major attention — and money — into Iowa. Fundraising reports from the Federal Election Commission covering the period from July 1 through Sep. 30 show Democratic Iowa Rep. Josh Turek raised roughly $13.88 million in the most recent period. That’s more than four times the amount raised by his opponent, U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee, who raised $3.25 million. Turek’s fundraising for the period exceeded Hinson’s campaign fundraising total for the election cycle at $13.52 million.
The margin is smaller between the two candidates in total fundraising over the entire election cycle, but Turek still leads at $20.15 million.
But campaign fundraising is not the only source of money in this race. Other political organizations have also spent a vast amount, buying ads both for and against Hinson and Turek in the lead-up to Election Day.
An analysis published by AdImpact found $93.3 million in aired advertising spending in Iowa by Sept. 30 from issue group and coordinated campaign buys. More of this funding — $55.1 million — has gone to ads supporting Hinson than to Turek, at $38.2 million, according to the report. Spending is expected to keep rising in the final two weeks before the election.
The outside spending comes as Iowa’s U.S. Senate seat is considered a “toss-up” by political forecasters heading into the midterms, which could play a critical role in determining which party controls the Senate. The seat is currently held by U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst, a Republican, who is not seeking reelection.
Further analysis from the Des Moines Register found the largest spenders in the race were the SLF PAC, aligned with the Senate Republicans’ Senate Leadership Fund, at $35.53 million and WinSenate, a Democratic super PAC at $28.27 million.
Libertarian Thomas Laehn, Greene County attorney, reported raising $11,033 in the most recent period for his U.S. Senate bid, bringing his election cycle total to $82,962.
Democrats hold fundraising edge in Iowa’s U.S. House races
Several of Iowa’s U.S. House races are also forecast to be hotly contested in 2026. All four of Iowa’s current U.S. representatives are Republican, but both races for Iowa’s 1st and 3rd congressional districts are rated by Cook Political Report as “leans Democrat.” The 2nd Congressional District race is rated as a “toss-up.”
The latest FEC reports show Democrats holding a lead in these three competitive races.
Bohannan maintains fundraising lead over Miller-Meeks
In the 1st Congressional District, incumbent U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks raised $1.72 million in the FEC reporting period, short of Democratic challenger Christina Bohannan’s $2.42 million in fundraising. Independent Michael Bridgford reported raising $148,447 during the period.
Miller-Meeks thanked her supporters for their contributions in a news release, calling the period “her best fundraising quarter yet.”
“I’m honored by the support of families in every corner of this district, Republicans, Democrats, and independents alike,” Miller-Meeks said. “They’ve watched me take on Big Insurance, take taxes off Social Security for seniors, bring home $209 million for our rural hospitals, and fight to stop corrupt insider trading in Congress. With their support, we’re going to finish the job.”
U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, running for reelection in Iowa’s 1st Congressional District, was joined by House Speaker Mike Johnson at a Davenport rally Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
But Bohannan’s campaign said in a statement on the latest fundraising period that their campaign’s totals came “without a dime of corporate PAC money,” and show the momentum for potentially flipping the seat from Republican to Democratic control in the upcoming election.
There have been other funding signals that show Miller-Meeks is expected to face a difficult bid for reelection. The Congressional Leadership Fund, a Republican super PAC, pulled funding from the Iowa 1st District race earlier in October.
Over the course of the campaign, Miller-Meeks has raised $9.27 million while Bohannan has raised $9.58 million.
Trone Garriott leads Nunn in fundraising
Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, D-West Des Moines, also boasted a fundraising haul of $2.36 million in the most recent FEC reporting period, putting her ahead of incumbent U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn at roughly $1.1 million raised in the same timeframe in the 3rd Congressional District race. This brings Nunn’s fundraising total for the election cycle to $6.05 million; Trone Garriott’s total to $7.65 million.
James outraises Mitchell in 2nd District
In the race to replace Hinson in the 2nd District, Democratic state Rep. Lindsay James raised more than former state lawmaker Joe Mitchell, the Republican candidate. James reported raising nearly $1.9 million to Mitchell’s $745,215 in the most recent period, while independent candidate Dave Bushaw raised $11,871. Libertarian candidate Rick Stewart, who is also running for the 2nd District seat, did not file a FEC report.
James said her campaign fundraising report showed “Iowans are ready for change.”
“Thank you to every person who supported this effort so far,” James said. “In Washington, I’ll be a voice against big corporations, private equity, and the ultra-wealthy that are buying our elections. I’m going to fight to lower healthcare and grocery costs, end the reckless war in Iran, and make sure every family in Iowa can build the life we know they deserve.”
While Mitchell did not release a statement on his campaign fundraising totals, he claimed in a social media post earlier in October that “over 60% of my opponent’s maxed out donors come from California, New York, and DC.” Mitchell has highlighted on the campaign trail that he is not accepting corporate PAC money, a position that distinguishes him from other GOP candidates.
McGowan leads fundraising in 4th District
The only Iowa race where the Republican candidate outraised the Democrat was in the 4th District, a longtime conservative stronghold in the state. Chris McGowan, the Siouxland Chamber of Commerce president, reported raising $173,476 in the most recent period, while Democratic former state lawmaker Dave Dawson raised $104,516.
Other statewide races share fundraising updates
An analysis from the environmental group Food & Water Watch of third quarter finance reports for Iowa’s secretary of agriculture campaigns found that Republican incumbent Mike Naig received large donation amounts from agricultural interest political action committees.
Iowa secretary of agriculture candidates Chris Jones, right, and Mike Naig debated on an Oct. 2 episode of Iowa Press moderated by Kay Henderson, center, and Donnelle Eller. (Screenshot courtesy of Iowa PBS)
Finance reports show Naig received $50,000 from the Iowa Farm Bureau Federation PAC, $20,000 from the Koch Industries PAC and around $80,000 more from pesticide, pork, corn and ethanol related donors. During the third quarter, Naig had more than 300 contributors with an average donation amount of around $1,800, according to the Food & Water Watch analysis.
Jones had more than 4,000 contributions during the same period, with an average donation amount of around $80, according to the environmental group, which has endorsed Jones.
Jones received $2,000 from the voter education branch of Plumbers and Pipe Fitters Local 125. Contributions were otherwise from individuals. Around 1,700 of Jones’ donations during the period were from individuals for $15 or less.
In the race for Iowa Attorney General, incumbent AG Brenna Bird, a Republican, reported raising more than $4.6 million in the reporting period, bringing her election cycle fundraising total to $11.49 million. This drove her ahead of Democratic challenger Nate Willems, who raised $3.16 million in the recent period and $6.3 million overall.
Incumbent Republican State Treasurer Roby Smith also reported outraising challenger John Norwood in the period at $143,664 to Norwood’s $72,193.
While Republican incumbents raised more in these three statewide races, Democrats pulled ahead in others: Taylor Wettach, the Democrat aiming to replace Sand as state auditor, raised $778,147 from mid-July to mid-October, more than Lt. Gov. Chris Cournoyer at $201,970. Ryan Peterman, the Democrat challenging Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate, also outraised his opponent in the period, raising $184,690 to Pate’s $48,265.
Cami Koons contributed to this report.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ school segregation case back in court as judges weigh potential constitutional violation
text:
Attorneys for civil rights groups appeared in court Thursday to try to revive their lawsuit against New Jersey over racial segregation in public schools. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters
Several years after civil rights groups sued New Jersey over racial segregation in public schools, attorneys returned to court Thursday to debate whether the state’s own enrollment data is enough to establish a constitutional violation.
During oral arguments before a three-judge appeals court panel in Trenton, attorneys representing the plaintiffs urged the judges to overturn a 2023 ruling that acknowledged persistent racial segregation in New Jersey’s schools, but stopped short of declaring it unconstitutional.
The state countered that enrollment numbers alone cannot establish a constitutional violation, and called for a more detailed look at individual districts.
The hearing was the latest development in a landmark lawsuit that could eventually change how New Jersey students attend public school. The case could have far-reaching implications for Newark and neighboring Essex County municipalities, where predominantly Black and Latino school districts sit near wealthier, majority-white suburban districts. Children who were in kindergarten when the lawsuit began are now in ninth grade.
The lawsuit was filed in May 2018 by the Latino Action Network, NAACP New Jersey State Conference, other civil rights organizations, and families. It argues that the state’s requirement that most children attend schools in the districts where they already live perpetuates racial segregation in violation of New Jersey’s Constitution, the only state constitution that explicitly bans segregation in public schools.
According to state enrollment data cited in the lawsuit, an average of more than 270,000 Black and Latino students, or roughly 46% of those students statewide, attended schools where more than 90% of students were nonwhite each year from 2015-16 through 2019-20.
In addition, Lawrence Lustberg, an attorney for the plaintiffs, pointed to decades of “pervasive” segregation in New Jersey’s public schools during Thursday’s hearing.
In 2023, both sides asked the court to decide whether the state was legally responsible without a trial. Superior Court Judge Robert Lougy denied both requests. After more than a year of unsuccessful mediation, a state appeals court agreed in July 2025 to review the ruling.
On Thursday, the plaintiffs argued that the trial court had improperly required them to demonstrate unconstitutional segregation throughout the state’s entire public school system, even though their lawsuit only focused on 23 “severely segregated” districts.
Those districts enroll roughly 15% of New Jersey’s public school students, Lustberg said. He highlighted Essex County, where predominantly Black and Latino districts such as Newark, East Orange, Irvington, and Orange border wealthier, majority-white communities, as evidence of why the state must address segregation across district lines.
“If Newark decides that they want to send their children to some other districts in order to desegregate their schools, they can’t,” Lustberg told the judges. “They don’t have that power.”
That authority, he argued, rests with the state education commissioner.
Judge Hany Mawla questioned whether the evidence was sufficient to rule in the plaintiffs’ favor without a trial, noting that the 23 districts represented less than 4% of New Jersey’s school districts and that experts had offered differing definitions of segregation.
Deputy Attorney General Francesco Ferrantelli Jr., representing the state, argued that the plaintiffs had failed to account for individual districts’ circumstances, including geography, educational opportunities, and parental preferences.
Pointing to Newark, he questioned whether students might prefer their current schools and what benefits they would gain from attending neighboring suburban districts.
Ferrantelli also disputed the plaintiffs’ claims of state inaction, citing existing school choice programs, charter schools, and state oversight. In addition, he argued that the plaintiffs had failed to prove intentional discrimination.
“They plead this case under the theory that they can prove it just by looking at enrollment data,” Ferrantelli told the judges. “That’s the entire case.”
Following the hearing, Lustberg criticized the state’s argument about a lack of sufficient evidence for unconstitutional segregation.
“Today, for the first time, they crystallize this argument that somehow numbers cannot be enough,” he told Chalkbeat. “But that is not consistent with the law.”
Several civil rights organizations not a party to the lawsuit also presented arguments supporting the plaintiffs.
Micauri Vargas, litigation counsel for the New Jersey Institute for Social Justice, told the court that segregation deprives students of opportunities to learn alongside classmates from different backgrounds, and leaves them to grow up as “strangers to one another.”
After the hearing, Vargas and Lustberg expressed frustration about the prolonged legal battle over the case. Vargas also said existing school choice programs remained too limited to provide meaningful options for many families.
“Every day that goes by where there’s no remedy for this is tragic,” Lustberg said. “Students in Newark are going to have to suffer with how long this is taking.”
Retired New Jersey Supreme Court Justice Gary Stein, who helped launch the lawsuit in 2018, called it one of the most significant civil rights cases in the state’s history, and that its outcome could have implications far beyond New Jersey.
Asking the state “to desegregate its schools is not just to wave a flag,” Stein said in an interview with Chalkbeat on Wednesday. “It’s for the purpose of giving those children a better opportunity to succeed in life.”
The appellate judges did not issue a ruling Thursday. They could uphold the lower court’s decision, reverse it, or return the case for additional proceedings.
A ruling in the plaintiffs’ favor could eventually lead to a separate phase of litigation over what steps New Jersey must take to address unconstitutional segregation.
Either side could also seek review by the state Supreme Court, which declined to take up the case in May 2026 before the appeals court had ruled.
Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools.

name: Mississippi Today
title: UMMC’s new cancer center aims to expand access to life-saving care in Mississippi
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
The University of Mississippi Medical Center broke ground Thursday on a cancer center officials say will help improve outcomes for patients in a state with some of the nation’s highest cancer mortality rates.
The new building is critical to the UMMC Cancer Center and Research Institute’s goal of achieving National Cancer Institute designation, which could expand Mississippians’ access to cutting-edge clinical trials and treatment options, officials said. 
“We have a real problem here in Mississippi with cancer outcomes,” said Dr. LouAnn Woodward, the medical center’s vice chancellor for health affairs, at the groundbreaking ceremony. “Mississippians need the highest level of cancer care and access to the latest clinical trials right here at home.” 
Dr. LouAnn Woodward, vice chancellor for health affairs at the University of Mississippi Medical Center, speaks during the UMMC Cancer Center and Research Institute groundbreaking ceremony in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The five-story building will be located on State Street across from the medical center and “bring together education, research and treatment under one roof,” according to the project’s fundraising website. The site is adjacent to the American Cancer Society’s Jackson Hope Lodge, which provides free lodging to cancer patients and their caregivers. 
The National Cancer Institute is a part of the National Institutes of Health and recognizes cancer centers that meet rigorous requirements for laboratory and clinical research and translate scientific knowledge into innovative treatments for patients. 
There are 74 NCI-designated centers nationwide, but none in Mississippi, Louisiana or Arkansas. Cancer patients in Mississippi seeking care at a designated center must travel out of state to receive care. Nearby states with NCI-designated centers include Alabama, Tennessee and Texas. 
If the cancer center achieves this designation, it will not only serve Mississippi families, but also people in neighboring states, Gov. Tate Reeves said Thursday. 
“We’re working to save lives well beyond our borders,” Reeves said. 
Gov. Tate Reeves speaks during the UMMC Cancer Center and Research Institute groundbreaking ceremony in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Speakers at the groundbreaking ceremony praised Woodward for her work advocating for the cancer center, noting the accomplishment is a fitting capstone to her more than four decades at UMMC. Woodward announced Oct. 15 that she plans to retire in June 2027. Dr. Alan Jones, the medical center’s associate vice chancellor for health affairs, will succeed her. 
Jones said the achievement of NCI designation will take time. 
“But we will achieve it, and we will change the outcomes of cancer patients,” he said. “That is our promise.”
Dr. Alan Jones, associate vice chancellor for health affairs at the University of Mississippi Medical Center, speaks during the UMMC Cancer Center and Research Institute groundbreaking ceremony in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Funding for the center has been drawn from state and federal sources and private donors. Reeves in April signed legislation appropriating $100 million in state funds to build the cancer center. 
Mississippi’s congressional delegation has supported the appropriation of $22 million in federal funds toward cancer research labs and the new cancer center building, and UMMC has requested $16 million in federal support for the project for the upcoming fiscal year, Woodward said. 
John and Sandy Black of Madison donated $25 million to support the new facility in 2025. The medical center has raised more than 80% of its $125 million capital campaign goal, according to a press release. 
A new building is just one piece of the medical center’s efforts to gain the designation. Dr. Rodney Rocconi, the director of UMMC’s cancer center, previously told Mississippi Today that achieving it will require the center to recruit faculty, expand its research capacity and demonstrate strong programming in community outreach and prevention.
Audience members including Attorney General Lynn Fitch and Insurance Commissioner Mike Chaney listen as Gov. Tate Reeves speaks during the UMMC Cancer Center and Research Institute groundbreaking ceremony in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Cancer is the second-leading cause of death in Mississippi, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The disease disproportionately affects Black Mississippians, who in 2022 had a 13% higher cancer mortality rate than white residents, according to a 2025 report by the Mississippi State Department of Health.
Only six counties in Mississippi fall below the national average of 143 cancer deaths per 100,000 people, according to 2020-2024 data from the National Cancer Institute. Some counties, including Humphreys, Tunica and Issaquena — all located in the Mississippi Delta — have death rates nearly twice as high as the national average. 
Eddie Moore, 44, of Clinton, was diagnosed with lung cancer in 2020 and given a prognosis of three months to live. He is still receiving treatment at UMMC. 
He said Thursday he is grateful for the treatment he has received at UMMC and believes the construction of a new cancer center will help more people like him.
“It’s a hope for the future,” he said.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: AOC stumps for Jackson as high profile figures descend on Maine ahead of election
text:
Troy Jackson, Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Maine, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York salute supporters after a joint campaign appearance at the State Theatre in Portland on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Jim Neuger / Maine Morning Star)Seated next to Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson in Portland, Democratic U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York described his attempt to oust longtime Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins as a battle about class. 
“The House and the Senate have always been institutions of the ruling class. What this institution tries to do is protect it from being intruded upon by working class Americans,”  Ocasio-Cortez told a packed State Theatre. “So they call people communists, they call them this, they call them that. But really what it is is they’re afraid of a waitress in the House, and a logger in the Senate.” 
Ocasio-Cortez, who worked as a server before running for Congress in 2018, joined Jackson, former logger and president of the Maine Senate, for a “Students vs. Billionaires” town hall on Thursday organized by More Perfect University, a progressive campus program launched in April by the media organization More Perfect Union to counter conservative campus groups such as Turning Point USA. 
The stop highlighting Maine’s U.S. Senate race, which is seen as key to Democrats flipping the balance of power in their favor, is one of several the program is making across the country ahead of the midterms. 
Fielding questions directly from attendees, Ocasio-Cortez and Jackson’s answers underscored their alignment across various issues, including Medicare for All and abortion rights. Ocasio-Cortez called out Collins for her vote for U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who had a hand in overturning Roe v. Wade, and telling the crowd the best way to support women is to vote for Jackson.
Jackson has not always held progressive stances, having changed his mind on abortion during his time in office, which he pointed out on Thursday. But he is now among the progressive candidates rallying against economic inequality and billionaire influence who are vying for seats in U.S. Congress. 
“When you have someone like Troy go to the United States Senate and call everything for what it is, it disrupts and makes it harder for everyone to get away with all of the glad-handing that goes on,” Ocasio-Cortez said. 
Ocasio-Cortez is one of several national figures who have visited Maine in the final weeks leading up to Nov. 3 to weigh into Maine’s U.S. Senate race. Democratic U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts joined Jackson at the No Kings protest over the weekend, and independent U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont campaigned alongside him earlier this month. Meanwhile, on Wednesday, former U.S. Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia joined Collins on the campaign trail.

Collins gets help with her independent pitch

As Manchin and Collins, former colleagues, visited local businesses on Wednesday — Simones’ Hot Dog Stand in Lewiston, the New Balance factory in Norway, among others — he praised her as the “soul of the Senate.” 
Manchin switched from a registered Democrat to independent in 2024, after having long been known as a moderate. Collins has been pitching herself as an independent voice as she tries to secure a sixth term. Vice President JD Vance helped her with that during his visit to Maine in August, and Manchin did so on Wednesday. 
“She’s not a Trump senator, she’s not a Republican’s senator or a Democrat’s senator,” Manchin said. “She’s an American Senator that represents her state of Maine, and that’s who she is — the most, the most independent-minded person I’ve ever met.”
Jackson has tried to tie Collins to President Donald Trump, arguing she is loyal to him when it counts. Ocasio-Cortez also made that case Thursday. 
The only GOP senator seeking reelection in a state Trump lost in 2024, Collins has been trying to distance herself from the president. That tight rope walk was evident on Wednesday, when Manchin directly blamed Trump for the state of the economy and Collins skirted the question. 
“There are lots of reasons why people are struggling,” Collins said, before pointing to higher inflation under former Democratic President Joe Biden. 
Manchin is now an advisor for Apollo Global Management, a private equity firm tied to past paper mill closures in Bucksport and Jay. (Also, Apollo Global Management’s CEO and founder Marc Rowan has contributed to Pine Tree Results, a pro-Collins super PAC.)
Former U.S. Senator Joe Manchin (left) and U.S. Sen. Susan Collins pose at a happy hour with friends and family at the Poland Spring Resort on Oct. 21, 2026. (Courtesy of Collins for Senator campaign)
The sitting president is always a factor in midterms elections, perhaps more so this year with Trump’s approval rating at historic lows. Both Jackson and Ocasio-Cortez were asked during the town hall what their day one agendas would be if Democrats take back the House and Senate. 
While Jackson said overturning Trump’s signature spending package to claw back funding for healthcare, Ocasio-Cortez pointed to the president’s “absolute weaponization of the Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation.”  
“Day one, we need to be opening investigations into the heads of every single one of these agencies,” she told the crowd. “I’m talking subpoenas. I’m talking investigations. I’m talking, if necessary and if the evidence leads us there, to court.”
Gen Z isn’t choosing a side. They’re choosing issues.

Young voters
Lola Fulham-FitzGerald, 15, brought her brother Cosmo Fulham-FitzGerald, 23, to the town hall on Thursday, which was the first campaign event either had ever attended. 
“It’s been a very long 10 years of every adult I know saying, ‘It didn’t used to be like this,’” Cosmo said, referring to the Trump era of American politics. He was 13 when Trump was first elected. Lola was five. 
“I’ve never experienced a world where it has been different,” Lola chimed in. 
The youngest generation that can vote, Generation Z, now roughly 14 to 29 years old, is disproportionately independent. Not to be construed as moderate, this growing bloc of the electorate has soured on both parties as they view the government as failing to protect and address their needs. 
Young voters could be consequential in midterms across the country and particularly in Maine, which CIRCLE, a nonpartisan research organization at Tufts University, considers the top state where these voters could sway Senate outcomes. 
Both Lola and Cosmo Fulham-FitzGerald are sick of the negative ads that have blanketed the state, largely paid for by outside interests. 
“I’d rather see, ‘This is what I can do or am going to do.’ I want to see personal genuine interest,” Lola said, adding that that is why the town hall appealed to her. 



Quotation







When you have someone like Troy go to the United States Senate and call everything for what it is, it disrupts and makes it harder for everyone to get away with all of the glad-handing that goes on.


– U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York


Jackson and Ocasio-Cortez shared stances on a range of issues throughout the town hall, calling for regulations on Artificial Intelligence and data privacy and more funding for public transportation, with Jackson saying he would like to see more trains connecting the state.
When a transgender college student said many in the trans community feel abandoned by the Democratic Party, Ocasio-Cortez said, “I think it’s what people hate most about politics, which is politicians who will jump on this side or that side of the line at a moment’s notice.”
When Maine Morning Star asked Collins about why she feels she is best fit to represent young Mainers during a campaign stop in Naples last month, the senator pointed to the same reason she thinks Mainers overall should support her: her power, particularly to ward off cuts from the Trump administration that would have harmed them. 
The senator listed her work preventing Trump from imposing caps on need-based federal financial aid for students known as Pell Grants, as well as preventing a freeze in admission and funding cuts to the Job Corps program, a free career training program for low-income young adults, among other efforts. 
“What we need to do is make sure that our young people have the tools and the support to get the skills that they need, so they can stay in the state of Maine,” Collins said.
Progressive push
Renee Caisse, a 20-year-old student at the Maine College Art and Design, wants to see more progressives in U.S. Congress, but also wants progressives not to cave to pressures of the Democratic establishment. 
“Sometimes the party may not be on their side,” Caisse told Maine Morning Star. “I want more progressive candidates to hold their ground.”  
Ocasio-Cortez said at the beginning of the town hall that there are a lot of consultants in Washington who would advise him to not sit beside her, as she is viewed by some as a polarizing figure. 
“I’m sure you probably heard some variation of that,” Ocasio-Cortez said to Jackson. “And it takes a lot to say, ‘You know what, no, I know my people. I know who I am and I’m gonna do things my way.’” 
A specific stance Caisse hoped Jackson and Ocasio-Cortez would stay firm on was opposition to U.S. aid to Israel. During the event, another attendee asked, “America or Israel first?” Both responded, “America first.” 
Jackson said no more blank checks to Israel. Pointing to all of the money the U.S. spends on foreign conflicts, Ocasio-Cortez said, “One of the things that I find so mind-boggling is that whenever we want to expand healthcare in this country, Medicare in this country, education, everyone’s first question in Washington is, ‘We have no money. How are we going to pay for this?’ As though the richest nation in the history of the world is a pauper.”
She added, “It’s about time that we flip that equation.”
After Ocasio-Cortez gave that response, Jackson said, “Why wouldn’t I want to sit alongside someone that just talked like that?”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Assembly panel OKs bill limiting federal agents, armed forces at polls
text:
Supporters of a bill limiting federal agents and armed forces at the polls say they’re worried about voter intimidation. (Photo by New Jersey Monitor)An Assembly panel approved legislation Thursday that would bar federal law enforcement and uniformed military service members from standing within 100 feet of polling places and ballot drop boxes, but a scrubbed vote on the Senate floor could prevent the law from being signed in time for this year’s elections.
The Assembly Oversight, Reform, and Federal Relations Committee approved the bill in a 4-2 vote along party lines, with supporters citing fears of voter intimidation. It would expand an existing prohibition on state and local police at polling places to encompass federal law enforcement and adopt provisions mirroring federal law that bars military personnel at polls that supporters worried would go unenforced under the Trump administration.
“We know that it’s really not a good sign for democracy when you see armed men anywhere near polling sites, not in Myanmar, not in Bangladesh or the Philippines, and not in New Jersey,” said Amber Reed, co-executive director of AAPI New Jersey.
The legislation, introduced just this week, would expand a law signed by former Gov. Phil Murphy in 2022 that barred election officials from requesting police presence at polling places to help maintain peace and good order and limited state and local law enforcement presence at polls to emergencies.
Supporters said the bill is needed because federal officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and President Donald Trump, have declined to rule out deploying federal agents to the polls on Election Day.
Erik Cruz Morales, director of democracy at the League of Women Voters of New Jersey, noted that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents appeared at polling places in some states during this year’s primaries and warned that concern over their presence or negative interactions with them could spur some to stay home.
“When voters are unsure whether ICE or federal troops will be at the polls, many weigh that cost and decide it’s not worth the trouble,” he told the committee. “That’s how voter suppression often works today, not through law that blocks the ballot but through enough doubt that people will stay home.”

The bill would also bar federal officials and service members from acting as election board members or as poll watchers — existing law bars police from doing so — though candidates on the ballot can act as challengers regardless of their jobs.
New Jersey’s attorney general would enforce the prohibitions through civil actions for injunctions and restraining orders in state Superior Court.
The legislation contains exceptions allowing individuals to vote and remain within their own residence if it falls within 100 feet of a polling place, and it would create a new exception allowing members of the New Jersey National Guard to come within 100 feet of a polling place or drop box to ensure, at the governor’s direction, access to the same.
Assemblyman Erik Simonsen (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Assemblyman Erik Simonsen (R-Cape May), who opposed the bill alongside the panel’s other Republican, offered an amendment that would have required voters to show identification at the polls, but no other member seconded the proposal, and it collapsed after failing to overcome that procedural hurdle.
“I believe if this was part of it, the identification part, there would be less need for anyone to monitor these drop boxes and other places,” said Simonsen.
Assemblyman Avi Schnall (D-Ocean), who chairs the committee and is one of the bill’s prime sponsors, said he did not second the amendment because it could have been the topic of its own hearing.
It’s unclear whether the bill will be law in time for this year’s elections. Though the Senate had planned to move the bill to a floor vote without a committee hearing during Thursday’s voting session, constitutional concerns from within the governor’s office knocked it off that course, said Senate President Nicholas Scutari (D-Union).
“We’re going to work on amendments. We anticipate bringing it up next voting session, but it just — I think perhaps people thought it might have been a little rushed and perhaps it might have not met constitutional muster, so we’re going to make sure,” he told reporters.
Sean Higgins, a spokesperson for Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D), declined to comment.
With the Nov. 3 elections now less than two weeks out, it’s unclear whether the upper chamber will reconvene in time to consider the measure. The Senate has no additional voting sessions scheduled before Election Day, though the full Assembly is slated to meet on Oct. 29.
New Jersey has a history with intimidation at the polls. The Republican National Committee in 1981 deployed off-duty police and sheriff’s officers to polling places in largely nonwhite voting districts.
Tom Kean Sr. (R) defeated Jim Florio (D) by 1,797 votes in the gubernatorial race that year, and Florio in part blamed the so-called Ballot Security Task Force for the Democratic loss. After a lawsuit, the GOP committee entered into a consent decree that admitted no wrongdoing but subjected similar deployments to judicial review. That consent decree lapsed in 2018.

name: VTDigger
title: National education funding expert takes the helm of the State Board of Education
text:
Tammy Kolbe, vice chair of the Vermont Board of Education, testifies before the House Education Committee at the Statehouse in Montpelier in February 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The state board tasked with setting education standards for Vermont’s schools elected a new chair: Tammy Kolbe, a researcher and national expert in education funding. 
Kolbe has served as acting chair of the State Board of Education since former chair Jennifer Samuelson suddenly resigned during a meeting last month, citing a host of personal reasons. Board members Wednesday unanimously elected Kolbe to carry out the rest of Samuelson’s term, which runs through the end of February. 
“It’s really an honor to be able to serve the state in this capacity,” Kolbe said in an interview.
The state board is tasked with regulating education standards and approving independent schools, among other responsibilities. The leadership transition comes as the board is working under tight deadlines to create standards to evaluate school merger proposals in the coming months. The board must also develop statewide graduation requirements for high schools by January. 
Rep. Emilie Kornheiser, D-Brattleboro, chair of the House Ways and Means Committee, which handles education finance policy, said she’s excited to have Kolbe serve as the board’s new chair. She considers Kolbe to be data driven and realistic about what’s possible, she said. 
“She has an incredibly broad view of what’s happening nationally, both in terms of best practice but also in terms of just how education institutions are functioning all over the country,” Kornheiser said in an interview. 
Kolbe said she works as a researcher advising the federal government and states on education policy. She was previously a professor of education leadership and policy at the University of Vermont. 
“Pretty much all I do is think about education policy and finance,” Kolbe said. 
Members of school boards around the state have begun meeting this fall to consider district mergers, as directed by this year’s education reform law, Act 170. 
The state education board is positioned to play an important role in the merger process. The board is tasked with evaluating the proposals of merger study committees and deciding if they benefit the state when pieced together, Kolbe said. 
Throughout the next couple months, Kolbe said, a panel of board members will be drafting a framework to evaluate whether proposed mergers are beneficial to the state. She said the board is trying to be proactive and transparent about its standards so that merger study committees know what to expect. 
During the Wednesday meeting board members also elected Cynthia Stuart, a consultant with a background in fiscal regulation, to serve as vice chair.
Eight of the board’s 10 members are appointed by the governor, while two members are appointed by the speaker of the House and the Senate Committee on Committees respectively. Board chairs are elected by fellow members. Kolbe could be reelected chair at the end of her term.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: PSC challenger seeks to advocate for landowners; incumbent calls herself ‘uniquely qualified’
text:
Republican Jill Kringstad, left, and Democrat Scot Kelsh are running for seats on the Public Service Commission. (Photos courtesy of the candidates)A challenger for a seat on the Public Service Commission says North Dakotans do not feel like they are being heard by state regulators, while the incumbent defended the processes used by the state agency. 
Democrat Scot Kelsh said people feel like developers of projects such as power lines and pipelines are “running roughshod” over landowners. 
Kelsh, a former Fargo firefighter and state lawmaker, is challenging Republican Jill Kringstad for a two-year term on the Public Service Commission. Kringstad was appointed by Gov. Kelly Armstrong in January 2025 to fill the seat once occupied by U.S. Rep. Julie Fedorchak, who resigned her PSC seat when she was elected to Congress in 2024. The candidates participated in a Plain Talk Podcast debate Thursday hosted by Rob Port and Chad Oban.



Kringstad touted a change in state law that she advocated for as improving the public input process for the agency. The change allows the PSC to first hold a technical hearing, where a developer can provide detailed information and recent updates, before the three-person commission. Then the commission can go into a community to take public testimony. 
She said the change helps eliminate people waiting hours for a company to present their case, a problem also identified by Kelsh. 
“I helped draft a bill while I was on staff, and then when I was appointed just last year, I was able to champion that through the Legislature,” Kringstad said. 
Kringstad also said the three-person commission must treat all parties fairly and follow the law when considering permits for power lines, pipelines and energy facilities. 
“It’s not our job to kind of cheerlead on behalf of developers and make sure that they get their projects through,” Kringstad said. “And if you have developers come in, as we’ve seen, who are more aggressive and don’t treat landowners with respect, then their project goes harder, as it should.” 
Kelsh said he agreed with the sentiment but that is not helping landowners who are feeling ignored by state government in general. 
“We need an advocate on the PSC who’s actually going to talk about that and advocate for public policy changes that are going to make it better for our landowners, not make it worse like it seems to be becoming right now,” Kelsh said. 
Democrat PSC candidates question attorney’s safety stance

Kelsh cited his 18 years of experience in the state House of Representatives and his ability to work across party lines as part of his qualifications for a seat on the PSC.  He served on Energy and Natural Resources and Finance and Taxation committees in the House. 
Kringstad called herself “uniquely qualified” to serve on the commission. She said her background in accounting and economics and her time on the PSC staff allow her to dig into cases before the PSC. 
She said that has helped her dissect electric utility rate increase requests that have come before the PSC. 
She cited the PSC’s work on a rate increase request from Xcel Energy. While Xcel requested a rate increase of more than 19%, the commission approved an increase of about 10%.
“Ten percent sounds like a lot,” Kringstad acknowledged, but noted that it was the first increase in four years. 
Kelsh acknowledged that electricity rates are low in North Dakota compared with other states but said some increases are the result of “bad decisions” by the utilities. 
The PSC has authority over investor-owned utilities but not electric cooperatives, which are common in North Dakota. 
“We really have to be careful it does not get away from us,” Kelsh said of utility rates. 
One issue where Kringstad and Kelsh agreed was that power providers should not be allowed to pass along costs associated with large-load customers such as data centers to residential and other existing customers. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
The PSC does not have regulatory authority over data centers but does have authority over the siting of some energy infrastructure affiliated with data centers such as power generation and power lines. 
Kringstad cited $38 million in credits returned to Montana-Dakota Utilities customers because of the development of the Applied Digital data center complex at Ellendale. But she said it is not always easy to identify those savings on a utility bill and would like to make those benefits more clear.
“That’s where I think we can bring some additional transparency,” she said. 
Kelsh is a native of Ellendale and has seen some benefits from the data center buildout in his hometown, such as enrollment growth in the schools and being able to afford repaving streets. 
While there was extra energy available on the grid when Applied Digital first started building there, he said he is concerned about power availability for data centers that are under construction or proposed in North Dakota. 
“Our grid and our generation capacity is just not there yet, and it will not be for years,” he said. 
Two of the three seats on the Public Service Commission are up for election this year. Republican Sheri Haugen-Hoffart is seeking another full six-year term. She is being challenged by Democrat Jon Pederson, a professor at Mayville State University.

title: Vance announces investment in domestic fertilizer manufacturing in Nebraska
text:
Vice President JD vance walking to podium to speak in North Platte on Oct. 22, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner) NORTH PLATTE —  JD Vance became the first vice president to visit North Platte on Thursday, campaigning for Sen. Pete Ricketts and Gov. Jim Pillen as they face challenging reelection bids. 
Ricketts and Pillen hit similar notes in their speeches before Vance arrived, attacking their top opponents, registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn and Democratic challenger Lynne Walz. Third Congressional District Rep. Adrian Smith told the crowd in his home district that Nebraska’s federal delegation is fighting for Nebraskans every day. 
Vance emphasized the importance of reelecting Ricketts, Pillen and Smith because they are fighting to preserve the “American Dream for the next generation.” 
“I think it is important as we continue to work hard to rebuild that American Dream to take stock of where we were just two years ago,” Vance said during his pitch to Nebraska voters at the D&N Event Center. “Joe Biden and Kamala Harris spent four years making life harder for people in Nebraska who actually make this country work.” 
The crowd listening to Vice President JD Vance speak in North Platte on Oct. 22, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
During his roughly one-hour speech, Vance highlighted President Donald Trump’s tax-and-spending law tax-cut provisions, ending the “Green New Scam” and rebuilding America’s energy economy. 
The vice president also announced Nebraska as one of the states selected for the Fertilizer Investment & Expansion for Long-Term Domestic Supply Program, which U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins announced earlier this year. Nebraska is one of seven states that will receive $99.8 million in proposed United States Department of Agriculture funding toward a $270.2 million project to deploy 20 modular ammonia manufacturing units. That project is part of a larger $1.3 billion investment nationwide.

As expected, the crowd was very friendly toward Vance and the other Republican elected officials. Vance and Ricketts got loud cheers when they attacked Osborn and Democrats. Audience members were wearing green and red “Make America Great Again” hats, and some held “Defend our future” and “Restoring Common Sense” signs. Two tractors were also near the stage. 
The Nebraska Republican Party chair, Mary Jane Truemper, said Republicans are “in a war … for the soul of this state and the country.” Truemper urged people to get out and vote as “bad things happen” when Republicans don’t vote. 
Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts and Gov. Jim Pillen waiting for Vice President JD Vance from Air Force Two in North Platte on Oct. 22, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Nebraska has seen more national attention than usual this midterm cycle as the political environment has worsened for Republicans. The 2nd Congressional District race often draws national attention as a swing district, but the Senate race has been competitive since the start of the cycle, and election analysts have highlighted the races for governor and the 1st Congressional District in recent weeks. 
Trump visited Grand Island earlier this month on a tour to shore up red states and increase GOP turnout. Senate Majority Leader Sen. John Thune went to Fremont this week to campaign with Ricketts. 
Like other notable Republicans who have visited Nebraska, Vance tried to paint Osborn as a Democrat. 
Vance hit the same points the Ricketts campaign has hammered at Osborn for the past year and a half — pointing to audio leaks, campaign fundraising and payments to him and his family for campaign work. Vance added that the former labor union leader is a “far-left partisan Democrat.” 
“Dan is smart enough to run away from the Democrat label even though that’s exactly what he is,”  Vance told the crowd. “I happen to think that you’re hell of a lot smarter than Dan Osborn thinks you are, which is why you’re never going to send him to the United States Senate.” 
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting has already started.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Millions from partisan outside groups pour into Colorado statehouse races
text:
The Colorado Capitol is pictured on the opening day of the Colorado Legislature, Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Outside partisan groups are spending millions of dollars this election cycle on competitive statehouse races in Colorado, and in some instances that spending is far greater than what the candidates themselves are putting up.

Democrats will almost certainly retain the majority in both the state House and Senate, but the question in November is whether they can secure a two-thirds supermajority, allowing them to override vetoes and put constitutional amendments on the ballot without Republican support. They are one seat shy in each chamber.
The state’s largest independent expenditure committees focused on electing candidates to the Senate and House of Representatives are spending an amount that’s similar to their expenditures during the last election cycle in 2024, spread out among a handful of competitive races. Those committees are not allowed to directly coordinate with candidates.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In Pueblo’s Senate District 3, that looks like over $2 million to support either Democrat Aaron Gutierrez or Republican Dana Charles as of Oct. 22, according to campaign finance filings. The district, currently represented by outgoing Democratic Sen. Nick Hinrichsen, will likely be one of the closest statehouse races in November. Democrats currently hold a 23-12 majority in that chamber.
The seat historically has been a Democratic stronghold in the state Capitol, and Hinrichsen won with 51.2% in 2022. But the county itself can be a political tossup — it voted for President Donald Trump in 2016 and 2024, but former President Joe Biden in 2020.
Outside spending numbers evolve quickly, as committees submit notices of spending to the secretary of state. The numbers in this story are from the morning Oct. 22, less than two weeks before Election Day.
Charles has raised a little under $130,000 this election cycle, but outside groups spent over $1.2 million supporting her campaign in October alone. Around $800,000 of that was from the Senate Majority Fund, which backs Republican Senate candidates and has focused spending heavily on Charles’ race and defending Republican Sen. John Carson’s seat in Highlands Ranch.
The Senate Majority Fund gets its money from donors including the federal super PAC known as GOPAC, the national Republican State Leadership Committee, The Anschutz Corporation and the Colorado Beverage Association.
The group spent nearly $289,000, for example, on one television ad buy and $273,000 on another ad buy one week later to support Charles and oppose her opponent, Democrat Aaron Gutierrez.
Charles also got a boost by around $242,000 in October in spending by Coloradans For Accountable Government, a group that also gets funding through GOPAC and the Colorado Conservative Leadership Fund. It is supporting Republicans up and down the ballot.
There is less spending on the Democratic side. Gutierrez benefited from a little under $400,000 in supportive outside spending in October. He has raised just over $130,000 for his own campaign this election cycle and has spent around $72,000.
All Together Colorado, a Democratic spending group, directed around $130,000 in October to support Gutierrez. All Together Colorado is funded by the Conservation Colorado Victory Fund, the “dark money” organization Sixteen Thirty Fund and union-related groups like Working Americans Building a Stronger America and the Association of Federal, State, City and Municipal Employees.
Most of the other spending in support of Gutierrez came from a group called Pueblo People for Change, which received all of its donations from the dark money group Fair Economy for Coloradans. That nonprofit, which doesn’t disclose its donors, spent heavily in this year’s primary to support moderate Democrats against more liberal opponents.
Gutierrez used the outside spending discrepancy in an appeal to donors on Facebook last week, writing that “the reality is that when outside groups are spending this kind of money, grassroots campaigns like mine need our communities to step up.”
Spending in Highlands Ranch and Loveland
The Senate Majority Fund also spent over $700,000 in October to support Carson, the incumbent Republican senator in Senate District 30, which covers south metro Denver communities such as Highlands Ranch and Lone Tree. Carson was appointed to the seat in 2025 and is facing a challenge from Democrat Kevin Leung. The Senate Majority Fund spent over $250,000, for example, for door-to-door canvassing efforts in the district and another $30,000 on direct mail ads.
Carson has raised about $143,000 for his own campaign and has spent around $112,000. In October, he also benefited from $31,000 in outside spending from Southern Colorado Business Action and $274,000 from Lower Energy Costs Colorado, a committee funded by the oil and gas trade organization Coloradans for Responsible Energy Development.
Leung, however, has had scant outside spending supporting him in October except for around $20,000 from reproductive rights nonprofit Cobalt and a few thousand from All Together Colorado. In fact, the Republican State Leadership Committee spent $80,000 for a digital ad against Leung.
The Senate Majority Fund is also spending money to support Republican Rob Woodward in Loveland’s Senate District 15, but it concentrated that spending in September. It spent just $30,000 in October compared to over $800,000 the month before. He had a $250,000 boost from Coloradans for Accountable Government. All Together Colorado spent around $340,000 for ads against Woodward.
Woodward’s opponent, Democratic incumbent Sen. Janice Marchman, saw $50,000 in spending from Coloradans Creating Opportunities, a group that reported contributions from the Sixteen Thirty Fund and Philip Morris International. The Blue Collar Action Fund also spent $15,000 on a mail ad for Marchman.
Less outside spending for House candidates
On the House side, there was about $360,000 in outside spending to support incumbent Republican Rep. Dan Woog in October. Woog is facing a rematch with Democrat Jillaire McMillan in House District 19, which covers north metro Denver towns such as Erie and Firestone. He has raised around $105,000 this election cycle.
New Day Colorado spent around $130,000 to support Woog during the month. That group’s donors include the Colorado Apartment Association, Phillip Morris International, Davita, the Rocky Mountain Business Unit and Occidental Petroleum. Woog also had modest backing from Americans for Prosperity, the group founded by the Koch brothers, and Weld Strong, which gets financial support from oil and gas companies.
Colorado Way Forward spent around $111,000 in October to support McMillan in October. The group’s donors include the Conservation Colorado Victory Fund, Sixteen Thirty, the Colorado Education Association, the Colorado Fund For Children and Public Education and union groups. McMillan has raised around $146,000 for her campaign.
Colorado Way Forward is also spending money to support Democratic candidates like Rep. Tisha Mauro, Tommy Butler and Stephanie Vigil.
Vigil’s unsuccessful 2024 race in House District 16 was the closest in the state, but the campaigns have seen comparatively little outside spending this cycle. Aside from Colorado Way Forward, Cobalt and Young People for All People spent the majority of the approximately $68,000 in support of Vigil in October. The district covers parts of central Colorado Springs.
Americans for Prosperity spent around $42,000 to support the Republican in the race, Jill Haffley, in October. Her campaign has raised $46,000 total.

name: VTDigger
title: Beta Technologies takes electric planes to new territories
text:
A BETA Technologies Alia vertical take-off and landing all-electric airplane is on display during the opening of BETA’s electric aircraft production facility in South Burlington on Monday, October 2, 2023. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Vermont-based aircraft manufacturer Beta Technologies has received federal certification to fly potential customers aboard its ALIA eVTOL, an all-electric aircraft capable of taking off and landing vertically.
The approval marks a new step toward commercial operations. 
“This is a critical milestone for Beta,” according to a written statement from a Beta spokesperson provided to VTDigger. “We’re focused on consistent, safe flying, and we’re excited to bring an aircraft designed, manufactured and tested in Vermont to the people and places that will put it to work.”
The certificate will allow Beta’s model — the all-electric ALIA eVTOL aircraft — to be flown with participants and operators in order to gather data for marketing surveys, according to a press release from the Federal Aviation Administration. With this certification, the planes will be allowed to take off and land in commercial airports, according to Frank Cioffi, president of the Greater Burlington Industrial Corporation.
If the process is successful, vertical take-off electric airplanes are one step closer to filling the horizon.

READ MORE

Beta Technologies, an aerospace and defense company based in Burlington, designs and sells electric aircraft as well as electric charging systems, components and propulsion systems for aircraft. The company has a global customer base, and employs almost 1,400 workers as of June 2026, according to past VTDigger reporting. The company created an aircraft family called ALIA aircraft, which consists of two different types of electric aircraft: the ALIA CTOL and the ALIA eVTOL.
The Special Airworthiness Market Survey Certificate — the first of its kind, according to the press release — is a milestone for Beta Technologies, Cioffi said. 
“It basically proves that the FAA believes in the safety and the construction and the viability of this aircraft to be landing in commercial airports,” Cioffi said. 
All-electric planes could open new economic possibilities for many different industries, Cioffi said, from medevac companies to special cargo companies. The cost of flights could potentially be mitigated by electric models, he said.
“And the ability to be able to take off and land in a vertical way just allows for so much more flexibility in the transportation of the plane as well,” Ciotti said.
The certificate is part of the eIPP program, or Electric Vertical Takeoff and Landing Integration Pilot Program, announced by U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy last September, which allowed eight different project areas to begin testing advanced air mobility aircraft. 
The projects include various state partners and aircraft manufacturers, and include everything from urban air taxi services to emergency medical response operations, according to the release.
These advanced air mobility aircraft models could improve road congestion, improve emergency services and medical transport, and help connect rural communities to urban areas, according to the original announcement.
Beta’s first flight under the certification went from Plattsburgh to Burlington, according to the Beta spokesperson.
“Next we’ll be flying with operators and key stakeholders so they can experience the aircraft firsthand,” the spokesperson said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico US Rep. Stansbury touts state’s universal healthcare push during Albuquerque visit
text:
U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) visited Albuquerque Oct. 22, 2026, to tout recent healthcare related earmarks and also express her support for a burgeoning state effort toward universal healthcare in New Mexico. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) on Thursday visited Albuquerque to tout roughly $11 million in funding her office has secured for an array of healthcare programs, including cancer research, mobile crisis centers and a sobering center. 
All of those programs, Stansbury said at a news conference at the University of New Mexico’s Comprehensive Cancer Center, complement a burgeoning proposal at the Roundhouse this upcoming session: universal healthcare.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The $11 million the congresswoman secured through congressional earmarks “is coupled with the work that New Mexico is doing…to hopefully one day be able to deliver universal healthcare to all New Mexicans,” Stansbury said. “And what I can say is, New Mexico is truly on the front lines in delivering healthcare.”
Several Democratic lawmakers have pointed to universal healthcare as the next step in a series of healthcare reforms and universal programs they’ve undertaken in recent years. Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland has also said she would prioritize developing a public option, which would allow all New Mexicans access to a government-funded healthcare plan that competes with the private market.  
New Mexico House Speaker Rep. Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque), who joined Haaland for her April unveiling of her healthcare agenda, likened Haaland’s plan for a public option to Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s efforts to use the state’s cash-rich permanent funds to pay for free university tuition and universal child care.
He said at the time that a public option is “always going to be the less expensive, most efficient, best way to deliver healthcare.”
Rep. Liz Thomson (D-Albuquerque), who chairs the Legislature’s interim Health and Human Services Committee, told Source NM after the news conference that the lawmakers will start “laying the groundwork” at the 60-day session beginning Jan. 19, with the goal of having a fully funded universal healthcare program by 2029. 
Thomson said she will carry several bills herself that would represent initial steps toward full universal coverage, including legislation that would cover all New Mexico children’s healthcare, all behavioral healthcare or all primary care. 
“We know it’s going to take a long process, but we’re ready to do the work,” Thomson told Source NM. 
Stansbury concluded her speech Thursday by declaring that “healthcare is a human right” and noting that she has co-sponsored a “Medicare for All” bill in the U.S. House of Representatives. 
“Until the United States has a healthcare system where every single person has access to care, we’re going to continue to fight every day to make sure that New Mexico is leading the way, and I’m confident we’ll get there,” she said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Family of toddler fatally shot by Senatobia police is shown unredacted footage by Mississippi officials in private screening
text:
Mukta Joshi is an investigative reporter at Mississippi Today. She is spending a year as a New York Times Local Investigations fellow examining immigration and criminal justice issues. She can be reached at mukta.joshi@nytimes.com.
BATESVILLE – The family of Kohen Wiley, the 1-year-old boy fatally shot by the Senatobia police this summer, gathered with state officials Thursday to view unredacted footage of the confrontation, two days after leaked clips were published by a local news outlet and widely circulated on social media.
The viewing was arranged by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation in Batesville, the family’s hometown, and was closed to the public. Only the toddler’s parents, grandmothers and two members of the family’s legal team were allowed inside. 
Veronica Roberson, the grandmother of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley who was fatally shot by a Senatobia police officer in June 2026, speaks at a press conference alongside the family’s attorney, Ben Crump, left, on on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026, in Senatobia. Credit: Mukta Joshi/The New York Times
The Mississippi attorney general, Lynn Fitch, said on Monday that her office would not seek criminal charges against Hunter Foster, the Senatobia officer who fired his weapon at a car while officers pursued two women accused of stealing diapers and baby clothes from a Walmart on June 14. 
Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, walked out of the meeting after watching the first clip, which had been captured by Foster’s body-worn camera. Wiley said she had already been hesitant to attend after seeing the leaked footage two days before. She said she felt she didn’t need to see any more, especially after Fitch said the shooting was justified. 
Kohen’s death set off local protests and raised questions about why the police needed to use deadly force over what appeared to be a minor crime.  
At least five officers chased the women into the parking lot and then drew their guns when a car carrying Kohen and the women backed out of a parking space and tried to flee. 
The car, driven by Latoya Ferrell, moved in the direction of two officers. The authorities publicly stated at the time that the car nearly struck one of them. In the body camera and surveillance footage leaked this week, it is difficult to tell if the car hit any of the officers. 
The state Department of Public Safety says a police officer responding to a shoplifting call on Sunday, June 14, 2026, shot at a car that drove in the officer’s direction, killing 1-year-old Kohen Wiley.  Credit: Courtesy of Carlos Haynes and Veronica Roberson
Foster, the only officer investigated by state authorities in the incident, fired his weapon four times, the footage showed. Foster has not responded to multiple requests from Mississippi Today reporters for comment over the past several months. Martin Zummach, Foster’s lawyer, said Monday that the attorney general’s decision was “expected” and “overdue.”
Wiley’s mother, Veronica Roberson, who attended the meeting Thursday, said footage from the shooter’s body camera clearly showed he was beside the car, not in front of it, when he fired some of his shots. State officials did not slow down the video or give a frame-by-frame presentation to the family, Ben Crump, the family’s lawyer, said.
The shooter’s body-cam footage was not included in leaked clips published this week by Darkhorse Press, a Mississippi news outlet. State officials are expected to publicly release the video now that the family has viewed it.
Roberson said that the family tried to ask officials about details of the encounter during the private screening, but they said they “weren’t going to get into all that.”
The footage shown in the screening began with a group of officers sitting in a room inside the Walmart, watching unrelated security footage, Crump said. A person who apparently worked at the store and had tried to stop Ferrell and Wiley near the exit then entered the room and said, “They’re running.” Video shows officers sprinting out to surround the car carrying the two women and the toddler. 
Roberson said that when they asked officials if the car had injured any officers, “they said the car had made contact with Foster.” 
The footage leaked this week shows the car driving toward Foster but turning away from him as it gets close to him. Foster puts his hand on the hood of the car and pivots to avoid being hit. He does not fall down. It is difficult to discern whether the car touches his body. He then continues running and chasing the car along with other officers after the car had passed. In subsequent footage, he is seen standing outside the hospital where Kohen was declared dead. 
Hunter Foster, right, received an award from the DeSoto County Sheriff’s Office in 2023, when he worked there as a deputy. He later went to work for the Senatobia Police Department. Credit: DeSoto County Sheriff’s Office via Facebook
Shortly after the viewing, Crump held a press conference in Senatobia and criticized the attorney general’s determination that the shooting was justified, repeating that the shot from the side was not justified. He questioned the officers’ drawing guns in response to alleged shoplifting, which would have amounted to a misdemeanor offense. Neither woman has been charged. 
Van Turner, the Mississippi lawyer representing Kohen’s family as a member of Crump’s legal team, said he would ask federal authorities to review the footage.
The Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus called for Fitch to give a detailed explanation of how she had reached her decision, and for an independent review of the Senatobia Police Department’s practices.
“Attorney General Fitch cannot reasonably expect public confidence in a decision the public has not been given the evidence to evaluate,” Representative Kabir Karriem, chairman of the caucus, said in a news release. “Announcing that a review is complete does not fulfill the responsibility to explain how a police encounter ended with a baby dead.” 
Mississippi Today Justice and Special Projects Editor Debbie Skipper contributed reporting.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Des Moines University partners with India health sciences university
text:
Des Moines University and Malla Reddy Vishwavidyapeeth University will collaborate on research and student exchanges focused on women's health. (Photo courtesy of Des Moines University)Health sciences universities in Iowa and India have paired up to provide opportunities for connection in education and research.
Des Moines University announced in a news release this week it has signed a memorandum of understanding with Malla Reddy Vishwavidyapeeth University in Hyderabad, India, to collaborate on research and student exchanges.
“This partnership reflects our shared commitment to advancing health sciences education, research and innovation on a global scale,” DMU President and CEO Angela Franklin said in the release. “When institutions come together around a shared purpose, they can accomplish far more than either could alone. We look forward to seeing what the future will bring through this impactful partnership with Malla Reddy Vishwavidyapeeth University.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Beyond student exchange and visiting scholars initiatives, the release stated the partnership will also support research into women’s health. Faculty at each university will be able to work together on research projects, grant applications and joint publications as well as “clinical studies and capacity-building efforts focused on improving women’s health outcomes.”
DMU Chief Research Officer Pravin Mishra said in the release the partnership will bring together not just the people conducting research and other work, but their “complementary strengths and a shared commitment to discovery,” which university officials hope will lead to patients across the world seeing better treatments and care.
Bhadra Reddy, chairman of Malla Reddy Vishwavidyapeeth University, said in the release that this partnership is a promising step forward in the institution’s “vision of building globally connected, research-driven health care education.”
“By bringing together the strengths of both institutions, we aim to create meaningful opportunities for academic exchange, scientific collaboration and innovation that can make a lasting difference to health care outcomes,” Reddy said in the release. “We believe that international partnerships such as this will empower the next generation of health care professionals and researchers to address global health challenges with knowledge, compassion and a commitment to excellence.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana Supreme Court rejects inmate’s bid to delay execution for brain scans
text:
Jeffrey Weisheit answers questions during his Oct. 16, 2026, clemency hearing at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. Board members questioned him about the murders of Alyssa and Caleb Lynch and whether he could safely serve a life sentence. (Screenshot from livestream)Indiana’s highest court unanimously rejected death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit’s request Thursday to postpone his execution for brain scans, saying the governor’s administration can arrange the testing without a court order, should it choose to do so.
“If the board or the governor finds the medical evidence relevant, the executive branch maintains its own authority to transport him without a court order,” the justices wrote.
Weisheit’s attorneys sought to move his execution to Nov. 19 and postpone clemency proceedings so experts could assess brain injuries they contend affected his behavior before the 2010 murders of 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb.
Weisheit was sentenced to death in 2013 for killing the children in a fire at his home near Evansville while their mother, his girlfriend, worked an overnight shift. His execution is scheduled to take place before sunrise Nov. 5 at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City.
No clemency decision had been announced Thursday. Board members said one was not expected before Friday at the earliest, however.
Story continues below.
Order - Deny rescedule execution
 
Braun will make the final decision after receiving a nonbinding recommendation from the Indiana Parole Board, which heard testimony Oct. 16 and 19.
The state’s high court said Weisheit cited no authority allowing it to control clemency proceedings.
The justices noted, too, that Weisheit’s attorneys had identified two other potential grounds for seeking an execution stay: a challenge to Indiana’s execution method and a request for permission to reopen post-conviction proceedings. Neither had been filed as of Thursday’s order, and the court said Weisheit had not initiated a proceeding that would give it authority to order his transportation for brain scans.
U.S. District Judge Sarah Evans Barker previously approved funding for potential brain scans but ruled Oct. 7 that she lacked authority to compel state officials to transport him for evidence gathering in a state clemency case.
The attorney general’s office opposed both emergency motions. A defense reply received Monday exceeded filing limits and lacked a motion seeking permission for the additional length, according to the docket.
During clemency hearings, Weisheit’s attorneys and family urged a sentence of life without parole. The children’s father also supported clemency. Their mother, though, urged officials to uphold the death sentence.
